docs.title: Start with a task
docs.text:
Try the offline demo to see planning, rejected evidence, a completion refusal and a verified result without an account or model spend.

AutoCode runs your coding agent through planning, approval, implementation and independent checks. Begin in a committed Git project. Approve the plan before implementation starts, and use the saved status to decide what comes next.

These five guides cover the first day:

  1. Install AutoCode — prepare Python, the CLI and your provider.
  2. Run your first task — ask for an outcome, answer questions and approve the plan.
  3. Understand a pause — read the current status and use the exact continuation command.
  4. Read completion evidence — see what was checked, what was accepted and what remains unverified.
  5. Review a pull request — check a change or take a GitHub issue through a task run to a PR with evidence.

Use the five navigation sections to find deeper guides. Search includes the full reference pages. The stage names come from the same canonical list as the CLI and dashboard.

If investigation reveals another repository, follow the multi-repository walkthrough to register a checkout, link runs, approve their plans and check them together.

latest follows master. The version selector also lists release tags as they are published, so a release's guide remains available after the implementation changes. Reliability results distinguish real-model trials from fake-provider checks and record their limits.

docs.title: Adaptive planning
docs.text:
The fixed AutoPlanner sequence sends every build request through the same stages, whatever its size:

requirements → plan → review → revise → final review → your approval

A one-line change pays for five model calls before you see a plan. A plan the Plan Reviewer has no objection to is still revised and reviewed again. A hard plan gets exactly one revision, and whatever the Reviewer still objects to comes back to you as questions.

Adaptive planning lets the evidence decide how much planning a request gets instead. It is on by default for new runs that use joint planning on the default planning flow (since 2026-10-02, after the two live comparisons below found fewer model calls and questions with the same plan quality). --no-adaptive-planning keeps the fixed sequence for a new run, and --adaptive-planning insists on adaptive planning, refusing a run that cannot use it. A saved run keeps the planning flow it was started with. It does not predict the job's size up front. Each decision is made by the first stage that has the evidence for it:

Decision Made by Evidence Effect Is the plan finished? Plan Reviewer Its own concerns, each marked blocking or not No blocking concern: an ordinary Planner draft goes to you, with the non-blocking concerns as notes. Otherwise the Planner revises. Progressive delegations keep revision and final independent review, which supply their approval authority. How many review rounds? The runner The draft's declared milestones and the files they touch (plan_size) A large plan (3+ milestones or 10+ files) gets 3 review calls instead of 2, so a revision is reviewed again before the final decision. Does feedback on a plan need requirements gathering? The runner, then the Planner The run's status: a complete plan waiting for your approval The Planner revises the plan you were shown, then the Plan Reviewer reviews it. The Planner can send feedback that changes what is being built back to Requirements. See below.

For this to work, the Planner's draft includes its initial_task (the first Builder task). In the fixed sequence only the final review writes one.

What does not change:

  • You approve every build plan. Adaptive planning removes model calls, never your approval.
  • Requirements always runs. It is the first stage of every run and follow-up turn and names the job (owner decision 2026-10-22, #1846, #1860). Until then a build request the Job recognizer judged clear went straight to the Planner; that skip is gone. While it names the job, Requirements also judges clarity by the recognizer's rule. Clarity then skips nothing; it keeps a small clear brief on one review allowance at the reduced Plan Reviewer effort (#1564), one rung below the configured one and fitted to the variants the reviewer's model declares (GLM 5.3 declares low, high and max, so a step from high lands on high, not medium; the move is recorded in effort_fits, #2020). A build named with --workflow build still runs Requirements, and nobody judges its clarity.
  • The setting applies only to new runs. A saved run keeps the planning flow it was started with: resuming with --adaptive-planning a run that lacks it, or with --no-adaptive-planning an adaptive one, is refused. Repeating the run's own choice, or passing no flag, is fine.
  • Questions work as before. On the fast path the Planner asks them itself.
  • The Tester and Completion Reviewer still judge the work, and bug-fix, review, design and discuss workflows are unaffected.
  • A plan that the Reviewer does block on takes today's path: revise, then a final review that settles every concern.

Where it lives: tools/autocode_adaptive_planning.py holds the decisions as pure functions. units/autoplanner.py (schema_for, after_challenge, after_revise, rerun_requirements), autocode_workflows.apply and autocode_goals.feedback apply them. State: workflow.clarity, workflow.requirements_skipped (only on runs saved before #1860), planning.adaptive (size, signals, review_limit, challenges, approved_at, final_stage), and revises_plan on a feedback event. autocode --status --json shows the decisions under planning_depth (task-run interface): the clarity, whether an older run skipped Requirements, the plan's size, the review allowance and whether the Plan Reviewer approved the draft early.

docs.title: Feedback on a plan you were shown
docs.text:
Without adaptive planning, feedback on a plan (--feedback, or typing a change in chat) restarts planning from the top, however small the change:

your feedback → requirements → plan → review → revise → final review → your approval

In an adaptive run, feedback sent while a complete plan waits for your approval goes to the Planner, which revises the plan you saw:

your feedback → plan (revises the plan you saw) → review → your approval

The review works as for any adaptive draft: with no blocking concern the plan comes back to you; otherwise it is revised and reviewed again. Feedback at any other point (while questions are open, or queued during a build) still restarts from Requirements.

Requirements is skipped because its job was done for the request you already planned; your feedback changes that plan. Three checks keep the shortcut safe:

  1. The runner checks the revision delivers your feedback. Your feedback becomes a requirement the Planner must trace, like the ones the Requirements stage writes: covered by an acceptance criterion or required behavior of the new plan, or the draft is rejected. This needs no model call. It stays a traced requirement until a Requirements report takes it in.
  2. The Planner can send it back. If your feedback changes what is being built (a different product, user or outcome, not an added or changed behavior), the Planner says so instead of revising (requirements_rerun), and the runner discards that draft and runs the Requirements stage. "Make it a web page instead of a command-line tool" is the example in the comparison corpus.
  3. The Plan Reviewer still reviews the revision, and is told to check that your feedback is applied as you said it and that nothing you asked for earlier was lost. The runner's existing guard already refuses a revision that drops or rewords a protected item (a criterion, behavior or exclusion) without citing your feedback.

You still approve the revised plan.

docs.title: Comparing it with today's pipeline
docs.text:
scenarios/run.py plan-compare plans each request in scenarios/planning.toml twice, once with today's pipeline and once with --adaptive-planning. Each run starts in a fresh copy of the request's seed and stops when AutoCode shows the plan for approval. A request with feedback then sends that feedback instead of approving, and stops at the next plan shown for approval; the feedback round is reported in its own columns. Nothing is built. The driver answers questions with AutoCode's proposed default, the same way for both variants.

PY=.venv/bin/python
$PY scenarios/run.py plan-compare --fake                      # plumbing: every adaptive path, scripted, seconds
$PY scenarios/run.py plan-compare --profile default --jobs 3 --i-authorize-live-model-spend

The evidence directory holds comparison.md (stages, review calls and blocking concerns, questions, tokens, model time and plan shape per request and variant), records.json, each run's state.json, and blind/. blind/ has each request's two final plans side by side as Plan A and Plan B, with the key in blind/key.json, so plan quality can be judged without knowing which variant wrote which.

docs.title: Results: live comparison with feedback, 2026-10-02
docs.text:
Each of the 11 requests in planning.toml was planned once per pipeline on the default routes (Requirements and Planner on GLM 5.3, Plan Reviewer on GPT-6 Sol). After the first plan, each run got the request's feedback instead of an approval and went on to the next plan shown for approval. The code under test was the feedback path above plus the re-review context for answered questions (feat/rereview-after-answers). Evidence: .scenario-runs/20261002T091307Z-plan-compare-default-ac6a8qs0 (not committed; blind/verdicts-before-key.md holds the verdicts written before the key was opened).

Today Adaptive Change First plan: plans reached 11/11 11/11 model calls 112 95 −15% questions to the user 26 16 −38% Feedback round: new plans reached 9/11 9/11 model calls 85 50 −41% plan-review calls 26 15 −42% tokens in / out 5.45M / 1.05M 4.50M / 0.63M −17% / −40% model time 267 min 157 min −41%

The first-plan numbers repeat the 2026-09-30 comparison (−15% calls, −37% questions). Four adaptive feedback rounds took two calls: the Planner revised the plan and the Plan Reviewer approved it at once.

Plan quality after the feedback was the same. Judged blind on whether the feedback was applied as stated and the rest of the plan kept: adaptive better in 3 pairs (deployment-planner, tenant-http-api, transactional-outbox), today's pipeline in 3 (small-json-flag, vague-reading-list, vague-timesheet-useful), 5 ties. Both pipelines sometimes added criteria nobody asked for.

Where the adaptive path fell short:

  • vague-reading-list ("make it a web page instead of a command-line tool"): the Planner produced no output for 300 seconds three times and the run stopped for a person, so the send-back to Requirements was never exercised live. A large change can exceed the idle limit before the Planner writes anything.
  • vague-timesheet-useful: the revision appended a section to the default report although the feedback said to keep that output exactly as it is, and the Plan Reviewer did not object.
  • Planner slips on the feedback path, each costing a report repair: a conflict_resolutions entry for a feedback-versus-plan conflict (2 runs; the Planner rule now says to use contract_changes instead), a blank feedback answer_id on an assumption (2 runs), and contract changes named by list instead of by item.

Today's pipeline missed a new plan twice: deployment-planner (both pipelines stopped for a person) and transactional-outbox (an Resolver blocker, "Planning recovery scope or inputs changed").

Earlier attempts at this comparison, stopped and restarted, found four Planner slips, each fixed on this branch or an accompanying one: a trace row without its requirement_id (now named by the runner when only one requirement can be meant; this branch), example_correction: null refused by the schema (fix/example-correction-null), a declared change whose item was wrapped in its list name (fix/contract-change-item-refs), and report fields written inside the contract (feat/rereview-after-answers).

docs.title: Results: live comparison, 2026-09-30
docs.text:
Each of the 11 requests in planning.toml was planned once with each pipeline on the default routes: Requirements and Planner on GLM 5.3, Plan Reviewer on GPT-6 Sol. That is one sample per request, and the same request can swing by several calls from run to run, so read per-request differences as noisy. The evidence is under .scenario-runs/20260930T180620Z-plan-compare-default-* (not committed).

Today Adaptive Change Plans reached (no errors) 11/11 11/11 Model calls 92 78 −15% Clear requests (8) 64 calls, 7 questions 52 calls, 1 question −19% calls Vague requests (3) 28 calls, 9 questions 26 calls, 9 questions about even Plan-review calls 27 27 same Questions to the user 16 10 −37% Model time 160 min 128 min −20% Tokens in / out 3.58M / 734k 2.93M / 566k −18% / −23%

Plan quality was about the same. Each pair was judged blind (Plan A and Plan B, key opened after every verdict was written) against the request and, where the request came from the catalog, against the hidden oracle tests. Adaptive was better in 3 pairs, today's pipeline in 2, and 6 were ties.

  • Adaptive better:
  • parallel-diamond: today's plan invented "raise ValueError for an unknown node", which a faithful build would fail on two oracle checks.
  • transactional-outbox: only the adaptive plan tested concurrency across separate Store instances, which is what the hidden test does.
  • feature-by-project.
  • Today better:
  • vague-timesheet-useful: the adaptive plan changed the default report output despite the answer "keep existing behavior intact".
  • tenant-http-api, slightly.

In each lopsided pair, the weaker plan had been through the same full review-revise-final cycle. So these look like model variance, not an effect of the pipeline.

Where the savings came from:

  • Skipping Requirements for clear requests. Nearly all of the question savings are here (7 questions → 1 on clear requests). The owner removed this skip on 2026-10-22 (#1860): Requirements now runs first on every run and names the job, in place of the recognizer's call.
  • Fewer planning restarts: 3 today, 1 adaptive. Most began when a revision renamed a protected contract item; the guard then asks the user, and planning starts over. Since 2026-10-25 a revision may apply the reviewer's blocking request to the Planner's own constraint or permission line in a plan nobody approved, and a redraft after AutoCode's own technical answer continues the reviewed cycle instead of starting over (workflow).

The live recognizer judged every request correctly: 8 clear, 3 vague.

What did not pay off as designed:

  • Early approval rarely fires. The Reviewer blocked on the first draft in 21 of 22 runs, usually on real test gaps. Adaptive approved early only twice: once at the first review (tiny-greeting), once at a re-review (deployment-planner).
  • The size rule over-fires. "10+ acceptance criteria" made 6 of 11 plans large, 3 of them single-milestone changes, which gave them a third review call. Those extra rounds did find real gaps (for example in extend-record-query), but they are why review calls came out even. Fixed after the run: size now comes from milestones and files only, which would have made only parallel-diamond large.
  • More bad citations. Planner revisions cited the Reviewer's own report under .autocode/ as evidence, and the report was rejected and repaired. This happened 3 times, all on the adaptive side, and 2 of them followed a second review. Since fixed for both pipelines by #192's SOURCE CITATIONS rule (merged after this run), which every planning stage after Requirements receives.

Found in both pipelines:

  • The protected-item guard turns test-name renames into user questions and full planning restarts. #192 (merged after this run) now tells the Planner to keep existing test names; its effect is not measured yet.
  • Planning restarts after a deferred approval are unbounded (docs/bugs/2026-09-30-unbounded-planning-restart.md).

docs.title: Compact planning for bug fixes
docs.text:
Compact planning is enabled for new joint-planning runs. --no-compact-bugfix-planning disables it; --compact-bugfix-planning explicitly enables it. A reproduced, localized bug can skip one paid planning call. On the ordinary bug-fix path Requirements runs, the Investigator reproduces the bug (investigate_bug), the Planner writes the plan draft (astra_discovery), the Plan Reviewer reviews it and you approve the displayed plan. On the compact path the runner writes that draft itself, deterministically, from two records it already holds: the Investigator's diagnosis (its root cause, invariant, regression cases, affected and test paths) and the Requirements record (every requirement row becomes a required behaviour, and the requirement trace is checked as a Planner's would be). The Plan Reviewer reviews the runner's draft exactly as it reviews a Planner's; a clean review goes to your exact-token approval, as an adaptive run's early approval does, and a blocking concern returns the run to the full path, where the Planner drafts with the review in its packet; the compact draft's review call is refunded, so the full path keeps the plan-review allowance it would have had. The draft is never approved by a policy. Everything after approval is unchanged: acceptance tests when configured, the Builder, the regression proof (each restore case fails on the original code and passes after the fix), the Tester and a separate Completion Reviewer by default. A new run may independently select --review-routing combined to combine testing and completion on the configured Completion Reviewer route. That explicit choice replaces separate enforced milestone-checkpoint routing; it is included in the displayed plan and binds to its exact approval. The independent regression and changed-code evidence gates still apply, and existing model/effort choices are retained.

The path is taken only when every trusted signal admits it; a model's word can keep the full path but never grant the compact one:

  • the run has compact planning enabled and plans adaptively, with joint planning;
  • Requirements named the bug-fix job (a pinned --workflow bugfix has no Requirements record);
  • the request does not prescribe test identifiers such as test_positive or TestPositive; those need the Planner's explicit acceptance bindings before review;
  • the Investigator reproduced the bug with a probe the runner ran, sized the fix small, and named a root cause, an invariant and at least one regression case;
  • the fix touches at most four files (affected and test paths together), and none of them, nor the diagnosis note, matches the project's declared sensitive-paths (project settings); without a declaration new runs save shipped conservative patterns for authentication, security, payments, billing, migrations, credentials, CI/build files and dependency manifests/locks. A project may replace these patterns, including an explicit empty list;
  • the contract validators accept the runner's draft; a refused draft keeps the full path, with the refusal recorded.

The decision, its reasons and the hashes it rests on are recorded once per job and shown by the status view as stage_policy (task-run interface). Existing runs keep their saved behaviour; a saved run refuses a changed flag.

docs.title: AutoCode inside your coding agent
docs.text:
← Back to README

Most people already work in Claude Code, Codex or Cursor. AutoCode can run as one step inside that agent instead of replacing it: the agent starts an AutoCode run in the repository, tells you where it stands at each stop, passes on your plan approval or answer, and reports the evidence when the run completes. Two integrations do this, with the same four operations:

Operation Claude Code skill (autocode_agent_step) MCP server (autocode_mcp) Start a run and work until it needs you or completes start "REQUEST" [--workflow KIND] -- FLAGS autocode_start Where the run stands (reads only) status [--full] autocode_status Pass on your decision, or continue answer, approve, continue autocode_respond The completed run's evidence report evidence [--markdown] autocode_evidence

Both reach a run only through the task-run interface (TaskRun and its status view), like any other integration, and use only the Python standard library: installing AutoCode is all either needs, and neither adds a dependency.

docs.title: What the agent may and may not decide
docs.text:
Your decisions stay yours. Every operation returns the status view's own fields that say what happens next, unchanged: status, done, pause_category, pause_category_label, needs, next_command, workflow and stop_reason, with the progress line, the explanation, the run_dir, and, while a plan waits for approval, the plan as autocode --show-goal prints it. The agent shows you these at each stop.

  • Plan approval (needs.kind approve_plan) takes needs.token from the view whose plan you approved. Approval authorizes AutoCode to change files, so the agent approves only when you say so; a token from an older plan is refused.
  • A question (answer) takes your answer and needs.resolver_token from the view you answered. One answer per call; the questions left return under a new token. When none are left, the run continues on its own.
  • Continue works only when needs.kind is continue: the run needs nothing from anyone.
  • Every other stop (a human review, a pause, a recovery, a budget, an operational request from the Resolver) is refused with the command you run yourself: next_command.

A refused call changes nothing. Engine, model and budget flags are set when a run starts (the skill's start -- FLAGS, the MCP server's own command line); later calls use the run's saved settings. Each call is recorded in the run's activity log with the caller agent-step or mcp.

A call returns when the run next needs you or completes, which can take as long as the work does. Raise your MCP client's tool timeout for long tasks.

docs.title: Claude Code skill
docs.text:
Copy examples/agent-step/skills/autocode to .claude/skills/autocode in your project, or to ~/.claude/skills/autocode for every project. Claude Code then uses it when you ask for AutoCode. The skill runs the step with the Python that has AutoCode installed: set AUTOCODE_PYTHON to that interpreter when it is not python3.

The steps can also be run by hand. Each prints one JSON summary; a refusal exits 1 with the reason on stderr:

STEP="python3 -m autocode_cli.autocode_agent_step"
$STEP start "Add a --json flag to the report command" -- --engine claude
$STEP status
AUTOCODE_RESOLVER_TOKEN=TOKEN $STEP answer QUESTION_ID "Use snake_case keys" --token -
AUTOCODE_APPROVE_GOAL_TOKEN=TOKEN $STEP approve -
$STEP continue
$STEP evidence --markdown

--workspace PATH (default: the current directory) selects the repository and --run-dir RUN the run when the workspace has more than one. A token argument of - is read from the variable the view's next_command names, which keeps it out of the process list.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text:
python3 -m autocode_cli.autocode_mcp --workspace /path/to/project -- --engine claude

The server speaks MCP over standard input and output. It serves one workspace, fixed when it starts, and everything after -- is the engine, model and budget flags for runs it starts: the agent cannot change them. For Claude Code, add it to the project's .mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "autocode": {
      "command": "python3",
      "args": ["-m", "autocode_cli.autocode_mcp", "--workspace", ".", "--", "--engine", "claude"]
    }
  }
}

The tools return the summary as JSON text and as structuredContent. A refusal is a tool result with isError and the reason, so the agent can read it. Tool arguments are checked against each tool's schema, and an argument it does not name, such as options, is refused.

docs.title: Verify a change you made
docs.text:
To have AutoCode's independent Code Reviewer judge a change the agent already made, start a review run that names the change and what it should do, then read the evidence:

  • skill: $STEP start "Review the uncommitted change in this workspace (git diff HEAD). It should ..." --workflow review -- FLAGS, then $STEP evidence --markdown;
  • MCP: autocode_start with {"brief": "Review the uncommitted change ...", "workflow": "review"}, then autocode_evidence.

A review run goes straight to the Code Reviewer (review_change), changes nothing outside review/, needs no plan approval, and proves each blocking finding with a test that fails on the change (the review workflow). Its evidence is the report it recorded (availability recorded): a review delivers no build, so unlike a build's report it is not rechecked against the workspace. To check a change against your own acceptance criteria with runner-executed checks as well, use autocode verify.

docs.title: AutoCode Arena (experimental)
docs.text:
Arena runs pinned repository issues through the existing public TaskRun interface, scores the candidate with evaluator-owned checks, and retains a SQLite attempt ledger. It never opens an issue or PR, pushes a patch, edits AutoCode itself, or promotes a version. The autocode-issue workflow remains the operator's route for an individual issue and eventual PR submission.

Install the checkout with pip install -e .. Commands can also be invoked as python tools/autocode_arena.py. The default store is .autocode/arena, ignored by Git; --arena PATH before the subcommand selects another evaluator directory. Use one operator at a time: concurrent catalog writers are not supported.

The planned reliability protocol pins tasks, repetitions, original limits and all-outcome reporting beside the catalogue. It contains no campaign results and is not an automatic runner.

docs.title: Start with the included projects
docs.text:
The checkout includes eight original pinned upstream bug cases in arena/catalog.json: three starter Python cases and five hard cases across Python, TypeScript and Go. A ninth declaration is a separate corrected TypeScript successor; it preserves the original case and results. Problem descriptions and self-contained oracles live under arena/cases/; the successor has its own description and shares the original TypeScript oracle. The catalog pins the full baseline and reference commit IDs; preparation fetches those commits, verifies that the baseline fails and the reference passes, and only then adds the case to the local Arena. TypeScript also receives the disclosed test-only adapter described below; its upstream pins remain in the catalog.

Case ID Project and upstream report Work to solve Starter split boltons-indexedset-update Boltons #474 Update an ordered set from several iterables while retaining order and tuple-valued members development humanize-intcomma-large Humanize #392 Format large positive and negative integers, including ordinary integer subclasses, without losing digits regression more-itertools-custom-exceptions More Itertools #1279 Preserve custom exceptions that evaluate to false and avoid formatting items when a custom exception is given holdout

From the checkout root, using its installed venv:

.venv/bin/python arena/prepare.py --list
.venv/bin/python arena/prepare.py --arena .autocode/arena \
  --case boltons-indexedset-update --case humanize-intcomma-large \
  --case more-itertools-custom-exceptions
.venv/bin/python tools/autocode_arena.py --arena .autocode/arena cases

Preparation requires GitHub network access but makes no model calls. It creates the Arena, so do not run init first. Use a fresh destination; preparation refuses to overwrite existing evaluator data. Add --case boltons-indexedset-update to prepare just one project. A failed preparation is retained for inspection; choose a new destination when retrying. Source repositories are in sources/, fixed reference trees in references/, and admitted cases in catalog.json and cases/ under that destination. Candidate attempts get their own frozen broken source tree without upstream history or remotes.

Omitting --case prepares all nine declarations. Install their dependencies first, including the external TypeScript build bundle and Go module cache below, and use --oracle-timeout 400 when including Go. Preparation does not install those dependencies or freeze their contents for you.

Run the development case with an authenticated native Codex CLI. The checkout's venv needs pytest for this project's test command; install it before starting an attempt. Keep the runner source and its dependencies fixed until the attempt finishes, because changes invalidate the recorded execution identity.

export PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH"
.venv/bin/python tools/autocode_arena.py --arena .autocode/arena \
  run boltons-indexedset-update --cohort baseline-v1 \
  --i-authorize-live-model-spend --approve-benchmark-plans \
  --timeout 3600 --option=--engine=codex \
  "--option=--test-command=$PWD/.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_setutils.py -q"
.venv/bin/python tools/autocode_arena.py --arena .autocode/arena report

This makes real model calls and approves the displayed benchmark plan through Arena's exact plan token. The one-hour deadline applies to each AutoCode CLI invocation, including a review and repair cycle. To use another configured provider, replace --option=--engine=codex with --option=--provider=NAME and add the model options that provider needs. --option forwards, exactly as typed, --engine, --provider, --single-model, the role model flags (--astra-model, --terra-model, --sol-model, --glm-model, --completion-model, --plan-reviewer-model, --requirements-model, --resolver-model, --investigator-model), the reasoning-effort flags (--reasoning-effort and each role's --*-reasoning-effort), --pin-model-role (repeatable), --test-command, --max-iterations and --joint-planning; Arena checks their choices and refuses any other flag, such as a workspace or run directory. The test command above is specific to Boltons; choose the corresponding project's test command for other cases.

These cases are public historical exercises. Their descriptions are explicitly marked evaluator-authored, problem-only adaptations of upstream issue and PR reports, not authenticated pre-fix issue snapshots. They omit solution text and comments. The checked-in source links and reference revisions remain evaluator material; this host-level setup cannot prevent a model from finding a public historical fix. The starter holdout is public and is not a secret or contamination-free benchmark. Use fresh private holdouts before drawing general improvement conclusions.

The starter oracles import the candidate source directly and use only Python's standard library. Humanize's generated version metadata is supplied in memory for source archive imports; its formatting implementation still comes from the candidate. These targeted checks do not replace each project's full upstream test suite. The catalog/preparation tool is distributed with the checkout, not the wheel.

For Humanize's native number tests, supply generated version metadata through the case-specific setup plugin:

PYTHONPATH="$PWD/arena/support/humanize" PYTEST_PLUGINS=arena_humanize_bootstrap \
PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \
  -p no:cacheprovider tests/test_number.py

Put those environment settings in the attempt environment or its configured test command. The helper supplies metadata only; number formatting comes from the candidate. The integer-subclass check was added after an earlier four-check candidate missed that boundary. Prepare a fresh store and cohort for the current five checks; earlier results retain their original score.

docs.title: Hard cases
docs.text:
The harder group exercises interacting algorithms and lifecycle boundaries in larger projects. The listed module counts describe the upstream reference fixes; AutoCode may produce a different correct implementation.

Case ID Upstream report Behavior Production modules in reference fix Split sympy-matrix-derivatives SymPy #25150 and linked reports Matrix gradients and Hessians, rectangular coordinates, noncommuting powers and tensor axes 11 development django-filteredrelation-join-lifecycle Django #33766, PR #16786 Conditions that spawn joins, filtered aliases, cloning and nested subqueries 3 regression pytest-stop-fixture-teardown pytest #11706, PR #11721 and PR #12048 Teardown and plugin reports after early stops, including multiple failing callbacks on one fixture 3 holdout typescript-dependent-destructuring TypeScript #35283, PR #46266 and linked reports Correlated union tags and payloads after destructuring, with assignment and error-preservation boundaries 2 development go-http2-hung-reset-health Go #59690 Canceled stream capacity, health acknowledgments, strict admission, healthy reuse and dead connection replacement 1 regression

The pytest case combines early-stop routing with same-fixture exception aggregation. Its reference is pinned to the early-stop reapplication, after both upstream fixes; the early-stop change was temporarily reverted between them. Three additional oracle checks cover same-fixture callbacks under maxfail, stepwise and setup failure, including callback counts and every plugin-visible exception. Earlier 9-check passes do not establish this stronger 12-check result: prepare a fresh Arena and cohort; never rescore or overwrite an existing attempt. The three-module count covers the two relevant fixes, not all intervening upstream changes.

These are public historical exercises. The holdout split controls which evidence an improvement proposal exposes; it does not make a public fix private. Fresh private tasks are needed for stronger generalization claims.

Prepare the three Python hard cases in a fresh destination:

.venv/bin/python arena/prepare.py --arena .autocode/arena-hard-v1 --oracle-timeout 120 \
  --case sympy-matrix-derivatives \
  --case django-filteredrelation-join-lifecycle \
  --case pytest-stop-fixture-teardown

Install runtime and test dependencies before freezing a cohort. The oracles need mpmath for SymPy and asgiref/sqlparse for Django. The tested upstream scopes also use pytest, numpy, hypothesis, attrs, py, pexpect and xmlschema. Keep every installed version fixed through all attempts. Disable third-party pytest plugin autoload with PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1; explicit setup plugins still load.

Use the checkout's absolute venv interpreter in --option=--test-command=.... These bounded upstream scopes cover the affected subsystems; they are not the entire SymPy, Django or pytest test suites:

Case Arguments after python -m pytest Per-process setup SymPy -q -p no:cacheprovider sympy/core/tests/test_diff.py sympy/core/tests/test_function.py sympy/core/tests/test_args.py sympy/matrices/expressions/tests sympy/tensor/array/tests/test_array_derivatives.py sympy/tensor/array/expressions/tests PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 Django -q -o 'python_files=test*.py' -p no:cacheprovider tests/filtered_relation tests/queries PYTHONPATH="$PWD/arena/support/django" PYTEST_PLUGINS=arena_django_bootstrap plus plugin autoload disabled pytest -o minversion= testing/test_runner.py testing/test_session.py testing/test_stepwise.py -q PYTHONPATH="$PWD/arena/support/pytest" plus plugin autoload disabled

The Django setup plugin uses candidate-local source, its existing test apps and two in-memory SQLite databases. Other database engines are outside this scope. The pytest sitecustomize helper prefers candidate source and supplies generated version metadata only when absent; nested pytester processes inherit that source. Neither helper installs or substitutes a runtime implementation. Apply each helper only to its own case and keep its files frozen through the attempt. The environment is inherited by AutoCode's collected, derived and replayed checks.

For example, the Django case can be launched with:

export PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH"
PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 \
PYTHONPATH="$PWD/arena/support/django" PYTEST_PLUGINS=arena_django_bootstrap \
.venv/bin/python tools/autocode_arena.py --arena .autocode/arena-hard-v1 \
  run django-filteredrelation-join-lifecycle --cohort hard-baseline-v1 \
  --i-authorize-live-model-spend --approve-benchmark-plans \
  --timeout 3600 --oracle-timeout 120 --option=--engine=codex \
  --option=--max-iterations=3 \
  "--option=--test-command=$PWD/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q -o 'python_files=test*.py' -p no:cacheprovider tests/filtered_relation tests/queries"

Use an oracle deadline of 120 seconds for these Python cases; pytest's oracle starts several isolated child suites. Benchmark approval still covers only the exact plan token, never questions, human reviews, recovery or quota overrides.

docs.title: TypeScript setup and native tests
docs.text:
The TypeScript controls used Node v25.9.0. Select and freeze the Node executable before preparation, and keep it unchanged through an attempt. Create the external build bundle from the checked-in lockfile:

arena_ts_deps="$PWD/.scenario-runs/arena-dependencies/typescript"
mkdir -p "$arena_ts_deps"
cp arena/support/typescript/package.json arena/support/typescript/package-lock.json "$arena_ts_deps/"
(cd "$arena_ts_deps" && npm ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund)
export ARENA_TYPESCRIPT_DEPS="$arena_ts_deps"
export ARENA_TYPESCRIPT_HELPER="$PWD/arena/support/typescript/arena_typescript_compiler.cjs"
export ARENA_NODE="$(command -v node)"
.venv/bin/python arena/prepare.py --arena .autocode/arena-typescript-v1 \
  --case typescript-dependent-destructuring --oracle-timeout 120

The lockfile pins TypeScript 4.5.2, @types/node 14.18.2 and @types/microsoft__typescript-etw 0.1.1. Record the installed bundle's content identity, the helper and the Node runtime before freezing the attempt. The pinned TypeScript package bootstraps the build: both the helper and oracle compile the candidate's own source in a temporary directory and load that fresh compiler. Generated candidate build files are not reused. The diagnostic metadata generator and table also come from the candidate.

The pinned upstream tree lacks the selected native test file. Preparation adds only tests/cases/unittests/arenaDependentDestructuring.test.cjs, containing three preservation guards that pass on the broken baseline. It commits those new tests as an adapted baseline and adds the identical adapter to the reference tree. Upstream runtime source and existing tests are preserved. arena/catalog.json retains the upstream baseline/reference pins; the prepared case's preparation.json records upstream_base_commit, adapted_base_commit, upstream_reference_commit and per-file hashes under test_overlay_sha256.

Use this direct native command in --option=--test-command=..., with the same environment inherited by AutoCode and its regression replay:

node --test tests/cases/unittests/arenaDependentDestructuring.test.cjs

The task must extend that file with its own named regressions and retain the three guards. Passing only the initial preservation tests does not establish a fix. The independent oracle checks 15 diagnostic behaviors, including cases that must continue to report errors. This is a focused compiler scope using an in-memory declaration library; it does not run the full historic Gulp/Mocha, conformance, language-service, emit or platform suites. Its external oracle deadline is 120 seconds.

docs.title: Corrected TypeScript case
docs.text:
Select typescript-dependent-destructuring-baselines-v2 to use the separately approved task scope. The original case's requirement to keep existing upstream expectations unchanged conflicts with the requested narrowing in tests/cases/conformance/controlFlow/controlFlowAliasing.ts: that existing test expects two errors and union payload types for an eligible destructured parameter. The corrected case permits necessary changes only to tests/baselines/reference/controlFlowAliasing.errors.txt and tests/baselines/reference/controlFlowAliasing.types. Preserve unrelated expectations, every upstream test input and definition, emitted JavaScript and symbol baselines, and the full original adapter prefix and all three guards.

.venv/bin/python arena/prepare.py --arena .autocode/arena-typescript-baselines-v2 \
  --case typescript-dependent-destructuring-baselines-v2 --oracle-timeout 120

This successor reuses the original oracle and adapter through fixture_case; its explicit preparation_note retains the approved successor instructions during normal preparation. Upstream commits and all 15 behavioral checks remain identical. Use the original adapter command for AutoCode's retained test gate, so candidate tests and the unchanged original guard overlay are independently replayed. Run the native compiler build and controlFlowAliasing conformance checks against the final candidate and its approved updated expectations. The original protected bundle remains retained; task permission does not authorize replacing it.

Keep original attempts and scores under typescript-dependent-destructuring. Record the corrected case's attempts under its separate ID and cohort. A corrected case pass does not retroactively qualify the original, and the declaration itself is no evidence that either case has passed.

docs.title: Go setup and native tests
docs.text:
The HTTP/2 case uses Go 1.25.5 with GOTOOLCHAIN=local. Its independent oracle uses testing/synctest in an external evaluator module; the candidate's upstream go.mod is preserved. Select the frozen Go executable through PATH (the local controls used /opt/homebrew/bin/go). Before going offline, run go mod download from a separate checkout of the catalog's baseline into an external GOMODCACHE. The pinned dependencies are golang.org/x/crypto v0.28.0, x/sys v0.26.0, x/term v0.25.0 and x/text v0.19.0.

Freeze the toolchain and module-cache contents before preparation. Give each attempt separate writable build and temporary directories outside its source; set GOCACHE, GOPATH, GOTMPDIR and TMPDIR to those directories. Then inherit the following offline settings through preparation and every native replay:

export GOTOOLCHAIN=local GOMODCACHE=/absolute/frozen/go-module-cache
export GOPROXY=off GOSUMDB=off GOWORK=off GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly
export CGO_ENABLED=0 GODEBUG=asynctimerchan=0
.venv/bin/python arena/prepare.py --arena .autocode/arena-go-v1 \
  --case go-http2-hung-reset-health --oracle-timeout 400

Use the following literal native command in --option=--test-command=..., with PATH selecting the frozen Go executable:

go test ./http2 ./http2/hpack -count=1 -timeout=120s -parallel=2

The task must add its own native Go regression tests. The evaluator-owned oracle's six checks use a scripted net.Pipe wire peer, public connection state and actual HTTP/2 frames. They distinguish strict waiting and pool reservations, health ACKs from peer PINGs, repeated healthy cancellation/reuse, dead connections exhausted at several concurrency limits, and single-use preservation. It builds and tests only a disposable copy. A passing child must have actually run and passed its requested named test; skipped or missing results and real process timeouts are evaluation errors. Retained controls record two additional local source-integrity checks separately; these do not add scored behaviors.

Use --oracle-timeout 400 during both preparation and attempts: compilation is bounded at 180 seconds and each probe at 20 seconds in Go and 25 seconds by its supervisor. The native command covers HTTP/2 and HPACK; it does not establish the full x/net suite, TLS interoperability, real TCP/firewall failure handling or performance across platforms.

“Hard” describes the selected interacting behaviors, not a measured ranking of model difficulty. Positive/negative oracle controls and native setup checks establish case validity; they do not establish live AutoCode success, general reliability or improvement across languages. Freeze external dependencies and retain fresh per-attempt evidence before making those claims.

docs.title: Declare a case
docs.text:
Choose an issue you have permission to evaluate, a local clone, and the full commit SHA before the fix. Supply a historical issue JSON snapshot for historical cases; fetching today's discussion may leak the fix. Arena does not infer the correct historical commit, scrub spoilers, or discover issues automatically.

Write a self-contained, trusted Python oracle, outside the candidate repository. It receives the candidate directory as its first argument and prints one JSON object with a nonempty checks list:

import json
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

workspace = Path(sys.argv[1])
result = subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, "-B", str(workspace / "greet.py"), "World"],
    capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=5,
) if (workspace / "greet.py").is_file() else None
ok = bool(result and result.returncode == 0 and result.stdout == "Hello, World\n")
print(json.dumps({"checks": [{"name": "greeting", "ok": ok}]}))

The oracle must exit 0 when it successfully evaluates either a passing or failing candidate. A crash, timeout, malformed result, duplicate/missing required check, or content mutation yields an evaluation error, never a passing result. Avoid writing into the candidate; use temporary directories and python -B for imports. The oracle is pinned as a single script. Its imported dependencies, services and environment are not transitively pinned; prefer self-contained offline checks.

Provide a separate known-good reference workspace. Ingestion actually runs the oracle against the frozen failing baseline and the reference. Both controls must behave as expected before the case enters the catalog:

autocode-arena init
autocode-arena ingest OSS-0001 \
  --repository /path/to/local/repo \
  --base FULL_COMMIT_SHA \
  --issue owner/repo#123 --issue-file /path/to/historical-issue.json \
  --oracle /path/to/oracle.py --reference /path/to/known-good-workspace \
  --check greeting --split development

Without --issue-file, ingestion uses the existing GitHub client to read the issue and its latest comments; GH_TOKEN / GITHUB_TOKEN work as in autocode-issue. The supplied snapshot is an evaluator declaration, not independently authenticated history. A control failure leaves its case directory for inspection; remove that new failed directory before retrying the same ID. Do not change a cataloged case; declare a new case instead.

docs.title: Attempt and score
docs.text:
autocode-arena run OSS-0001 --cohort baseline-v1 \
  --runner /path/to/autocode-v1 \
  --i-authorize-live-model-spend \
  --option=--provider --option=YOUR_CONFIGURED_PROVIDER
autocode-arena report --cohort baseline-v1

Each attempt gets a fresh repository with only the frozen source tree and one local base commit. It has no upstream remotes, later commits or copied hooks. Issue and oracle snapshots remain outside it. The Arena layer never reads TaskRun's private state.json; status and approvals go through its public API.

By default the attempt stops at the operator's plan gate. For automated benchmark runs, explicitly add --approve-benchmark-plans; Arena saves the displayed plan and approves its exact current token. This is benchmark automation, not human acceptance. Questions, review criteria, recovery and quota overrides are never automatically answered. --timeout bounds each TaskRun CLI invocation, not the entire experiment; --oracle-timeout bounds each independent evaluation.

The attempt directory retains status, checks, content identity, the candidate patch (including new files), and result JSON. SQLite retains the authoritative final observation. Stopped attempts are final snapshots; manually continuing the underlying TaskRun does not rewrite their score. Use a fresh attempt for comparison. Interrupted attempts remain RUNNING in the ledger and block the comparison gate.

Outcome Meaning PASS Runner claims completion and all independent checks pass FALSE_COMPLETE Runner claims completion but an independent check fails STOPPED Runner pauses or requests input; not proof of a correct stop FAIL Runner does not complete and is not in a recognized input/pause state ERROR Execution or evaluation could not establish a verdict

Exit codes: PASS 0, STOPPED 2, other attempt outcomes 1; invalid requests 2. Reports show both false completions per attempt and per completion, with explicit denominators. Raw public usage is retained; dollar cost stays unknown rather than equating subscription tokens with an API invoice. There is no inferred human time, maintainer acceptance, or independently measured test coverage.

--fixture uses the existing greeting-only scripted Codex provider, refuses other engines/providers, and needs no live-spend authorization. It tests plumbing; fixture results cannot qualify an AutoCode version. It does not solve arbitrary OSS issues.

docs.title: Controlled improvement
docs.text:
autocode-arena propose --cohort baseline-v1
# Investigate the development failures, implement a candidate in another checkout.
# Run every declared case freshly under baseline-v1 and candidate-v2, then:
autocode-arena compare --baseline baseline-v1 --candidate candidate-v2

propose saves development failures, failed check names, and investigation areas. Uninvestigated root cause remains UNDETERMINED: an oracle failure alone cannot establish whether the bug was in requirements, planning, implementation or validation. It deliberately does not disclose holdout failures in an improvement proposal or automatically generate a self-modification. The operator can give this evidence to AutoCode's ordinary planning/build workflow and review the proposed change.

After investigation, autocode-arena annotate ATTEMPT --report attribution.json appends evidence references and free-text suspicion without modifying the saved attempt or its outcome. A confirmed diagnosis also needs --reviewer NAME and pinned independent fail-before/pass-after regression reports. propose includes eligible development attribution and still excludes holdout failures. Changed evidence makes the diagnosis unknown again; no annotation promotes a candidate. See failure attribution records for the shared Arena and scenario contract and its limits.

Declare distinct development, regression and holdout cases before comparing. The gate requires exactly one baseline and one candidate attempt for every catalog case, a single source version per cohort, identical case/configuration/approval policy, live evidence, no incomplete evaluations, no candidate false completion, no previously passing case lost, and at least one solve improvement on holdout. Repeated attempts cannot be cherry-picked inside a cohort. A successful gate emits CANDIDATE_FOR_HUMAN_REVIEW, never promotion. This small-sample rule is an engineering gate, not statistical proof of generalized improvement. Repeated use of a holdout contaminates it; rotate fresh holdouts and keep them out of improvement workspaces.

docs.title: Trust and validation limits
docs.text:
These are trusted-code experiments, not a containment boundary for hostile OSS. Candidate code, build tools and evaluator code can execute on the same host, with its permissions. Process deadlines and the existing birth-identity supervisor help with ordinary failures; a separate directory does not prevent an agent from reading or altering evaluator files. Use a separate isolated machine/container with no credentials for unfamiliar code. Catalog, snapshots and SQLite are operator-owned: hashes detect accidental edits but are not signatures against a hostile writer.

The tests exercise CLI parsing, positive/negative oracle controls, fresh frozen checkouts, TaskRun approval boundaries using a scripted interface, persistent outcomes and comparison rejection cases. They substitute oracle transport and the TaskRun boundary; they do not establish live-provider performance. The shared supervisor and TaskRun have their own integration suites. A live Arena attempt that reaches the changed path is still required before marking the PR ready.

docs.title: Reliability table
docs.text:
Dated sweep rows live in docs/reliability-sweeps.json. The published table is generated, never edited by hand (#694):

python tools/reliability_table.py docs/reliability-sweeps.json > docs/reliability-table.md
python tools/reliability_table.py docs/reliability-sweeps.json --readme   # short README copy

Fake-provider and live-model rows are separate tables and are never mixed. Each row names the master commit the sweep ran on. Add a row after a sweep with the date, profile, commit, mode, run/pass/false-completion counts and a note that points at the run's bug file or evidence directory. The generator refuses a row whose counts do not add up or whose mode is neither live nor fake. A test compares the committed table and the README copy with the generator's output, so regenerate both after changing a row.

A row may also record what each case cost (#721) as case_costs, one entry per case run, with the money fields of that run's status view (autocode --status, the JSON view's cost block) copied as they are:

"case_costs": [
  {"case": "bugfix-iso-weeks", "run": "<run directory name, or null>",
   "estimated_usd": 0.412, "reported_usd": null, "spent_usd": 0.412, "cap_usd": 5.0}
]

null means unknown, never zero: no rate in the price table, or nothing recorded. The table shows it as unknown, and a null cap_usd as no cap. spent_usd is the known spend the cap is compared with, so it is a floor when a stage had no rate. Pasting the whole cost block is fine; the other keys are dropped. The generator checks each amount with the status view's own rule (autocode_cost.check: null or a finite, nonnegative number) and refuses a boolean, a negative or non-finite number, a string, a missing money field, a sample without a case name, or more samples than the sweep's runs. Each mode's table then gains a Cost per case section, and the row shows the median of its known spent values.

docs.title: Channel bridge: GitHub issues as the front door
docs.text:
← Back to README

The channel bridge runs autocode bridge on the same persistent Linux host as the core. A team member opens an issue with the bridge label; the bridge starts a durable run (it survives the bridge, the terminal and the SSH session). When the run reaches a human gate — Requirements questions, the plan approval, a pause — the bridge posts it to the issue. The requester replies in the issue; the bridge takes exactly the action the status view names. Between gates nobody is needed: the worker plans, builds, tests and reviews on its own, and the finished change comes back as a draft pull request carrying the run's canonical evidence.

GitHub is the first channel (issue in #2035, a slice of the remote-service roadmap #2022). Slack and Jira adapters follow on the same bridge core; this page is their contract too.

docs.title: Set up the host
docs.text:
One trusted persistent Linux host, prepared like any durable-workflow host: systemd user manager 254 or newer with linger already enabled (the bridge never configures the host; modes list --json names the reason when it is missing), a clone of the repository to build in, an engine the runs will use, and a GitHub token with access to read issues and post comments (GITHUB_TOKEN).

autocode bridge check     # config, project, GitHub token, durable availability
autocode bridge run       # the daemon; one per host (a lock file refuses a second)

Everything is configured through the environment:

Variable Meaning AUTOCODE_BRIDGE_GITHUB_REPO OWNER/REPO, the single repository this bridge serves. AUTOCODE_BRIDGE_PROJECT the persistent checkout to build in (default: the daemon's directory). AUTOCODE_BRIDGE_LABEL the label that takes an issue (default autocode). AUTOCODE_BRIDGE_ACTORS a JSON array of GitHub logins allowed to steer runs. Replies from anyone else are ignored. AUTOCODE_BRIDGE_OPTIONS a JSON array of launch options (engine, models, --test-command). Every human or run action flag is refused here. AUTOCODE_BRIDGE_POLL_SECONDS seconds between polls (default 10). AUTOCODE_BRIDGE_OPEN_PR 1 to also push the branch and open the draft PR on completion; the default only prepares it. AUTOCODE_BRIDGE_OWNED 1 for the explicit no-systemd mode: runs live with the daemon process, as the GitHub Action's runs do. A daemon restart interrupts them; prefer the durable mode on a host that supports it.

docs.title: The requester's flow
docs.text:
1. Open an issue describing the outcome you want and add the bridge label. AutoCode takes it, comments to say so, and starts the run.
  2. Answer in a comment when the run asks a question. Each question carries its id and, when they exist, its options; a single open question takes the whole comment, several take ID: your answer lines.
  3. Read the plan it posts — the acceptance criteria, how each will be checked, constraints and permission boundaries. Reply approve to accept it, or reply with what to change (that goes back to the Requirements Gatherer, and the revised plan is posted for a fresh decision). If the run is one of a change set (autocode changeset link), the bridge also posts the other runs. Once every run waits with a complete plan, it posts their plans too, and approve set approves every plan together (change sets in clients). approve still releases this run alone.
  4. Walk away. If the run pauses or a role's model runs out of quota, the bridge posts why and what to reply (resume, or model NAME).
  5. On completion the bridge commits the change on the run's branch and prepares the evidence pull request (and opens it when configured).

docs.title: The rules the bridge keeps
docs.text:
The bridge is a client of the task-run interface, exactly like the terminal chat and the headless conformance client:

  • Tokens never leave the host. Every decision is taken against a fresh status view through autocode_taskrun, with the current token read from that view and passed in the child's environment. Issue comments carry questions, options and plan text — never a control token.
  • Free text never approves. Only the exact words approve, approved, y, yes or lgtm at a plan gate count, and only when a complete plan was posted first. Anything else becomes feedback to the planning stage.
  • An approval binds to the plan that was shown. The bridge records the token of the plan it posted; if the plan changed since, the approval is refused and the new plan is posted instead. approve set binds the same way to the change set's plans it posted, and takes only the set approval autocode changeset status names. Words written before a gate was posted can never answer it: each gate remembers which comments it has already consumed.
  • Person-only stops stay person-only. Pauses, retries and blockers are relayed with their reason, and acted on only by an allowlisted actor's explicit reply. Nothing resumes on its own.
  • Refusals are reported, never retried. When the core refuses an action (a stale token, an answer outside the options), the bridge posts the refusal and re-reads the run. A comment the status view cannot act on is posted as a gap to report against the CLI or the view — the bridge works around nothing.
  • One bridge, one action at a time per run. The daemon holds a host lock; each run takes one action per comment, and the durable worker envelope owns every advancing command.

Between gates the bridge only watches: the run itself runs to its next stop under the durable worker, whether or not the daemon is up (it reconciles from its records when it returns).

docs.title: Operating
docs.text:
autocode bridge status [--json] lists every bridged issue, its current gate and its run. Records live under $XDG_STATE_HOME/autocode/bridge (override with AUTOCODE_BRIDGE_HOME), owner-private, outside every task workspace; the per-issue worktrees, run state and the autocode issue records they carry stay in the project's .autocode/issues, so a person can always pick a run up with autocode chat --run-dir ... or autocode issue status N on the host.

A refused start (durable execution unavailable, a missing engine, a leftover branch) is posted to the issue and recorded with its reason; the bridge does not retry it automatically. Remove the record to let it try again.

docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text:
← Back to README

Use autocode for tasks and its subcommands for related work. autocode --help shows the short command overview; autocode --help-all lists every run option, and autocode COMMAND --help shows that command's options. This reference lists the accepted public flags, including advanced run controls. Role/model selection is in Models; provider setup is in Providers. Every command accepts -h / --help.

docs.title: Entry points
docs.text:
Command What it does autocode "Your rough idea" The normal entry point. Runs the full plan → approve → build → validate → complete loop (or stops at the next required checkpoint). replay RUN --into WORKSPACE/.autocode/runs/NAME Re-drive a saved run offline with recorded provider events and fresh verification checks; see Replay. replay RUN --export DIR Export a bounded recording; --recorded-checks on replay simulates historical checks without current completion evidence. autocode resume Continue the unfinished run of this project or task worktree (see Which run a command acts on). Never starts a new task. On a paused or blocked run (PAUSED_*, BLOCKED_*, *_REWORK_REQUIRED, RESOLVER_PENDING) it also acknowledges the stop, as --resume-paused does, so the run goes on: no new budget or recovery allowance, though the per-cycle report-repair and resolver attempt counts restart. A design conflict (PAUSED_DESIGN_CONFLICT) is only shown until you edit the design and pass --resume-paused. Its companions (--retry-failed-stage, --grant-recovery N, ...) need no --resume-paused after it. Plain autocode with no task, run from a script or with output redirected, relaunches a running run the same way but only shows a stop; in an interactive terminal it opens autocode chat. autocode status The same as autocode --status: read-only status of that run. Command words are recognized wherever they stand among the options; a task whose whole text is resume, status or explain goes after -- (autocode -- status). autocode explain The same as autocode --explain: explain the saved run's stop and the offered next command. Reads only; no model call, run lock or workspace changes. autocode demo [--directory PATH] Watch an offline sample plan, demo approval, build, rejected evidence and completion acceptance with the bundled fake provider. No account or model spend. Creates a new temporary directory by default, keeps its run and evidence records for inspection, and refuses an existing --directory. See Offline demo. autocode verify Check an existing working-tree change, branch or patch against caller-supplied criteria; retain independent review, replay and external-change proof in the canonical evidence format. See Standalone verification. autocode coordinate status\|advance\|bind\|approve\|choose\|cancel\|resume\|budget\|planning-budget\|access Coordinate a terminal-chat bug across authorized local repositories, approve member and joint-test plans together, bind verified candidates, prove the combined fix and publish linked PRs. The chat takes the core's named actions; see Automatic multi-repository fixes. autocode chat [BRIEF] [--mode ID] [-- RUN_OPTIONS] Talk to a run in the terminal, the way the VS Code extension does: it prints the run's conversation, asks you only for what the status view leaves to you (an answer, a plan approval, a reply) and runs exactly the command the view names. Plain autocode in an interactive terminal opens it too. With a brief it starts a new run in the project (--in-place, with the start flags of the --mode from autocode modes list, else its default). Without one it picks up the project's open run (or --run-dir RUN), lets you choose when several are open, and asks what you want done when none is. Leaving at a prompt changes nothing. While a stage works, Ctrl-C asks for the view's pause after the current step, a second Ctrl-C interrupts the step and a third stops AutoCode; the chat never exits while AutoCode still runs. A brief that starts with - goes in --brief=TEXT. Where the view names no action it can take, it prints the command to run yourself. Exits 0 when the run completes, 2 when it waits for you. See Terminal chat. autocode conversation start\|attach\|read\|send\|refresh\|handoff Core Requirements conversation journal tied to one task run: queue human messages, explicitly refresh its draft and inspect the handoff. See Core Requirements conversations. autocode ui Figma design (and optional --build handoff to implementation). autocode tasks Run a multi-lane task flow file; accepts --json. autocode components Build the components of an architecture record in parallel and combine them (see Task lanes); with --integrate TARGET --run-local, also start the combined system with Docker Compose and run its smoke check (see Running the combined system locally). autocode dashboard Local browser dashboard. autocode unattended Agent wrapper that refuses operator decisions and reports a stop (see Unattended callers). autocode issue brief\|start\|status\|continue\|plan\|pr Read a GitHub issue, work on it through the task-run interface, put the plan waiting for approval in a pull request as a plan file for review (plan), and prepare a pull request (see GitHub issues). autocode bridge run\|check\|status The channel bridge daemon: take labeled GitHub issues, start durable runs, relay questions, plan approvals and pauses to the issue, and take an allowlisted actor's reply as the exact action the status view names (see Channel bridge). autocode changeset link\|status\|approve\|check-command\|verify\|waive\|reopen\|order\|pr-body\|list Start a run in another registered project for work a run's request places there, show the change set the linked runs form, approve all their plans at once, check them together with an integration command, and write the section each pull request carries (see Linked runs). autocode arena init\|ingest\|cases\|run\|report\|propose\|annotate\|compare Run independent benchmark cases, append evidence-backed failure investigations and compare candidate cohorts (see Arena). autocode checkpoint --workspace PATH --run-dir RUN --compare CHECKPOINT Compare retained code or restore it by the exact inspected token (--working shows what the Builder has changed so far, display only); accepts --json (see Saved code checkpoints). autocode merge [WORKTREE] [--workspace PATH] [--into BRANCH] [--json] Merge a delivered task worktree into its base branch (see Task lanes). autocode capture --output FILE -- COMMAND Run a command with exact output retained for retrieval (see Exact output). autocode output read\|retrieve Read or retrieve exact retained file bytes (see Exact output). autocode visual-capture --config FILE / autocode visual-check --policy FILE Capture visual references or run a source-owned visual check (see Visual checks). autocode compare-baseline Compare Vitest failure evidence (see Execution). autocode review-pr URL [--post] [--out NEW_DIRECTORY] [--json] -- PROVIDER_OPTIONS / autocode-issue review-pr Fetch the exact PR head into an owned checkout, run Code Reviewer only, and print authenticated findings/evidence. --post submits COMMENT only after every new-side anchor and the head are rechecked (see Pull request reviews). autocode review --workspace PATH [--run-dir RUN] Inspect pending human-review criteria and their recorded evidence, then approve, reject with a note, or skip. Reads decisions from terminal or piped input. --show and --json display without prompting; decisions never start a model. See Human review. autocode serve start\|stop\|status [--workspace PATH] [--run-dir RUN] Run the run's development server in the foreground from the project's saved serve command (Project settings) on a free loopback port until Ctrl-C or autocode serve stop; stop ends it and waits (--timeout); status shows whether it is configured, running and its address (--json). See Development server. autocode forget [--workspace PATH] [--json] Clear only the learned project record; keep explicit configuration, saved runs and evidence. See Project memory. autocode clean-worktrees [--yes] [--json] List, then with --yes remove, task worktrees whose runs are complete and whose branch holds their work; records are archived and branches kept (see Task lanes). autocode prune-run RUN [--yes] [--json] (or --run-dir RUN) List, then with --yes delete a run's settled evidence bytes: finished verification-copy trees (tool-containment-*/scratch) and settled job-source stores (<attempt>.source/). Manifests, receipts and hashes are retained, so what was there stays provable; state.json is never modified. Anything still named at file level by state, owned by a live stage or a pending failure recovery, or the newest of its kind is kept with the reason shown. autocode bundle RUN [--out FILE] [--with-diff] [--json] (or --run-dir RUN) Write one redacted archive of a run for a bug report (default WORKSPACE/.autocode/bundles/RUN.tar.gz; a run clean-worktrees archived to PROJECT/.autocode/archive/TREE/runs/RUN takes the project as its workspace, and --with-diff then diffs its base commit against the kept branch): the replay recording replay RUN --export writes, so a maintainer can replay it; state.json, activity.jsonl, the stage reports, the check-replay receipts and the last 200 lines of each provider event stream; the resolved settings, doctor --json output and the version. Every file it writes passes the credential redaction exports use, plus the values of secret-named environment variables; a recording that redaction would still change is left out, and the manifest says why. No workspace source unless --with-diff adds the run's diff (against its base commit, else the uncommitted work). manifest.json lists each file's sha256; cite the printed manifest hash in a bug report or a docs/bugs/ note instead of pasting logs. The run directory is only read. autocode --version Print the executing package version and its source commit when known. An installed package without a source checkout reports commit unknown; it does not borrow the workspace commit. autocode completion bash\|zsh\|fish Print a shell completion script read from the CLI's parsers: the commands, every public option of the main command with its choices, and file names after an option that takes a path. A subcommand completes from the parser it reads: its options, its commands (output read, arena run) and their options, or its argument's choices (completion bash). capture, registry, intervention and dashboard complete only --help. Load it with source <(autocode completion bash) (zsh the same, after compinit; fish autocode completion fish \| source), or save it; see Shell completion. autocode models [--provider NAME] [--workspace PATH] [--json] [--prices] [--selection] List the models your plans offer, grouped by plan (subscription or pay per token) and tier (cheap worker, strong judge, Resolver only), and check the route every role of a new run takes. Without --provider it follows the project's engine setting as doctor and a task do: a claude project lists the Claude Code provider, and a codex project is told its routes are fixed (default models) rather than sent to OpenCode. Suggests a replacement for any route you cannot use; exits 1 when one is missing (see Models). A profile default the provider no longer offers is not a gap when automatic selection replaces it with a route it does offer: the verdict then weighs the selected routes and names each replacement, because the profile defaults are only the fallback a run uses when selection cannot field a set (#1995). --prices prints the dated price table instead, and the rate each default route is priced at, or "no rate" (never a zero price); it runs nothing and works offline. --selection reads the tool's own model and login listings (still no model calls) and prints what automatic selection would choose - the route per role with its price and reasoning level, why every other qualified model lost, and which chosen routes the access check would still probe; exits 1 with the account-terms stop when the connected accounts cannot field an independent checker (Choosing models automatically). autocode setup [--install opencode\|kilocode] [--json] Connect the backends AutoCode runs on, once after installing it (#2049): checks Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Kilo with each one's own login listing; in a terminal, when neither OpenCode nor Kilo is installed, offers to install OpenCode 1.18.33 with npm (one yes/no; --install installs the named hub without asking); offers each installed, signed-out one its own sign-in, where you connect ChatGPT, GLM, MiMo or API keys; then says which backend new runs use and, in a terminal, offers to choose each stage's model and reasoning level on it (autocode stages choose; the first time Enter means yes); finally it lists each stage's choice, or without one the route each role takes. It launches no model. Without npm it names the Node.js download and the command to run. --json asks nothing and installs only what --install names and returns backends (the autocode connections rows, checked, with install_command when missing) and new_runs_use. Exit 1 when no backend could start a run. autocode stages [list\|choose\|set\|reset] [STAGE] [--model MODEL] [--effort LEVEL] [--backend NAME] [--workspace PATH] [--json] See and change the model and reasoning level each stage of a new task runs, kept per backend in ~/.config/autocode/stages.toml (Choosing each stage's model). list (the default) shows each stage, what it does, and its model and level, marked as your choice or the default; choose asks for every stage in turn in a terminal, with advice on what suits it, and saves the answers together; set STAGE --model MODEL --effort LEVEL changes one stage (a stage is its route name, such as terra, or its job, such as builder), refusing a model the backend does not offer, a level the model does not take, or a model the stage's checker or producer runs; reset [STAGE] forgets one stage's choice, or every stage's. Without --backend it uses the backend a new run in --workspace would take. --json returns the view clients render as one dropdown per stage (Stage choices for clients). Every new task reads the choices before it begins; a flag or the project's .autocode/config.toml still wins, and a task already running keeps its own. It launches no model. autocode doctor [--workspace PATH] [--engine opencode\|codex\|claude] [--json] Check Python, psutil, Git, each engine (OpenCode must be 1.x; Codex must be logged in), that the workspace is a Git repository with a commit, and the projected run storage (workspace size x its measured ~3x copy growth: worktrees, verification copies, attempt snapshots) against free disk space — a doomed filesystem is a ✖, a tight one a warning with the numbers. Prints the fix for anything missing; exits 1 when not ready. Passes only when the engine a new run uses is ready, resolved as a run resolves it: --engine codex is Codex; without --engine, the engine the project's files set (Project settings) counts as that flag; otherwise (no engine, or --engine opencode) the provider AUTOCODE_PROVIDER or default_provider in ~/.config/autocode/config.toml names, else OpenCode. That provider must answer and list the route each role of a new run takes - its default model, or the route automatic selection replaces that default with (opencode models, as autocode models checks; #1995). AUTOCODE_PROVIDER=codex names a provider config, not the Codex engine. A ready Codex alone does not pass; doctor names --engine codex as the single-login alternative. --engine claude, a project's engine = "claude", or a claude default provider, checks Claude Code instead: claude on PATH and claude auth status --json, run in the agents' environment, reporting a Claude subscription login (engine:claude; an API key, Bedrock or Vertex is refused, by the same check a run makes: the agents' environment and the project's .claude/settings.json), its conformance row, and its routes; a user claude.toml it ignores is a warning. Doctor shows no Claude rows for other runs and never prints the account's email or organization. Lists the settings a new run takes from the project's files (Project settings) and fails on a file a run would refuse. A user settings row shows the keys ~/.config/autocode/config.toml sets (default_provider, plan_review_call_limit), warns on a key the user file does not take, naming the project's .autocode/config.toml for a project key such as engine, and fails on a file that is not TOML. When a new run launches built-in OpenCode stages, names the kernel tool boundary they get on this machine (containment: macOS Seatbelt or Linux bubblewrap and its version, with OpenCode 1.18.33, by the check run setup makes; --json adds it as containment with backend, backend_version and problem, or null for a Codex, Claude Code or configured-provider run), as a warning that does not fail doctor when such a run would be refused without --allow-uncontained-tools (Execution). The Linux CLI first drops only CAP_SYS_ADMIN and CAP_SYS_PTRACE from its bounding set and re-executes once; the session row records a verified drop. Set AUTOCODE_NO_CAPABILITY_DROP=1 to opt out. If either capability remains available, this row still fails because every stage launch, the demo included, refuses it; it names the fallback (an ordinary user, or setpriv --bounding-set=-sys_admin,-sys_ptrace). Other kernel prerequisites are not established by this check. Runs without psutil and reports it missing. Never reads credentials. autocode registry location\|list\|add\|import\|forget-deleted Run registry API; add PATH registers a committed local project without starting a task, and forget-deleted --workspace W --run-dir R drops the entry of a run whose directory no longer exists (see Registry API). autocode registry roots add\|list\|remove\|discover Configure and inspect bounded, local source roots used by cross-repository bug discovery, independent of the launch directory. autocode registry repositories add\|list\|remove Register a standalone committed checkout outside the configured source roots. autocode runs [--all] [--needs] [--json] Every run of this project, including those in its task worktrees under .autocode/worktrees and its issue worktrees (or, with --all, of every registered project, each row then naming its workspace), in one read-only table, each JSON row titled with the first line of its task (title): what each run's own status view says it needs, and the command that answers it. Needs-first order, then working, then settled, then runs whose checkpoint cannot be read; the row shows how long since the checkpoint was written. A RUNNING checkpoint whose controller left a ready receipt for it (saved by an answer, approval or follow-up, left for the person to continue) is listed under needs you as Ready to continue, with ready_to_continue: true in its JSON row. Nothing here starts, resumes or changes a run. Where a saved run's status alone cannot tell an uncertain attempt from one whose retained report only needs repair, the row points at autocode --run-dir RUN --status instead of offering a command that could set accepted work aside.
