An audited native reference revision also records the previous and current file URLs. Removed entry nodes fall back to the current file root; replacement files appear in the reviewed input list. Engine, authentication, role routes, pins and limits stay unchanged. Identical relocated reference bytes keep their case identity; file names alone do not require fresh visual proof. Shared token aliases are reconciled by library key while original file-local IDs remain in the retained source receipts.

docs.title: Externally reviewed product scope (version 2 inventories)
docs.text:
A complete version 2 source inventory may contain historical frames outside the approved app. Supply both --figma-approved-scope PATH and --figma-approved-scope-sha256 SHA256 with --figma-manifest. The trusted operator pin authenticates a reviewed artifact bound to the complete manifest and every approved case/state/viewport/reference row. A bundle cannot grant its own scope by declaring an approval file. No admission keeps the strict legacy requirement to map every discovered frame and full resource into cases.

All original pages, nodes, actual component owners and variants, variable modes and aliases, fonts, assets and prototype endpoints still undergo full-source validation and remain retained. Scoped case refs must equal their actual transitive dependencies; historical resources cannot be linked as false usage. The retained scope_admission stores only a portable artifact path and its SHA, with byte-identical authority beside the bundle. Saved-run reload rechecks it; new-run flags cannot silently replace a saved pin.

At the stopped, reconciled reference-revision boundary, pair both scope flags with --revise-figma-manifest, the inspected old --expected-design-hash and a concrete --design-change-reason. A scoped run requires a newly reviewed artifact bound to the complete replacement manifest. Ordinary resume cannot replace a pin, and unchanged manifest bytes cannot swap scope authority. The old bundle and its exact authority remain in reference history; the replacement pauses for independent plan review and fresh affected-case validation. The public TaskRun.revise_design accepts the same optional approved_scope and approved_scope_sha256 keyword pair. Revision never grants implementation, image acceptance or human artifact acceptance.

The public inventory retains full-source availability blockers and the exact used/retained frame and resource partition. App readiness and completion use verified delivery blockers for actual app dependencies; historical missing resources remain visible full-source gaps and do not become available. The separate full-resource qualification still needs its own evidence. A scoped --dry-run reports an unretained read-only input preview, without saving scope or running models. Admission and plan review never imply rendered fidelity, independent visual PASS, or human artifact acceptance.

docs.title: Install and run
docs.text: ← Back to README

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
You need macOS or Linux (Windows through WSL), Python 3.11 or newer, Git, pipx, and npm (Node.js) to install the engine.

Linux provides the kernel provider boundary. macOS can run tasks with portable supervision, which cannot prove that every detached provider descendant exited. Use supported Linux for the stronger process-ownership guarantee and for the provider-backed regression checks in this guide. WSL must meet the same Linux kernel requirements.

If prerequisites are missing, on Ubuntu install python3-venv, pipx and git with your package manager; on macOS install Python 3.11+, Git and pipx. Node.js/npm is needed to install Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or Kilo with npm. API keys go in OpenCode or Kilo; the built-in API-key connection is retired.

1. Install AutoCode.

pipx install autocode-supervisor
pipx ensurepath
# Open a new terminal so PATH includes pipx's executables.
autocode --version
autocode demo

Or use the published Homebrew tap:

brew install charlieanna/tap/autocode

The published version verified on 2026-10-27 is 0.8.2 on both PyPI and Homebrew. These commands install the tagged release, not current master; this guide's latest documentation can describe newer features and fixes. Use the advanced checkout/master installation when you need those changes. The release verification record distinguishes distribution smoke checks from task/provider qualification. If pipx's Python is older than 3.11, add --python python3.11. The demo is offline: no sign-in or model spend. Once installed, you do not need to activate a virtual environment in every shell.

Connect your accounts once. Run autocode setup right after installing. It checks Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Kilo. When neither OpenCode nor Kilo is installed it offers to install OpenCode with npm (--install kilocode installs Kilo instead), then offers the sign-in of each installed one that is not signed in, and says which backend your tasks will use. API keys (Z.ai, MiMo, OpenAI, Anthropic) go in OpenCode or Kilo. It then asks which model and reasoning level each stage runs, with advice for each, and every task uses that choice; change it any time with autocode stages choose (Choosing each stage's model). After that a task needs no flags.

Already have an engine signed in? Reuse it. When OpenCode is not installed and nothing names an engine (no flag, no default_provider, no project engine), or OpenCode is installed with no account at all, a new run takes the first backend this machine has connected: Claude Code signed in to a subscription, then Codex, then Kilo. It prints the choice (Engine for this run: Claude Code. …), and autocode doctor checks that same backend. So with only Claude Code or only Codex signed in, skip step 2 and go to the project setup in step 3 with no flags. To choose explicitly, add --engine codex or --engine claude to doctor and to the task; a flag selects a route for that command only and never changes your saved defaults or existing runs.

2. Install the engine and sign in. The default engine is OpenCode. The terminal adapter accepts 1.x and 2.x; this quickstart pins 1.18.33, the version with historical macOS native-tool qualification. Its default routes use two accounts: the Requirements Gatherer, Planner and Builder run GLM 5.3 on a Z.ai Coding Plan, and the Plan Reviewer, Tester and Completion Reviewer run GPT-6 Sol through ChatGPT (Models). So OpenCode needs two logins:

npm install -g opencode-ai@1.18.33
opencode auth login     # choose OpenAI and sign in with your ChatGPT account
opencode auth login     # choose Z.AI Coding Plan and enter its API key
opencode auth list      # both are listed now

One login instead of two? Not on OpenCode's default routes. There are two single-login routes. Codex with a ChatGPT account: install it, sign in once, and add --engine codex to autocode doctor and to every task below.

npm install -g @openai/codex
codex login

Or Claude Code with a Claude subscription (the built-in claude provider): install Claude Code, sign in once, and add --engine claude to autocode doctor and to every task below.

claude auth login
autocode doctor --engine claude

3. Make a project and check everything. A task works in a Git repository with at least one commit:

mkdir hello-autocode && cd hello-autocode
git init
git commit --allow-empty -m "Start"
autocode doctor

If Git asks who you are, run git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email you@example.com once, then commit again. doctor prints ✔ or ✖ for Python, psutil, Git, the engine and the project, with the fix next to each ✖, and ends with ready for a first task. For OpenCode it also reads opencode models (this can take up to a minute) and shows a ✖ routes line naming the login still missing when a role's default model is not offered, as the first task would refuse to start; autocode models shows the full list. With --engine codex it checks the Codex login instead, and with --engine claude the Claude Code login. For an OpenCode run its containment line names the kernel tool boundary the stages get on this machine (macOS Seatbelt or Linux bubblewrap), or warns, with the reason, that the run would be refused without one (native tool containment).

4. Start the first task.

autocode "Write hello.py that prints a greeting, with a unittest test for it"

On Linux the provider-ownership requirement applies to every task-stage engine. OpenCode's separate tool policy also needs an explicit choice: see native tool containment for the explicit choice to use OpenCode's own permission checks on Linux. That choice concerns tool access; it does not bypass Linux provider process ownership. The macOS portable supervision limitation remains as described above.

In a terminal this is a chat. AutoCode may ask a question or two (type the answer, or an option's number). Once it has understood the request it asks before spending on planning: Prepare a reviewed plan? with what that spends, then Prepare plan? [y/N]:; type y. It then shows the plan: what will be built and how each requirement will be checked.

5. Approve. At Approve this plan? [y/N], or type what to change: type y. Nothing is built before this; anything else you type goes back to the planners as feedback. After approval the Builder, Tester and Completion Reviewer run on their own until the task completes or needs you.

6. See the result. The task runs in its own Git worktree, so your checkout is not touched. When it completes, AutoCode prints what was done and checked, then Delivered on branch autocode/<task>-<id> (<commit>). Look at it and merge it:

git log --stat autocode/<task>-<id>
git merge autocode/<task>-<id>

If you closed the chat, autocode status shows where the run is and autocode resume continues it. Workflow explains each stage; CLI lists every command.

docs.title: If setup stops
docs.text: What you see What to do autocode: command not found Run pipx ensurepath, open a new terminal, then autocode --version. For a venv install, activate that venv or use its bin/autocode. Missing engine or login in doctor Select the engine you actually connected. Use the same --engine codex or --engine claude for doctor and the task; the unqualified command uses the configured/default route. Missing Git project or HEAD Run in the project root and make its first commit. Starting in a folder of sibling repositories does not select them as a set. A missing model route Follow the named route/login fix. An installed CLI alone does not establish access to every selected role's model. Provider session boundary unavailable on Linux doctor's session row names the cause. The CLI automatically drops CAP_SYS_ADMIN and CAP_SYS_PTRACE from its Linux bounding set and re-executes once before touching run state, so root containers normally need no prefix. A successful drop is reported on stderr and in doctor; no other capability is dropped. Set AUTOCODE_NO_CAPABILITY_DROP=1 to manage this yourself. If the kernel refuses the drop or re-exec, existing stage admission still applies: use an ordinary user or, where permitted, setpriv --bounding-set=-sys_admin,-sys_ptrace autocode .... Other boundary requirements are unchanged; see provider ownership. doctor is not a complete kernel-admission test. Another repository is not registered Set the same AUTOCODE_HOME in each terminal and use autocode registry add /path/to/committed/checkout; see the multi-repository walkthrough.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.11+
  • Git
  • OpenCode 1.x or 2.x connected to ChatGPT and Z.ai (the default engine). Live-checked with OpenCode 1.18.31. OpenCode 2.x uses --standalone and a provider/model#effort model id. Strict tool containment and verified visual delivery stay qualified only for OpenCode 1.18.33.
  • Linux or macOS, with different provider cleanup guarantees; see provider process ownership. Supported Linux is used for provider-backed qualification. Windows needs WSL with the same Linux kernel requirements. Native Windows support is not planned; Native Windows records what was audited and what remains.
  • Optional: Codex CLI for --engine codex (one ChatGPT login) and the Figma path; Claude Code for --engine claude (one Claude subscription login). Installation does not change Codex, OpenCode or Claude Code settings.

Native process supervision uses the psutil runtime dependency, which pipx and pip install with AutoCode. Works against any committed Git workspace; no IdleCampus files or services are required.

docs.title: Windows through WSL
docs.text:
Run Git, Python and AutoCode inside WSL. Prefer a fresh checkout on the Linux filesystem, such as ~/src/autocode, to avoid sharing ownership and environment state with Windows tools. The repository's .gitattributes keeps text checkouts at LF even when core.autocrlf=true; binary assets retain their bytes. This policy applies to fresh checkouts and does not rewrite an existing dirty tree. Save any real edits before replacing a checkout with line-ending-only churn; do not commit that churn to recover it.

A virtual environment created by Windows has Scripts/, Lib/ and Include/, while the Linux commands in the README require .venv/bin/. Create the environment with Linux Python inside WSL. If the shared checkout already has a Windows .venv, keep it separate and create a Linux environment outside the checkout:

python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/autocode-wsl
~/.venvs/autocode-wsl/bin/python -m pip install --editable .
source ~/.venvs/autocode-wsl/bin/activate

If Git reports detected dubious ownership for a Windows-mounted checkout, first verify that you trust that specific directory. You can then allow its exact path, replacing this example with your checkout's absolute path:

git config --global --add safe.directory '/mnt/c/Users/YOU/workspace/autocode'

Avoid safe.directory '*', which trusts every repository. A checkout on the Linux filesystem usually avoids this mounted-directory ownership mismatch.

docs.title: Advanced: install from a checkout
docs.text:
To follow current master without maintaining a development checkout:

pipx install git+https://github.com/charlieanna/autocode

Use pipx reinstall autocode-supervisor to refresh an existing pipx Git installation from its saved source. This is separate from the published PyPI release; check autocode --version and retain the source commit when reporting behavior. Do not assume two builds with the same package version contain the same master changes. Choose one active installation rather than relinking a Homebrew command over an existing pipx/development command.

For working on AutoCode itself, or trying an unreleased change. Run directly from a checkout (its Python needs psutil, as in the project's .venv):

python3 /path/to/autocode/tools/autocode.py "Build a greeting CLI" \
  --workspace /path/to/project --reasoning-effort high

Install the checkout once with pipx, editable so your changes apply, to invoke it from any project:

pipx install --editable /path/to/autocode

Or install into your own virtual environment:

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install .
.venv/bin/autocode "Build a greeting CLI" --workspace /path/to/project

A virtual environment's bin directory is on PATH only while the environment is activated (source .venv/bin/activate), and only in that shell. In a new shell, typing autocode answers command not found: activate again, call .venv/bin/autocode, add that bin directory to PATH in your shell profile, or use the pipx install above, which puts autocode on PATH for every shell.

docs.title: Sanity check
docs.text:
Confirm the install, then check the machine and your project before the first task:

autocode --version
autocode doctor --workspace /path/to/project

--version prints the commit when run from a checkout and commit unknown from an installed package. doctor names anything missing (Python, psutil, Git, the default engine, a committed Git project) with the fix next to it, and exits 1 until the machine is ready. Its path row warns, without failing, when a new shell would not find autocode on PATH, and names the directory to add or the pipx install. It checks the engine a new run would use: OpenCode, or the provider set as the default below (with no --engine and with --engine opencode alike), including that it offers every role's default model; --engine codex checks Codex instead.

docs.title: Shell completion
docs.text:
autocode completion bash|zsh|fish prints a completion script read from the CLI's own parsers: the commands, every option of the main command and of each subcommand, with their choices, a subcommand's own commands (autocode output read), and file names after an option that takes a path. Load it in the current shell, or save it where your shell reads completions:

source <(autocode completion bash)   # or save it as ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/autocode
source <(autocode completion zsh)    # after compinit; or save it as _autocode in a directory on $fpath
autocode completion fish | source    # or save it as ~/.config/fish/completions/autocode.fish

capture, registry, intervention and dashboard complete only --help. A saved script lists the options of the version that wrote it, so write it again after upgrading.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text: Pushing a version tag publishes to PyPI; see Releasing.

docs.title: The normal invocation
docs.text:
From inside any committed Git project:

autocode "Your rough idea"

Or target another committed Git workspace:

autocode "Your rough idea" --workspace /path/to/project

That starts joint requirements planning: a Requirements Gatherer clarifies the outcome, a Planner drafts a task DAG, and a Plan Reviewer challenges it. You approve the plan before any Builder starts. See Workflow.

docs.title: Advanced entry points
docs.text:
Use the whole workflow through autopilot, or invoke one unit at its saved boundary:

autopilot "Build a greeting CLI" --workspace /path/to/project --chat

# Or invoke individual units at their saved boundaries:
autoplanner "Build a greeting CLI" --workspace /path/to/project --chat
# After approval, this stops before any Builder starts.
# Each unit continues the project's unfinished run (add --run-dir RUN when it has several):
autocode-build --workspace /path/to/project --no-chat
autoreview --workspace /path/to/project --no-chat
# If review requests rework, diagnose it without launching a Builder:
autoresolver --workspace /path/to/project --no-chat
# Let Autopilot continue through any remaining build/review cycles:
autopilot --workspace /path/to/project --no-chat

Each unit command stops successfully before dispatching another unit. autocode --unit autoplanner|autocode|autoreview|autoresolver provides the same selection; omitting it runs all units.

docs.title: Engine and planning flags
docs.text:
New runs use joint Requirements Planner/Plan Reviewer work by default. An approved three-role OpenCode run can add Planner (GLM) work at a clean execution boundary with --joint-planning --resume-paused. Its approved work and existing sessions remain; the Planner joins the next brief revision.

Native Codex, including Figma runs, supports --engine codex --joint-planning: requirements gathering, planning, and plan review run in separate read-only Codex sessions using the existing ChatGPT login. The three routes inherit the saved planning model unless explicitly selected with --requirements-model, --glm-model, and --plan-reviewer-model (bare GPT names). Adding joint planning to a saved Codex run at a clean execution or discovery boundary backs up the checkpoint, retains the work and existing sessions, and restarts at requirements gathering. The reviewed plan needs fresh approval before further implementation. Saved runs retain their engine and limits.

docs.title: Default provider
docs.text:
New runs use OpenCode unless you choose otherwise. --provider <name> picks the tool for one run. To change the default for every new run and for the dashboard, set AUTOCODE_PROVIDER=kilocode or add this to ~/.config/autocode/config.toml:

default_provider = "kilocode"

A Kilo provider needs the Kilo CLI on PATH. On Linux, install the pinned release; a launch there refuses any other version, because its restricted read-only and planning stages need that release's kernel shell. macOS has no kernel shell, so its checkers use Kilo's own shell with edits denied and any Kilo release launches:

npm install -g @kilocode/cli@7.8.3
kilo auth list

A saved run keeps the provider it started with, and --engine codex runs still use Codex. autocode doctor then checks the default provider instead of OpenCode. AUTOCODE_PROVIDER=codex does not select the Codex engine: it names a provider config codex.toml, and doctor reports it missing. Use --engine codex for Codex. autocode-dashboard --provider <name> overrides the default for the dashboard; its model pickers list that tool's models.

See also: CLI · Providers · Models

docs.title: Queued interventions
docs.text:
← Back to README

The browser can submit a durable change request without competing for the workspace writer lock or changing state.json:

["autocode", "intervention", "submit", "--workspace", "/project", "--run-dir", "/project/.autocode/runs/run", "--request-id", "request-123", "--kind", "feedback", "--text", "Keep the partial implementation", "--json"]
["autocode", "intervention", "submit", "--workspace", "/project", "--run-dir", "/project/.autocode/runs/run", "--request-id", "pause-124", "--kind", "pause", "--json"]
["autocode", "intervention", "inspect", "--workspace", "/project", "--run-dir", "/project/.autocode/runs/run", "--json"]

docs.title: Submission
docs.text:
submit writes only the canonical run's .autocode/runs/<run>/interventions.json under a separate short-held inbox lock. It validates the Git workspace, canonical run containment, direct regular state.json, checkpoint workspace pointer, and rejects symlinked inbox or lock paths. The versioned receipt has id, kind, original text, monotonic order, submitted_at, observed_goal_token, and boundary_pause_requested. Both feedback and pause requests set that boundary intent; they never start a provider or write state.json from the submitting process.

Request IDs are idempotency keys over id, kind, and original text: an identical retry returns the original durable receipt without another record, while changed text or kind under the same ID returns request_conflict. Concurrent submissions are serialized by the inbox lock and receive durable order values. Corrupt, unsupported, unavailable, locked, invalid, or failed-write inboxes return JSON errors and exit 2 without claiming a receipt. inspect is read-only, creates neither inbox nor lock, and reports only pending requests; it does not claim that a currently running older binary can consume them.

docs.title: Consumption
docs.text:
The workspace-lock owner checks the inbox after recovery and before every provider admission, and after every saved stage result, including question, approval, review and completion exits. Inbox acceptance and admission are serialized by the short inbox lock: a request accepted before admission is consumed first; one accepted after admission waits for that stage's saved boundary. The inbox lock is never held while a provider runs. Consumption writes the applied receipt ledger and feedback event to authoritative state.json before removing inbox records. A crash before that state write leaves the request pending; a crash after it is recovered by recognizing the applied ID and retrying only inbox acknowledgement. If interruption follows inbox acknowledgement but precedes the final state write, owner recovery clears the obsolete acknowledgement marker only when every marked ID is already applied. Receipts retain their original IDs, text and order.

Applied feedback saves a brief_feedback provenance event, preserves stage artifacts and partial edits, archives stale validation/review authorization, invalidates goal approval, and pauses with astra_discovery selected. It never starts Requirements discovery automatically: invoke the existing explicit Continue action as an argument array, for example ["autocode", "--workspace", "/project", "--run-dir", "/project/.autocode/runs/run", "--resume-paused"]. The revised brief still requires its exact displayed approval token. Pending feedback also blocks goal approval, artifact approval and completion until the owner consumes it.

A pause-only request preserves the selected next stage and any valid goal approval. It pauses at the next safe boundary with a pause_intent; --resume-paused records its acknowledgement and resumes that selected stage. If the run was already held at another pause (any PAUSED_* status, or an operational pause's AutoResolver request, answered or not), the intent records that pause as held_pause, also when the same batch carries feedback. A second pause keeps the held_pause of the first. Feedback applied on its own records one too when the held pause is operational, unless that pause offers feedback (an exhausted plan-review budget, or a validation-only stop whose request names --feedback). --resume-paused then acknowledges the intervention and returns the run to that pause, whose own resume rules apply in the same command: an operational pause is released only by its own authority, and the stop reason says so. That authority includes the one re-evaluation of corrective information already sent for its request, when the intervention left the run as that information found it; a --resume-paused that finds the pause still queued applies it under the held pause before that re-evaluation, so the order of the two commands does not matter. An invocation that acknowledged that pause itself (for example with the exhausted bound's flag or --grant-recovery) releases it before applying the batch, so nothing is held then. --retry-builder is not such an acknowledgement here: it is checked only after the batch is applied, so the batch is applied under the held pause, the retry is not applied, and you send it again with --resume-paused. --pause-after-stage and the existing run-local pause-requested file continue to stop at saved boundaries. --status is read-only and adds interventions with inspector versus recorded-runner capability, pending IDs/count, pause intent, applied receipts, inbox errors and blocked conditions.

Use --astra-model, --terra-model, --sol-model, or --completion-model to explicitly override a role. Resuming keeps the saved engine, provider mapping and limits unless overridden.

docs.title: Intervention ordering and recovery
docs.text:
Each request ID retains its original receipt after application. An identical explicit retry returns it without requeueing; changed text or kind under that ID is a conflict. Receipt order increases across consumed batches. The observed goal token is read under the inbox lock when accepting the request.

Submission and provider admission share the short inbox lock. Preparation occurs before admission; a request accepted first prevents the next provider launch. A request accepted after admission is queued while that stage finishes. The lock is released before waiting for the provider or asking for terminal input. Pending requests also prevent a prepared answer, goal approval, artifact approval or operator completion from committing. Stage results and recovery preserve completed work and consume earlier requests before committing any completion authorization.

The owner commits pause effects, feedback invalidation and applied receipt IDs in one authoritative state write before removing inbox requests. Restart recovers both acknowledgement crash windows without applying an ID twice. Pause confirmation requires the saved paused state, not merely a receipt. Explicit --resume-paused acknowledges a saved pause; feedback still requires Requirements discovery and a newly displayed exact-token brief approval before implementation can resume.

Applied receipts include applied_at; explicit continuation adds resumed_at to previously applied receipts. Status exposes these durable timestamps. Submission retries omit these owner-only fields and continue to return the original acceptance receipt.

See also: Dashboard · Workflow · Registry API

docs.title: GitHub issues to pull requests
docs.text:
← Back to README

autocode-issue takes a GitHub issue, runs AutoCode on it in a branch of its own, and turns the finished run into a pull request whose body carries the run's evidence. It sits on top of the task-run interface and changes nothing about how a run plans, builds or completes.

It never makes a decision that belongs to you. Approving the plan, answering questions, accepting reviews and resuming pauses stay with you; the tool prints the exact command for each. It refuses to prepare the change's pull request from a run that has not completed. Nothing is pushed unless you pass --open. On a team, it can also put the plan in a pull request for review before anything is built (below).

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text:
Run these from inside a clone of the repository whose issue you want resolved. Its dependencies must be installed there, and the origin remote must point at GitHub.

autocode-issue brief #812                      # the brief AutoCode would get; no side effects
autocode-issue start #812 -- --engine codex --test-command "uv run pytest"
autocode --show-goal --workspace WT --run-dir RUN
autocode --approve-goal TOKEN --workspace WT --run-dir RUN
autocode-issue continue #812                   # repeat after each answer or approval
autocode-issue status #812                     # where it stands and the next command, at any time
autocode-issue pr #812                         # commit the change and write the PR body; no push
autocode-issue pr #812 --open                  # push the branch and open a draft pull request

start and status print WT, RUN and TOKEN for you, with every command filled in.

In a terminal, start and continue open the run's chat (autocode chat --workspace WT --run-dir RUN) whenever the run needs you: answer its questions, give plan feedback and approve the plan there, as in any other chat. Leave the chat and the commands above still work. --no-chat keeps them alone (a script or CI), and --chat asks for the chat even when the output is not a terminal. The run also appears among the project's own chats (autocode runs, the terminal chat's /runs), under its worktree.

  • ISSUE can be a URL, OWNER/REPO#N, or #N for the repository behind --remote (default origin).
  • AutoCode options go after -- on start. That covers the engine, the models, and --test-command. They are saved and reused by continue. Without them, the run reads the project settings committed in .autocode/config.toml or [tool.autocode] (CLI).
  • --note TEXT adds your own guidance to the brief, for example "keep the public API unchanged".
  • --issue-file FILE reads the issue from a JSON file in GitHub's issue shape instead of the API. Use it offline, or to edit an issue before running it.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Step Effect start Creates branch autocode/issue-N-<title> and a worktree for it at .autocode/issues/OWNER-REPO-N/, both from --base (default HEAD). Starts a task run in that worktree with the brief. Records the link in .autocode/issues/OWNER-REPO-N.json. brief The issue's title, URL, labels, description and up to 30 of its newest comments. The description and comments are quoted and marked as the reporter's words, not instructions. The brief adds no requirements of its own. AutoCode's requirements stage traces every requirement to the issue text or your --note. pr Refuses unless the run is complete and its canonical evidence report is current. Checks that report before staging or committing. Commits every change except .autocode/ on the issue branch. Writes the PR body to .autocode/issues/OWNER-REPO-N-pr.md. pr --open Pushes the branch to --remote and opens a draft pull request against the branch that was current at start (override with --base). If --remote is a fork, the head is FORK-OWNER:branch. --ready opens it ready for review instead of as a draft. plan Refuses unless the run is waiting for its plan to be approved. Exports that plan as a plan file and commits it, as the only change, on branch autocode/issue-N-<title>-plan made from the run's base commit (after a merged plan pull request, on -plan-2 from the base branch). Writes that pull request's body to .autocode/issues/OWNER-REPO-N-plan-pr.md. See Reviewing the plan in a pull request. plan --open Pushes that branch and opens a draft pull request with the same base, fork and --ready rules as pr --open.

The PR body says Resolves OWNER/REPO#N and includes the run's exact canonical evidence.md, with the issue wrapper and diffstat. The paired evidence.json and evidence.md live in the run directory. They report what AutoCode recorded:

  • the intended outcome
  • each acceptance criterion with its result and evidence
  • for bug fixes, the runner's fail-before/pass-after regression proof
  • the review findings and their status
  • for a build, bug fix or design, who approved the plan and each review, accepted completion, edited the plan or resumed a pause, with the Git identity, host, command and any --as name recorded for each, none of it verified (Who approved). A report written before AutoCode listed approvals has no such section, and neither does a pull request body built from it, until AutoCode saves the completed run again; reading its status does not.
  • the diffstat, the run and the base commit

The report also records actual roles/models, durations, available usage and provider provenance. Missing usage stays unknown. A declaration such as --evidence-provenance fake or live describes the caller's setup; a model's name alone cannot establish live inference. The task-run interface authenticates the saved pair against the current run and source before delivery. A missing, changed or stale pair must be repaired/revalidated in the owned run; preparing the PR does not silently regenerate evidence. A passed completion gate is evidence for review, not proof of correctness.

docs.title: Reviewing the plan in a pull request
docs.text:
On a team, what will be built is worth reviewing before AutoCode builds it. When start or continue stops with the plan waiting for approval, put it in a pull request instead of approving it at once:

autocode-issue plan #812                       # commit the plan as plans/issue-812.md on its own branch; no push
autocode-issue plan #812 --open                # push that branch and open a draft pull request
  • What it commits. The plan is exported as autocode plan --export writes it, through the task-run interface. It is committed as one file on branch autocode/issue-N-<title>-plan, made from the commit the run started from. The commit is built without a checkout: your checkout, the issue's worktree and the run do not change, and nothing is approved. --path PATH puts the file elsewhere in the repository, as a path from its top level, never under .autocode/.
  • The pull request. Its title is Plan: TITLE (#N), and its body gives the plan revision and the file's goal hash, says how to edit the file, and says that merging approves nothing. The run's directory is named, not its path on your machine. If the export masked credential-shaped text, the body says so: the run refuses the file until those values are restored.
  • A changed plan. While the pull request is open, run plan again after the run's plan changes, for example after --feedback. The new plan is committed on top of the branch, so the same pull request shows the change. An unchanged plan reuses the commit. It never replaces commits it did not make: if the branch moved, it refuses, and if reviewers pushed edits to the pull request, the push is refused. A branch deleted here holds nothing to replace, so plan makes it again at its last plan commit. A merged plan pull request is never reused (see below).

Reviewers edit the file in the pull request as Reviewing a plan in a pull request describes. Merging it approves nothing. Once plan --open has opened it, status prints its URL and the command that loads the merged file into the issue's run, to run once it is merged and pulled into your checkout; loading and approving stay with you:

autocode --goal-file /path/to/project/plans/issue-812.md --workspace WT --run-dir RUN
autocode-issue continue #812                   # in joint planning the Plan Reviewer reviews the loaded plan first
autocode --approve-goal TOKEN --workspace WT --run-dir RUN

The approval stop names the file and its goal hash. The merged file goes back into the run that drafted the plan; starting a new run from it is not available yet (A team's plan review).

autocode-issue counts the pull request as merged once the base branch, here or as last fetched from the remote (plan fetches it first once it has committed a plan, with or without --open), holds a different file at its path than the plan branch started from, whatever the merge method, and whether or not the plan branch was deleted with it (gh pr merge --delete-branch deletes it here too). Until the run's plan moves past the one the merged pull request carried, plan refuses and pushes nothing, and status prints the --goal-file command. After that, for example once the Plan Reviewer revised the loaded plan, status stops printing it: loading the file again would replace the newer plan. To have the changed plan reviewed again, plan starts a new pull request, on branch autocode/issue-N-<title>-plan-2 (then -plan-3) made from the base branch that holds the merged file, so it shows only what changed since.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
• Token: reads GITHUB_TOKEN, or GH_TOKEN if that is unset.
  • Reading issues: a public issue needs no token. A private issue needs one with read access.
  • Opening a pull request: needs a token with pull-request write access to the issue's repository.
  • Pushing: uses your own git credentials for the remote.
  • GitHub Enterprise: set AUTOCODE_GITHUB_API=https://HOST/api/v3.

docs.title: Label-triggered Action example
docs.text:
The example workflow and its handler use the same issue CLI and public task-run interface. Applying the configured label starts a run and posts its current status with exact human commands. Applying it again reattaches to the same issue worktree and run, without advancing it or approving anything. After a person answers or approves on the runner, a manual workflow dispatch with the issue number continues it. A completed, authenticated run is pushed and opened as a draft PR; the Action never merges.

This example requires a dedicated persistent Linux self-hosted runner with the autocode-issues runner label. Its project clone, AutoCode installation and provider configuration must be outside GITHUB_WORKSPACE and RUNNER_TEMP. The workflow's checkout is only the trusted default-branch handler code. It must never clean or replace the persistent project. GitHub-hosted ephemeral runners need a complete state-restoration design beyond this example; uploading one run directory as a cache does not preserve its Git worktree or ownership.

Set up the runner once:

  1. Install AutoCode in a dedicated venv and configure a working provider as in providers.md. Clone the target repository to an absolute persistent path, keep its approved base branch current, and install its test dependencies where issue worktrees can use them. Configure the Git author identity and push credentials for its origin remote. For HTTPS, gh auth setup-git can use the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN; verify this under the runner account. An SSH credential is another option.
  2. Copy the example workflow to .github/workflows/autocode-issue.yml and keep examples/github-issue/issue_action.py available on the default branch. The persistent venv must contain the compatible AutoCode version. For this repository, the handler is already present; another repository must copy it.
  3. Configure repository Actions variables:
Variable Value AUTOCODE_ISSUE_PROJECT Absolute persistent target clone, such as /srv/autocode/widgets. AUTOCODE_ISSUE_PYTHON Absolute venv interpreter, such as /srv/autocode/venv/bin/python. AUTOCODE_ISSUE_ACTORS Required JSON allowlist, such as ["maintainer-login"]. AUTOCODE_ISSUE_LABEL Label to start/reattach, default autocode. Create that label. AUTOCODE_ISSUE_OPTIONS JSON argv list of provider/models/test options, such as ["--engine", "codex", "--test-command", "python -m unittest", "--evidence-provenance", "live"].
  1. Permit Actions to create pull requests in repository settings, and permit the job's contents: write, issues: write and pull-requests: write permissions. Configure provider credentials on the dedicated runner; do not put credentials in the options variable. If a GitHub App token replaces GITHUB_TOKEN, set AUTOCODE_ISSUE_COMMENT_AUTHOR to its actual bot login in the step environment so duplicate recovery recognizes only its own comment.

The allowlist is checked both before the job starts and by the handler. Before any issue work or comment/PR write, the handler also requires the triggering actor's current repository permission to be write or admin. It checks GITHUB_TRIGGERING_ACTOR, so a rerun by another person does not inherit the original person's authorization. GitHub maps maintain to write and triage to read in this API. Custom role names alone are not accepted as authorization. See GitHub's actor variables and collaborator permission API.

Repository writers in that allowlist can start provider work, consume its budget and eventually push a draft branch. Use a dedicated runner whose credentials and repository access fit that trust boundary. Issue text is passed as quoted task data; event fields and issue text never enter a shell. The handler rejects saved approval, answer, delegation and resume actions in AUTOCODE_ISSUE_OPTIONS, including --no-requirements. Do not add automatic approval commands to the workflow.

The handler saves --no-adaptive-planning itself: ordinary joint planning can otherwise allow a Plan Reviewer to approve automatically. Explicit --adaptive-planning is refused. An attachment created elsewhere without this opt-out is retained but refused; inspect its approval policy instead of silently changing it or treating an automated decision as human approval.

docs.title: Human approval and continuation
docs.text:
Apply the label to an open issue. The Action comment prints the exact autocode --show-goal, autocode --approve-goal TOKEN, workspace and run directory commands. Sign in to the persistent runner as its operator, use the configured venv's autocode, and read the displayed plan. Then execute the printed approval command for that exact token, or provide the requested answer/feedback/recovery action. Changed plans require their new token. The Action never infers approval from a label, comment or dispatch.

Choose Run workflow for the copied workflow and enter the issue number. Dispatch before approval simply reports the same human stop. Repeat the human action and dispatch when another approval, question, review or operational pause occurs. A final dispatch opens a draft PR only when the ordinary completion gate and canonical evidence inspection pass. Its body embeds the exact retained evidence.md. Repeated dispatch after opening reuses the saved PR URL, without another provider run, push or PR.

docs.title: Persistence, duplicates and recovery
docs.text:
Keep the whole persistent clone and its Git objects/worktree registration, .autocode/issues/OWNER-REPO-N/ worktree, corresponding version-1 issue attachment .autocode/issues/OWNER-REPO-N.json, the owned run's artifacts and the .autocode/issue-action/ comment receipt. The attachment's worktree, run_dir and saved options are the supported link; the handler asks TaskRun for run facts and never reads child state.json. Paused runs remain on disk between workflow invocations and machine restarts.

Per-issue Actions concurrency plus a local nonblocking lock prevents duplicate handlers from taking over a run. Duplicate labels only report it. One owned bot comment is updated; if GitHub accepted the comment before the local receipt was saved, the handler finds its marker and author rather than posting another. A partial initial launch, damaged attachment, unavailable GitHub permission check or mismatched comment receipt fails closed and retains the files. Inspect the saved attachment and use autocode-issue status and the public task-run commands to diagnose it; do not delete an existing run to make a retry succeed. GitHub accepting a PR just before its local URL is saved may need a human to reconcile that PR before retrying. The example does not promise transactions across GitHub and local storage.

After review and merge/closure, an operator can remove this issue's worktree with git worktree remove, then its attachment, Action receipt and issue branch when they are no longer needed. Preserve evidence first if required. Do not delete another run's .autocode contents. No automatic cleanup runs while an issue is paused.

docs.title: Offline CI smoke
docs.text:
tests.test_issue_action invokes this same handler against the existing fake greeting provider, a loopback HTTP GitHub stub and a local bare Git remote. It checks the initial approval stop, duplicate reattachment/comment recovery, refusal to infer approval on dispatch, explicit test-human approval, continuation to one draft PR, and its exact canonical Markdown. Negative controls cover unauthorized/rerun actors, wrong labels, concurrent ownership and saved approval bypasses. It uses no public GitHub mutation or paid models. The normal CI suite discovers it on every PR through --all-fast and on master.

.venv/bin/python -m unittest tests.test_issue_action -v

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One run per issue. A second start for the same issue is refused. Resume its retained run first. Deliberately starting over requires preserving any needed evidence, removing that issue's worktree (git worktree remove), record and branch; the Action never does this automatically.
  • Dependencies are not copied into the worktree. A bug fix's regression proof needs a test command that works there. Pass --test-command, or install dependencies in the worktree first.
  • You still review and merge. The pull request is a draft by default. "Complete" means AutoCode's completion gate passed. It does not mean the change is safe to merge.
  • One issue at a time. Several issues can run at once, each in its own worktree, but nothing schedules them. Each one still stops for your approval.

docs.title: Reviewing a pull request
docs.text:
autocode review-pr reviews an existing pull request without changing your local project or starting Requirements, planning, approval or building. The autocode-issue review-pr alias runs the same command.

autocode review-pr https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/pull/NUMBER -- \
  --provider opencode --single-model zai-coding-plan/glm-5.3 --reasoning-effort high

Provider authentication must already work (Providers). The command reads the PR title/body as untrusted context, fetches its captured head from the base repository's pull ref, and creates a detached checkout under a new owned .autocode/pull-reviews/ directory. --out NEW_DIRECTORY chooses another new output directory; existing outputs, parent traversal and symlink aliases are refused. The current project and other runs are never reused. Query/fragment anchors are accepted, but the URL's HTTPS hostname and port must match the configured GitHub API (AUTOCODE_GITHUB_API for Enterprise).

The Code Reviewer reads the exact diff against the captured base's merge base, leaves findings and targeted tests under review/, and retains its normal obligation to demonstrate blocking behavior with a failing test or an explicit test limitation. Source changes outside the permitted review/run artifacts are refused. A report based on an additional scratch patch is refused: the proof must use the fetched head itself. If the workflow pauses, the command exits 1 and names the retained run for inspection; it does not approve or repair it.

Successful output includes the head SHA, findings, their evidence, and the authenticated canonical evidence report. --json prints these in one JSON result. review-pr.json retains the checkout/run identity, and result.json retains the successful result. Review canonical reports retain their recorded availability: review completion is not build delivery. The layer separately checks that the reviewed head/source and report bytes are unchanged, and refuses stale/invalid canonical bindings. New review reports expose the SHA-256 of the exact runner-written review/findings.json bytes through the existing public workflow_result.artifact_sha256 slot. Legacy reviews keep an unknown hash and cannot be published through this command; start a new review instead. Findings are read from a stable regular file with a 4 MiB bound, without links, redirected parents, duplicate JSON keys or nonfinite numbers.

autocode review-pr https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/pull/NUMBER --post -- \
  --provider opencode --single-model zai-coding-plan/glm-5.3 --reasoning-effort high

--post requires GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN with permission to create PR reviews. It creates COMMENT only, with one comment per finding; the review summary includes the exact canonical evidence Markdown. That report has no Approvals section. Only build, bug-fix and design reports list who approved; a review never asks for an approval, so the post carries no approval record and no Git identity or host of anyone who resumed the review. Every finding must name a changed file and a positive line/span entirely present on the diff's new side. Removed files, unavailable/truncated GitHub patches, invalid spans and stale heads refuse the whole write. The command reauthenticates the local report/source and rereads the open PR's head immediately before POST. GitHub may still change after that read; the submitted review's commit_id remains the captured reviewed head. Repeating --post creates a separate review. GitHub posting tokens and Git authentication helper/header values are blanked at the TaskRun child boundary; normal provider configuration stays available.

The companion pull request Action uses trusted installed AutoCode/provider tooling on an explicitly configured runner. It reviews without posting by default, and keeps its result as a workflow artifact. Follow its setup; never install AutoCode or provider tooling from the PR with secrets available.

docs.title: macOS app
docs.text:
← Back to README

macos-app/ contains a native macOS app that hosts the same dashboard in its own window, with every conversation and task action routed through the autopilot controller: the app starts the dashboard server with --runner tools/autopilot.py, so messages, answers, approvals, feedback, continue actions, and the status/intervention/registry reads all execute as python tools/autopilot.py …. Project-free planning conversations still talk directly to OpenCode, and attaching one to a project launches through autopilot.

cd macos-app && ./build-app.sh   # builds dist/Autopilot.app (needs Xcode CLT)
open dist/Autopilot.app

The server binds to a free loopback port, and quitting the app stops only the dashboard server; runner processes are independent and keep their saved state. See the macOS app readme for details.

See also: Browser dashboard

docs.title: Models, roles, and escalation
docs.text: ← Back to README

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Every stage of a run has a role. Role names describe responsibilities, not mandatory models — each role can select any provider/model from opencode models (or a Codex-compatible provider):

Role Job Requirements Read-only requirements handoff, no task DAG Planner Draft the task DAG and evidence-backed revision Plan Reviewer Challenge the draft; owns final planning decisions Builder Implement one bounded task Tester Independent validation, separate session Completion Reviewer Complete/rework decision, separate session

Model overrides use the role names: --requirements-model, --glm-model, --plan-reviewer-model, --astra-model, --terra-model, --sol-model, --completion-model, --resolver-model, and the matching --<role>-reasoning-effort flags. --utility-model is a cheaper route for the stages that only classify or reformat (the utility route). See CLI. When constructing a new Requirements route from provider defaults, an explicit --requirements-model wins; otherwise --glm-model supplies its initial model. Changing the Planner on resume keeps the saved Requirements model. Its reasoning effort remains a separate selection.

Conversation handoffs apply their independent profile after this initial configuration: --glm-model selects the profile's Planner while Requirements keeps its profile default unless --requirements-model selects it explicitly.

Accounts that expose only one usable model can start a run with --single-model MODEL. This assigns that model to every role, including the Planner, Builder, Tester and review roles, while shared or role-specific reasoning flags still apply. It explicitly relaxes cross-model verification; the review stages remain separate sessions and gates, but they are not independent model-family checks. --single-model implies joint planning and cannot be combined with per-role model flags.

docs.title: Default models
docs.text:
New OpenCode runs (the default engine) use these routes through the configured provider connections. The cheaper model does the volume and the more expensive one judges it: GLM plans and builds, GPT-6 Sol reviews the plan and checks the build. A verifier never shares its producer's model family by default. GPT-6 Astra is the Resolver's default; explicit choices may use it in other roles. The --single-model exception is described above.

Role Default model Reasoning Escalation ladder Requirements zai-coding-plan/glm-5.3 medium None Planner zai-coding-plan/glm-5.3 high None Plan Reviewer openai/gpt-6-sol high None Builder zai-coding-plan/glm-5.3 medium None; a stuck Builder gets one GPT-6 Sol XHigh attempt (retry policy) Tester openai/gpt-6-sol high Sol High → XHigh → Max Completion Reviewer openai/gpt-6-sol medium Sol Medium → High → Max Resolver (--resolver-model) openai/gpt-6-astra high Astra High → XHigh → Max

A role escalates only while its exact model and reasoning level are on its ladder. The ladders live in one place (tools/autocode_route_ladder.py, shared with the Builder retry policy), and one function there, next_route, decides each climb: the next rung, or why the role stays where it is (a pinned or custom-provider route, a route on no rung, the last rung, or a climb already made for the same failed iteration). A new run persists the ladders under route_ladders in its settings, with rungs removed that its provider does not offer: the provider's published list, and the model list a new run reads for its routes before its first model call (Builder retry policy covers the stronger attempt). Each escalation, and each ordinary Builder retry, later records how its struggle ended, and autocode --status counts those stamps as escalation_outcomes. The runner stamps every one still open passed when the run completes on work a validation passed, or when the Completion Reviewer or Resolver assigns the next task while the last validation passed, and paused at the Builder's retry-limit pause. At that assignment it leaves the Builder's own open when the work was sent back since that validation, by a retry-policy charge or a correction task (the work failed, and a stronger attempt the charge just made has not run yet), or when the run's records do not say when that validation's attempt started, so a send-back cannot be ruled out. autocode --status also lists each escalation as a row of escalations (a climb, or the Builder's stronger attempt): the job and stage it was for, the route it climbed from and to, what its escalated attempts cost, and whether the work then passed, failed again, paused or is still running, with one line each on stderr (status view). The row judges each escalation by its own work, so read a row's outcome for how one escalation ended; when its struggle has ended, its stamp agrees. A stamp is the struggle's, though: a climb a later climb replaced takes the struggle's end too while its row reads failed_again, and so does an ordinary retry, which has no row. Before the struggle ends the stamp is open while the row may already read passed; completing the run or accepting completion via --accept-completion stamps open entries passed. The default GLM Builder, any GLM Tester or Completion Reviewer, and the Plan Reviewer are on no ladder: they keep their configured route, and a verifier that keeps struggling pauses the run instead. The Builder instead gets its retry policy's one stronger attempt. If you configure the Builder on openai/gpt-6-sol (with GLM checkers), it climbs Sol Medium → High → XHigh → Max. No role other than the Resolver escalates onto GPT-6 Astra.

The Planner has one stronger attempt of its own (autocode_planner_escalation, owner decision 2026-10-23). In an adaptive run, when the Plan Reviewer's second challenge in a planning cycle still has a blocking concern about the revised plan, the next revision runs on Claude Opus 5.5 High, or on GPT-6 Sol High when the Plan Reviewer is a Claude model. Only a blocking concern counts: schema errors, silences and output caps go through report repair and recovery as before. A target is used only when the run's provider serves it, the saved accounts permit it, it is a different model from the Planner's and it is outside the Plan Reviewer's family; otherwise the Planner stays. The climb is a reasoning_escalations row with trigger plan_sent_back, the Planner's session is rotated, and the route stays climbed for the rest of the run, so a run climbs at most once. A second challenge runs only when the review allowance leaves room for it (a large plan, plan_review_call_limit of 3 or more, or 0, in ~/.config/autocode/config.toml): under the default allowance of two calls the first revision goes straight to the final review and the Planner never climbs. If the stronger revision is still blocked, the final review returns the open concerns to you as blocking questions.

Two scripted scenarios check these rows end to end, through autocode --status --json (catalog). In escalation-converts the Builder's stronger attempt fixes what its ordinary attempts could not: one row, from the Builder's route to GPT-6 Sol XHigh, one attempt with its cost, passed, and the run completes; escalation_outcomes stamps that attempt and the ordinary retry before it passed too. In escalation-ladder-end that attempt fails too: the row reads paused, as both stamps do, and the run pauses at PAUSED_BUILDER_RETRY_LIMIT with the stuck-stage Investigator's diagnosis in its stop reason. scenarios/test_escalation.py also checks that a --builder-strong-model the tool does not list refuses the new run before any model call.

The Resolver runs on a route of its own, resolver. It starts as a copy of the astra route, which the per-task Planner (astra_plan) runs on; autocode models lists that route as "Resolver and per-task Planner (--astra-model)". The Resolver's route is created the first time a Resolver stage runs, or by --resolver-model. Which flag sets it:

  • On an OpenCode-engine run (the default), --resolver-model and --resolver-reasoning-effort set the Resolver's route alone. --astra-model and --astra-reasoning-effort set the per-task Planner's route, and reach the Resolver only while its route has not been created yet.
  • A Codex-engine run (--engine codex), and a saved run without joint planning, ignore --resolver-model and --resolver-reasoning-effort: the Resolver starts from the astra route that --astra-model and --astra-reasoning-effort set.

Only the Resolver's route climbs the Astra ladder. The per-task Planner keeps its configured effort however often its reports are rejected, so a Resolver route copied from the astra route later starts at the configured effort, not a climbed one. A run saved before this was fixed kept the Astra ladder under astra in route_ladders; it is read as the Resolver's ladder, and the saved state is not rewritten. A climb is not a settings change for the recovery packet the Resolver works from: the climbed attempt is held or admitted by that packet's causal-progress check, as the attempt before it was.

The one-stage jobs use the Plan Reviewer's model on a route of their own: the Investigator (bug fixes), the Analyst (discuss) and the Designer (design reviews), the last two with effort capped at medium. A run without a Plan Reviewer route falls back to the Resolver's. The Code Reviewer (code review) runs on the Tester's route.

Other engines keep their own defaults, set where each engine is configured:

Engine or provider Defaults --engine codex gpt-5.6-terra for the Builder; gpt-5.6-sol for the Resolver, Tester and Completion Reviewer (DEFAULT_ROLE_MODELS in tools/autocode_configure.py); with --joint-planning, Requirements and the Planner take the Resolver's model and a new Plan Reviewer takes gpt-6-astra, or gpt-5.6-sol when the Planner runs gpt-6-astra (CODEX_PLAN_REVIEWER_MODELS) --engine claude (or --provider claude) claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 for the Builder; claude-sonnet-5-5 for Requirements, the Planner and the Tester; claude-opus-5-5 for the Plan Reviewer, the Resolver and the Completion Reviewer; every role at medium (tools/providers/claude.py, Claude Code provider) --provider kilocode openai/gpt-5.6-terra for the Builder, zai-coding-plan/glm-5.3 for the Planner, openai/gpt-5.6-sol for every other role (tools/providers/configs/kilocode.toml) a user-level provider whatever its ~/.config/autocode/providers/<name>.toml [roles] specify Dashboard Codex console gpt-5.6-* defaults; any valid bare Codex model name can be selected, with configured GLM routes using Z.ai

Autocode advances exactly one rung after durable evidence that the current role struggled: an invalid completed response after report repair is exhausted, an operator-abandoned uncertain response, a Builder batch with no source progress, or failed validation routed back for implementation or revalidation. The next request uses the stronger rung and a fresh role session. Autocode does not silently replay the failed request, advances at most once for the same failed iteration, and never overwrites an explicit custom model/provider route. Under a money cap that request is priced before it launches, from the role's last attempt's tokens at the climbed route's rate; when that projection would take the spend past the cap, the run pauses PAUSED_COST_LIMIT, naming the rung and the arithmetic, instead of launching it. Under an active-time budget you set it is timed the same way, from the role's last attempt's duration, and pauses PAUSED_TIME_LIMIT instead. A Builder climb is also timed against a milestone budget you set, and pauses PAUSED_MILESTONE_BUDGET when it would take the milestone past that budget.

Note on role names. The CLI flags keep the older tier names — --astra-model (the per-task Planner, and the route the Resolver starts from; see above), --terra-model (Builder), --sol-model (Tester) — because those names are in saved run state. They are not model choices: --terra-model zai-coding-plan/glm-5.3 selects the model used for the Builder role.

docs.title: Choosing each stage's model
docs.text:
You choose the model and reasoning level of each stage once, and every new task uses them (owner decision 2026-10-30). autocode setup offers this right after connecting your accounts; autocode stages choose asks again whenever you want to change them, and autocode stages lists what each stage runs now. For each stage it says what the stage does, gives advice on what suits it, and lists the models your backend offers with the reasoning levels each model takes:

Stage What it does What suits it Requirements Turns your idea into requirements; asks you only about real ambiguity A capable all-round model at medium Planner Drafts the plan and revises it after review A capable model at high Plan Reviewer Challenges the plan and makes the final planning call; its model also runs the Investigator, the Analyst, the Designer and the Design Reviewer Your strongest judge at high, never the Planner's model Builder Writes the code for one task; several run in parallel A fast, cheaper model at medium Tester Checks each Builder's work and proves its tests fail without the change; its model also writes the acceptance tests and runs the Code Reviewer A strong model at high, never the Builder's Completion Reviewer Decides whether the task is done or goes back for more work A strong judge at medium, never the Builder's model Resolver and per-task Planner Steps in when a stage stops progressing; plans each task's steps Your strongest model at high

The workflow jobs have no list of their own: each starts from the stage that names it. The Investigator of a bug fix takes the Plan Reviewer's model and level; the Analyst, the Designer and the Design Reviewer take its model at a capped level; the acceptance tests and the Code Reviewer run on the Tester's. A Plan Reviewer level you did not choose runs one rung lower on a small, clear task (adaptive planning); a level you chose is kept.

The models come from your backend: for OpenCode and Kilo, the models your connected accounts serve, with the reasoning levels and family their own listing declares (a model that cannot call tools is left out); for Claude Code, Haiku, Sonnet and Opus; for Codex, the GPT models AutoCode runs on it. A configured command provider without declared account routes offers the models in its own configured list; AutoCode leaves account and billing details unknown, and the provider checks the selected model again before launch. A model the stage's checker or producer already runs is shown as not available, with the reason, because a checker never grades its own model's work (independence); on Claude Code and Codex two different models of that vendor may check each other. No price is read.

The choices are kept in ~/.config/autocode/stages.toml, one table per backend, so switching backends uses that backend's own choices. Each new task reads them before it begins, as if you had typed that stage's --ROLE-model and --ROLE-reasoning-effort flags, and prints Stage choices from … naming the stages it took. A flag on the command line and the project's own .autocode/config.toml still win for that run; --single-model takes no saved choice, and a shared --reasoning-effort keeps the saved levels out. A task already running keeps the routes it started with. A stage you have not chosen keeps its default, or the route automatic selection picks for it (below). autocode stages set STAGE --model MODEL --effort LEVEL and autocode stages reset [STAGE] change one stage without asking.

docs.title: Choosing models automatically
docs.text:
New CLI and TaskRun.start runs choose models automatically from the selected tool's connected accounts for every stage you have not chosen yourself. No model flags or pinned profile are needed. One tool serves the run by default; explicit per-role tool bindings and model/effort flags still win. A fully pinned profile keeps its existing preflight and recovery policy because there is no automatic choice to make. --single-model keeps its explicit same-model policy. Saved runs retain their routes and permitted alternatives without discovering new accounts.

Use --no-auto-select to retain fixed defaults. If discovery is unavailable or cannot field independent checkers, the default launch prints the reason and tries the fixed routes under the normal catalogue, billing and independence guards. Explicit --auto-select instead refuses before spending. Preview the choices and exclusions with autocode models --selection --provider NAME; this reads local listings only.

Selection also needs the installed OpenCode version to have a row in the conformance matrix whose result allows ordinary runs (known-good or accepted-for-ordinary-runs, #2060). On any other version the default launch prints why and uses the fixed routes, and --auto-select refuses. autocode doctor shows the installed version's row; a new version qualifies once tools/provider_conformance.py has passed on it and its row is added.

OpenCode and Kilo reasoning variants come from their local verbose model listings. An unsupported qualified level is omitted so the model uses its default. When older tools cannot report variants, the recorded qualification level is used. Preflight proves each distinct model/effort on its actual tool within the run's time/cost cap; receipts survive resume. Recovery checks independence against the current saved routes, including explicit assignments and catalogue substitutions. It stays within the saved connected accounts, and exhaustion asks for intervention. A model a flag pinned (--terra-model, and the other per-role flags) is never switched on its own: its stop asks, as before automatic selection. A stuck-run Investigator reuses an independent saved reviewer route and its supported level; it cannot silently use a fixed paid-gateway default. Explicit --investigator-model remains an override. A newly connected account is never silently added.

The rules the choice keeps:

  • A minimum standard per role. A model is only ever chosen for a role when the dated qualification table (tools/autocode_route_qualification.json) lists it for that role, with the evidence that admitted it: AutoCode's own runs qualify a model, and a public benchmark admits it only provisionally until such a run confirms it. The table changes by pull request, like the price table it is priced from. A model not in the table is never chosen automatically, however cheap. After a live run proves a route, tools/qualify_routes.py --run-dir RUN --scenario NAME --profile PROFILE merges that run into the table, refusing anything that did not declare --evidence-provenance live and finish TASK_COMPLETE; it launches no model. Each merge also appends a runs record to the entry: the date, run, scenario and profile, the role's accepted attempts on that route, and their minutes and cost (null when an attempt did not record one). autocode models --selection shows each listed entry's evidence, such as provisional: no AutoCode run yet or the number/date of recorded runs (#2059). Historical minutes, cost_usd and attempts cover only accepted attempts on that role/model; their display labels the scope, excluded failed/repair amounts and known-run denominator. New records additionally carry versioned attempt_accounting for all attempts on that role/model, including rejected, timed-out, interrupted and report-only work. Duration is summed recorded active time, not task wall time. Provider-reported and historical-estimated amounts stay separate, with known subtotals and coverage; missing/uncertain usage is not zero. Native shared receipts retain the existing accounting attribution. New attempts also freeze bounded execution_identity at launch: role slot, engine/tool, exact model, effective effort and runner commit when known. Public accounting carries those facts; qualification records group them under execution_evidence with known/unknown attempt counts. They are not reconstructed from later settings. Billing classification is recorded only for the exact saved selected model/tool, with its basis; a permitted account pool is not proof of the account charged. Direct connections record configured endpoint origin, protocol, provider key slot and SHA-256, keeping tenant paths and credentials out of public evidence. Other backends' endpoints remain unknown when not recorded. Blank/null effort preserves the provider-default convention; a modified or unknown runner commit is not a complete code-byte fingerprint. These records do not establish cross-endpoint compatibility, an external benchmark verdict or comparative merit. Legacy and all-attempt cohorts are not pooled. None of these role measurements is a whole-task cost per accepted fix, an invoice or new comparative qualification. Rejected/repair-only attempts still do not qualify a route, and no historical record is silently backfilled. Provisional entries stay selectable (owner decision, 2026-10-26) until benchmark runs have filled these records.
  • Within a role's qualified models, the cheapest route wins. A subscription route counts as cheaper than any pay-per-token one, then the price-table cost orders them, and a route whose access is already proven beats one that would need a probe. The checkers are never downgraded to save money: they start on their cheapest qualified model, and only a failure ever moves a role up. A role whose table entries carry a preference is ordered by it first: the Plan Reviewer is GPT-6 Sol when the ChatGPT login is connected, then Claude Opus, and MiMo is not used for review (owner decision, 2026-10-20: MiMo spent 32-45k reasoning tokens and up to 15 minutes per plan review). With neither connected, the run stops before any work and offers those two logins. A model the table marks excluded for a role is never chosen for it, even when a profile pinned it and a live run completed on it; tools/qualify_routes.py names the exclusion instead of adding an entry, so the Plan Reviewer's MiMo v2.6 Pro exclusion is that record. The Builder likewise prefers GPT-6 Luna at medium effort (owner decision, 2026-10-21), then GPT-6 Sol, then MiMo v2.6 Flash, then Claude Opus, then the cheapest of GLM 5.3, MiMo v2.6 Pro and DeepSeek (owner decision, 2026-10-20: on ladder-07 a Luna Builder took 36-66 s and a Sol Builder 66 s against MiMo v2.6 Pro's 404-474 s, and the whole task 16-35 min against 34-46 min). A small task's first Builder attempt still runs at low effort (autocode_light_builder). Because a checker never grades its own family, an OpenAI Builder is checked by GLM as Tester and Completion Reviewer; when only GPT models could check an OpenAI build, MiMo Flash builds instead. The Completion Reviewer prefers GPT-6 Sol only when no GPT model built. Requirements, Planner and Tester stay on the cheapest qualified models.
  • Independence is never lowered quietly. Every producer and checker pair stays on different model families (tools/autocode_verifier_independence.py); when the connected accounts cannot provide that, the run stops before any work and says what is missing in account terms ("connect a second model family"), never by suggesting --single-model. GLM, MiMo, Claude and OpenAI's GPT models are each one family, so no Claude model checks another Claude model's work, and no GPT model another GPT model's (Luna's build is never tested by Sol), on Kilo, OpenCode or a custom provider (owner decision, 2026-10-20). The built-in Claude Code and Codex engines reach only their own vendor's models, so there different models of that vendor check each other (for example Sonnet's work is reviewed by Opus); a model never checks itself.
  • No invented reasoning levels. A route gets a reasoning level only when the model advertises it; otherwise the model uses its own default.
  • Explicit choices win. --<role>-model, --provider, --role-transport and --single-model constrain or replace the automatic choice, and saved runs keep the routes they were started with.

The choice is one deterministic function from the discovered candidates and the accounts you allow to one route per role, or a stop that names what is missing. Each chosen route is recorded with its origin (auto_selected) in the route record the status view shows. autocode models --selection shows the whole reasoning: the logins the tool reports, the route chosen for each role with its cost, and why every other qualified model lost (not connected on any login, a preferred or cheaper qualified route won, or it would check its own family's work).

Before the first stage, the model-access preflight probes exactly the chosen routes that are still unproven, one tiny call each at the role's own reasoning level, within the run's cost cap — including built-in OpenCode routes, which saved-run probes never touched. On OpenCode and Kilo a probe runs as a bare agent with no tools and a one-line system prompt, a few hundred input tokens instead of the coding agent's ~18k. The Resolver's own model (usually GPT-6 Astra) is probed only before the first stage that runs it, since most runs never need a Resolver (#1744).

docs.title: Builder retry policy
docs.text:
New standard-workflow runs use a persisted Builder retry policy per approved milestone: the configured Builder gets one ordinary retry, then one stronger attempt (default openai/gpt-6-sol at xhigh reasoning, not Astra), then a safety pause. Set --builder-strong-model MODEL when creating a run to select a different model. A --single-model run keeps the stronger attempt and its checkers on the selected model, changing reasoning effort rather than changing the model. A tool registered with a TOML file can name its own stronger model, and the model its checkers move to, in a [builder_retry] table (Providers); --builder-strong-model still wins. The built-in claude provider declares Sonnet for a Haiku Builder, with Opus checking that attempt. When the run's provider config lists its models (models = [...]) and the strong model is not among them, the run gets no stronger attempt: the Builder gets one more ordinary retry in its place, then pauses, and --builder-strong-model (or [builder_retry]) must name one of the listed models. A new run whose provider lists its models (autocode models: OpenCode, the claude provider, or a tool with models or models_command) checks the stronger attempt against that list, the one it reads for its routes, before any model call. The attempt needs the strong model and, when a Tester or Completion Reviewer the attempt would move (see below: not pinned, not on a custom provider) runs that model or its GLM or MiMo family, the checker model it moves to. When the list lacks either, the run has no stronger attempt: the Builder gets one more ordinary retry in its place, then pauses with a stop reason that names the missing model (saved as not_offered in the run's builder_retry settings). A --builder-strong-model that needs a model the list lacks refuses the new run instead, so the gap shows at creation rather than as a failed launch partway through the run. A pinned or custom-provider Builder never makes the stronger attempt, so its policy is left as it is. A Builder failure whose cause the runner cannot tell from its evidence goes to the Investigator to be classified before this policy charges it. A milestone may have as many failures classified as this policy takes (its ordinary retries, the stronger attempt or the retry in its place, the failure it pauses on, and each failure that did not count, see below), so classifying never stops a milestone before the policy would; the next milestone, or a later turn's new plan, starts its own. Classifications do not count toward the run's three stuck-stage investigations (Workflow), and turning those off (max_calls_per_run = 0) turns classification off too: such a failure pauses as PAUSED_BUILDER_CLASSIFICATION. Under a money cap the stronger attempt is priced before it launches, from the last Builder attempt's tokens at the stronger model's rate; when that projection would take the spend past the cap, the run pauses PAUSED_COST_LIMIT with the arithmetic instead of launching it.
