Under an active-time budget you set it is timed from the last Builder attempt's duration, and pauses PAUSED_TIME_LIMIT when it would take the run past that budget, or PAUSED_MILESTONE_BUDGET when it would take the milestone past a milestone budget you set. Explicit model pins and custom providers are never overridden. Existing saved runs without this policy retain their previous routing. Restarting/resuming cannot reset an exhausted budget. Scope violations, approval requests and transport safety pauses are not automatically retried by this policy.

Each charged failure is checked against the milestone's earlier ones (its evidence ledger, tools/autocode_evidence_ledger.py). A failure's items are the checks that exited nonzero, the criteria not met and the open blocking findings in the latest validation and review; its signature is those items with the files the Builder changed.

  • A repeat, a failure with the signature of an earlier one, has no new evidence, so it skips the remaining ordinary retries. It goes straight to the stronger attempt, or pauses once that is spent or the run has none. The stop reason then says the last failure repeated an earlier one.
  • Progress, a failure whose earlier failing items are all resolved (each check exits 0, each criterion passes, each finding is closed) and that fails only on new items, does not count toward the limit. The Builder retries on the route it has now, and a pause stays a pause. A run that keeps finding new problems is still bounded by its milestone time budget, the stalled-review limit, the iteration limit and any money cap.
  • Anything else, including a failure with no failing items, counts as before.

Each decision in builder_retry_decisions records which of these it was as novelty (new, repeat or progress). A failure saved before the ledger existed has no signature, so the next failure cannot count as progress.

The stronger attempt must not be checked by its own model. The rule is the cross-model guard's (tools/autocode_verifier_independence.py), so its families count: when the Tester or Completion Reviewer runs the stronger model, or another model of its GLM or MiMo family, it moves to the policy's checker model (zai-coding-plan/glm-5.3 by default, or checker_model under [builder_retry]) for the rest of that milestone (keeping its effort, or high for a climbed xhigh/max) and returns to its route at the next milestone. The decision records the switch as checker_models. Runs saved before this switch existed use the default checker model. Pinned and custom-provider checkers are never moved; the cross-model guard pauses the run instead. A new run refuses a --builder-strong-model that is the checker model or shares its family, since the moved checkers would then check their own model's work. On a tool whose Builder model has no provider/ prefix (the built-in claude provider), a Tester or Completion Reviewer moves only when the cross-model guard would refuse it (it runs the strong model in the tool's spelling, or another model of its GLM or MiMo family) and the checker model is one the run already routes a role to; one that may only spell the strong model another way (openai/X for X) cannot move. When one cannot move, the run pauses (PAUSED_BUILDER_RETRY_LIMIT) before any route changes, and the stop reason says why. provider/model names, as KiloCode uses, keep the rule above.

A parallel Builder cannot move the checkers that will check its batch. When its stronger attempt would run on the checkers' model, it stops with SERIAL_ESCALATION instead (decision defer) and leaves that attempt to the run. The run integrates the Builders that finished, and the unchanged checkers validate them. The deferred milestone is never run in parallel again. When it is next assigned, the run makes the stronger attempt itself, serially, with the checker switch above and without a human. The retry budget carries over from the Builder, so this is still the milestone's last attempt before the safety pause. If every Builder in a batch defers, nothing is integrated and the run starts on the first of them straight away. A Builder route pinned while the milestone waited is not overridden; the run pauses instead.

An implementation attempt with no source changes is no progress, not a build candidate. The dashboard's named milestone checkpoints distinguish recorded implementation/tool activity from independent verification; tool completions alone never verify criteria.

docs.title: Explicit model selection
docs.text:
Explicit provider/model choices use OpenCode for every role. For example:

autocode "Your rough idea" \
  --glm-model openai/gpt-5.6-sol \
  --astra-model zai-coding-plan/glm-5.3 \
  --terra-model openai/gpt-5.6-terra \
  --sol-model openai/gpt-6-astra

This overrides four routes through OpenCode; the Completion Reviewer keeps its default. No Codex login is required for the default workflow. Bare model names for the legacy astra and sol CLI roles are expanded to openai/model on OpenCode. Explicit legacy --engine codex runs retain their separate Codex routing.

AutoCode accepts every well-formed model route listed by the configured provider, including mimo-token-plan/, free, Flash, highspeed and newly listed models. Model defaults and tier labels guide selection; they are not allowlists. Explicit conversation handoff choices retain their model and reasoning effort. Visual review also accepts an explicit model instead of requiring Astra.

Before launching an OpenAI role, AutoCode accepts either OAuth or API authentication reported by opencode auth list, or explicit API environment configuration. Missing or ambiguous authentication pauses without choosing another connection. Other providers retain their configured connections. No credentials are copied. Actual model entitlement is managed by the provider CLI; a listed model can still fail at request time. Producers and their reviewers must keep independent routes.

The dashboard shows the live opencode models catalogue in all four pickers, grouped by provider, plus explicit reasoning selectors for the Plan Reviewer, Builder, Tester, and Completion Reviewer. Each unchanged default route is labeled explicitly.

Resuming keeps the saved engine, models and separate role sessions. Start a new run when switching between Codex and OpenCode; their session IDs cannot be reused across engines. Saved runs retain their original role engines and sessions; no existing run is migrated by a dashboard selection.

docs.title: The utility route
docs.text:
Some calls in a run only classify or reformat and need no frontier model. --utility-model MODEL (new runs only) sends those stages to a cheaper model:

autocode "Your rough idea" --utility-model ollama/qwen3:8b

The stages it serves are listed in one place, UTILITY_STAGES in tools/autocode_roles.py. Today that is the Job recognizer (recognize_workflow), which picks one of the five workflows on a flow without a Requirements stage; elsewhere Requirements names the job (#1860). The route copies the Plan Reviewer's engine, provider and reasoning effort and replaces only the model (--utility-reasoning-effort sets its own effort). A run started without the flag saves no utility route, so every stage keeps the route it had before. The flag is refused on a saved run.

A stage that writes code or judges evidence is never put on the utility route: the Planner, Builder, Plan Reviewer, Tester, Completion Reviewer, Resolver, Designer, Design and Code Reviewers, and the Investigator. A weak utility model can therefore misroute a request (the console line after recognition names the workflow and how to override it with --workflow) but cannot produce or accept work. Builder-failure classification stays on the Investigator because it judges the failure's evidence, and report-only repair keeps the route of the stage whose report it repairs.

A local model runs through OpenCode's local providers (for example Ollama or LM Studio, configured in OpenCode): name it as provider/model the way opencode models lists it, and the launch checks it is listed like any other route. No local model has yet been qualified on the utility route; run the conformance probe for your provider/model before relying on one, and record a reliability sweep before changing the default.

docs.title: When a model is not in your plans
docs.text:
A new run first asks its provider which models your plans offer (opencode models). If a role's model is not listed, the run stops before any model call and shows:

  • every model your plans offer, grouped by plan, each marked subscription or pay per token and with its tier: cheap worker (plans and builds), strong judge (checks) or Resolver tier. A model AutoCode has no tier for says "tier unknown"; MiMo token-plan, free and Flash routes are included.
  • a replacement for each missing role. It prefers a subscription over per-token billing, then the tier the role wants, and never shares a model (or GLM family) with the role it checks or is checked by. Any listed model can be offered, including GPT-6 Astra for other roles and OpenAI routes authenticated with an API key.
  • the flags to start the run with, for example --sol-model openai/gpt-6-luna.

In --chat, you can accept all the replacements and the run continues with them, as if you had passed the flags. AutoCode never changes a model without you. A saved run is not re-routed this way: resuming keeps its models, so start a new run instead.

autocode models shows the same list at any time and checks every role's default route; see CLI. autocode models --prices shows what each model's tokens cost instead: the dated price table tools/autocode_prices.json (updated by pull request) and the rate each default route is priced at, or "no rate" for a model without a row, whose cost is then unknown rather than zero. The money cap (--max-cost-usd, Money cap) counts spend at these rates.

docs.title: Reasoning effort
docs.text:
A role runs at one reasoning effort, chosen from the variants its model declares. Kilo and OpenCode report those variants in their local model listings; when a tool reports none, AutoCode records the effort as unverified and the tool's own check decides. The flags are --reasoning-effort LEVEL for every role and --<role>-reasoning-effort LEVEL for one (--glm-reasoning-effort, --astra-reasoning-effort, --terra-reasoning-effort, --sol-reasoning-effort, and the matching flag for the other jobs).

An effort AutoCode derives itself — a reduced Builder tier, a climb on the effort ladder, a single-model run — moves to the nearest declared variant and records the move as effort_fits. An effort a person named never moves. When the model does not declare it, the run pauses as PAUSED_EFFORT_UNSUPPORTED before the stage launches, naming the model, the level you chose and the levels it does declare. Answer with one of those and continue:

autocode --answer effort-glm=high
autocode --resume-paused

The status view's needs carries the same question as needs.effort (question_id effort-ROLE, role, job, model, requested, declared, nearest), and --answer records the level you name as your own choice. A level the model does not declare is refused with nothing saved. See KiloCode.

docs.title: When a role's quota runs out
docs.text:
A provider that reports a used-up quota, usage limit or credits stops the stage with PAUSED_BUDGET, and so does a used-up daily, weekly or monthly plan limit sent as an HTTP 429 (Z.AI's "Weekly/Monthly Limit Exhausted"); a per-minute rate limit does not. The stopped attempt is kept and never replayed. Unless the run can switch the role on its own (see the end of this section), AutoCode asks you which model the role should continue on, for example:

[route-sol] Tester's quota is exhausted; name the model to continue on

The question names the job on screen (Tester, Builder, Completion Reviewer, …). It has no proposed default, is never delegable (--delegate-all refuses it) and the scenario driver never answers it for you. Answer it with a model:

autocode --run-dir RUN --answer route-sol=gpt-6-luna --resolver-token TOKEN
autocode --run-dir RUN --resume-paused

The answer sets the stopped attempt aside exactly as --abandon-stage does (partial work and evidence retained, the role's session dropped), saves the model on the role, and records the change. --resume-paused then runs the role again on a fresh session with the new model. The same thing without answering the question: --abandon-stage ATTEMPT, then --resume-paused --sol-model gpt-6-luna (or both in one invocation). --sol-model alone is refused while the stopped attempt is still uncertain. Setting the attempt aside never raises the role's reasoning effort: a quota stop is not a sign the model struggled.

A model is refused, and the run stays paused with the question open, when a launch would refuse it:

  • it is for a different engine: a Codex run takes a bare name (gpt-6-luna), an OpenCode run a provider/model (openai/gpt-6-luna); sessions never move between engines;
  • OpenCode does not list it (opencode models);
  • it breaks the cross-model rule: a checker never shares its producer's model, or its GLM or MiMo family (Builder/Tester, Builder/Completion Reviewer, Planner/Plan Reviewer);
  • it is the model that just ran out (or was refused, below).

Every change, through the answer or the resume flag, is appended to the run's user_events as a route_assignment (role, job, from, to, engine, stage, attempt, events path, time, via answer or resume_flag). A resume flag the launch refuses (another engine's format, a cross-model clash) is not recorded. The status view shows each role's current route under routes — its model, engine, the job it runs, the reasoning_effort a launch passes (null for the model's own default), the provider tool that launches it, the account its model bills (null when the engine's own login decides) and the origin, why the route is what it is — and the changes under route_assignments; while the question is open, needs.route names the role and its current model. The new model stays on the role until you change it again, including past the next milestone.

A run that chose its models automatically (Choosing models automatically) first switches the role on its own. It takes the next qualified model on an account the run already uses, keeps every checker independent of its producer, and prints a line such as Builder: MODEL stopped (PAUSED_BUDGET); switched to NEW_MODEL on ACCOUNT without asking. The switch sets the stopped attempt aside the same way an answer does, is recorded as a route_assignment whose actor is runner, and counts as an automatic recovery. When the new model bills another way than the stopped one (a subscription route replaced by a pay-per-token one, by the billing discovery recorded), the record carries billing: {from, to}, which the status view's route_assignments shows, and the line ends ; it bills pay per token where MODEL was subscription (#2061). AutoCode asks instead when no such model remains, when you pinned the role's model with a flag, when a pause was requested, and for native runs and workflow jobs. The same switch applies to content-filter and output-limit stops.

A run on fixed routes (--no-auto-select, or a launch whose automatic selection fell back to them) has no fallback list or configuration table: its quota stop is always your decision. Capacity errors retry the same model, rate limits pause as before, and authentication failures never ask for a model.

docs.title: When the stopped role is a workflow job
docs.text:
A workflow job (the Code Reviewer, Designer, Design Reviewer, Analyst, bug-fix Investigator or Design inventory) that stops on quota pauses differently: its attempt is set aside at once and the job takes one exact retry, bound to the run's configuration (PAUSED_JOB_FAILURE, needs.kind retry_job; see CLI). The stop names the job, the model and the provider's words, and the status view's needs.route carries the same model question. You answer it with the job's retry token instead of a resolver token, then retry with the new token it issues:

autocode --run-dir RUN --answer route-sol=gpt-6-luna --job-retry-token TOKEN
autocode --run-dir RUN --resume-paused --retry-failed-stage --job-retry-token NEW_TOKEN

The answer applies the same checks and records the same route_assignment. The old token stops working, so the job never runs again on the model that stopped without your saying so. --abandon-stage and a --sol-model flag are refused at this stop (the flag would make the exact retry stale; only putting back the model the retry is bound to is saved), and so is the flag next to an --abandon-stage that sets the job's uncertain attempt aside: set it aside on its own, then answer. The answer itself changes nothing but the job's model; given with another setting it is refused and nothing is saved, and so is the answer next to the retry (--resume-paused --retry-failed-stage), since the retry needs the new token. Once you have named a model, the status line and recovery card ask only for the retry on it. The Architect (Designer, Design Reviewer), Analyst and Investigator routes have no flag at all: the answer is the only way to move them. After a quota stop the shown token also retries the job unchanged, once the quota resets. The stuck-stage Investigator (investigate_stuck) is the exception: its route is rebuilt for every investigation, so its stop keeps only the exact retry (--investigator-model pins the model of the next investigation).

docs.title: When a provider's content filter refuses a response
docs.text:
A provider whose content filter refuses a stage's response (OpenCode's ContentFilterError, a content_filter error code, or an OpenCode or Kilo stream whose last step finished with reason content-filter) stops the stage with PAUSED_CONTENT_FILTER, whether the provider exited with an error or exited 0. The stop names the job, the refused model and the provider's words:

Builder: the provider's content filter refused the response on xiaomi-token-plan-sgp/mimo-v2.6-pro (ContentFilterError: The response was blocked by the provider's content filter); the same model is likely to refuse it again.

The same model is likely to refuse the same request again, so the attempt is kept and never replayed. AutoCode handles it as a quota stop: a run that chose its models automatically switches on its own where it can (above); otherwise it asks the question a quota stop asks, answered the same way:

[route-terra] Builder's model was refused by its provider's content filter; name another model to continue on

The question also lists the run's other configured models, from other providers, that would pass the launch rules above, or says that none does (in the GLM/MiMo profile the only other model is the Tester's GLM, which the cross-model rule refuses for the Builder). The list is advice, never a default. Setting the attempt aside never raises the role's reasoning effort, and the route_assignment records PAUSED_CONTENT_FILTER as its pause_status. Only the provider's error event or a final content-filter finish reason classifies the stop: the model's own text ("The request was rejected ...") never does. When no error event follows the finish, the provider's words in the stop are content_filter: OpenCode's last step finished with reason content-filter.

A refusal in a response the provider returned with exit 0 from a session the run did not expect, or one that names no session, stays PAUSED_UNCERTAIN_STAGE ("Provider returned a missing or unexpected session ID") and asks no model question. --resume-paused keeps it uncertain ("Recovered response belongs to an unexpected session"), and so does a resume after AutoCode stopped before it saved the provider's exit or interrupted it. A workflow job stopped this way names the session, not a refusal. Only a provider that exited with an error has such a refusal typed, as at its first stop. A stage that timed out stays PAUSED_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT on resume, from any session, as at its first stop, and the automatic timeout recovery may set it aside. --answer route-ROLE=MODEL is accepted only where the request asks it, so while such a stop is open (or one a run paused on before a finish-only refusal was typed), the role's model flag alone (--terra-model) is refused and names only the other route: --abandon-stage ATTEMPT, then --resume-paused --terra-model MODEL.

A refused workflow job pauses for its exact retry, as a quota stop of a job does (above): name another model with --answer route-ROLE=MODEL --job-retry-token TOKEN, then retry with the new token. That answer refuses the model that was refused. Until you name one, the status view's needs.action is that answer and the recovery card offers no retry. The job's own retry token still replays the refused model if you retry without naming one.

docs.title: When a response reaches its output limit
docs.text: An authenticated terminal output-limit stop (PAUSED_OUTPUT_CAP) switches models on its own on a run that chose them automatically, as a quota stop does (above). Otherwise it asks for another model on the same engine with the existing availability and checker-independence rules. The answer retains the incomplete attempt and usage; continuation is explicit. Builder and Requirements never automatically retry this stop on the same model. See Output cap for cap settings and the existing bounded read-only report repair.

docs.title: A parallel Builder stopped on its model
docs.text:
A Builder in a parallel batch that stops on quota, a content-filter refusal or an authenticated output limit asks the same model question, naming its milestone:

[route-terra] Builder (milestone M1)'s model was refused by its provider's content filter; name another model to continue on

Answer it the same way, with --answer route-terra=MODEL. The answer sets that member's stopped attempt aside, runs only that milestone's Builder again on the model you name, and keeps the other Builders' results. As for a serial Builder, it also moves the run's Builder route, so later Builders (the next serial milestone, later batches) run on that model too. The answer is checked against the model that member ran on, even when another member's answer already moved the route, and it must not share that model's GLM or MiMo family. The models a refusal's question lists pass the same checks. When two members stop, AutoCode asks about them one at a time.

Changing another role's settings while a member's question is open withdraws the old request and asks that member's route-terra question again under the new settings. Use the fresh request's token to answer it.

While the question is open the status view offers no per-member retry for a member stopped on any of these causes: the question is the next step. AutoCode never reruns a member stopped by its provider's content filter or output limit on that same model: --retry-builder M1 is refused while its route is still that model, so it runs again only on the model your answer names. A member stopped on quota can still be named with --retry-builder M1, which runs the same model again (for example once its quota has reset).

A settings change beside --retry-builder is saved only when the retry is accepted. The member reruns on its own saved Builder route: a Builder model, provider or reasoning effort change beside its retry is refused with nothing saved. To change a member stopped on quota, refusal or an authenticated output limit to another model, answer its route-terra question instead. Saving a different Builder route separately also does not move the member's route. A later --retry-builder refuses the mismatch and names the member's saved settings and the run's current settings. If that member's model question is open, answer it to choose the model; the answer keeps its other frozen route settings. Otherwise restore the run's Builder settings to that member's route in a separate command, then retry it. AutoCode does not silently copy the run's route into the child.

If you answer the request with corrective information (--resolver-response provide_information) or leave it paused instead, no model is named and no question stays open. One command continues from there, and the stop reason, the status view's needs.action and the recovery card all name it: autocode --resume-paused --retry-builder M1. For a member stopped by its provider's content filter or output limit, it reads that member's saved stop again and asks its route-terra question again; nothing launches. For a member stopped on quota, it reruns the member unchanged. A plain --resume-paused stays paused there and names that command; the request itself never advises "then autocode resume" at a member's stop. Changing the Builder's route with --resume-paused --terra-model MODEL after the information moves the run's route, not the member's, so AutoResolver asks that member's question again.

See also: Providers · Workflow · CLI

docs.title: Work that spans several repositories
docs.text:
← Back to README

One AutoCode run changes one repository. Its workspace is one Git tree. The checkpoints, diffs, protected tests and the Builder's declared changes are all bounded to that tree, and a Builder write outside it is treated as a fault.

That matters when a request needs changes in more than one separately versioned repository. A ticket that adds a field to an API service and records it in a history service is two pieces of work. A run started in the API repository can deliver only the API half.

docs.title: Automatic bug fixes from terminal chat
docs.text:
This flow is part of current master and is not in the published 0.8.2 release: the pipx/Homebrew commands in the README install a tagged release without it. Install from master with the checkout installation first, and connect a backend your chat can use — including Kilo, which the default-provider guide covers with its pinned Linux release.

Configure the local source roots once. Discovery searches every configured root, even when a chat starts elsewhere. Register standalone checkouts that sit outside those roots explicitly:

autocode registry roots add /work/fulfillment
autocode registry roots add /work/shared-services
autocode registry repositories add /srv/standalone/history-consumer
autocode registry roots list

Then start plain autocode in a terminal (or autocode chat) from any directory and provide the ticket only. A clear bug identified by Requirements enters the coordinated flow without a workflow flag or separate Requirements confirmation; genuine unanswered business questions still need clarification. On a supported Linux host, use an owned chat (the default) and set up your coding backend with /connect. AutoCode investigates the configured local catalog; /repos displays roots and discovered repositories. This catalog is setup, not a repository list to add to each bug. An explicit AUTOCODE_HOME selects the same user-level catalog from any launch directory; project-local run registries remain in place. Checkouts need committed product code, a branch identifying the delivery base, a GitHub origin, Git push authentication, and gh auth login, GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN for PR creation. /repos shows authentication readiness. Before creating a worktree, AutoCode checks repository write access and that the local baseline matches the remote delivery branch. Missing checkouts must be made available before their work starts. Discovery is bounded to configured roots and standalone registrations; it does not clone remotes or search the whole disk.

The Investigator traces the symptom through code. Grounded repository names resolve against registered directory, GitHub or package names. A unique match is selected automatically; ambiguity or missing access stops for your input. Model-supplied paths and URLs do not authorize a checkout. Further discoveries join the same coordination, including A → B → C dependencies absent from the request. Every member works in an isolated, pinned worktree. Original product files remain untouched.

If the set expands after a member finishes, AutoCode reopens completed peers and shows a fresh cohort approval with the new member. Earlier approvals cannot release implementation against the expanded set.

AutoCode prepares the joint-test plan from the pinned repository baselines before any Builder starts. The chat shows every repository plan and that joint plan in one approval offer, bound to the original request and its clarifications, discovery snapshot, selected repository identities and exact plan tokens. No member or joint Builder runs before that approval. AutoCode retains the selected role routes, efforts and run limits. A configured money cap is shared across sequential launches using the core's known-cost accounting; unknown cost remains unknown. If that cap stops the run, chat shows the shared known spend and asks for a finite whole-set cap, followed by confirmation. Leaving it blank keeps the set paused. The explicit change retains all earlier spending and other limits; it does not approve a plan or waive verification. A changed checkpoint must be read again. Each member's flow gate covers its own executable local path. The joint plan names a real combined regression without putting it inside a member's completion flow. After each member passes its checks, the core exposes a named coordinate bind action that snapshots the exact candidate trees, including deletions, into the already-approved joint workspace. The integration Builder then runs that plan. Corrections discovered in the integration copies return through member follow-ups and a complete revised coordinated plan. When every revised plan keeps the contract the person approved, the coordinator carries that approval and records it; a revision that changes what was approved is shown for approval again. A failed independent check retains its diagnostics for the bounded retry. The limits are 12 repositories and three joint attempts.

Independent review and runner execution must establish fail-before/pass-after evidence. Integration copies must match the member trees exactly. Missing checks, waivers and individual PASS reports cannot authorize publication. AutoCode commits the checked files, pushes reserved branches and creates linked PRs with exact revisions and the joint evidence binding. Reopening the chat reconciles existing publications; an uncertain result never authorizes a second PR creation. PRs are not merged automatically.

/pause cancels further coordination and requests a boundary pause from active members, retaining files and existing PRs. While the coordinator is working, Ctrl-C takes that same cancellation action; the screen labels it accordingly. Individual runs use Ctrl-C for a boundary pause. The TUI consumes the public coordination contract. Once the cancellation has settled, the public resume offer can recover the saved work under an explicitly selected spending policy, including no spending cap when the person chooses zero. This does not approve plans or restart models; the existing participant gates still govern continuation.

docs.title: Manual change sets
docs.text:
• Requirements and the Investigator notice the other repository. When the request or the code they read shows that part of the work belongs elsewhere, the report says so in its workspace_scope. The runner keeps a reported part only when its quote is verbatim in the request or a saved answer, or when it cites a file in this repository that shows it, such as a client of the other service. Other claims are dropped. This includes work discovered while reproducing a bug that the initial request did not mention. The same public scope and ready briefs make that repository available for linking.
  • It asks you before planning. A kept part stops the run with one question. Answer This repository only to plan this repository's part. The plan then lists each other part in its scope exclusions as Not covered: changes in TARGET: WORK, so the approval screen shows what this run will not deliver. To change the request instead, give feedback. To stop instead, leave the question unanswered: the run's status (scope.briefs) holds a ready brief for each repository, this one first, to start a run with in each. A reproduced bug still waits on its unanswered questions. A follow-up with an existing plan also asks about newly discovered external work: an earlier choice cannot cover another turn or different work. Later model reports retain grounded obligations until human feedback permits Requirements to revise the scope. Answering the scope question requires a refreshed plan and its explicit approval.
  • You can link a run in the other repository. autocode changeset link starts a run in a registered project with that repository's ready brief and records the two runs as one change set, which both runs' status shows under scope.linked (Linked runs). Each run still plans, builds and completes on its own.
  • You can approve the linked plans together. autocode changeset status shows every run's plan and one set token, and autocode changeset approve approves them all at once. A plan that changes in any run withdraws the token (Approving the set).
  • You can check the linked runs together. Name an integration command, such as the consumer's tests against the producer's checkout, with autocode changeset check-command. autocode changeset verify runs it once every run is complete. Its evidence identifies the command, execution target, member runs and their code; a change to any of those withdraws it. Replacing the check also clears its previous waiver. A concurrent record change refuses an old result instead of attaching it to a new check. A failed check can reopen the run that diverged, or you can waive that check with a reason. autocode changeset pr-body writes the section each pull request carries, with the merge order (Checking the set together).
  • The terminal chat shows the change set. Its side panel lists the linked runs, and /changeset shows every run and asks before approving the plans together or running the check. /runs groups the chats of one change set (Change sets in clients). VS Code's Run details does the same with one button. On a GitHub issue, the channel bridge posts every run's plan and takes approve set.
  • Component builds stay inside one repository. autocode components builds several components in parallel, but every component worktree comes from the same repository's HEAD, and integration applies their changes to a worktree of that same repository (Parallel tasks and components). It cannot drive two existing sibling repositories.
  • A parent folder is not a multi-repository workspace. If you start AutoCode in a plain folder that holds several repositories, it creates a new, empty project under that folder instead of working in them. If the parent is itself a Git repository with the services as nested repositories or submodules, changes inside them appear to the parent only as a gitlink, so its diffs and test checks do not see them. Treat both as unsupported.

docs.title: Walkthrough: a bug reveals another repository
docs.text:
This walkthrough describes explicit changeset commands for callers that manage their own integration check. Terminal bug chats use the automatic flow above.

Suppose you report “Submitting an order records the wrong total” in order-api. The Investigator finds a call to history-service and reports that its consumer also needs to accept the corrected payload. You did not need to name that repository in the original request. The pause is triggered by the grounded report; it is not a guarantee that a model will discover every dependency.

1. Use one registry across the repositories. In every terminal used for this change set, choose the same location before starting runs:

export AUTOCODE_HOME="$HOME/.autocode"
autocode registry location
autocode "Submitting an order records the wrong total" \
  --workspace /path/to/order-api --engine codex --workflow bugfix

Use your chosen engine consistently; codex here is an example. Without an explicit AUTOCODE_HOME, task startup uses the project's registry storage (a task worktree's project, not the worktree), which registry list and runs --all read when run inside that project. For runs already created elsewhere, set the shared home and import their existing project roots with autocode registry import /path/to/project. Import reads saved runs and launches no model.

2. Keep the scope question open while selecting the other checkout. Copy the source run directory from AutoCode's output. Inspect the exact target and ready brief under scope.external_parts and scope.briefs:

api_run=/absolute/path/to/the/source/run
autocode --run-dir "$api_run" --status --json

Select an existing committed checkout yourself. The linked run works directly in the selected checkout, so give it a dedicated Git worktree when you want to keep your normal checkout separate:

git -C /path/to/history-service worktree add \
  -b autocode/history-fix /path/to/history-fix
autocode registry add /path/to/history-fix
autocode registry list
autocode changeset link --run-dir "$api_run" \
  --target history-service --workspace /path/to/history-fix -- --engine codex

Replace history-service with the exact target the status reported. registry add registers a committed local Git root without a task or model request. It does not clone repositories, change branches or approve code changes. A target that was not reported, or a checkout you have not registered, is refused.

3. Bring both runs to their plan approval. changeset status lists each run's directory, current need and continuation command. Open each run's chat:

autocode changeset status --run-dir "$api_run"
autocode --run-dir "$api_run" --chat
# Use the linked run_dir printed by changeset status:
autocode --run-dir /absolute/path/to/the/linked/run --chat

In the source chat, answer the scope question This repository only. This means this run owns the API side; the linked run owns history's side. Linking itself does not answer the question. Read the exclusions in both plans and make sure their payload fields, examples and acceptance checks agree. Leave individual plans unapproved while preparing approval of the set.

4. Review and approve the plans together. In the terminal chat use /changeset, or read the CLI's complete plans and run the approval command it prints:

autocode changeset status --run-dir "$api_run"
# After reading every plan, substitute the token just shown:
autocode changeset approve --run-dir "$api_run" --set-token TOKEN_JUST_SHOWN

No token is offered while a member still needs answers or planning. The token binds all current plans. An interrupted partial approval holds every Builder; read status again and retry with its current token. After approval, continue each run with its printed next command or autocode resume --run-dir RUN. If history discovers a third repository, link it from history's run in the same way: it joins this set and all current plans need fresh approval.

5. Name a real check of the combined behavior. The command must exercise both delivered versions. For example, if history has a tests.test_api_contract module that reads the producer checkout from AUTOCODE_CHANGESET_WORKSPACES:

autocode changeset check-command --run-dir "$api_run" --in history-service -- \
  python3 -m unittest tests.test_api_contract
# Once both runs have completed their own checks:
autocode changeset verify --run-dir "$api_run"
autocode changeset status --run-dir "$api_run"

Provide that project-specific test; AutoCode does not generate it from the command above. AUTOCODE_CHANGESET_WORKSPACES is a JSON mapping from the target names in changeset status to the actual run workspaces. Read it in the test instead of hard-coding your original checkout. The command runs in the selected member's workspace. A failed check leaves the set unverified; use autocode changeset reopen --run-dir "$api_run" --target history-service when that member needs correction. A waiver requires your explicit reason.

6. Prepare delivery. Review the merge order and include the generated change-set section in each pull request:

autocode changeset order --run-dir "$api_run" order-api history-service
autocode changeset pr-body --run-dir "$api_run" --target order-api
autocode changeset pr-body --run-dir "$api_run" --target history-service

Use the exact target names from status, including the source name. These commands record order and print text; they do not publish or merge pull requests.

docs.title: Verification and current limits
docs.text:
The deterministic regressions drive the public CLI/TaskRun interface with offline providers. They test runner behavior, not a live model's ability to discover an arbitrary service dependency.

Case Coverage TUI symptom → A → B → C discovery → fixes → joint regression → three PRs tests/test_coordination_tui_e2e.py: public chat actions, real Git repositories and actual producer/consumer calls, independent fail-before/pass-after proof, offline GitHub publication and cross-links Locally passing but incompatible member; lost PR response and reopened chat The same full-flow test requires a revised coordinated plan, a second joint regression, no publication before correction and exactly one PR per repository; changed joint-test bytes withdraw completion Missing or ambiguous repository, missing credentials/access, stale approval, cancellation, changed source/remote, exhausted joint retries tests/test_coordinate.py: refusal or bounded correction before launching/publishing; tests/test_control_tokens.py keeps coordination approval tokens out of provider environments Initial bug request omits the other repository; Investigator cites a local service client tests/test_bug_questions.py: pause before planning, public registration of a fresh checkout, linked start, reciprocal links, no Builder, explicit local-only answer New external work during a follow-up with an existing plan tests/test_scope_question_cli.py: asks again and invalidates earlier authority Invalid target or unregistered checkout; stale or interrupted set approval tests/test_changeset_cli.py: rejects unknown members, stale tokens and Builder dispatch after partial approval; retry and explicit standalone release A → B → C membership tests/test_changeset_store.py: one canonical set; duplicates and ambiguous legacy overlap refused Real producer output disagrees with the consumer expectation tests/test_changeset_delivery_cli.py: real command fails, blocks joint completion, and can reopen the affected run Code/check changes, waiver replacement and concurrent check edits tests/test_changeset_delivery.py and delivery CLI tests: old evidence cannot accept a different command or version

These are focused regressions, not one live, end-to-end multi-service production trial. Bounded live Kilo MiMo/GLM TUI attempts on 2026-10-27 discovered all three fixture repositories but stopped on planning/report validation before builds, joint testing or real PR publication. See the retained qualification evidence and remaining convergence issue #2208. Live end-to-end delivery is not yet verified. The current implementation also has these limits:

  • Discovery inventories repositories beneath configured roots and standalone registrations. The model still has to ground each repository's role in the ticket and source files; AutoCode does not search the whole disk or clone missing repositories.
  • Automatic coordination currently supports owned terminal chats on Linux and local Git repositories containing ordinary files. Symlinks, submodules and durable_local coordination are refused explicitly; saved execution policies are never silently changed.
  • Independent verification also requires preservation evidence from the original combined suite. If that suite cannot collect or supplies no complete passing test evidence, the result remains unverified and bounded retries stop with diagnostics.
  • The manual change-set API leaves linking and the check command to its caller. Automatic TUI coordination discovers and links the repositories, then uses one consolidated approval for member plans and the joint-test plan. A plain parent folder is not itself a multi-repository run; configure it as a local source root for automatic discovery.
  • In the manual change-set API, without a named integration command, verification.done means all individual runs completed. It does not prove the producer and consumer agree. Name the check before treating the overall bug as resolved.
  • Manual change-set approval binds member plans; automatic coordination binds member and joint-test plans together. A separately versioned shared-interface contract and the remaining guided onboarding work are tracked in #2066.

docs.title: The manual workflow
docs.text:
Without a change set, coordinate the repositories yourself:

  1. Write one brief per repository. Each brief states the shared requirement, the interface both sides agree on (field names, payload examples, an API schema fragment), and that this run owns only this repository's side.
  2. Start a run in each repository, the producer first when one side consumes the other: autocode in each checkout, or autocode --workspace PATH. Or start the other repository's run with autocode changeset link so the two are recorded together.
  3. Read and approve each plan against the same interface. A plan that changes the interface needs the same change in the other repository's plan.
  4. autocode runs --all lists the runs of every registered project, grouped by project, and the terminal chat's /runs and /open switch between them.
  5. Before merging, run the consumer's tests against the producer's branch, and link the two pull requests to each other with the merge order.

Without a change set, nothing checks that the two halves agree.

Configured source roots are workspace search boundaries. Git metadata on a root itself does not hide independent child checkouts. Discovery recognizes Git identities without repository-name prefixes; ordinary discovered checkouts are traversal leaves. Depth, directory and containment limits remain explicit.

Discovery skips generated Python environments identified by pyvenv.cfg, independently of their directory names. File symlinks are not traversed; directory symlinks escaping a configured root still make discovery incomplete.

docs.title: Named test proof
docs.text:
A plan's test: test_c1_example criterion requires that named test to pass with the change and not before it. A guard: criterion must pass before and after. When every criterion the proof covers is a guard: and the change adds or edits no test (it may change nothing, as a validation-only re-check does), the guards rest on tests the project already has: the proof runs the suite on the base and the candidate, and each guard's named test must pass on both. A test: criterion still needs a change, unless the person granted the test-only regression-proof exception.

A guard that names its test exactly (guard: test_c4_adds) may name a test the project already has in a file the change leaves alone, as a final check does for the criteria earlier milestones proved. The targeted run covers only the changed test files, so the whole suite also runs on the original code with the change's test files (its tests, fixtures and goldens), and such a guard is matched against the tests that pass there and on the candidate, with these limits:

  • a test whose own name appears in any changed code file is left to the targeted run (a changed test file) or not used (a changed product module that defines it); a document that mentions it does not count;
  • if that suite run times out or does not report every test, a guard left without its test is unverified rather than refuted;
  • with git-ignored test files that the proof copies into its trees, the whole suite is not consulted, so a guard cannot rest on an ignored file, and the failure says so;
  • a case matched by its id alone (a diagnosis's T4) is never matched this way, since another fix's test_t4_... is not its test;
  • one failing variant of a matched test breaks the guard, even when it failed before the change too: the same function in the same file or module, with other parameters, as a Go subtest, or run by another class. A failing test elsewhere that only shares the name does not;
  • a node:test file that spawns another test runner is refused here as everywhere.

When the change edits no test file, the guards are matched against the base suite's own pass-to-pass, by the case id as well as by exact name, so a guard may name several tests; one of them failing beside a test it matched breaks the guard.

Preservation normally rests on base tests that still pass. When the original code holds no test file and its suite had nothing to run (an empty collection, or a known runner with no test directory), the change's own tests stand in (#2259). Any of them that pass on the original code and on the change show its existing behavior was kept, and the full candidate suite must pass. Without such a test the proof stays UNVERIFIED, and its reason tells the Builder to add one; no person is asked. A base holding only documents, manifests, data files or a short extensionless text note has no behavior to preserve at all. An exit code or a printed PASS test_c1_example is not enough to identify which case ran. AutoCode currently attributes tests from Python unittest/pytest, Go, Node's built-in node:test runner, Vitest 4, and an explicitly configured JUnit XML report from another test runner.

A literal Go check with an explicit empty selector (go test -run '^$' ./...) may validate compilation in a plan. Its exit must be zero, but it supplies no named-test results or behavioral proof. Unknown flags, benchmark/fuzz requests, and custom test-program arguments retain the normal test-result requirement. Submitting an empty-selector command as a regression or suite still cannot satisfy that proof: it must execute named tests.

The identifier right after test: or guard: is the one the runner proves; an explanation may follow after — or in parentheses. Without one, the test is named after the criterion ID (test_c1_...; Go's TestC1... matches it).

Use a bare Python test name, such as test_health, after test: or guard:. Qualified selectors such as tests.test_health.HealthTests.test_health, including those inside paired Markdown backticks, are not supported as proof declarations: a new draft, or a saved draft at approval, is refused before building. No module, class or method is inferred from a suffix. Supported Go test/subtest names and annotations remain valid. Prose, placeholders and declarations naming multiple tests retain the criterion-ID fallback; they do not bind a qualified selector. An already approved proof is not rewritten; changing it needs a goal edit and approval of the new exact plan.

When the user's brief asks for Go tests by name ("add Go tests TestFixedReturnsTwo and TestFixedPreservesCrash"), the plan declares those exact names, in the user's spelling: test: TestFixedReturnsTwo, guard: TestFixedPreservesCrash, one criterion each. A requested test the runner cannot run to a pass (one that skips without a database) may instead be named by an ordinary criterion, and no other test with it, for the Validator. Planning stages are told the names, and the runner refuses a draft, before it is installed or approved, that leaves a requested name unaccounted for, declares a respelling of it (test_fixed_returns_two), or declares another identifier (or none it can read, as in test: TestFixedReturnsTwo.) while its method or criterion text names the requested one, as in prose saying it "resolves to" it (#498). A name counts as requested when the user wrote it right after "test", "tests" or a Go test-shaped "func" signature (or in a list introduced as tests, each name with or without a description). Name-first requests such as "Add TestA, a real regression ... plus TestB and TestC" also count. Negations, examples and alternatives do not. The proof must run Go tests, and the project must not already declare the name as a top-level test in a *_test.go file. Comments, strings and callable production APIs (func TestConnection() error, "a func named TestConnection that returns an error", "a func called TestConnection in product.go") do not make a test existing or requested; "a func named TestParse in parser_test.go" or "a func named TestA, a regression test" does. This inventory does not replace Go compilation or execution proof. A subtest path such as TestCacheExpiry/expired is requested as the user wrote it (a quoted one with its spaces as underscores, as Go runs it): planning stages and refusals ask for test: TestCacheExpiry/expired. Declaring that path, a path under it or its whole test function accounts for it; another subtest of the function does not, since the runner binds that one to its own outcome only. "Instead of", "rather than" or "not" right before the path withdraws that path; before the function, the function and the paths of it an earlier message asked for. The user's own --edit-goal is never refused by this check and settles which requested names stay; an edit of a design job's plan, which "Build it." archives when it plans the build afresh, settles nothing for the build. TestMain and TestXxx are never tests to write. Other frameworks, and bug fixes proven by their diagnosis's cases, keep the criterion-ID convention. The details and limits are in docs/bugs/2026-10-06-native-proof-names.md.

For Node, register each case as a real test, keeping its existing assertions and fixture helpers:

const {test} = require('node:test');
const assert = require('node:assert/strict');
const {add} = require('../app.cjs');

test('test_c1_adds_two_numbers', () => {
  assert.equal(add(2, 3), 5);
});

Run it with node --test tests/cases.cjs. Use unique case names within each suite and await asynchronous assertions. AutoCode detects node:test imports in changed test files and derives the targeted command. It runs identical tests against the original and candidate source in isolated worktrees. Keep the project's existing suite (including custom npm scripts) and protected tests; --test-command can continue to run that suite.

AutoCode attaches its own structured reporter to direct node --test commands. It checks completed event streams and final counts, ignores test stdout, and does not count skipped, todo, empty-file or ambiguous duplicate results as named passes. Import and fixture-hook failures cannot demonstrate a reproduced bug. Missing or incomplete evidence stays unverified. The adapter uses the documented Node TestsStream custom reporter API, including final summary events available in current Node 22 and later releases. The reporter handles Node 22.14's omitted ordinary-test type while preserving suite identity; a missing type in retained proof files is still invalid evidence.

For Vitest 4, keep the tests in their existing framework. Give each case a unique name, such as test('test_c1_adds_two_numbers', ...), and use npx --no-install vitest run tests/example.test.js. An npm test script containing a single vitest run command is supported too, including npm --prefix frontend test. AutoCode attaches its owned reporter, reads a fresh structured result file, and excludes its internal .autocode/ test backups. Missing or skipped cases, duplicate identities, interrupted reports, and unsupported versions cannot supply named passes. Collection and hook failures are separated from application failures. The reporter uses Vitest's reporting lifecycle and v4 hook-result metadata; qualification currently covers Vitest 4.1.6.

A node:test case must assert the behavior itself. A case that runs another test runner through child_process (npm test -- -t NAME, npx vitest, Jest, Mocha or node --test) passes on that runner's exit code, and Vitest exits 0 when a -t filter matches no test, so a misspelt or renamed case would pass without running (#380). AutoCode reads each node:test file that a case's test lives in and does not match a case to a test in a file that spawns a test runner; the proof names the file. Running the product's own CLI from a node:test case (node cli.js add x) is fine. The check only sees commands the file spells out; a wrapper is not named proof in any form.

Where the runner can select the proving tests, each runs three times on the candidate, inside the scratch tree the proof already has, and a test: criterion's test also runs three times on the original code. A test that passes on one run and fails on another is unstable: it does not count as proof, the evidence names the test and its runs, and completion stops until the test is fixed. Retrying the proof leaves the same disagreement. Guards repeat on the candidate only. Only the proving tests repeat, so a stable proof costs two extra executions of those tests, not of the suite.

When the project already has a coverage tool, the proving-test command runs once more to record diff_coverage: each changed product hunk, the hunks no proving test executed, and the changed files the report did not measure. That run cannot change the verdict, and nothing is installed into the project.

Shell pipelines, custom reporters, ordinary npm/Jest/Mocha summaries and custom assertion scripts do not currently provide named proof. A direct supported targeted command can accompany an existing package-script suite. If the project cannot use a supported runner, settle that compatibility blocker during planning; do not downgrade an approved named criterion to prose to make a run finish.

docs.title: JUnit XML from other test runners
docs.text:
Use --test-report junit:RELATIVE_PATH with an explicit --test-command to attribute Java, Kotlin, .NET, Rust or Ruby tests through their runner's JUnit XML output. For example, the catalog's Java case runs one real JUnit class:

autocode --workspace /path/to/project "Count partial pages" \
  --test-command 'mvn -o -B -q -Dtest=PageCountTest test' \
  --test-report junit:target/surefire-reports/TEST-example.PageCountTest.xml

Install the project's locked dependencies before running offline. The ordinary suite command is also used for the candidate/original-source regression runs when --regression-command is omitted. If provided, the regression command must produce the same relative report path. Keep every named guard: case in the command's selected tests as well as the new test: cases.

The selection persists in the run and is also available as project settings:

# pyproject.toml
[tool.autocode]
test-command = "mvn -o -B -q -Dtest=PageCountTest test"
test-report = "junit:target/surefire-reports/TEST-example.PageCountTest.xml"

A saved command/report correction uses the existing reconciled --resume-paused repair boundary before the Tester or combined checkpoint. It cannot replace evidence during an active command or late acceptance. Generic JUnit commands have no portable selector: stability repeats the unchanged command only when its complete report contains exclusively the proving cases. Otherwise the stability record reports that they ran once, without widening to an unrelated whole suite. Existing reporter selection is unchanged.

This interface accepts one XML file per command, not a directory or glob. Use a single test class/project or a runner that writes one combined report. The path must stay inside each proof tree. Each command starts with that report removed, so a previous result or a command that does not rewrite it cannot supply proof. The runner captures the fresh XML beside its execution receipt and pins its hash; changing that captured artifact invalidates the proof. Missing, malformed, zero-test, incomplete or inconsistent reports cannot establish a named pass. Failure/error/skipped outcomes retain their meanings; a nonzero command exit with no genuine failing case cannot demonstrate a regression. This does not change the existing Python, Go, node:test or Vitest reporters.

JUnit suite preservation pins the base test bodies and recognized build-system selectors before running them over the candidate product. Standard Maven, Gradle, .NET, cargo-nextest and RSpec commands have this boundary; an unknown command cannot establish preservation merely by writing valid XML. Changes to unclassified suite inputs remain UNVERIFIED. Existing Rust product files can also define inline tests, so changing such a file currently leaves preservation UNVERIFIED, even when its reported cases pass. The same conservative boundary applies when an existing product file may contain nonstandard test definitions. Command-selected custom build/test files, unbound project paths and arbitrary build properties also leave preservation UNVERIFIED until their base inputs can be bound. The trusted command still runs; its XML cannot prove that those hidden definitions stayed intact.

Runner setup examples (configure unique test names matching the named criteria):

  • Maven / Java: pin JUnit Jupiter and Maven Surefire in pom.xml. Run mvn -Dtest=PageCountTest test; use junit:target/surefire-reports/TEST-example.PageCountTest.xml. Surefire emits XML per class; -Dtest selects the class. Surefire reports, single-class selection.
  • Gradle / Java or Kotlin: keep JUnit XML enabled and run ./gradlew test --tests example.PageCountTest --rerun-tasks; use junit:build/test-results/test/TEST-example.PageCountTest.xml with Gradle's default layout. reports.junitXml.outputLocation changes the directory; align the report flag with it. Re-running tasks avoids treating Gradle's up-to-date result as fresh execution after the report was removed. Gradle XML reports.
  • .NET / VSTest: add the compatible JunitXml.TestLogger NuGet package to the test project, then run from that project's directory: dotnet test Tests.csproj --framework net8.0 --logger "junit;LogFilePath=junit.xml"; use junit:junit.xml. Select one project and target framework so outputs do not overwrite each other. This is a third-party JUnit logger. dotnet test --logger trx writes TRX, not JUnit XML, and is not accepted by this interface. JUnit logger, Microsoft's TRX documentation.
  • Rust / cargo-nextest: in .config/nextest.toml, set:

toml [profile.default.junit] path = "junit.xml"

Run cargo nextest run and use junit:target/nextest/default/junit.xml. The path is relative to the profile's store directory; with --profile ci and [profile.ci.junit], it becomes target/nextest/ci/junit.xml. JUnit output is configured in the profile, not with a --junit command flag. Nextest JUnit configuration. - Ruby / RSpec: include rspec_junit_formatter in the project's bundle and run bundle exec rspec --format RspecJunitFormatter --out junit.xml; use junit:junit.xml. Keep the formatter in the same dependency group as RSpec. Formatter usage.

The feature-java-page-count catalog case exercises this interface with real Maven 3.9.9, JUnit Jupiter 5.11.4 and Surefire 3.5.2. Its independent Java oracle rejects wrong behavior and a green regression that also passes on the original source. The other setup examples document their runners' interfaces; they are not claims of locally executed qualification for those ecosystems.

docs.title: Mutation check
docs.text:
A proving test can fail without the fix and pass with it and still not pin the behavior: assertEqual(3, page_count(11, 5)) holds for a correct ceiling and for a fix that is wrong when there is only one, partial page. Once a named proof passes (its verdict final, after the case check), the runner looks for that by changing the product code one small step at a time and running the proving tests against each change (#699, tools/autocode_mutation_check.py, with the changes from tools/autocode_mutants.py).

  • Where. Only the changed lines of the change's product .py files, in the proof's own candidate scratch tree. Tests, files the change does not touch, type stubs (.pyi), files that are not UTF-8 (ASCII counts, however the coding cookie spells it), files that do not parse with the runner's Python and files with a carriage return no line feed follows (Python and git number their lines differently) are never changed; the record notes why.
  • What. Six operators: negate a condition (if, while, a conditional expression, assert, a comprehension filter or a case guard); swap a bound (< and <=, > and >=); drop a branch (an if body or its else becomes pass, a decorated definition with its decorators; an elif is mutated as its own if); return a constant instead of the value; shift an integer bound by one: a literal beside <, <=, > or >= (an ==, !=, is or in operand is not a bound); and bind another constant where a bool, number or string literal is assigned to a name (TEXT = "hello" becomes TEXT = ""), so a line whose whole behavior is the value it binds has a site a test can see. Each mutant replaces the bytes of one syntax node, keeps every line number, must compile, and must change its statement exactly as intended; a site that fails one of these, or cannot be checked at all (a statement nested too deep, an integer too long to print), is skipped with a note and the next one takes its place. TYPE_CHECKING and __main__ guards, f-strings, annotations and branches that already do nothing are left alone.
  • How many. Current task proofs enumerate the eligible sites on every changed line within the existing mutation budget. Unrun sites stay explicit obligations. The older advisory collector and standalone review study retain their six-site sample per file. The same source and selection give the same sites.
  • How long. One 900-second budget, the same limit as a check replay, covers one unmutated run and every mutant. Current task proofs select the independently observed passing candidate-suite tests by exact ID; when the suite is a command the runner cannot narrow to those tests (a project's own gate script, such as python project_gate.py), they select the proof's regression command and the tests it passed on the candidate instead, so a project gate does not leave every changed line without evidence. Older advisory collectors select only the named proving tests. Each mutant uses its own empty bytecode cache and its own modification time, so a compile cached by a Python the tests start themselves is never reused. A mutant may take ten times the unmutated run's duration, at least 60 seconds, and never more than the budget left: with fast proving tests one that never returns cannot spend the budget, but with slow ones it can use the rest of it. No mutant starts with less than 60 seconds left; those, and a mutant the budget cut short, are not_run.
  • Which proofs. Python unittest and pytest only for now. A Go, node:test or Vitest proof gets a note and no run.

A mutant that makes a proving test fail is killed. One that every proving test still passes has survived, and is reported beside each due test case whose test passed with it (keyed by the same test-case ids as case_tests), for example test_partial_last_page_is_counted passes with pager/__init__.py:9 changed (`>` -> `>=`). The status view shows the record as evidence.mutation_check (the task-run interface), the evidence report lists each survivor under the regression proof, and the Tester and the Completion Reviewer receive it with the proof. The runner combines exact-source coverage and authenticated mutation observations in changed_code_evidence (#2474). A line merely executed without a meaningful assertion does not pass. A named test must actually fail under the mutation; a setup/collection failure, missing test, interrupted command or timeout grants no positive evidence.

Every changed executable line needs demonstrated mutation evidence or a precise reason checked by the existing independent Tester. This is its code-review responsibility within the existing workflow, and cannot be self-approved by Builder. A survivor can be equivalent (no test could observe the change); the Tester can record that specific reason against the current offered gap ID and pin its source/test/check evidence. An unavailable tool alone is not a blanket exception. Empty survivor lists and the old six-site sample never prove that all changed lines were tested.

The core returns unresolved exact lines to Builder for two bounded repair rounds, then uses its existing Investigator path and saved run limits. It records those decisions and the fallback in the public verification view and final report. Missing project coverage tooling uses demonstrated mutation evidence alone where available; otherwise the line remains open for independent judgment. No project dependency is installed. Blank/comment-only lines, Python declaration-only lines and non-executable lines excluded by an authenticated statement map are omitted. Legacy proofs and standalone review mutation studies remain advisory records; active task completion requires current evidence rather than inferring it from those older records. A proof that did not pass runs no mutant.

It complements the check replay's sanity gate (tools/autocode_test_quality.py), which rejects test bodies that assert nothing at all. A test that asserts something, but not enough, passes that gate and shows up here.

docs.title: Tests in a reviewed patch
docs.text:
The review workflow keeps two test groups separate. A reviewer's delivered finding tests must fail on the change to prove its blocking findings. They are not the passing tests used for mutation checks.

For an explicit change_patch, the runner selects added or modified standard Python test files from that patch, excluding review/. It applies the pinned patch in its clean scratch copy, runs those original tests, and selects only complete, observed passing test IDs. Every selected ID must pass again before mutants run. It never executes the model's free-form tests_run strings or falls back to the whole suite.

The check changes only product lines actually added by the patch, excluding context lines, tests and unchanged files. It uses the same Python operators, six-mutant file limit and one 900-second budget. Missing patches, unsupported runners, absent test selections and changes without eligible mutation sites produce an explicit not-run note. An empty selection is not evidence that the tests reject wrong code. Unknown process cleanup remains a hold.

Review results expose subject: reviewed_patch_tests in evidence.mutation_check, with the patch hash, selected files and test IDs. Survivors are keyed by those actual test IDs, rather than invented acceptance criteria. The findings artifact and canonical workflow_result.mutation_check retain the same report; Markdown presents it under Review test mutation check. This creates no named regression proof and changes neither the review verdict nor the finding-test requirement.

docs.title: Contained Tester Evidence
docs.text:
A contained Tester cannot bind or connect sockets. If the named regression tests exercise real HTTP/end-to-end behavior, it must not run that network-dependent regression command again: inspect the named tests and cite the runner's existing clean-copy proof, not a model claim of execution. At launch, the runner checks the proof's source revision against the current source, its receipt hash, and the integrity of its check artifacts using the existing completion-proof validator. The entire presented proof must also match the runner's fresh handoff projection, including JSON types. Only then is runner_regression_proof_current true; missing or altered handoff evidence is not authenticated even when the saved runner proof is valid. A PASS receipt alone is not sufficient authority. The tests must assert the approved flow, not only health or static behavior; missing, stale, incomplete, failed, skipped or zero-test proof cannot establish HTTP PASS.

The Tester still executes permitted independent non-network checks and captures their receipts in tool_containment.scratch. It cites regression_proof directly (verdict, source_revision, case_tests, checks, path), never through a check that reads run files, which are absent from clean replay. This changes no network permissions, replay policy or completion requirements. Uncontained Testers retain the existing instruction to run the regression command themselves.

docs.title: Go test prerequisite metadata
docs.text:
A test may import a package from an already selected transitive module whose indirect requirement or checksum is missing from the root manifests. Where the approved plan permits it, the acceptance Tester may add that loading metadata alongside its tests. The core admits only additive indirect requirements at the original Go selection and missing checksums verified against offline cached module artifacts. Existing requirements, versions, module/toolchain directives and checksums cannot be replaced or removed through this exception.

The runner retains both native graph observations and exact manifest hashes, including any change in transitive module selection. Those observations grant no plan approval: a version constraint in the approved plan still applies. The Builder must retain admitted metadata byte-for-byte, including for blind tests. The final regression comparison uses identical admitted metadata on original and corrected production source, while the original suite baseline keeps its original inputs. Compilation failures never establish a bug reproduction. Other dependency changes remain on the ordinary proof path and are not overlaid onto the original source as test prerequisites.

docs.title: Declared public pilot inputs
docs.text:
Use tools/autocode_pilot_prep.py when a task depends on public proof files or an immutable patch. Store them at non-ignored project-relative paths, such as pilot-public/PUBLIC-PROOF.md and pilot-public/pr42.patch, and mention those exact paths in the task brief. Ignored files do not enter Git-enumerated source copies; copying all ignored directories would also copy secrets and outputs.

Create a JSON manifest with an inputs list. Each entry declares path, type (file), mode (for example 0644), byte size and sha256. Compute these fields from the intended public files. Absolute paths, parent traversal, directories, leaf symlinks and symlink ancestors are rejected. Matching bytes outside the selected root cannot qualify a declared input inside it.

.venv/bin/python -B tools/autocode_pilot_prep.py \
  --workspace /absolute/project \
  --manifest /absolute/public-input-manifest.json \
  --brief /absolute/pilot-brief.txt \
  --report /absolute/project/.autocode/prep-report.json

The coordinator creates a fresh .autocode/prep/<id>/source worktree from HEAD plus Git-enumerated dirty and untracked candidate inputs. It deliberately omits dependency links and recursive directory copies. Existing prep copies, ignored credentials, build outputs and dependency trees stay excluded. The preflight checks type, mode, size and SHA-256 in both the original workspace and this actual copy. A missing or mismatched input prints a setup error and exits 2 before any TaskRun or model provider starts, with a non-ignored-path remedy. The copy remains available for inspection; a new invocation allocates a different directory.

The bug-fix workflow's actual Investigator also selects tracked and ordinary untracked inputs from each Git source inventory, including dirty source and initialized nested Git components. Its copy excludes ignored credentials, dependencies and outputs. It rejects source aliases that would materialize an ignored target. The prepared-copy handoff names the exact directory in which the Investigator runs its checks; it does not need a parent-directory search.

On success, the coordinator starts the task in the original workspace through the public TaskRun interface. The JSON report names the checked copy, inputs, HEAD and run directory. The opt-in coordinator does not change ordinary AutoCode startup or automatically provision ignored inputs. It does not answer questions, consume plan approval or declare completion. If a required artifact is ignored, move only that public artifact to a non-ignored location and update the manifest and brief; do not disable Git isolation.

Offline boundary tests use the maintained fixture provider. Its requirements and plan reports cite tracked and ordinary untracked source paths, excluding runner artifacts and caches before limiting citations. Both lexical paths and resolved symlink targets must identify eligible source inside the workspace. The fixture selects directly stored files from the Git inventory, so ignored targets and dangling source aliases cannot become citations. An empty workspace retains its task fallback. The success case stops with needs.kind=approve_plan and done=false. The ignored input case invokes no provider and creates no task-run directory. The inventory guard remains a separate baseline behavior test.

.venv/bin/python -B -m unittest tests.test_autocode_input_preflight tests.test_input_inventory_guard tests.test_autocode_pilot_prep tests.test_pilot_investigator_cli tests.test_taskrun
.venv/bin/python -B tools/run_suite.py --changed --jobs 2
.venv/bin/python -B scenarios/run.py run --fake

docs.title: Project memory
docs.text:
A completed task can remember project preferences for the next task in the same repository. The learned record is .autocode/project.json, separate from the settings a person deliberately chooses in .autocode/config.toml or [tool.autocode].

AutoCode records the observed test framework and a shareable test command, reusable conventions actually answered by a person, observed model routes, and the names of pause states that needed a person. Unknown facts remain null. It writes after the completed checkpoint and evidence; learning cannot approve a task, change its verified result, or make completion fail.

docs.title: Reusing an answer
docs.text:
Requirements can tag its own question IDs as project conventions. Before saving one, the runner joins the exact question to the issued clarification, the actual human answer and its source record. It saves the question and answer verbatim, not a model paraphrase. Proposed defaults, delegated answers, machine decisions and unasked questions are ineligible. Permission, spending, quota, external side effect and task-outcome decisions are not reusable authorization.

The next task gives these historical answers to Requirements as project data. For example, an unchanged preference about test naming need not be asked again. The new brief and current answers take precedence. Memory is never inserted into this task's answer ledger, acceptance criteria or human-source citations, and every required plan and completion approval still belongs to the new task.

docs.title: Defaults and configuration
docs.text:
For the test command, precedence is:

  1. The current command-line flag.
  2. .autocode/config.toml.
  3. [tool.autocode] in pyproject.toml.
  4. The learned project record.
  5. Built-in detection/defaults.

The record has no per-package entry, so its framework and test command describe the whole repository. A run started with --package does not take the learned test command, and does not save its framework or test command into the record; it still saves conventions, routes and pause states. The explicit project files still apply to it. See Monorepo packages.

Framework and route observations provide context and diagnostics. They do not select a provider, change engines/models, set budgets or grant permission. A known generated Python suite can use a portable python3 launcher rather than storing the previous machine's interpreter path. Custom commands are retained only when safe to share.
