A saved run keeps the provider it started with, and --engine codex runs still use Codex. autocode-dashboard --provider <name> overrides the default for the dashboard; its model pickers list that tool's models.

See also: Models · Install · CLI

docs.title: Conformance matrix
docs.text:
Generated by python tools/provider_matrix.py --write from tools/provider-matrix.json. Do not edit by hand. A version the offline conformance suite has not been run against is untested — never guess. Run the suite with python tools/provider_conformance.py --fake (no model calls).

Engine Version Transport Containment Visual Result Date Commit Note opencode 1.18.33 opencode qualified qualified known-good 2026-10-08 a8852cf4 The version the glm53-mimo three-case reliability sweep ran on (docs/bugs/2026-10-06-opencode-2.md). opencode 1.18.31 opencode untested untested known-good 2026-10-01 68e89aa4 Live-checked in the 2026-10-01 glm53-openai sweep; containment/visual stay qualified only for 1.18.33. opencode 2.0.20 opencode-standalone refused refused accepted-for-ordinary-runs 2026-10-06 9a31a8e8 Uses --standalone and a provider/model#effort id. A 2.x binary fails the containment and visual checks closed until it has its own conformance pass (docs/bugs/2026-10-06-opencode-2.md). codex native codex n/a n/a known-good 2026-10-03 b96a633e Native Codex probes in docs/provider-conformance.md; ChatGPT login required. kilocode registered-adapter kilocode n/a n/a known-good 2026-10-03 b96a633e Registered KiloCode adapter; see docs/provider-conformance.md. autocode direct-1 direct-compatible qualified n/a known-good 2026-10-26 ed2a01957 The direct engine's own runtime, kernel-contained shell and event stream against a loopback model fixture (#2055); covers the OpenAI/OpenRouter-compatible API-key transport. Sessionless engine: build and validate boundaries. The Anthropic-messages transport and Google remain pending.

docs.title: Connection setup and company backends
docs.text:
autocode connections list --json lists built-in Kilo, OpenCode, Codex and Claude Code and user-registered providers (Codex is an engine, --engine codex; its row says whether it is installed and signed in). connections check --provider NAME --json checks credentials without model traffic. connections login --provider NAME opens the backend's own interactive sign-in. AutoCode does not store a second copy of keys, SSO sessions, or AWS credentials. Kilo/OpenCode login lets the backend choose its supported API-key or browser flow; existing route/billing checks still apply before a task launches.

A company GoCode adapter can keep its corporate authentication and Bedrock routing. AutoCode does not require it to go through Kilo or OpenCode. In a registered provider's user-level TOML, optionally add:

[connection]
login_command = ["your-company-cli", "its-documented-login-command"]
status_command = ["your-company-cli", "its-documented-login-status-command"]

These are argument arrays executed without a shell. Use the company's documented commands; the names above are placeholders, not GoCode commands. The status command must make no inference requests: exit 0 for credentials present, 1 for sign-in required, and another code for a failed check. Its stdout/stderr is withheld from clients. The interactive login command owns its terminal output. Without these optional commands AutoCode reports login as unchecked and offers no guessed sign-in command. Provider files are trusted user configuration; files in a project are never discovered as connection definitions.

docs.title: AutoCode direct connections (issue #1493)
docs.text:
Retired (owner decision 2026-10-30, #2049); removed in the next release. AutoCode offers four backends: Claude Code and Codex as engines, and OpenCode and Kilo for every other account and API key. Add API keys there (opencode auth login, kilo auth login). A direct connection that is already configured still appears in autocode connections list, and --provider autocode still runs on it until then; nothing offers it to a new user, and connections setup and connections add print that notice first. The rest of this section describes it until it is removed.

AutoCode includes its own text/tool runtime. It does not require Kilo, OpenCode, Codex, Claude Code, or another coding-agent executable. In VS Code open Connections → AutoCode · Direct connection → Set up AutoCode, or run:

autocode connections setup
autocode connections add openai
autocode connections check --provider autocode --json
autocode "hi" --provider autocode --joint-planning --spec-first

Setup is interactive in a terminal and launches no model. Choose mimo, zai, openai, openrouter, claude, or a custom compatible API. connections setup keeps one provider per connection; connections add PROVIDER (issue #2055) configures several providers at once, each with its own key in the same private store, and assigns each role to its provider — for example Planner/Builder/Requirements on an OpenAI key and the independent reviewer/tester roles on a Claude key, so verifier independence is satisfied without flags. add reports immediately when the resulting routes are not independent; re-adding a provider with a blank key rotates nothing and keeps the other providers' keys. Google's Gemini API is refused until its own transport ships; openrouter reaches many vendors today through one key. A version-1 single-provider connection keeps working and upgrades in place the first time a second provider is added.

API choice Protocol Authentication Response limit field MiMo Chat Completions api-key max_completion_tokens Z.ai Chat Completions Bearer key max_tokens OpenAI / OpenRouter / custom compatible Chat Completions Bearer key max_completion_tokens Claude Anthropic Messages x-api-key, version 2023-06-01 max_tokens

MiMo and Z.ai require an explicit base URL, including its version path. Use the exact endpoint and matching key for your billing route: ordinary API access and Token/Coding Plan subscriptions have separate endpoints. Setup shows the API examples and requires you to choose; it never falls back to another billing route. OpenAI defaults to https://api.openai.com/v1; OpenRouter defaults to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1; Claude defaults to https://api.anthropic.com/v1. Endpoint overrides require HTTPS (HTTP is allowed only for loopback fixtures). This setup accepts API keys, not ChatGPT or Claude subscription logins. Kilo continues to own its separate sign-in and routes.

MiMo/Z.ai assistant messages retain reasoning_content across tool turns. Claude uses native tool_use/tool_result blocks and replays signed thinking blocks in order. Unsupported content and incomplete responses fail closed. Nonempty Chat Completions effort overrides are sent as reasoning_effort and must be supported by that model. Claude effort overrides are currently refused; its default reasoning is used. Redirects are refused, with no automatic parameter change, retry or provider fallback. Bedrock is outside this scope.

Model IDs are those the endpoint accepts, not Kilo/OpenCode routing aliases. Setup groups Planner/Builder/Requirements and independent reviewers/testers; the existing verifier-independence rules still apply. Reopening setup with blank model answers preserves every saved role assignment. models --provider autocode lists the configured roster; unconfigured model escalation is refused.

The API key lives in a separate auth.json file, mode 0600, under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/autocode/direct/ (default ~/.config/autocode/direct/), whose mode is 0700. This is a private local file, not an OS keychain. The credential is bound to the API endpoint: changing the endpoint requires an explicit key for that destination, and in a multi-provider connection each provider's key is bound to that provider's endpoint alone. Status and launch arguments never contain key values. Listing connections reads metadata only; Check setup validates local setup, not live model access. configured and setup_required are distinct. Key rotation for the same endpoint preserves transport identity; changes to the API provider, endpoint, models or runtime change it and trigger the saved run's existing drift checks. Configuration is never read from project files.

Select Use for new chats after setup. This does not replace an existing Kilo/GoCode connection or change its model routes. CLI callers explicitly pass --provider autocode; setup does not silently change the global default.

The existing supported-Linux provider supervisor owns each launch and cleanup. Model-requested commands run only through AutoCode's existing kernel shell boundary, with credentials removed, no network, protected run files, and the stage's read/write authority. Read-only execution uses the existing verification copy mechanism. There are at most 32 model responses per stage and eight tool calls per response, an 8192-token requested response cap, a 60-second HTTP read bound, and a 90-second tool bound; outer task/stage/spend limits still apply. Tool output is bounded at 65536 bytes and explicitly marked when truncated. Actual tool output and exit codes supply evidence; model prose cannot manufacture command events. Reported input/output usage is retained across requests, including failed turns; output counts include reasoning. A separate reasoning-token breakdown is not yet reported by this runtime. Missing token fields and prices remain unknown.

This initial runtime supports text and shell tools with a fresh context per stage. It does not provide native image qualification, in-process file tools, MCP tools, or external-agent session resumption. Local HTTP fixtures and supported-Linux task tests verify protocol and safety behavior; they do not establish live model access. The implementation stays draft pending live qualification with an explicitly configured connection.

Protocol references: OpenAI Chat Completions, MiMo API and Token Plan setup, MiMo Chat Completions, Z.ai Chat Completions, Z.ai thinking replay, and Claude Messages.

docs.title: Automatic routes for new runs
docs.text: New runs automatically select qualified models from the chosen tool's connected accounts, preferring subscriptions and preserving independent checking. No per-role model flags are needed, including with TaskRun.start(workspace, brief). Explicit model, effort and tool overrides win; saved runs keep their choices. --no-auto-select retains fixed defaults. --auto-select requires selection to succeed instead of falling back when discovery or an independent checker is unavailable. See automatic model selection for discovery, reasoning levels, bounded preflight, recovery and the read-only selection preview.

docs.title: Registry APIs
docs.text:
← Back to README

Autocode automatically records every real new run and ordinary resumed run before a provider can start. The registry is a small per-user pointer index, not a copy of state.json, logs, prompts, credentials, or provider configuration. It is stored at $AUTOCODE_HOME/registry.json; when AUTOCODE_HOME is unset, the storage root is ~/.autocode. Set AUTOCODE_HOME for isolated installations and tests.

A task started without AUTOCODE_HOME records its run in its project's own registry, <project>/.autocode/registry/registry.json, including a run in a default task worktree under .autocode/worktrees. So, with AUTOCODE_HOME unset, registry list and autocode runs --all run inside a project read that project's registry as well as ~/.autocode; a run in both is listed once, and an unreadable project registry is reported as a project_registry_unreadable diagnostic. With AUTOCODE_HOME set they read only that registry.

The browser application should invoke these commands as argument arrays, without a shell, using the same environment as the runner:

["autocode", "registry", "location", "--json"]
["autocode", "registry", "list", "--json"]
["autocode", "registry", "import", "/selected/root", "--max-depth", "3", "--directory-budget", "10000", "--json"]

docs.title: location and list
docs.text:
location and list always emit versioned JSON and are read-only: they do not create the storage directory or lock file, start/resume a task, migrate a checkpoint, or alter a task file. location returns registry_version, storage_root, registry_path, and exists. list returns registry_version, workspaces, runs, and diagnostics. Run records contain stable canonical-path-derived id, workspace_id, workspace, run_dir, and task_id when the run-level checkpoint identity is available. Listings derive only a small current summary (status, phase, next_stage) from a valid referenced checkpoint.

Each listed run has an availability value. available includes that summary; workspace_missing, workspace_invalid, checkpoint_missing, checkpoint_malformed, containment_invalid, checkpoint_unsupported, inaccessible, and malformed_record retain an honest stale or invalid pointer instead of pruning or repairing it. An absent registry is a successful empty result with the registry_absent diagnostic. Corrupt or unsupported registry storage returns JSON with an error object and exits 2 without replacing the file. Successful location/list operations exit 0.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text: Registration resolves workspace and run aliases before deriving IDs. The run must be contained by the canonical <workspace>/.autocode/runs directory and its direct state.json must identify that same canonical workspace. The registry stores no alias and repeated aliases deduplicate. Updates use fsync-backed atomic replacement under a dedicated registry lock with a one-second bounded wait. A runner first holds its workspace writer lock, then obtains the registry lock only for the central read/update/write, releases it, and only then proceeds toward a provider stage. Registration failures pause the preserved run as PAUSED_REGISTRY; fix storage and explicitly resume the same --run-dir to retry its stable identity.

docs.title: Shared source catalog
docs.text:
Cross-repository bug discovery uses a source catalog shared across launch directories. Set AUTOCODE_SOURCE_CATALOG_HOME to select its AutoCode home; an explicit AUTOCODE_HOME selects the same home when the source-specific setting is absent. With neither set, the catalog lives in ~/.autocode/source-catalog.json. Terminal chat keeps this user-level location even when its ordinary run registry defaults to the project. Existing run registries are unchanged.

Authorize locations once:

autocode registry roots add /work/services
autocode registry roots add /mnt/fulfillment
autocode registry repositories add /work/standalone/history-consumer
autocode registry roots list

roots add authorizes bounded recursive discovery beneath one canonical local directory. repositories add authorizes one committed Git checkout outside the roots. Remove entries with roots remove PATH or repositories remove PATH. These commands change only the catalog; they do not start a task, clone a remote, or edit a source checkout. roots discover --max-depth 8 --directory-budget 20000 --json performs read-only inventory and reports whether traversal was complete. Reaching a bound, an unavailable root, an unreadable repository, or a symlink escaping its configured root is explicit in diagnostics.

Discovery validates Git roots and committed revisions, does not follow directory symlinks, and prunes common generated/dependency directories. Worktrees and clones with the same normalized remote and tree collapse to one baseline; distinct trees for one remote remain candidates marked as an ambiguous baseline. The response includes catalog_identity and source_snapshot hashes so a coordinated task can bind its scope to the exact catalog and discovered source revisions. A changed catalog or baseline must be rediscovered before approval or execution.

The catalog is separate from the run registry. It contains local paths and Git identities only. It does not clone repositories or authorize a repository based on model output or ticket text.

docs.title: registry add
docs.text:
autocode registry add /path/to/project [--json] registers an explicitly selected, existing Git checkout or worktree with at least one commit. It accepts the root, not a subdirectory or a bare repository, and canonicalizes aliases. It creates no run, launches no provider and changes no project files. Repeating it returns already_registered: true. Invalid roots or corrupt/conflicting registry data return an error object and exit 2 without replacing existing records.

Use this to make a fresh local checkout available to changeset link without a dummy task. Use one explicit AUTOCODE_HOME for registration, source runs, linked runs and change-set commands. Task text and model output never invoke registration, and clients' named-action contracts are unchanged.

docs.title: registry forget-deleted
docs.text: autocode registry forget-deleted --workspace /path/to/project --run-dir /path/to/project/.autocode/runs/RUN [--json] drops the registry entry of one run whose directory no longer exists: a run the person deleted by hand, or one removed with its worktree by an older clean-worktrees. It never deletes files, and refuses (invalid_deleted_run) while the run directory exists, so the entry of a run recreated meanwhile is kept. autocode runs --all names this command on the row of such a run.

docs.title: registry import
docs.text:
registry import discovers and registers existing runs. It requires an explicit selected directory, resolves that root canonically, and searches the root at depth zero through depth 3 by default. --max-depth must be a nonnegative integer; --directory-budget must be a positive integer and defaults to 10000. The budget counts each unique canonical directory inspected, including the selected root and direct run candidates; canonical aliases do not consume the budget twice. Repository internals (.git), .autocode contents, and run contents are pruned from general workspace discovery.

Import follows only canonical directories contained by the selected root, deduplicates aliases and cycles, and reports aliases that escape it before reading their candidate contents. It validates each discovered canonical workspace, run and direct state.json using the same containment and readable checkpoint rules as registration. Valid legacy checkpoints do not need an approved goal and their bytes are never migrated or changed. Canonical path identities, rather than task_id, determine uniqueness: two distinct runs with the same task ID remain distinct; repeated imports report already_registered.

The JSON result includes selected_root, effective bounds, directories_inspected, imported, already_registered, diagnostics, and complete. Expected malformed, inaccessible, escaped, duplicate, or out-of-bound candidates are diagnostics. Budget exhaustion, inability to enumerate a workspace or its .autocode/runs candidates, unreadable traversal branches, and escaped aliases set complete false and exit 1, so retry with a narrower root or deliberately larger bound. Fully enumerated candidates with invalid individual checkpoints remain diagnostics without making the traversal incomplete. Invalid arguments/root and registry lock/storage/write failures emit an error or registry_error object and exit 2; candidate registration validation failures such as a non-Git workspace conservatively use that same registry_error exit and abort the pass. Any earlier acknowledged imports remain durable and it is safe to retry. Import never starts or resumes providers and does not modify imported task files.

See also: Dashboard · Interventions

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
← Back to Install

AutoCode is published to PyPI as autocode-supervisor by .github/workflows/publish.yml. It uses PyPI trusted publishing: GitHub proves to PyPI which repository, workflow and environment is uploading, so there is no API token to store or rotate.

docs.title: Published baseline
docs.text:
PyPI and charlieanna/homebrew-tap already publish 0.8.2, checked on 2026-10-27. The tag points to 86fdb7920f46a935405840f78c8c3bff0ed3422b (2026-10-21), not current master. See the distribution verification record. Existing versions/tags must not be republished or moved to ship later master fixes: choose a new version and follow the release process below.

The one-time publisher/environment/tap instructions below describe setup for an installation that does not already have them. Do not create a second PyPI project or overwrite the existing tap as part of a release.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
1. On PyPI, signed in as the account that will own the project, open Your account → Publishing and add a pending GitHub publisher: project name autocode-supervisor, owner charlieanna, repository autocode, workflow publish.yml, environment pypi. The first upload creates the project; after that the publisher is listed under the project's Settings → Publishing.
  2. On GitHub, Settings → Environments → New environment named pypi. Add yourself as a required reviewer if each release should wait for a click, and limit its deployment tags to v*.

docs.title: Each release
docs.text:
1. Set version in pyproject.toml (for example 0.8.0) and merge that to master.
  2. Tag the merged commit with v and the same version, and push the tag:

sh git fetch origin git tag v0.8.0 origin/master git push origin v0.8.0

  1. The publish workflow refuses a tag that differs from v plus pyproject's version, builds the sdist and wheel, checks the wheel installs and reports that version, then uploads both (after the pypi environment's approval, if you set one).
  2. Check it: pipx install autocode-supervisor (or pipx upgrade autocode-supervisor), then autocode --version prints the new version and commit unknown.

PyPI never accepts the same file twice. Once an upload has succeeded, fix a bad release with a new version, not by moving the tag.

docs.title: Homebrew
docs.text:
Homebrew installs AutoCode from a tap, charlieanna/homebrew-tap, whose Formula/autocode.rb pins the PyPI release's source archive and each runtime dependency by sha256. People then install with:

brew install charlieanna/tap/autocode

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text: Create the public GitHub repository charlieanna/homebrew-tap with an empty Formula/ directory. Homebrew finds charlieanna/tap by that name.

docs.title: Each release
docs.text:
After the PyPI release above has succeeded, from a checkout of the release tag:

python3 scripts/homebrew_formula.py 0.8.0 > ../homebrew-tap/Formula/autocode.rb
cd ../homebrew-tap
brew install --build-from-source ./Formula/autocode.rb && brew test autocode
git commit -am "autocode 0.8.0" && git push

The script refuses a version other than pyproject.toml's and a release with no source archive on PyPI. The formula builds a virtualenv on Homebrew's Python and links only the public autocode command; brew test checks that it reports the release's version.

docs.title: Cadence and qualification decision (#2048)
docs.text:
The proposed two-week release cadence remains an owner decision, not an enabled schedule. No automation or calendar promise is created by the installation correction. Until a cadence is agreed, releases use the explicit version/tag process above.

Before choosing the next release pin, review that revision's required CI, packaging/install checks and applicable supported-host/provider reliability record, preserving failed, skipped, unknown and unrun results. A distribution smoke pass or a prior tag's live sample does not qualify all newer master behavior. Record the exact candidate, missing evidence and agreed release gate;

docs.title: 2048 remains open for this policy decision. Do not publish the current master
docs.text: under the already-published 0.8.2 identity to avoid that decision.

docs.title: A pinned reliability campaign declaration
docs.text:
arena/campaign.json is the PLANNED first protocol slice of #634. It declares 13 tasks and two repetitions each: 26 scheduled rows. It contains no run results, and no campaign has been executed for it. It is a measurement specification, not a command accepted by the current Arena or scenario CLI. tools/reliability_ledger.py checks a published attempt ledger against it and reports the portfolio (below), and tools/reliability_import.py fills ledger rows from scenario and Arena result records (below). Automatic execution and fresh holdout rotation remain separate work in #634.

The tasks include the three hard Python Arena cases; the existing bug-fix, feature and greenfield scenarios; the transactional import, ledger, durable queue, outbox and event-replay ladder; interrupted verification reuse; and a review followed by a fix in the same run. Verification reuse is explicitly fixture evidence because its interruption comes from the scripted fault. Other tasks declare live execution. Their results must be reported separately.

docs.title: What is pinned
docs.text:
The source revision fixes the complete AutoCode and evaluator inputs. The manifest additionally records the selected profile, policy file hashes, full upstream base/reference commits and checks, and each task's entire definition tree, including briefs, seed, reference, broken controls and hidden tests. The build-comparison profile is copied from the existing profile definition; its existing role keys, models, efforts and extra options are preserved.

A definition hash is SHA-256 of compact ASCII JSON containing sorted rows [repository_relative_path, git_mode, sha256_of_blob_bytes]. Symlinks use their Git blob bytes and 120000 mode; they are not followed. files counts the rows. Tests read the local Git objects at the declared source revision, so later catalogue/profile changes do not rewrite this protocol's inputs. The manifest can be tested without importing an oracle, preparing projects, fetching upstream repositories or launching a provider:

.venv/bin/python -B -m unittest -v tests.test_reliability_campaign

The declared Python, psutil, native provider and package versions are future admission requirements, not evidence that those environments were qualified for all tasks. Before any attempt, capture and freeze its installed project and test dependencies and the actual runtime identities. Verify the original failing and passing controls, preserve all setup failures, and obtain the normal live-spend/approval authorization. The current Arena option whitelist does not consume this profile declaration; a future executor must prove its actual configuration matches, rather than assume a profile name applied it.

docs.title: Limits and attempt accounting
docs.text:
Scenario max_steps and harness wall time come from their original catalogue definitions, including the 90-minute ISO-week case and five-minute interrupted verification case. There is no blanket timeout override. Arena keeps the documented 3,600-second per CLI invocation timeout, 120-second oracle bound and three-iteration cap. These are not a 3,600-second total campaign ceiling; this declaration adds no total campaign ceiling or budget refill.

The report compares each attempt's spent budget with these limits. An attempt that spent more than a declared limit did not run under the pinned budget: it blocks a comparison, and a PASS that did is not counted as a verified delivery. A harness that stops an attempt at its limit can record slightly more than the limit; the report still shows it as over, since a ledger row cannot tell that from a larger budget.

Freeze the manifest hash before admission. Every schedule ID must appear exactly once in the published attempt ledger, including failures, errors, skips, unexercised or interrupted work and unattempted DEFERRED rows. Keep the native status/verdict, actual models/efforts, independent oracle evidence, elapsed time, interventions and spent budget. Unknown usage or cost stays null, never zero. Publish failed comparisons beside successes; do not replace a failed repetition with a successful retry. A new attempt needs a new declared schedule, with the original evidence retained.

AutoCode saying complete alone is not delivery proof. Preserve the existing Arena and scenario verdicts: an Arena STOPPED result does not by itself prove that stopping was appropriate. Fixture passes do not qualify a live version; incomplete attempts block comparison and no result automatically promotes code. The Arena holdout split consists of public historical cases, not private or contamination-free holdouts. This finite protocol makes no statistical reliability or model-effectiveness claim.

docs.title: Attempt ledger and portfolio report
docs.text:
The ledger is the published record of a campaign: one JSON object naming the declaration's id and the SHA-256 of its exact bytes, and one row per scheduled attempt. Start from the template, which records every scheduled attempt as DEFERRED (not attempted), and replace a row as its attempt ends:

.venv/bin/python tools/reliability_ledger.py template arena/campaign.json > ledger.json
.venv/bin/python tools/reliability_ledger.py report arena/campaign.json ledger.json
.venv/bin/python tools/reliability_ledger.py report arena/campaign.json ledger.json --json

The report command reads files only. It runs no AutoCode, oracle or model, never rescores a native outcome and never promotes a version. It refuses a ledger, with exit status 2, when:

  • a scheduled attempt is missing, appears twice or an unscheduled one is added (a retry needs a new declared schedule; the original row stays);
  • the ledger names another declaration or its bytes changed after admission;
  • a row lacks a declared attempt field or adds an undeclared one;
  • a fixture row is relabeled live, or a native outcome is not one the task's harness produces;
  • a native PASS contradicts its own status (a stop on a task that expects completion) or carries a failing oracle check;
  • a non-PASS row has no reason, or a DEFERRED row carries a status, oracle result, elapsed time, usage, cost or spent budget (an attempt that spent anything ran, and keeps its native outcome).

It also refuses a declaration that weakens the acceptance rules it applies, lists a native outcome that has no portfolio outcome below, or declares a task without a limits object whose values are finite nonnegative numbers: the spent budget is compared with those limits, so a task cannot leave them out.

Each row holds the declared fields. source_revision is the full commit that ran, or null when the record does not establish one (a checkout with uncommitted changes, or an Arena runner that is not the declared revision); a null revision is reported as a deviation. oracle_checks is a list of {name, ok} or null when ungraded, interventions_decision_or_repair a list of {kind, note} with kind decision (a legitimate answer or approval) or repair (a person fixed the work), and elapsed_seconds, estimated_usd and each spent_budget value a nonnegative number or null when unknown. spent_budget names its amounts after the task's declared limits (harness_minutes and max_steps for a scenario; cli_invocation_seconds, oracle_seconds and max_iterations for Arena). Each declared limit is reported as within, over or unknown: a spend equal to the limit is within it, and a missing or null spend is unknown, never within. runtime_identity names the pinned runtime versions and a dependencies freeze record; actual_models_and_efforts has the profile's provider, models and effort shape. An imported Arena row also keeps the runner options as forwarded (runner_options) and option_deviations, a list of strings naming each option that differs from the declared configuration (below). A live row that lists any is reported as a deviation; a value that is not a list of strings is refused.

The report puts every attempt in exactly one portfolio outcome:

Portfolio outcome Native outcome and evidence Verified delivery PASS at a completion status, every oracle check passing (for Arena, every declared upstream check present), evidence references, the declared revision, runtime and live profile, and no repair Verified delivery after a human repair The same, with at least one repair intervention Appropriate stop PASS at a stop on a task that expects a stop; none of this campaign's tasks does Native PASS without complete evidence A PASS missing checks or evidence, recorded on another or no revision, runtime or profile, or over a declared limit False completion FALSE_COMPLETE Stopped (appropriateness not established) Arena STOPPED or scenario HONEST_BLOCKER Ended without completing or stopping Arena FAIL Error ERROR Skipped or never reached SKIPPED, NOT_EXERCISED Ungraded RUNNING, INTERRUPTED_UNGRADED, PENDING_UNGRADED Not attempted DEFERRED

Live and fixture attempts are counted in separate sections and never pooled. Each section also reports decisions and repairs, cost across every attempt including failures (an unpriced attempt keeps the total unknown, beside the known subtotal), cost per verified delivery without repair, and elapsed time. Each section counts the attempts within every declared limit, over at least one, and with a spend unknown. A comparison is reported as blocked while any attempt has no judgement, differs from the declared revision, runtime or profile, or spent more than a declared limit. Evidence references are the evaluator's declarations: the report checks their presence, not their authenticity.

docs.title: Importing native results
docs.text:
tools/reliability_import.py fills a ledger's DEFERRED rows from the records the harnesses already write. The evaluator names the scheduled attempt each record belongs to; nothing is matched by guessing:

.venv/bin/python tools/reliability_import.py arena/campaign.json ledger.json \
  --scenario scenario/bugfix-iso-weeks/01 .scenario-runs/RUN/result.json \
  --arena arena/sympy-matrix-derivatives/01 .autocode/arena-hard-v1 ATTEMPT_ID \
  --runtime-identity runtime.json

--scenario takes a scenario run's result.json (or its evidence directory). --arena takes an Arena store directory and an attempt ID, and reads that attempt from the store's results.sqlite3, opened read-only. Both repeat. The ledger is updated in place, and the command prints each imported attempt's native outcome and portfolio outcome with any gaps, deviations or overruns.

The native verdict, status and oracle checks are copied as recorded, never rescored. What a record does not establish stays null:

  • A scenario run records its commit and whether tools/ held uncommitted changes; with changes, the revision is null. That flag covers tools/ only: a scenario record does not pin the scenario's own definition, oracle or checks, so an edited scenario under scenarios/ is not detected. Arena records a content identity of its runner's tools/, not a commit: the revision is the declared one only when that identity equals the declared revision's, read from local Git objects, and null otherwise.
  • An Arena store records each case's base commit, required checks and the SHA-256 of the oracle it ingested, and a digest of the whole case definition that each attempt repeats. The import reads the case as Arena does: a case whose digest no longer matches its definition, or whose digest is not the one the attempt ran against, is refused. Its oracle digest must equal the digest of the declared task's oracle.py at the declared revision, read from local Git objects; another oracle is refused. The import, and its tests, therefore need the pinned commit in local Git objects (git fetch --unshallow in a shallow clone).
  • A scenario run's cost is the status view's spent amount only when that view says it is complete; a floor is not the attempt's cost. Arena does not price attempts, so its rows' cost stays unknown.
  • The scenario harness measures its wall-clock drive time (harness_minutes) and its recorded CLI calls (max_steps). Arena measures none of its declared limits per CLI invocation, so they stay unknown.
  • A live scenario run records its resolved profile. Arena records the runner options it forwarded. The import reads the provider, and the model and effort AutoCode gives each role, from them in AutoCode's order: --single-model names every model, a role's own effort flag overrides --reasoning-effort (which the scenario harness writes as the builder's effort), and --resolver-model and --resolver-reasoning-effort override the resolver's --astra-* flags. It also compares the options as a whole with the declared configuration: the scenario harness's flags for the profile (--provider, --joint-planning, the profile's extra options and the role flags) and the task's --max-iterations cap. Each option that is missing, added or set to another value is recorded in option_deviations and reported as a deviation, so such an attempt's PASS is not a verified delivery. --test-command is not compared, since the declaration leaves each case's test command to the evaluator. A scripted (--fake) or hybrid run is fixture evidence and cannot fill a live row. A hybrid run is recognized by the -hybrid part of its mode, which the harness sets before it sets up the hybrid route, so a hybrid run skipped before that setup is fixture evidence too.
  • Neither record holds the runtime versions or the dependency freeze. --runtime-identity adds the evaluator's admission record (a JSON object with the pinned runtime keys and dependencies) to every row the call imports; without it, those rows report the runtime as not recorded.

Each answer and gate the harness gave on the person's behalf, and Arena's benchmark plan approval, is recorded as a decision, its note naming the answer's source or the gate. Neither harness records a repair: if a person repaired an attempt's work, add a repair intervention to its row by hand.

The import refuses, with exit status 2 and the ledger unchanged, when the ledger already fails a check of the report, a row already holds an attempt (a retry needs a new declared schedule), a record would fill two rows, the record is of another task or kind, an Arena case in the store pins another base commit, other checks or another oracle than the declared task or changed after the attempt, or the resulting ledger fails any check of the report.

A scenario attempt the harness admitted but never graded has an attempt.json and no result.json; the import refuses it rather than judge whether its process is still running. Import it once it finishes. When scenarios/run.py stats reports it INTERRUPTED_UNGRADED or PENDING_UNGRADED, write its row by hand: that native outcome, oracle_checks null, the run's evidence directory in evidence_refs, whatever the attempt record establishes (revision, profile, elapsed time) and null for the rest, and a reason. The report checks the hand-written row like any other.

docs.title: Replay a saved run
docs.text:
← Back to README

Replay drives a fresh AutoCode task run with a saved brief, model routes and provider events. It makes no model calls. Normal replay runs the current verification checks again; a previous PASS cannot establish a current PASS. The original run and its evidence remain unchanged.

# Export a portable recording from a saved run.
autocode replay /work/project/.autocode/runs/RUN --export /work/recording

# Re-drive it in an empty, isolated workspace at this exact fresh run path.
autocode replay /work/recording --into /work/reproduced/.autocode/runs/reproduction

# A saved run can also be replayed directly; export happens before launch.
autocode replay /work/project/.autocode/runs/RUN \
  --into /work/reproduced-again/.autocode/runs/reproduction --json

The destination must be an immediate child of the new workspace's .autocode/runs/. The workspace must be empty before replay prepares its recorded initial source. Existing run directories, including empty ones, and symlink destinations are refused. A replay is created at its selected path; its bound artifacts are never moved from a temporary run directory.

An explicit initial --workflow choice is replayed only at creation. A job chosen by the model keeps its recorded Job recognizer dispatch; replay does not infer a workflow pin from the final job or skip that dispatch. Older bundles without this explicit choice retain their original validation behavior.

The recording includes only the selected source payloads, stage artifacts, launch policy and semantic operator decisions. It does not carry the original provider configuration, credentials, environment, Git hooks or approval tokens. Its source and artifact payloads have digest and size checks. Inspect a bundle before sharing it: source files and model-authored prose can themselves contain private project data.

Every recorded provider dispatch must match the current stage, occurrence, model route, session continuation and source. Plan approvals and answers also must match the current public request, including a plan's scope exclusions and Git delivery terms. Older recordings that omitted those fields cannot authorize new nonempty exclusions or a commit obligation; replay refuses that mismatch. Replay displays the new plan and uses fresh tokens from that run. It never invents an answer or adopts an old token after a mismatch. A project's require-approver does not apply: no person approves in a replay (Required approver).

Replay stops with REPLAY_REFUSED when a payload is missing, changed or outside the supported format, or when the current controller asks for an unrecorded stage or different operator decision. It cannot reconstruct already overwritten evidence. A historical hash snapshot is sufficient only when its exact bytes can still be recovered from a saved source capture, a Git revision or a matching current file. The final tree cannot substitute for a missing intermediate tree. A recording that ended before a trustworthy provider exit cannot be emitted as a completed attempt.

A recorded answer may name an identity that digests where the original run happened, such as the independent Tester's changed-line gap_ids (each one digests the proof's source revision and execution context). The recording keeps what each one stably identifies (the gap's exact file, bytes and line), and replay re-derives the current value from that identity. A citation of the proof file itself binds to the replay's own proof, whatever its directory is named. A gap whose file, bytes or line differ in the replay is not rebound, and a replay whose Tester runs without a current changed-line proof refuses rather than guess. The archived check commands compare without the interpreter's location: /usr/bin/python3 -m unittest discover -v on the recording host is the same obligation as the replay host's own python3.

Replay preserves the Plan Reviewer's archived effective reasoning effort instead of reducing it again for a small task. Review allowances still apply, and each dispatch must match its recorded route exactly. Optional provider light_effort values remain part of the portable role configuration.

The format stores the saved role configuration, not its complete configuration history. If one role used different efforts at earlier stages, its final saved effort may not reproduce those stages; replay refuses that mismatch. It does not guess an earlier tier for legacy recordings.

The first recording format supports serial Builder dispatches. Export refuses concurrent Builders, retained protected-test files or commands, and external visual or Figma startup. Those paths need additional portable evidence; export does not drop them to make a recording appear replayable. An empty protected-test binding is recreated by the fresh runner.

Fresh checks also require the evidence their current verifier expects. Some older report-file provider archives lack retained tool-command receipts; replay refuses those paths instead of copying old supervision records into current proof. The original check summary must also be retained. For older runs without its explicit reference, export requires one owned summary matching the saved digest; a missing or ambiguous match causes refusal.

docs.title: Recorded checks
docs.text:
autocode replay /work/recording \
  --into /work/simulated/.autocode/runs/reproduction --recorded-checks --json

This explicitly simulates archived checks instead of running them. A simulated completion is REPLAY_COMPLETE, with replay_result.simulated true, completion_current false and done false. Its recorded verdict describes the historical run; it supplies no current delivery or canonical completion proof. Missing, invalid or mismatched check evidence causes refusal, never a fabricated PASS. Use normal replay when current check results matter.

Recorded checks currently support serial runs with one milestone covering all approved criteria. Multiple milestones, active progressive execution, protected oracles, and brief, lifecycle or visual evidence obligations are refused. The usual semantic checks still require the current contract, task, criteria, findings and human reviews to match; an archived PASS cannot override a gap. Recorded regression checks also require an authenticated pristine Git baseline and proof for every required named case. Missing or unsupported baseline mappings cause refusal.

docs.title: Public task-run interface
docs.text: The CLI uses TaskRun, including its ordinary approval and answer methods. Status adds replay_progress with the recording digest, check mode, dispatch count and next recorded dispatch, plus replay_result for a simulation result. replay_source exposes the bounded export projection of the saved run. These fields do not grant approval or establish evidence authenticity; the exporter and ordinary runner still validate the artifacts they consume.

docs.text:

docs.title: Task-type scenarios
docs.text:
← Back to README

The runner must handle more than one kind of engineering request. This catalogue freezes one scenario per request type, each with an independent oracle that scores the delivered workspace. The oracle never reads the runner's own reports and never uses a candidate's green tests as the sole verdict. Runner honesty scenarios (crash, budget, lying Builder) live separately under test-scenarios/; the complexity ladder they both serve is the progressive testing plan.

ID Request type What is asked What the oracle executes BUGFIX-01 Fix a bug in committed code Blank or whitespace-only name must exit 2 with usage; existing tests kept; no README or file changes Five invocations; seeded test names still present; candidate suite passes on the candidate and fails on the seeded bug (the regression is real); README byte-identical; no extra files FEATURE-01 Add a feature to an existing project list --tag TAG case-insensitive filter in a seeded notes CLI with saved data; old commands and store format unchanged Delivered notes.json must exist and be byte-identical to the seed; filters on mixed-case tags against a scratch copy; no-match, empty tag and missing value behavior; scratch store unchanged after reads; add still works; seeded tests kept and suite passes ARCH-01 System architecture task ADR, architecture/components.json, per-component contracts, stub packages, and a checker that enforces the declared import boundaries ADR sections; exact component set, required edges, acyclic, disjoint ownership; contract operations are callable in services/<id>/api.py; AST import checks include relative, comma-separated and nested-package imports, excluding docstring examples. The delivered checker must pass the candidate and an allowed-import control, then reject an injected forbidden static import without a traceback or syntax error. Injection preserves docstrings and future imports PROGRAM-01 Large requirement: many components, parallel build, combine, deploy descriptors Catalog, cart, checkout and gateway as separate stdlib HTTP processes, shared contracts, run_local.py, an e2e test, and compose descriptors Checks all four contracts/<shape>.json files for object type and required field declarations. Runs delivered run_local.py on free ports; independently drives the gateway journey (list, add two items, checkout total, cart cleared, empty-cart 409, order lookup, unknown order 404); sends SIGTERM and checks launcher exit and closed ports within five seconds. Delivered unittest e2e discovery must run at least one test and exit successfully; assertion quality is not checked. Compose lists all four services; descriptors are never executed UI-01 Design → implementation (Figma stand-in) Implement a frozen design/spec.json as one self-contained web/index.html plus a stdlib structural test Static: ids, labels, role=status, viewport meta, DOM order, no external resources, tokens. In Chromium via Playwright: state/disabled maps, transitions, cancelled note, one-row desktop layout, stacked 44px targets at 375px, no horizontal scroll. Without a browser the result is DEFERRED, never PASS

The pre-existing LIVE-01, LIVE-02, LIVE-05 and LIVE-06 scenarios stay registered unchanged. python3 tools/live_trial.py --list prints the whole registry.

docs.title: Where the pieces are
docs.text:
• tools/task_scenarios.py: seeds, briefs and oracles. PROGRAM-01 runs as one run with parallel milestone Builders.
  • tools/scenario_references.py: a handwritten reference delivery per scenario. They are the oracle's positive control and a starting point for a scripted fixture provider; they are not model output.
  • tests/test_scenario_oracles.py: exercises positive and targeted negative controls. The references pass (UI defers without a browser); seed-only controls do not pass; and targeted breakages fail on the expected row (a fix without a regression test, a case-sensitive filter, a filter that rewrites or deletes the store, a vacuous architecture checker, relative and comma import violations, unrelated checker crashes, a wrong checkout total, an uncleared cart even with green no-op candidate tests, missing contracts, empty or miswired launchers, failed shutdown, empty or failing e2e suites, a missing service, a wrong UI transition, an unstacked mobile layout). Positive controls include alternate stdlib JSON serializers.

docs.title: Running a scenario
docs.text:
Offline oracle controls (no provider, no model spend):

python3 -m unittest tests.test_scenario_oracles

Score a workspace you delivered by any route (a manual run, a dashboard run, a task worktree). The report lands in the evidence bundle:

python3 tools/live_trial.py BUGFIX-01 --score-only /path/to/delivered/workspace

Drive a scenario through the real CLI. The driver seeds the workspace, launches autocode, serves the explicit human gates (--answer, --approve-goal) from the saved state, and scores the result with the oracle. The runner's own completion claim is never the verdict:

# Harness check only: the scripted fixture provider implements LIVE-01.
python3 tools/live_trial.py LIVE-01 --profile fixture --workspace /tmp/trial

# Authorized live trial of a task type.
python3 tools/live_trial.py FEATURE-01 --profile glm53-mimo --workspace /tmp/trial \
  --i-authorize-live-model-spend

Exit codes and verdicts follow testing: PASS (0), HONEST_BLOCKER (2, a recorded pause rather than delivered work), FALSE_COMPLETE/FAIL/ERROR (1). --score-only exits 2 for DEFERRED.

--i-authorize-live-model-spend never authorizes deployment. PROGRAM-01 generates descriptors as ordinary code, and nothing is deployed.

docs.title: When a scenario counts as reliably passing
docs.text:
The live qualification rule (#110, as practised): a rung passes only with 3 fresh live PASS runs in a row on one profile, with zero FALSE_COMPLETE, each judged by that scenario's own oracle. Fresh means every run starts from a clean checkout with no reused workspace or run state. A rung passes on any one profile, and the profile that passed is recorded (for example glm53-openai, default, claude-tiers). Fake runs (--fake) are used on every change; live runs are spent only at qualification rungs and need explicit spend authorization.

The FX04 frozen-reference fixture for LIVE-04's 7-state × 3-viewport matrix was not created. That matrix is owned by the Figma design-coverage track (#250 coverage manifests, #251 rendered comparison, #297 deterministic PNG comparison); tests/test_catalogue_t12.py records the remaining gap.

docs.title: Limits, stated plainly
docs.text:
• All five task types were attempted on 2026-09-26 with the glm53-mimo profile. None delivered a completed product within the recorded budgets: planning and report repair exhausted the attempts. The registry records ERROR, not PASS; VALIDATION.md distinguishes external interruptions from enforced deadlines, includes independent post-stop scores, and records source/driver identities. These bounded failures are not a ranking of the models or proof that the tasks cannot be solved. Offline controls still cover only references and selected defects. A later BUGFIX-01 retest with stable report-repair inputs reached the Builder but still exhausted its 1,200-second budget without delivery; its baseline remains ERROR.
  • One case per task type is a capability example, not a general pass rate.
  • The scripted fixture provider implements only the greeting scenario, so --profile fixture exercises the harness for LIVE-01 only. Other scenarios need a live profile or --score-only on a delivered workspace.
  • UI-01 is a stand-in for the Figma route. The real design workflow (autocode ui ... --build, Figma) needs the Codex Figma plugin and has no offline oracle. UI-01 tests the implementation half against a frozen reference; it does not test Figma inspection or design generation.
  • ARCH-01 examines static Python imports, not dynamic imports or the semantic quality of architecture decisions. Its paired checker controls rule out the demonstrated syntax/import-crash false positives, not every possible unrelated failure or an adversarial checker tailored to the controls.
  • PROGRAM-01 checks contract field declarations, not complete JSON Schema type semantics. Delivered e2e discovery checks successful, nonempty execution, not assertion quality or candidate-test coverage. Independent HTTP checks decide the sampled behavior even when the candidate tests are green no-ops.
  • PROGRAM-01 checks compose service names, not image builds, networking or deployability. Its brief asks for descriptors that are never executed in the task. Nothing is deployed.
  • These oracles execute candidate Python locally; they are not a security sandbox. Subprocess deadlines and process-group cleanup bound ordinary hangs and clean up ordinary descendants, but do not contain hostile code or children that detach into a different process group. Launcher shutdown checks cover SIGTERM and listener closure, not every Ctrl-C race or possible non-listening background worker.
  • The driver serves default answers to open questions and approves the displayed plan token. That is test automation, not a person's judgement; do not count a driven run as human acceptance where a criterion requires human review.

See also: Testing plan · Testing

docs.title: Spec-first runs
docs.text: --spec-first (off by default; new runs with joint planning on the default flow) changes two points of a build, so that what you approve is what gets built (#1200).

docs.title: 1. You confirm the requirements before any plan exists
docs.text:
Every time Requirements produces a handoff, the run stops with one question (needs.kind answer, id requirements-review-…) beside the handoff's own open questions. It shows what Requirements understood: the outcome, the behaviors, the acceptance examples, the constraints, what it left out and its assumptions.

  • Answer plan to start the job: the Planner for a build, the Investigator for a bug fix, the Code Reviewer or the Designer for a review or a design.
  • Answer anything else to correct it: Requirements runs again with your answer and asks again.
  • --feedback works as usual.

The handoff names the job Requirements understood (job: build, bugfix, review, design, discuss, or none while no outcome is named yet), and the question says what approving starts. Only a build or a bug fix needs behaviors and acceptance tests; a review, a design or a question names its outcome and nothing else. A question is never asked to be approved: once Requirements understands it and has nothing to ask, the Analyst answers it straight away. The Job recognizer runs only when Requirements named no job (#1846). Every run, chat or not, starts at Requirements and has it name the job (#1860); what spec-first adds is the confirmation before the job starts.

Adaptive planning never skips Requirements on such a run. Planning, plan review and plan approval are unchanged.

Without the setting, a complete handoff goes straight to the job Requirements named: planning for a build, the Investigator for a bug fix, the Code Reviewer, the Designer or the Analyst for the others. A handoff that has only questions so far, with no behaviors or acceptance tests yet, still stops the run for your answers on any flow, and Requirements runs again with them; only the confirmation of a complete handoff is spec-first's own.

docs.title: 2. The Tester writes the acceptance tests before the Builder
docs.text:
After you approve the plan, and before the first Builder call, the run goes to write_acceptance_tests. The Tester (the Validator's model, on a session of its own) writes one test per approved test:/guard: case, named as the case says, changing only test files. The runner then runs those files on the code as it is:

Case Required on today's code test: (new behavior) the test fails, or its file cannot load because the product lacks what it imports guard: (must keep working) the test passes

A report that breaks this is rejected, and the Tester's retry gets the runner's result.

When the code already does what a test: case says, the Tester keeps the test and reports the case as already working; once the runner sees that test pass, it sends the plan back: it relabels that case guard: (must keep working), the Plan Reviewer reviews the corrected plan, and you approve it as any plan. Then the Tester runs again. A case sent back once that disagrees again, a case no test can show, and a bug's reproduction that already passes stop the run with PAUSED_ACCEPTANCE_TESTS; --feedback revises the plan.

A bug fix's cases are its Investigator's, plus any test:/guard: cases its plan adds: the Tester writes the reproduction tests, which must run and fail before the fix (a file that cannot load is no reproduction), and the preserve tests, which must pass. A reproduction that already passes pauses the run (PAUSED_ACCEPTANCE_TESTS): the diagnosis and the code disagree, and only --feedback can say which is right. A test: case the plan itself added that already passes is not that disagreement; it is sent back relabelled guard: and reviewed again, exactly as in a build (#1868).

In a plan with milestones, the Tester writes the cases due when a milestone is reached; a parallel batch gets the cases of every milestone in it at once. Tests for milestones not yet built are written later, so they never fail an earlier milestone's checks.

The Builder then works with the Tester's lines fixed. Its prompt names the files. It may add tests to them (a plan can name further tests in the same file), but every line the Tester wrote must stay, in order. When an attempt changes or deletes one, the runner puts the file back and sends the Builder straight back, naming the file (twice per plan; after that the attempt is rejected). A parallel batch whose patch removes or changes a Tester line is not integrated (PAUSED_ACCEPTANCE_TESTS; --retry-builder rebuilds that member). A test weakened by an added line (a skip, an early return) still fails the final regression proof, which needs each case's test to fail without the change. The status view's acceptance_tests field shows the files, the cases and how each test behaved on the code before building. The final regression proof (fails without the change, passes with it) is unchanged.

docs.title: Blind tests (--blind-tests)
docs.text:
--blind-tests (off by default; implies --spec-first) runs the Tester before the Builder starts, but isolates the test code from the Builder entirely (#702):

  • The Tester writes the tests and the runner verifies them on base code (test: criteria must fail; guard: must pass).
  • The runner archives the tests in evidence and removes them from the workspace.
  • The Builder gets no prompt note naming the test files, and workspace protection is not applied because the files are not in the workspace. The Builder never sees the test implementation.
  • Before independent validation (sol, astra_checkpoint) and completion review (astra_review), the runner executes the archived tests in a candidate scratch worktree.
  • Any test failure in the candidate scratch tree opens a blocking runner finding (source="runner"), preventing completion and appearing in open findings for review. When tests pass on candidate, the finding resolves.
  • The status view's acceptance_tests field marks blind: true.

docs.title: Task lanes and multiple tasks
docs.text: ← Back to README

docs.title: Connected task lanes
docs.text:
Use autocode tasks (or autocode-tasks) when several complete Autocode tasks must run in order or independently. Tasks inside one lane run sequentially in the same worktree, so later tasks see earlier source changes. Different lanes use different worktrees and may run concurrently. Every item invokes the normal UI or code loop; the task runner does not replace planning, validation or completion gates.

{
  "version": 1,
  "name": "dashboard release",
  "lanes": [
    {
      "id": "application",
      "tasks": [
        {"id": "design", "mode": "ui", "task": "Design the operations dashboard"},
        {"id": "build", "mode": "code", "task": "Build the dashboard", "ui_from": "design"},
        {"id": "polish", "mode": "code", "task": "Polish loading and error states"}
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "documentation",
      "tasks": [
        {"id": "guide", "mode": "code", "task": "Write the operator guide"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

autocode tasks flow.json --workspace /path/to/project --max-parallel 2

The command saves its checkpoint under .autocode/task-flows/. A code task can pause at its normal plan-approval or intervention boundary; its run_dir appears in the JSON result. Review or resume that ordinary Autocode run, then invoke the same task-flow command again. Completed UI tasks can feed a later code task through ui_from. --dry-run validates and previews the lanes without creating worktrees.

Parallel lanes intentionally remain separate branches. Autocode does not guess how to merge parallel source changes. Put dependent tasks in one lane, or explicitly merge completed branches before starting a task that combines them.

docs.title: Building components of an architecture in parallel
docs.text:
autocode components ARCHITECTURE --workspace REPO takes a design already committed in REPO — components.json, dependency_trace.json and contracts/*.schema.json — and builds each component as its own AutoCode task run under REPO/.autocode-components/<id>, in parallel with any component it does not depend on. A component owns only components/<id>/; this is checked against its actual changes at integration, not only requested in its brief.

autocode components architecture --workspace /path/to/project --joint-planning

Without --auto-approve, a component that needs a plan approved, a question answered, or a review accepted stops there; inspect and resume it directly with autocode --workspace /path/to/project --run-dir RUN_DIR --status, using the run_dir this command prints for that component. --auto-approve answers those for every component automatically, including approving the displayed plan — an explicit person's decision to delegate, not a default choice.

--integrate TARGET combines every finished component's changes into TARGET (created fresh from the repository's HEAD if it does not exist yet), left uncommitted for review, the same way a single AutoCode task leaves its own work. An existing TARGET must be the top directory of a worktree of the same repository; anything else is refused before a file is written. Components are always parts of one repository; for work in separate repositories see Work that spans several repositories. Extra flags for the underlying task runs (models, reasoning effort, provider) go after --options, shell-quoted.

docs.title: A component with a Figma design
docs.text:
Design the screen before starting the component build. In components.json, give that component a ui_run pointing to a completed, accepted AutoCode UI run. Relative paths resolve from the architecture directory, not from the component worktree:

[
  {
    "id": "web",
    "description": "Team dashboard using the accepted screen design",
    "requirements": ["R1"],
    "depends_on": ["api"],
    "publishes_contracts": [],
    "consumes_contracts": ["team"],
    "ui_run": "../.autocode-ui/runs/ACCEPTED-RUN"
  },
  {
    "id": "api",
    "description": "Team API",
    "requirements": ["R2"],
    "depends_on": [],
    "publishes_contracts": ["team"],
    "consumes_contracts": []
  }
]

The UI run may live outside the repository. Its accepted handoff and artifacts are validated before any component starts. The component receives its ownership and contract brief plus the accepted UI brief through the ordinary --ui-run build path. It still owns only components/web/, and plan approval and independent implementation review remain required.

Alternatively, use "figma_file": "https://www.figma.com/design/FILEKEY/Project" to supply an existing Figma reference. That URL alone does not establish an accepted design run. Choose one field per component. Components without either field keep their ordinary text brief.

Figma implementation requires the existing native Codex Figma workflow, ChatGPT login and the connected Figma plugin; use --engine codex for this build. Any other explicit --engine is rejected before components start. See Figma design and implementation for setup and visual verification. Implementation and review inspect the live file because it can change remotely. This command consumes an existing design; it does not create a design run.

Progress is saved in .autocode-components/manifest.json as each component starts and stops. Running the same command again continues the build: finished components are left alone, and a component that stopped for input picks up from where it stopped, in the same worktree and run. You can answer or approve that component's own run directly first, or pass --auto-approve the second time. If components.json, a contract or an accepted UI handoff changed since the saved build, the command refuses to resume, because the saved components were built against the old contracts or designs; remove .autocode-components/ to rebuild from scratch. A worktree the manifest does not record is refused too, rather than guessed at. Rerunning with the same --integrate TARGET is safe: a component whose exact result TARGET already holds (the same content and file mode at every path it changed) is left alone and listed in the summary's integration.already_applied, and a component that finished since is added. A component is applied only to a TARGET that holds none of its result yet, so a rerun never applies a change twice. Otherwise integration stops at that component and names the paths that differ. If TARGET was edited there or is checked out at another commit, the message says to integrate into a new target. If HEAD itself changed those paths since the component was built (for example, an earlier integration was committed and then edited), a new target would differ the same way, so the message says to rebuild the component: remove its worktree .autocode-components/<id> and run the command again.

docs.title: Declaring how a component runs
docs.text:
A row of components.json may carry an optional runtime block saying how that component runs once the system is combined. It is checked before any component starts, and it adds instructions to that component's brief, which tells each Builder how its component will be run. --run-local starts the components this way (see Running the combined system locally).

For a runnable architecture request naming components.json and runtime, smoke or Compose, the architecture Planner receives this runtime grammar and must deliver a runtime block for every component plus smoke.json as design data. The smoke flow must cross component boundaries, not merely check health. This is architecture work; it does not start Docker or authorize deployment.

{
  "id": "gateway",
  "description": "Forwards note requests to the store",
  "requirements": ["R2"],
  "depends_on": [],
  "publishes_contracts": [],
  "consumes_contracts": ["note"],
  "runtime": {
    "kind": "service",
    "port": 8002,
    "start": "python3 server.py",
    "health": "/health",
    "runtime_depends_on": ["store"],
    "env": {"GREETING": "hello"}
  }
}

There are four kinds:

  • service: a long-lived HTTP server. It needs port and an HTTP health path.
  • worker: a long-running process with no port, for example a queue consumer. It has no port; health is optional.
  • database: built from its own dockerfile (a start command on the Python image cannot run a database). It needs port: the port is never published, but the database's Builder and the Builders of the components that connect to it are all told it, since none of them sees the others' code. health is a command and is required.
  • library: never started on its own. Its block is exactly {"kind": "library"}, and nothing may name it in runtime_depends_on.
Key Kinds Rules kind all Required: service, worker, database or library. port service, database (required for both) The port inside the container: an integer from 1 to 65535. start service, worker A shell command of one line, at most 1000 characters. It runs with /bin/sh -c in /app, in an image built from python:3.12-slim with components/<id>/ copied to /app. $PORT in it is expanded inside the container. dockerfile service, worker, database (required) A relative path inside components/<id>/, which is its build context: /-separated segments of letters, digits, ., _ and -, with no empty, . or .. segment, at most 128 characters. The Builder writes the file. A service or worker takes exactly one of start and dockerfile. health service (required) An HTTP path that answers with a 2xx status once the service is ready: it starts with /, contains only letters, digits, ., _, ~, / and -, has no .., and is at most 128 characters. health worker (optional), database (required) A command run inside the container that exits 0 once it is ready: a JSON array of 1 to 32 nonempty one-line strings, such as ["pg_isready", "-U", "app"]. runtime_depends_on service, worker, database The components it connects to while running, each listed once. Each must be a service or a database, never itself, and the graph must have no cycle. It is separate from the build-time depends_on. env service, worker, database At most 32 extra environment variables. Names are upper case (A-Z, digits and _, not starting with a digit, at most 64 characters); values are strings of one line, at most 1000 characters. PORT and the names generated for a runtime dependency are reserved.

The block is refused if it has an unknown key, or if any string in it contains a backtick, a NUL, a line break (CR, LF, VT, FF, NEL, U+2028, U+2029 and the other characters Python splits lines on) or a lone surrogate (a \ud800-style escape that is not half of a pair). A row key that looks like a misspelled runtime (runtme, run_time, runtimes) is refused too; other unknown row keys are still ignored. The id of a component that runs (service, worker or database) must be a lowercase DNS label that starts with a letter (a-z, digits and -, at most 63 characters, not ending in -), because it becomes its container's host name and part of environment variable names. It must not be localhost, ip6-localhost, ip6-loopback, ip6-localnet, ip6-mcastprefix, ip6-allnodes or ip6-allrouters: inside every container those names mean the container itself, so a component connecting to one would reach itself. Library ids follow the ordinary component-id rule. Each refusal names the component and the key, and the command stops with a usage error before any component starts.

Each running component's container gets, in this order: PORT (when it has a port); for each runtime dependency, its address; then its own env. A service dependency store gives STORE_URL=http://store:8001. A database dependency db gives DB_HOST=db and DB_PORT=5432. A - in an id becomes _, so link-api gives LINK_API_URL. env values are used literally: they are committed with the architecture, which a model may have written, and nothing is taken from your own environment. Do not put real secrets in them.

The Builder's brief gains these sentences right after the line naming the directory it owns, before any contract lines:

  • A service: it runs as a long-lived HTTP service in its own container, must listen on 0.0.0.0 (not only on 127.0.0.1 or localhost) at the port in PORT, and must answer GET <health> with a 2xx status once it is ready.
  • A worker: it runs as a long-running process with no HTTP port and nothing connecting to it, and must keep running until it is stopped rather than exit when it is idle; with health, that command must exit 0 once it is ready.
  • A database: other components reach it only over the combined system's internal network, never through a published port; it must accept connections on its port on 0.0.0.0; its health command must exit 0 once it accepts connections.
  • With start: its container is built from python:3.12-slim with components/<id>/ copied into /app, and runs that command in /app. The command and any health command are quoted exactly as written, non-ASCII characters included.
  • With dockerfile: provide that file; it can copy only files from inside components/<id>/, and its image must start the component.
  • For each runtime dependency: reach it only through the variables above, never through a hard-coded host or port.
  • With env: the extra variables its container gets.
  • A library: it is not started on its own.

These sentences are obligations, so each component's Requirements stage traces them like the rest of its brief. Declare runtime blocks before the first build. A block lives inside components.json, so adding or editing one changes the saved build's identity, and a later run refuses to resume ("the architecture changed"); remove .autocode-components/ to rebuild. Records without runtime blocks build exactly as before.

docs.title: Declaring the smoke check
docs.text:
The architecture directory may also hold smoke.json, beside components.json and contracts/: the HTTP requests that show the combined system works. It is read only by --run-local, which starts the combined system on your machine (see Running the combined system locally); otherwise AutoCode ignores the file. It is not part of the saved build's identity, so editing it never forces a rebuild.

{
  "version": 1,
  "steps": [
    {"name": "create a note through the gateway", "service": "gateway", "method": "POST",
     "path": "/notes", "body": {"text": "hello"}, "expect_status": 201,
     "expect_json": {"text": "hello"}, "capture": {"note_id": "id"}},
    {"name": "read it back through the gateway", "service": "gateway", "method": "GET",
     "path": "/notes/{{note_id}}", "expect_status": 200, "expect_json": {"text": "hello"}},
    {"name": "the store holds it", "service": "store", "method": "GET",
     "path": "/notes/{{note_id}}", "expect_status": 200, "expect_json": {"text": "hello"}}
  ]
}

The file has exactly two keys: version, which is 1, and steps, a list of 1 to 30 steps. Each step is one request:

Key Rules name Optional: 1 to 80 printable characters on one line, unique across steps. Defaults to step N. service Required: the id of a component of kind service. A worker has no port and a database's port is never published, so check a database through a service that uses it. method Required: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE. path Required: starts with /, at most 300 characters of printable ASCII with no spaces, and no :// or @. It may carry a query string. body Optional: any JSON value, sent as application/json. Not allowed on GET or DELETE. expect_status Required: the exact HTTP status expected, an integer from 100 to 599. expect_json Optional: the JSON the response must match. An object matches when each of its keys is in the response and matches there, so the response may carry more keys; lists and other values must be equal, and true is not 1. capture Optional: {"variable": "key"} pairs. Each takes the value of a top-level key of the JSON response, which must be a string or an integer, for later steps. Variable names are lower case (a-z, digits and _, starting with a letter, at most 32 characters) and each is captured by one step only.

A later step uses a captured value as {{variable}} in its path or in a string value of its body; a step cannot use a value before an earlier step captures it, and {{ may not appear anywhere else: not in name, in expect_json, or in an object key of body, where nothing is filled in. In the path the value is percent-encoded, / included, so it stays one path segment or query value. In the body a string that is exactly {{variable}} becomes the captured value itself, so an integer stays an integer; inside a longer string the value is inserted as text.

Unknown keys, duplicate keys and anything outside these rules are refused, naming the step and the key; NaN, Infinity and a number too large to send (such as 1e999) are refused as invalid JSON. Steps run in order, each request going to its service's port on 127.0.0.1, without a proxy and without following redirects, and the check stops at the first step that fails. Nothing in smoke.json is run as a command.

docs.title: Running the combined system locally
docs.text:
autocode components architecture --workspace /path/to/repo --integrate integration --run-local

--run-local needs --integrate TARGET, and Docker with Compose v2 (the docker compose plugin, 2.17 or newer) and a running Docker daemon on this machine. Before any component is built, the command refuses with a usage error unless every component declares a runtime block, at least one is a service, the runtime dependencies have a start order, smoke.json is valid and sends requests only to services, docker compose version --short reports 2.17 or newer, docker version reaches the daemon, and that daemon is local: its endpoint is selected using Docker's precedence: nonempty DOCKER_CONTEXT first, otherwise DOCKER_HOST, otherwise the current/default context resolved by docker context inspect. Context resolution and rejection of a remote endpoint happen before daemon contact. The validated endpoint must be a unix:// or npipe:// socket. A daemon reached over tcp:// or ssh:// would publish the ports on its own machine, where the checks on 127.0.0.1 cannot reach them. --keep-running and --health-timeout are refused without --run-local.

The resolved local socket is pinned with docker --host <endpoint> for daemon checks and every subsequent startup, health/port query, log, teardown and recovery command. Changing the ambient context does not redirect an in-progress run. autocode doctor reports optional Docker, Compose and local-daemon readiness; missing or unsupported setup is WARN-only, not a blocker for ordinary builds. Doctor diagnoses setup but does not install Docker or start its daemon.
