After every component has finished and been integrated cleanly (otherwise the summary's local_run.status is not_run), it:

  1. Checks that TARGET holds components/<id>/ for each component that runs, and the dockerfile of each that declares one.
  2. Writes the Compose file to <workspace>/.autocode-components/.local-run/<project>/compose.json, never into TARGET or any tracked file. The leading dot keeps it apart from component worktrees, .autocode-components/<id>, since no component id starts with a dot. <project> is a new Compose project name for each run, autocode- and 12 hex digits, passed with -p.
  3. Starts the components in runtime-dependency layers, one layer at a time, with docker --host <endpoint> compose -p <project> -f <file> up -d --build --no-deps <ids>, and waits for the whole layer before starting the next: a service once GET <health> on its published loopback port (from docker compose port) answers 2xx; a worker or database with a health command once Compose reports it healthy; a worker without one once it is running. A container that exits or turns unhealthy fails at once, reported as <id> is not running (state <state>). Each layer may take --health-timeout SECONDS (a positive, finite number; default 120) to become ready.
  4. Runs the smoke steps in order against 127.0.0.1:<published port>, stopping at the first that fails.
  5. Tears the project down with docker --host <endpoint> compose ... down -v --remove-orphans --rmi local, on success, on failure and on Ctrl-C alike. This also removes the images the run built: every run is a new project, so they would otherwise pile up. --keep-running deliberately leaves it running instead and prints that down command to stop it.

A failed teardown or uncertain owned CLI-helper cleanup changes the result to failed, even if every smoke step passed. torn_down stays false and cleanup_detail explains why; stop_command is shell-quoted from the exact argv (including endpoint, project and file) for recovery. Intentional --keep-running is distinguished by kept_running: true, not misreported as successful teardown.

On a failure, the command prints which component or step failed and the last 50 lines of that component's logs (docker compose logs --tail 50). When no single component is to blame (up failed for a layer of several components, or docker compose ps failed while waiting on a layer), it prints the last 50 lines of each component in that layer. Progress goes to standard error. The JSON summary gains a local_run key: status (passed, failed or not_run), project, compose_file, layers, ready, ports (the published host port of each service), steps (each step's name, service, method, the path sent, the status received, ok and detail), failed_component, failed_step, detail, logs, torn_down and stop_command, docker_endpoint, cleanup_detail and kept_running. The exit status is 1 when the local run did not pass, including cleanup failure.

docs.title: Multiple tasks in one project
docs.text:
New implementation tasks automatically get separate Git worktrees and branches, so two terminal commands or dashboard conversations can use the same project:

autocode "Add billing history" --workspace /path/to/project
autocode "Fix search navigation" --workspace /path/to/project

Each task starts from the project's committed HEAD, on an autocode/<task>-<id> branch under .autocode/worktrees/. The original checkout and its uncommitted changes are retained. Commit changes first if new tasks should include them. Dependencies and ignored environment files are not copied into the new worktree. The command prints the task workspace and branch; the dashboard discovers its run through the registry. Each worktree has its own runner lock, checkpoints, and code. Two writers still cannot operate on the same worktree.

AutoCode's own directories (.autocode/, .autocode-components/, .autocode-ui/) each hold a .gitignore containing *, so run state, logs and nested task worktrees never appear in git status or get staged by git add -A in your checkout or in a task worktree. Your own .gitignore is not touched, and a .gitignore you already put in one of these directories is left as it is.

docs.title: When a task finishes
docs.text:
When a run in a task worktree completes, AutoCode commits the delivered source to the task's branch (autocode/<task>-<id>, author AutoCode <autocode@localhost>) and prints the branch and commit. Only the branch moves: the worktree is detached at the commit it started from, with the delivered changes still in its files, so the completion evidence (pinned to the worktree's HEAD) stays current and you can still inspect or run the result there. Later work in the same worktree, such as a rework after feedback, is committed on top at its next completion. Runs started with --in-place and components are never committed this way.

Review and merge the branch like any other, for example git merge autocode/<task>-<id> from your checkout. Then remove finished worktrees:

autocode clean-worktrees --workspace /path/to/project         # list what would be removed
autocode clean-worktrees --workspace /path/to/project --yes   # remove it

A worktree is removed only when every run in it is TASK_COMPLETE, its source is exactly what its branch holds, and no runner holds its lock. Its .autocode/ records (run state, logs, evidence) are copied to .autocode/archive/<worktree>/ first; the branch is kept. Anything else is listed with the reason it is kept. Worktrees an autocode program recorded are kept: that command is archived on the archive/program branch, and clean-up leaves what an older checkout's program owns. The dashboard and registry show a removed worktree's runs as workspace_missing.

Resume from the project while the task is its only unfinished run, or from inside the task worktree, or name the run from anywhere:

cd /path/to/project/.autocode/worktrees/TASK && autocode resume
autocode --run-dir /path/to/project/.autocode/worktrees/TASK/.autocode/runs/RUN

Existing runs retain their original checkout. --in-place explicitly starts a new task in the selected checkout. Only one run's agents work in a checkout at a time: a second run started there (or resumed there) while another run's agents are working prints which run holds the checkout and exits with status 2, changing nothing. Run the same command again once the other run stops, or start the task without --in-place so it gets its own worktree. Answering, approving or giving feedback to a waiting run launches no agent and is not blocked. AutoCode never merges branches; see When a task finishes for committing and removing worktrees.

See also: Figma design · Workflow

docs.title: Worker and design prerequisites
docs.text:
Start with --task-preflight qualification/preflight.json. Version 2 retains the basic manifest's inputs, checks, phases, recovery and resume flow. Every check adds execution: "runner" or "worker" and timeout_seconds (positive finite seconds, default 120). Runtime files may also be project-relative. Check arguments and fixtures are operator-approved inputs, never commands chosen by a model.

{
  "version": 2,
  "inputs": [],
  "runtime_files": [],
  "checks": [{
    "id": "named-imports", "phase": "planning", "execution": "runner",
    "argv": ["{python}", "{runtime}/autocode_preflight_unittest.py", "--named", "tests.test_example"],
    "contract": {"kind": "command"}, "timeout_seconds": 120,
    "recovery": "Correct the named import while preserving the test, then resume"
  }]
}

Admission runs at the provider launch boundary, including parallel workers and report repairs. Worker probes use the actual selected executable, role, model, sandbox and scrubbed child environment in both the workspace and its nested source copy. Native Codex uses its model-free sandbox helper with the selected read-only/workspace-write policy. OpenCode uses its actual agent and debug agent --tool; effective permissions are checked first because that diagnostic path auto-allows ask. Unresolved approvals block admission; the runner never grants permissions. Read-only planning can check design files with read even when bash is denied. OpenCode tool permissions are not an OS sandbox. Command providers currently fail closed for required worker probes: they have no supported model-free adapter. Runner checks cannot substitute for a required worker check. No probe falls back to a model call.

Version 2 checks poll pause requests and clean up their process group. Reuse requires unchanged bindings, including the worker, approved plan, command, runtime helper sources, inputs, packages and configuration. Set reuse: false for capabilities whose availability can change without a file change.

docs.title: Browser and deterministic fixture setup
docs.text:
Add a check like this to checks:

{
  "id": "browser-setup", "phase": "build", "execution": "worker",
  "reuse": false, "timeout_seconds": 120,
  "argv": ["node", "{runtime}/autocode_preflight_browser.cjs", "qualification/browser.json"],
  "contract": {
    "kind": "browser",
    "viewport": {"width": 652, "height": 188, "device_scale_factor": 1},
    "canvas": {"alpha": "composite", "background": "#ffffff"},
    "fonts": ["Inter"], "ready": ["catalogue-completed", "catalogue-nonempty"]
  },
  "recovery": "Restore the approved browser/fonts or correct fixture initialization, then resume"
}

The browser configuration supplies the same viewport/canvas, plus fixture: "qualification/browser-fixture.cjs", fonts: [{"family":"Inter","path":"qualification/Inter-Regular.woff2"}] and these explicit ready conditions:

[
  {"id":"catalogue-completed", "selector":"#catalogue", "attribute":"data-complete", "equals":"true"},
  {"id":"catalogue-nonempty", "selector":"#catalogue", "attribute":"data-nonempty", "equals":"true"}
]

The fixture exports async setup({page, context}) and async teardown({context}). Initialize the approved deterministic state in setup and release servers/resources in teardown, including on failure. The readiness attributes must reflect completed fixture/application state; do not set them just to satisfy a probe. Tests of a later unavailable state must start from the completed nonempty catalogue. This cannot prove every test race-free.

The helper uses the project's installed Playwright (playwright_module can select an approved installed package), launches Chromium, loads the actual font bytes, checks viewport/DPR, captures PNG bytes at the expected dimensions, then closes the context/browser. executable can select an approved browser; none is installed automatically. readiness_timeout_ms defaults to 10000 inside the outer deadline. Zero exit alone is insufficient: one structured AUTOCODE_PREREQUISITE={...} result must match every contract field and confirm setup, launch, capture and teardown. Declare fixture/config/font files in inputs and external browser/package identities in runtime_files. Add a distinct check with phase: "validate" when visual review also needs it.

docs.title: Figma inputs and readable context
docs.text:
A version 2 visual task requires design alongside checks. Store the approved export manifest and its files in a non-ignored public directory. Every declared file/frame/state needs one readiness case:

{
  "manifest": "qualification/design/manifest.json",
  "cases": [{
    "id": "composer.empty", "encoding": "mcp-text",
    "context_parts": ["qualification/readable/part-0000.txt"],
    "assets": ["qualification/send.svg"],
    "fonts": [{"family":"Inter", "path":"qualification/Inter-Regular.woff2"}],
    "canvas": {"alpha":"composite", "background":"#ffffff"}
  }]
}

Include the manifest, screenshots, raw context, every context part, asset and font in inputs with approved hash/size/mode. The public manifest must match the run's retained design manifest and any explicit Figma file/node URL. Both source roots are checked. Missing exports, omitted frames, altered references and inputs lost from the source copy block dispatch. Remote Figma access is not inferred from a URL or login: export the approved references first. Preflight never edits the Figma source or substitutes implementation captures.

Before approving the prerequisite manifest, split long escaped context into lossless parts that provider read tools can display completely:

python tools/autocode_preflight_design.py qualification/design/context.json \
  --encoding mcp-text --output qualification/readable

Encodings are text, json-string, or mcp-text (ordered MCP text blocks). Concatenated parts must equal the complete decoded source exactly; each part is at most 1600 UTF-8 bytes. They are not summaries. The gate records raw and decoded hashes, actually reads parts and PNG exports through the worker, and gives every stage the ordered paths and provenance. A matching worker browser contract must declare the viewport/DPR, canvas and fonts; its font receipt must identify the exact approved files. alpha: "preserve" requires background: null; composite requires an explicit six-digit color. These are capture prerequisites, never visual fidelity approval.

docs.title: Named proof eligibility
docs.text:
Use contract.kind: "proof", an explicit test_changes_allowed boolean and cases such as [{"id":"C1","selector":"test_product.T.test_c1","kind":"fail_to_pass"}]. Kinds are fail_to_pass and preserve; selectors carry the criterion ID using the same naming rule as the proof engine. Approved plan changes invalidate readiness and must match the case bindings.

The bundled unittest helper's arguments are ["{python}","{runtime}/autocode_preflight_proof.py","--inventory","qualification/controls.json"]. The inventory has selectors and controls: {"baseline":"qualification/base","reference":"qualification/reference","broken":"qualification/broken"}. Each directory contains its approved test and corresponding implementation. Each runs in a fresh interpreter in both source contexts, including unittest setup/teardown. Keep the fixture sources public and hash-bound.

Every named case must pass the reference and fail its broken control. Fail-to-pass cases must fail the baseline; preserve cases must pass it. ERROR, SKIP, aggregate-only output, omitted selectors and teardown failures block readiness. Fail-to-pass proof requires added/changed tests, so a policy forbidding all test changes blocks that incompatible contract before dispatch. Obtain an approved correction rather than relabelling a failed run, removing protected tests or weakening a proof marker. Fixture controls qualify the proof interface; the final candidate still needs fresh independent proof.

docs.title: Task prerequisites before paid dispatch
docs.text:
Start a run with --task-preflight MANIFEST.json to check operator-declared prerequisites before planning, building or validation. This is an opt-in gate for ordinary runs. Existing runs without a manifest retain their behavior.

A prerequisite runs in both the project workspace and a source copy beneath the actual run's .autocode/runs/.../preflight/.../scratch/candidate directory. The copy, linked dependencies, scrubbed environment, interpreter selection and process cleanup come from the verification engine. This catches setup that works at the project root but fails in the runner's nested copy. The runner does not guess a collection command from an arbitrary test command or execute a whole failing acceptance suite as a prerequisite.

docs.title: Basic command manifest (version 1)
docs.text:
Use version 2 for actual worker execution, browser readiness, readable Figma exports and proof eligibility. Version 1 remains a runner-environment command contract.

{
  "version": 1,
  "inputs": [],
  "runtime_files": ["/absolute/path/to/browser-executable"],
  "checks": [
    {
      "id": "named-and-discovered-tests",
      "phase": "planning",
      "argv": [
        "{python}", "{runtime}/autocode_preflight_unittest.py",
        "--named", "tests.test_example",
        "--discover", "tests", "--top-level", "."
      ],
      "recovery": "Correct the module import without removing tests, then resume",
      "reuse": true
    },
    {
      "id": "browser-and-font-access",
      "phase": "build",
      "argv": ["node", "qualification/check_browser_setup.cjs"],
      "recovery": "Restore the approved local browser/fonts and resume",
      "reuse": false
    }
  ]
}

argv is a nonempty argument array, not a shell script. {python} selects the repository's verification interpreter, {workspace} selects the current workspace or scratch root, and {runtime} selects this AutoCode runtime's directory. Both contexts must return zero. Commands are trusted operator inputs: do not declare model-generated commands, live providers, installs, product edits or an acceptance test whose intended baseline behavior fails. Probe output belongs in ignored temporary paths. Source mutation stops dispatch and preserves the workspace changes for inspection.

Each check requires a unique ID, a phase (planning, build or validate), arguments and a concrete bounded recovery instruction. Builder and parallel orchestration admission use build; Validator, checkpoint and completion review use validate; other stage boundaries use planning. Declare the checks needed for each phase; a check declared only for validation does not protect planning.

inputs declares public source-copy dependencies using the existing input inventory format:

{
  "path": "qualification/reference.png",
  "type": "file",
  "mode": "0644",
  "size": 1234,
  "sha256": "64 hexadecimal characters from the approved file"
}

inputs and runtime_files are task-wide prerequisites, checked in every phase. Phase-specific needs can be checked by that phase's explicit command instead. The file must match in both roots, including mode and hash. A matching ignored file omitted from the source copy blocks dispatch with its path and remedy. Store public proof assets in a non-ignored location; do not copy private run state to satisfy this check. runtime_files identifies external capability files whose current contents/metadata must invalidate receipt reuse. This does not copy them or approve their use by a provider.

A zero model/tool limit no longer makes a version 1 prerequisite unbounded: it uses a separate 120-second prerequisite timeout. No model route or stage budget changes. Version 2 declares a positive finite timeout per check.

docs.title: Collection helper
docs.text:
autocode_preflight_unittest.py loads named modules and/or discovery in separate interpreter processes, so discovery's sys.path additions cannot hide a broken named import. It rejects loader errors, empty collections and duplicate test identities. --expected-ids inventory.json additionally requires an exact operator-approved identity list for each selected mode, for example {"named": ["tests.test_example.Example.test_a"], "discovery": [...]}. Hash-bind that inventory through inputs; retain the canonical suite's declared scope and exclusions. This helper neither chooses a smaller suite nor runs methods. --exclusions exclusions.json audits collected discovery IDs mapped to nonempty reasons without removing their identities. Paired --setup module:function --teardown module:function hooks check the approved fixture lifecycle independently in each collection interpreter. Hook failures are setup errors; collection still never executes test methods.

Output says COLLECTION_READY and tests_executed: false. Collection and all other prerequisite receipts cannot establish test PASS, fail-to-pass proof, visual fidelity, independent acceptance or task completion. Existing proof and acceptance gates still execute independently.

docs.title: Receipts, reuse and recovery
docs.text:
--status / TaskRun.status() exposes task_preflight, including phase, READY/BLOCKED, errors and the retained receipt path/hash. During execution, the existing runner_check view identifies task_preflight and the probe log. The sole writer of the task_preflight state record is autocode_task_preflight.guard; status reads it without establishing proof.

Reuse requires the same phase and unchanged source snapshot, manifest, runtime Python sources, selected interpreter/executable identities, repository venv package records, scrubbed environment, declared inputs/runtime files, saved model routes, verification commands, limits and design-manifest identity. The receipt itself must still match its hash. Failed checks are never reused. A phase change, changed bindings or tampered receipt triggers fresh execution. Observable file/environment bindings do not reveal every dependency or OS permission change: declare relevant external files and use reuse: false for volatile capability/remote access probes.

On failure the run stops as PAUSED_TASK_PREFLIGHT before the affected provider dispatch. Inspect the exact log, apply an authorized bounded setup correction, then use the ordinary --resume-paused operation. To correct the manifest itself, supply --task-preflight NEW.json --resume-paused at that exact stopped boundary, with no active/uncertain stage or runner check. The CLI saves the old and new manifests in a user event; historical failure receipts remain. It does not install dependencies, alter pins/caps, approve a plan or weaken test gates.

docs.title: Scope of readiness
docs.text: Version 1 checks run in the runner test environment. Version 2 explicitly selects runner or worker execution; its status distinguishes worker_permissions_checked from native provider_sandbox_attested. The status view includes per-check receipts and design provenance. Readiness is never inferred from a login, a binary on PATH or a collected test name. It does not establish visual fidelity, race-free tests or candidate correctness.

docs.title: Task-run interface
docs.text:
← Back to README

How a program drives one AutoCode task run: start it, read where it stands, answer what it asks, and let it continue. This is the only supported way for code outside the runner (the scenario harness, autocode issue, the coding-agent skill and MCP server, and the planned architecture and multi-component layer) to control a run. Such code must not import runner internals such as autocode.py or read state.json directly; that file has about 140 keys and changes without notice.

A task run is bound to one workspace, one Git tree. The multi-component layer drives several task runs, but all of them come from the same repository; it cannot link runs in separate repositories. See Work that spans several repositories.

Every step is one CLI invocation, and the run's state lives on disk. A caller that crashes can reattach to the same run directory with TaskRun(workspace, run_dir), or with TaskRun.attach(workspace) if it never learned the run directory (it returns the workspace's only run, or None). In a workspace where someone else may also run AutoCode, note TaskRun.runs_in(workspace) before the start and pass it as attach(workspace, exclude=...), so that only a run created since can be adopted.

docs.title: Automatic coordination from chat
docs.text:
For an unresolved bug with grounded external scope, view.coordination names status_command, next_command and cancel_command. The terminal client reads autocode coordinate status --run-dir RUN --json and executes only its named actions. It does not read child state, select repositories or compose tests. /repos displays the shared local source catalog; configure its roots with autocode registry roots add PATH and standalone repositories with autocode registry repositories add PATH.

Initial Requirements and Investigator requests receive a pinned, bounded inventory of all configured sources, including external roots. The launch directory is optional context. Catalog file citations use catalog/ID/path:line and are accepted only when the cited ordinary file matches the pinned Git blob. The task retains the inventory at planning/source-catalog.json; changed catalogs, revisions or altered receipts cannot silently replace its evidence. Built-in read-only intake shells receive only the validated catalog directories as extra read roots; this grants no Builder write authority. Clear source-grounded bug requirements flow into the complete plan without a separate Requirements confirmation. Genuine unresolved business questions still pause for an answer. This also applies to the coordinator's joint verification task, whose workflow is build: its saved current joint identity or first-start intent authenticates that machinery. A retired, mismatched or ordinary standalone build retains its normal Requirements flow. No Requirements confirmation is recorded on the person's behalf, and the consolidated plan still requires exact approval.

view.request_sources carries the authenticated live human source texts as {id, kind, text} records, including Requirements clarifications. It excludes model prose and discarded answers. Coordination pins those exact records and carries their text into every member and joint brief. A changed source inventory invalidates the saved coordination and its approval, even if the opening task and repository scope are unchanged. Older unapproved, idle coordinations adopt the current inventory and refresh incomplete member briefs through public, receipted feedback actions. Interrupted feedback is reconciled against its public chat receipt; an uncertain outcome is never submitted twice. Approved or active work cannot use this recovery to replace its request.

The version-1 coordination view identifies the anchor, record revision, phase, member workspaces/runs/PRs, done, needs, and optional next_command and approval. The joint-test baseline and plan are prepared before any Builder. One approval binds the original request and its human-source inventory, source-catalog snapshot, repository membership and pinned baselines, plus every exact member and joint-plan token. Clients reread before approving. Pass its token privately as --token - with AUTOCODE_COORDINATION_TOKEN; providers never receive that variable. A missing or changed token authorizes nothing. A later revision of the coordinated plans (after a joint mismatch repair or a replanned joint test) whose every member and joint plan keeps the approved contract (acceptance criteria, constraints, permission boundaries, scope exclusions and Git delivery) is approved by the coordinator under that same approval as the automatic carry_approval step, recorded in the coordination state with the targets it covered; a revision that changes any of those, or adds a repository the person has not seen, is offered for approval again. A criterion's source citations are provenance, not a term: a repair's follow-up instruction becomes a run source and may add citations without changing the approved work (#2565). Repository-choice actions exist only for current catalog candidates. After member runs complete, a named coordinate bind action snapshots exact candidate trees, including deletions, for the already-approved joint test. Cancellation prevents further dispatch and submits only current members' named boundary-pause actions.

An approved automatic producer member whose due criteria are all guard: cases may deliver preservation tests alone. Its proof requires those named tests to pass on both the baseline and candidate, without a permission answer. Any product change retains the ordinary bugfix fail-before/pass-after requirement. Standalone bug fixes and the joint verification task do not receive this member allowance; the joint gate still requires the real combined regression to fail on baseline and pass on exact candidates. Completion review rechecks the proof when its preservation mode changes, even after repeated failures on unchanged source. A passing preservation proof also expires when that mode no longer applies; stable contexts keep normal reuse. A fresh authenticated preservation proof can retire an obsolete private completion blocker caused solely by the old product-code-only proof rule. The core archives the prior runner receipt and private proposal, then runs independent completion review. It grants no completion or approval and never withdraws published questions, permission requests, or blockers for other causes. When the spec-first Tester already wrote every due guard, an unchanged Builder may submit those exact archived test files for fresh independent review. The core checks approved producer membership, case coverage, receipt/source identities, file hashes, ownership and unchanged snapshots. This records a candidate handoff; regression proof, review and the joint gate still run normally. Concurrent member checkpoints wait up to ten seconds for the shared approval record lock. A longer hold still refuses the write; contention never releases approvals or starts a provider without its ordinary admission checks. If a linked repository assignment is recorded before its child action is refused, the coordinator offers that assignment again while the child still holds the exact scope question. Reopening takes the existing named advance action; it requires no repository selection or human answer. Other questions and stale scope identities remain untouched, and assignment grants no plan approval. A runtime-only repair may refresh the authenticated scope receipt before retiring it, including a prior refused-action pause. Source, contract, settings, accounting and other frontier changes still invalidate it; no answer or approval is manufactured. A fresh authenticated proof can also settle a runner finding on unchanged source when the retained earlier proof failed entirely at Go test collection because its disk was full. The core checks owned receipt chronology, matching source, log hashes and supervision receipts, and refuses any actual failing test name, mixed error or stale scope. Reviewer findings still require that reviewer to resolve or retract them; no product edit is manufactured for an environment repair, and no completion or approval follows from this reconciliation alone.

At a settled shared-cost stop, needs.kind=budget names the current finite cap, known accumulated spend, accounting completeness, minimum_cap_usd, and its own next_command argument array. Terminal chat shows these, fills only its --max-cost-usd N slot with the person's finite amount, confirms the whole-set total, rereads the offer and sends its token privately using AUTOCODE_COORDINATION_TOKEN. coordinate budget rejects changed checkpoints, active workers, uncertain or cancelled operations, insufficient amounts and zero/unlimited caps. It retains prior member, integration and verifier costs and all other settings. An existing sufficient shared cap may be reasserted. The action acknowledges only the displayed member's cost pause through TaskRun, with that run's current public recovery token and its derived share of the cap. It grants no plan approval, proof waiver or general recovery retry. Durable intent precedes the resume; an uncertain reply is retained for inspection and never automatically replayed. No saved member state is edited by coordination.

A settled cancellation offers needs.kind=coordination_resume. Its named coordinate resume --token TOKEN --max-cost-usd N action retains all work, attempts and accounting and launches no model. Terminal chat confirms the selected policy and rereads the exact kind and token. A finite amount keeps the planning allocation unchanged; an explicit 0 removes the shared spending cap and disables its planning allocation limit. The retained allocation and prior cap stay in history. Subsequent participant advances receive an explicit zero cap so they cannot silently inherit an old spending limit. Other limits, routes, approvals and verification gates remain unchanged. A child pause still requires its own public recovery. Active or uncertain work, incomplete pricing, changed source/catalog/checkpoint and duplicate requests refuse. Cancellation receipts are retained; a newer cancellation always takes precedence.

New coordinations with a finite cost cap reserve 70% for implementation and verification. Their shared planning allowance is 30% of the original cap, including the anchor's planning, every member's planning, report repairs and all retained joint attempts. While a run is planning its derived whole-run cap also respects that allowance; approved implementation uses the remaining task envelope. Replanning, viewer restart and reasserting a shared cap do not renew the planning allowance. Exhaustion refuses further dispatch, including when a projected next attempt exceeds the allowance. Unpriced planning returns needs.kind=blocked without a spending action. Saved coordinations without this policy retain their original limits. At a settled planning stop with complete pricing and unused whole-set money, needs.kind=planning_budget offers a distinct coordinate planning-budget action. The explicit --max-planning-cost-usd N is a total planning allocation, not an additional grant; it cannot exceed the whole-set cap minus nonplanning spend. Its token binds the durable coordination and public participant/source, route, approval, accounting and attempt frontier. The action records the old allocation and all spending, launches no model and approves no plan. Replaying its token refuses without changing the allocation. Terminal chat shows the bounds and unchanged total cap, confirms the amount and rereads before sending the private token. A child cost pause still needs its separate existing public acknowledgement. No restart or same-cap acknowledgement increases planning money. Unavailable, uncertain, active or unpriced work remains blocked.

These are stage-boundary checks, not a guarantee about the price of an in-flight request; toolchain and baseline readiness remain separate prerequisite checks.

The coordinator drives each member using TaskRun. related_profile is the public configuration export: selected role routes, efforts, providers, run limits and policies, without sessions or approvals. Fresh related runs accept a pinned --related-profile FILE --related-profile-sha256 SHA256; this cannot be applied to a saved run. TaskRun.assign_linked_scope(identity) consumes only a current core-owned changeset assignment. It retires the exact covered scope question; it neither invents a human answer nor approves a plan.

An integration task starts from original baselines, then receives the candidate copies only through the named binding action. It runs the approved joint test and returns differences to members through follow-ups. A revised plan renews the single coordinated approval. Publication requires every member's canonical completion evidence, exact matching integration copies, and the integration run's current authenticated completion report with independent criterion verdicts and runner fail-before/pass-after proof. Approved prose methods and named test:/guard: bindings remain unchanged. A native verification receipt has kind: task_run; its record names the canonical report, and its binding and digests are rechecked through TaskRun's inspected status before publication and on reopen. Its model costs are already counted in the joint run. Older completed plans without a native regression-proof record still use standalone verify; their records retain the existing freshness reader. A present but stale or failing native proof is refused rather than falling back. The coordinator owns durable publication intent and reconciles branch/PR identity before any retry. It never merges. Manual change-set completion alone is not automatic coordination completion.

A coordinated member names the repositories that own its external work by their exact member names (or a genuinely grounded repository name); its member context says so, and a role label such as Checkout display member is refused by the report contract, so the normal bounded report repair attempts the correction. A repair that does not converge leaves the member stopped on that visible failure; the refused obligation is never silently dropped (ordinary filtering of ungrounded scope is unchanged). For labels earlier runs already accepted, discovery resolves the trailing member role noun against the authorized catalog only, and only when the catalog's own exact, noun, parenthetical and coordinated matches found nothing: every alias-prefix identity is enumerated, a job word or phrase naming another repository refuses the label, one identity that is already linked and still available reuses that member automatically, and anything else stays the person's repository gate.

Automatic coordination currently runs in owned terminal chats. A durable_local anchor is refused without changing its saved execution policy. See multi-repository setup and limits.

docs.title: Per-attempt execution identity (#2059)
docs.text:
New provider launches add bounded execution_identity to their saved attempt and public usage.accounting.attempts row. Schema 1 records the actual route slot, engine/tool, model, effective effort, runner source commit when known, a saved selected-route billing classification/basis, and optional configured endpoint identity (origin, SHA-256, protocol and API provider slot). It contains no key, credential URL, tenant path or environment dump. An endpoint hash describes the configured target, not an observed HTTP redirect or invoice. Opaque backend endpoints and unrecorded billing remain null; account/model discovery is unchanged.

The effective reasoning_effort is separate from launch_route's saved route configuration: existing fit/first-Builder policies may differ. Empty/null effort can mean the provider default and is not replaced with a guessed level. Invalid or contradictory identity records project as unknown; old attempts are not backfilled from the viewer's current settings/runtime. These are additive measurement fields, not action authority, route qualification or a new client.

docs.title: Remote team service proposal (#2023)
docs.text: The single-host team-service contract proposes an additive authenticated service over this interface. It is not implemented or approved. Current local tokens and Git/--as provenance do not authenticate a remote person. The proposal records opaque remote envelopes, current named-action bindings, separate admission/execution/delivery states and explicit public core gaps. Its synthetic examples are design data, not live responses. No existing client, task policy, route, approval or host configuration changes through this documentation. The owner decision is needed before implementing the service extension or its dependent runtime slices.

docs.title: Python client
docs.text:
tools/autocode_taskrun.py wraps the commands below.

TaskRun.start(..., run_dir=path) selects an exact fresh run directory, an immediate child of workspace/.autocode/runs. Existing directories and symlinks are refused before a provider launches. The optional destination is used by saved-run replay; the run is created there without moving bound artifacts afterward.

When the workspace is a plain, non-empty folder, the core bootstraps a task project inside workspace/autocode-projects/ and runs there. A destination named under the selected folder's .autocode/runs keeps its name: the run is created under the bootstrapped project instead, and commands may keep using the selected folder and that name as the run's handle. The status view names the effective workspace and run_dir. When the launch does this bootstrapping, the run also says so once in its chat history (view.chat.messages, message id workspace-bootstrap), naming the folder that was selected and the project the work happens in, so a client shows the move instead of leaving the person to infer it from view.workspace.

This example accepts the displayed plan and chooses question defaults or the first listed option. An interactive client should collect the person’s answer instead, using the token from the view they saw. Operational recovery needs a separate decision.

from autocode_cli.autocode_taskrun import TaskRun, TaskRunError

run = TaskRun.start(workspace, brief, options=("--engine", "codex"))
view = run.advance_until_input()
while not view["done"]:
    need = view["needs"]
    if need["kind"] == "answer" and need.get("resolver_scope") in ("blocker", "operational_exhaustion"):
        break  # Inspect recovery guidance; respond_operational() handles these requests.
    if need["kind"] == "approve_plan":
        view = run.approve_plan(need["token"])
    elif need["kind"] == "answer":
        # One question per pass: an answer consumes the request, and the questions
        # left come back in the returned view under a new resolver_token.
        question = need["questions"][0]
        # Decision questions may have no default; choose among their options.
        view = run.answer(question["id"], question["proposed_default"] or question["options"][0],
                          resolver_token=need.get("resolver_token"))
    elif need["kind"] == "continue":
        view = run.advance_until_input()
    else:
        break   # review, planning_budget or resume: a decision for the caller or a person

TaskRun.start works directly in the given workspace (--in-place): the caller owns the workspace, typically a worktree it created, so start one run per workspace at a time. Files uncommitted or untracked there at the start are the code the run starts from (base_commit), not part of its change. options (engine and model flags) are passed whenever the run starts or advances. Any rejected command raises TaskRunError with AutoCode's message.

An AutoCode self-build requires an executing controller outside the task workspace, so the task cannot edit the code that runs it. With such a controller (an installed autocode, or another checkout), an AutoCode checkout is an ordinary project and TaskRun.start or --in-place works in it directly, main checkout included; an ordinary CLI launch creates its own worktree by default. An unsafe new run or advancing invocation is refused before starting a provider. Saved status, explanations and dry runs remain readable without changing the checkpoint.

view.runner and view.evidence.runner identify the controller that last saved the run: its package directory (path) and source revision (commit, with +modified for local source edits). view.evidence.base_commit identifies the Builder's starting code separately. Legacy runs without a saved identity report runner: null; an installed package without source revision metadata reports commit: null. Status never substitutes the current installation or Builder revision for this saved identity. The existing resume warning names a change in the controller revision.

To build AutoCode itself with the controller from that same source checkout, keep that checkout fixed and create a separate workspace:

git -C /path/to/autocode worktree add --detach /path/to/autocode-self-build HEAD
/path/to/controller-venv/bin/python /path/to/autocode/tools/autocode.py \
  "Fix the selected issue" --workspace /path/to/autocode-self-build --in-place

Use the existing provider and model flags for the run. Keep the controller checkout and its environment unchanged until the run has stopped. An installed controller is also safe when its package directory is outside the task worktree.

Inputs fixed when a run starts, such as --ui-run, --test-root and --package, belong in start_options instead of options: TaskRun.start(workspace, brief, options=("--engine", "codex"), start_options=("--ui-run", str(design_run))). They are passed once; later advances and reattachment use the saved settings. For scoped Python proof, use start_options=("--test-root", "components/api/"); the root selects tests, not generic write ownership. Generated component runs bind their original ownership declaration to this caller-selected root before plan approval and execution. An older shipped component run with no saved root uses only its exact, single original generated ownership declaration to derive a transient root for admission and regression proof. It does not rewrite the original task, settings, approval, user events or historical evidence. An explicit root must still match; generic rootless tasks gain neither a test root nor write authority from model text.

At PAUSED_COMPONENT_PLAN, needs.kind remains resume for compatibility. First check needs.new_run_required: when true, needs.action is fresh_run, needs.edit_required is false, and needs.feedback_action is null. The original caller declaration is missing/ambiguous or the saved root disagrees with it. These immutable inputs cannot be repaired by editing the model's plan. Preserve the stopped run and use TaskRun.start for a fresh component run in a separately caller-owned workspace, with the correct generated declaration and matching launch-only root. That new plan still requires approval. Feedback at this stop is rejected before recording an event or scheduling a new model draft. Never change the original task or saved root to make the old approval usable.

With a valid caller binding, needs.edit_required is true instead: incorrect body paths or deferred/prohibited mandatory flow can be repaired. Follow needs.action (--edit-goal FILE) or needs.feedback_action (--feedback TEXT), then inspect and approve the new draft with its newly displayed token. The old approval token cannot approve it. Plain resume leaves the checkpoint unchanged and launches no Builder; adding --test-root on resume cannot repair a launch-only setting. A valid older rootless run needs no root flag to edit its plan. The recovery card, progress line and issue/finder guidance distinguish these two cases without promising that an unchanged resume repairs either one.

A caller that keeps each invocation's output, such as its stdout.log, stderr.log and exit code, reads it from the client:

  • TaskRun.last_advance is the subprocess.CompletedProcess of the latest call that starts or advances the run (start, advance, resume and retries), also when AutoCode rejected it. Status reads and user actions never replace it.
  • TaskRunError.process is the CompletedProcess of the CLI call that failed. It is None when the error is not a failed call: a call that could not run or did not finish (a missing working directory, a timeout), attach finding several runs, or a guard such as advance_until_input's no-progress check, which is raised after its calls finished; last_advance still holds the latest advancing call. A start that fails may still have created its run: TaskRunError.run_dir names it when it created exactly one.
  • A call that outlives timeout raises TaskRunError naming the call and its limit (status did not finish within 60 s), followed by the end of each stream that reached the caller before the limit, or no output reached the caller before the limit. TaskRunError.partial_output holds that (stdout, stderr) whole; it is None for every other error. It is what arrived, not everything the call printed: unless PYTHONUNBUFFERED is set, the CLI's stdout to a pipe is block-buffered, and a call stopped at its limit can lose what is still in that buffer.
  • TaskRun.cwd (cwd= on start and attach) is the CLI's working directory, so relative paths in options and start_options resolve against it. None, the default, keeps the caller's. A continuation from restore_checkpoint keeps it.

Operator-declared prerequisites can be supplied once with --task-preflight in start_options. A failed prerequisite pauses before paid dispatch and is visible in the additive task_preflight status field. See task-preflight.md for phase selection, copied input checks, receipt reuse and supported correction; readiness does not replace proof.

docs.title: Chat projection for ordinary task runs
docs.text:
A clean user-requested pause may set needs.confirmation_required: false on its ordinary resume offer. The person's Resume click then needs no second confirmation dialog. The need remains person-only: clients must not automatically resume it. Missing or true preserves the client's existing confirmation policy; failure recovery, held operational pauses, retained attempts, report repairs and terminal stops do not receive this exception. Numeric allowance changes still need their explicit confirmation. Named commands and CLI admission checks are unchanged.

The additive view.chat contains messages (stable id, role, text), an opaque context, and an optional input offer. Messages project existing human receipts and saved completed replies. At a follow-up, the prior reply is retained under that turn's historical record; display text grants no approval and does not become a new requirement. Status reads do not write a transcript. The Requirements question the run waits on is a message whose id starts with requirements-question- and names that question, so each new question is a new message a client shows once (#1792).

During a running step, optional progress is an array of core-authored display lines: the inspected current activity, saved task/requirement counts and up to three recent finished attempts in this turn. An attempt finishing does not mean its report was accepted or its checks passed. Unknown activity stays unconfirmed; queued and stopped steps are not described as running. Clients render these lines without deriving stage names or success from private state. Older cores may omit the field.

While a supervised step works, optional activity is an array of at most 20 display events from the running attempt's own provider event file, oldest first: {kind, text, status} with kind one of command, edit or tool, status one of running, done or failed, and, for an edit, the paths it names (relative to the project when they are inside it, at most 8). text is one bounded line: a command's first line, the files changed, or the tool called. Model prose, reasoning and tool output are never copied, and only the tail of a file inside the run directory is read. done and failed describe the tool call, not the work: a command that exited 0 is not a passed check, an edit is not an accepted change, and nothing here is proof, approval or authority to retry. Activity that is not confirmed as supervised, a finished or stopped step and a paused run have none, and the field is then omitted. Codex-style items (also what the built-in Claude provider writes) and OpenCode or Kilo tool parts are read; other event shapes show nothing. Older cores may omit the field.

While a supervised step or parallel Builder works, optional log is the terminal chat's live agent log (owner decision 2026-10-21): an array of display entries {id, agent, kind, text} from each working attempt's own provider event file, oldest first per attempt, at most 40 per attempt and 8 parallel Builders. agent is the job's screen name, with the task for a Builder (Builder · task M2); id stays the same across reads so a client can keep entries beyond the newest and update a growing one in place. kind is thinking (model reasoning), message (model prose), or one of activity's command, edit and tool with the same status and paths. Unlike activity, reasoning and message prose are copied: collapsed to one line, credential-shaped text redacted, and cut to the newest 400 characters. Tool output is never copied. Each parallel Builder's attempt must itself be confirmed as supervised, and only a file inside that attempt's run directory is read. The entries are display only, never a report, proof, approval or authority to retry. The field is omitted when nothing is working. Older cores may omit the field.

During spec-first Requirements chat, phase: "requirements" lets clients show the conversation without the empty task dashboard. An assistant message may have streaming: true; its text is provisional display content from the active Requirements attempt, never an answer, approval, report or tool receipt. Kilo text deltas are filtered to the current assistant message; reasoning and tool output are excluded. Requirements reuses its own saved provider session while independent plan reviewers retain separate sessions. Requirements answers the first message of a spec-first run, whatever it says: a greeting or an off-topic question gets a short answer and a question about what to build or change. Until Requirements finds work to do, the person's newest reply becomes the task; the source log keeps the first message and each reply as separate sources. Requirements names the job it understood (#1846), as it does on every run (#1860). A question goes straight to the Analyst without a confirmation; any other job starts once the person approves what Requirements understood. The Job recognizer runs, after that approval, only when Requirements named no job. Model access probes for planning and execution roles wait until the user confirms the requirements.

When the only pending question is the core's current requirements review, review offers its question_id, exact answer, label and bound summary. A client may display that summary and submit the ordinary named answer action. This confirms the understanding and starts the job Requirements named: plan preparation and review for a build, the investigation for a bug fix, the review or the design work. The label and spend_confirmation say which. The resulting execution plan still needs its own displayed-token approval. The optional review.spend_confirmation supplies the modal's title, detail and confirm-button label before submitting that review's planning answer. match: "trim_lower" mechanically matches the answer after whitespace trimming and lowercasing, as the core does; corrections do not trigger the planning modal. This spend confirmation never approves an execution plan. The optional notice explains a stop or ongoing work in ordinary language; chat clients keep diagnostic headings, empty counts and pause categories in Run details. A notice never grants an action beyond the view's named command.

A build plan can explicitly request local delivery with git_delivery: {"kind": "atomic_commit", "message": "…"}. Use null when no local commit is requested; older reports may omit the field without granting delivery authority. This field is part of the sealed plan and is shown alongside its approval. A fresh passing runner regression proof allows the controller to create the scoped commit before the independent Tester inspects it. The committed revision receives fresh runner proof and independent verification before completion. Plans without executable regression cases retain the final completion boundary. Existing Git hooks are honored. Stage workers must leave delivery to the controller. Push, merge and deployment are separate actions.

Delivery refuses preexisting dirty launch work, staged changes, changes outside the approved affected paths, or an unrelated moved HEAD. If a worker nevertheless commits, the controller can reconcile a clean, linear chain witnessed by this run's successful Builder source captures under the same approved plan. It preserves the checked files and replaces that chain with the approved atomic commit, records the original commits in the delivery receipt, and requires fresh proof and review. Unwitnessed commits, merges and dirty trees remain refused. A durable receipt prevents repeating a successful commit after a lost response. Uncertain Git writes or source changes in a hook stop for reconciliation. The supported routes are the ordinary build review workflow and the bugfix workflow. Older plans promising an atomic commit only in prose require a revised, explicitly approved structured delivery contract; prose cannot authorize a Git write and cannot silently satisfy the completion gate.

input is null when free text is not an admitted action. Otherwise it names kind (feedback, follow_up, or resolver_response), a display label, and next_command with one literal MESSAGE placeholder. A client replaces that argument with the person's text, checks that the command names the same workspace/run, and runs it as an argument array without a shell. Compare against the view's workspace and run_dir fields: after bootstrap relocation they name the run's effective location, which can differ from the handle the client started with. The headless conformance client's message_command() implements this same parsing boundary.

A client compares the displayed context with a fresh status before submitting; if it changed, retain the draft and ask the person to review the new checkpoint. The ordinary CLI independently rechecks admission when saving the action. At a semantic Resolver or completion stop (RESOLVER_PENDING or PAUSED_COMPLETION_GATE with needs.kind=resume), permitted corrective feedback uses this same named offer. Terminal chat lets the person type the correction at the Continue prompt. A held operational pause, blocker or human-review gate does not gain a feedback bypass; the existing pause-authority policy still decides. One blocker stop does gain it, as its own decision rather than a bypass: after a blocker was answered with provide_information and the response holds the current frontier at an approved contract, that hold exists to take the contract decision it asked about, so the view offers the same feedback action and the CLI admits --feedback (and, consistently, the --edit-goal path the stop reason names). The correction invalidates the approval and starts ordinary re-planning toward a fresh, unapproved draft and a fresh approval — fresh set approval too, for a linked run. The informational reply alone still changes nothing (#2434). An operational resolver_response offer binds provide_information to the current Resolver request ID and token in needs. It supplies corrective information only; retry grants, scope changes, model routing and resuming remain separate actions. Resolver frontier bindings also include the runner's Python source contents, using relative names rather than its installation path. A runner repair expires an old response hold so ordinary continuation can reconsider the stop. This grants no approval, permission or additional recovery allowance; unchanged runner contents retain the hold even when installed in another directory. In spec-first chat runs, a message at plan approval is interpreted by the saved Requirements route when the client continues. Questions receive an assistant reply while preserving the reviewed plan and its token; requested or mixed corrections enter normal requirements/review again and need fresh approval. Free text, including approval-like messages, never approves the plan. The existing --feedback action and feedback input kind remain the client contract; no client intent parsing is needed. Exchanges are stored as plan_message user-event receipts (ID, original text, contract token, return stage, then intent and reply_after). They are not requirement sources unless a change is forwarded once as ordinary brief feedback. Legacy nonchat feedback keeps its correction behavior.

Saving feedback or a follow-up launches no model. A button explicitly offering to send and continue may then follow the ordinary needs.kind=continue action. It may never infer a plan approval, answer another question or release an operational pause. Approval remains bound to the displayed plan token. Older cores without chat leave free-text input disabled for an existing run.

This projection is separate from the explicit Requirements journal below: ordinary run clients do not create or drive a second conversation controller.

docs.title: Core Requirements conversations
docs.text:
TaskRun.start_conversation(workspace, text, request_id="first-message") starts a core-owned journal and one ordinary task run. attach_conversation(workspace, run_dir=...) validates an existing conversation; read_conversation() reads its journal and current public run view without changing either or invoking a model. Provider, model, effort and budget selections use the same ordinary runner settings as start(), through a creation allowlist shared by Python and the CLI. The core session always uses joint planning, stops for explicit plan approval, and accepts --planning-v2 for separate Planner and Plan Reviewer stages. The default joint flow presents a Requirements planning draft and an independent Plan Reviewer. Ordinary planning review limits still apply: a budget pause remains a pause, and conversation refresh grants no extra review calls or approval. Creation inputs belong in start_options; later advances use saved settings.

send_conversation(text, request_id=..., expected_revision=...) queues a human message only. Use the revision returned by the inspected conversation and retain the request ID for a retry of that same message. It does not call feedback, answer, or a model. refresh_conversation(request_id=..., expected_revision=...) explicitly commits the pending human batch through the ordinary saved-action boundary, then advances the same controller to its next question or approval stop. A question refresh also supplies its question_id and current resolver_token; exact answer and operational-recovery rules still apply. Stale revisions, conflicting request IDs and stale question tokens are refused.

During joint planning, technical decisions with a proposed default are resolved internally and sent through drafting and review again. They are retained as user_events receipts with actor=autocode and kind=technical_decision, outside the human answers ledger and chat history. They cannot authorize a protected contract change or approve a plan, and they never renew the plan-review allowance: the redraft continues the planning cycle that asked, carrying its spent review calls, its first review and its revision (planning.inherited_review in the saved state), and with one review call left the final review decides on the redraft. Genuine questions about the requested outcome, behavior, cost, permissions or side effects still require a human answer, as do unresolved facts and rejected assumptions. A repeated identical technical question goes to report repair instead of another planning loop. Non-joint runs keep their existing question path.

handoff_conversation(expected_revision=..., expected_plan_token=...) records the reviewed current draft's handoff to that same run. It does not approve the plan or start a second task. Read the current plan and use the separate approve_plan() action only when the operator authorizes implementation. The original handoff source digest stays immutable; later human feedback retains its own provenance. Assistant text and unapproved drafts never become mandatory requirements merely because they appear in the journal. The browser dashboard and macOS app still use their existing path.

The additive view.conversation is None for ordinary and legacy dashboard runs. A core conversation exposes actionable status/needs (including current questions and resolver tokens), messages, pending_message_ids, revision/applied_revision, saved human actions and request acknowledgements, accepted planning_records/history, current_draft/draft history, and Reviewer findings under review. Each accepted record identifies its actual saved role, model and effort; declared_seed_routes records only explicit creation context and uses runner-default when no model was named. A queued message makes the shown draft stale until refresh completes its ordinary independent review.

A completed identical refresh or an unchanged revision with no pending human messages dispatches nothing. If a client exits after saving a request, its runner-owned acknowledgement reconciles that exact source event on restart. If it exits after marking planning delivery as advancing, an unresolved outcome is held for ordinary inspection/recovery; repeating refresh never blindly replays a paid call. The immutable initial handoff and all accepted/rejected stage artifacts remain evidence on the same run. read and attach save nothing and cannot approve it.

The public CLI has the same operations:

autocode conversation start --workspace "$PROJECT" --text "Build a greeting CLI" \
  --request-id initial -- --provider opencode --joint-planning
autocode conversation read --workspace "$PROJECT" --run-dir "$RUN"
autocode conversation send --workspace "$PROJECT" --run-dir "$RUN" \
  --text "Use standard-library Python" --request-id language --expected-revision 1
autocode conversation refresh --workspace "$PROJECT" --run-dir "$RUN" \
  --request-id draft-2 --expected-revision 2

Every conversation command prints JSON on stdout. Provider/model/effort/budget options follow -- on start; unit overrides, approval and automatic approval are refused. Attach/read are read-only. Sending several messages does not silently refresh between them. Only an explicit refresh asks the ordinary controller for its next result.

A rejected conversation answer can be corrected without replaying it. Read the current question and token first. If the runner retained an input rejection, queue the corrected text with send_conversation(..., supersedes_request_id="old-message-id") or CLI send --supersedes-request-id old-message-id, at the current revision. The original message and sealed rejection remain visible. Only that rejected, unapplied message leaves the pending batch; saved actions, active or unknown delivery, and unattempted inputs cannot be replaced. Refresh the correction with a new request ID and the current question/token. A stale supplied token is refused before a request is sealed.

docs.title: Controller ownership and recovery
docs.text:
status()["controller"] reports the current invocation's birth-bound owner, last saved checkpoint and completed stage, declared CLI return code, and ready or stopped disposition. A hard exit has no collected return code; that field stays null. Deliberate answers, approvals and unit handoffs retain an explicit ready receipt and keep their ordinary continuation behavior. A rejected user command records its actual exit code 2 while retaining the ready checkpoint; it does not imply a lost controller or a successful action.

If the controller disappears between stages, status projects PAUSED_CONTROLLER_EXIT with a concrete --resume-paused command. Reading status or attaching does not rewrite the checkpoint. The next advancing CLI saves that pause under the existing run lock; resume_paused() acknowledges it and continues the saved stage. The checkpoint digest must still match before the receipt identifies that stage or return code as the current boundary. Retained provider attempts and runner checks keep their existing recovery actions. A live owner or provider and a busy exclusion lock remain active; unverifiable ownership is reported precisely without guessing absence. Existing approval, source and provider cleanup gates still apply.

A controller exit while applying a returned, accounted report also projects this pause after fresh inspection confirms all supervised processes stopped with successful cleanup and the regular report file remains inside the run directory. status()["controller"]["completed_stage"] is true at that boundary. Resume revalidates the retained report without abandoning it or replaying that provider call. Usage, model routes, limits and plan-approval gates stay in force. An unaccounted, interrupted or missing result keeps its existing recovery controls.

docs.title: Pausing a working run
docs.text: While a run works (a live stage, a fresh birth-bound controller, or a controller holding the run's locks), status()["pause"] names the boundary pause of queued interventions: label, effect, requested and next_command, an argument array following autocode for intervention submit --kind pause --json. Its REQUEST_ID placeholder is the client's own id for this request, so a retried submission returns the original receipt instead of queueing another. The current step finishes and is saved, then the run pauses with its next stage selected; the ordinary --resume-paused action continues it. While a pause request waits for that boundary, requested is true and next_command is null. The field is null when nothing is working, when the recorded runner cannot consume interventions, and for a stopped run. It never interrupts a step in progress or stops the run.

docs.title: Durable local workers
docs.text:
Durable execution is an explicit new-run choice. modes list --json adds an execution object with default owned and a durable_local availability row. The latter carries the exact next_command argument-array envelope:

["autocode", "worker", "launch", "--workspace", "WORKSPACE", "--run-dir", "RUN_DIR",
 "--checkpoint", "CHECKPOINT", "--"]

For a fresh run, fill its absolute selected workspace, fresh immediate run destination, and CHECKPOINT with -; append the ordinary literal new-task arguments. Continuing a durable run uses view.execution.next_command, whose paths and checkpoint are already bound, followed by the existing named action and its exact human tokens. No shell is involved. The wrapper owns workspace, run-directory and noninteractive flags; do not repeat those inside the action. The core checks the checkpoint again under the existing run lock before configuration, reconciliation, a new controller epoch or provider dispatch. An admitted human answer, feedback, approval or resume keeps that same controller in the ordinary loop until the next human boundary; it does not depend on a viewer taking another Continue action. Explicit unit stops and inspection actions retain their boundaries. Attaching to an idle saved durable run reads only: the TUI offers Enter to take its current named Continue action, after rechecking that exact boundary. It does not silently dispatch on reconnect.

worker launch seals a private launch-intent receipt before calling the service manager. The default request ID fingerprints the exact action, checkpoint and private authorization-token fingerprints; an explicit --request-id may instead identify the caller's request. Identical repeats reconcile that one receipt; changed content conflicts. A dispatching receipt can never re-arm itself, even if the service was collected or its response was lost. worker inspect ID and worker launches --workspace PATH [--run-dir PATH] are read-only. The launch reply's inspect_command names the inspection action. ready acknowledges a matching committed run/controller binding; it does not assert worker liveness, successful provider execution or task completion. Those remain in normal status.

The first adapter uses an already configured Linux systemd user service, Type=exec, without a PTY or inherited input/output pipes, persistent private output, no automatic restart and existing linger. Admission refuses an unavailable manager, systemd before 254, missing linger or editable controller/launch storage inside the task workspace. Only the manager's matching MainPID and InvocationID can enter the exact receipt on the pinned runtime and host boot. The existing core controller, task lock, checkout lock and provider supervision retain ownership. Runtime changes, missing run folders and uncertain persistence refuse adoption; reboot is interruption, not automatic replay. The launcher never enables a service or changes host login policy.

TaskRun.start_durable(workspace, run_dir, brief, ...) returns (run, receipt) without waiting for model completion. run.inspect_launch(receipt) reconciles its named read and adopts effective bootstrap paths only after binding. Read the normal status, retain the action and exact human decision tokens, and call run.dispatch_durable(named_command, view=inspected_view) to launch one action. It returns another receipt. The synchronous start/advance APIs retain their ordinary owned-worker semantics; using them to write a durable run is refused. The client driver reads no private task or launch file. Other clients may observe a durable run; they need the named worker transport before writing it. An ordinary root CLI write is refused rather than silently changing worker lifetime.

view.observation contains the selected effective paths, a token for canonical committed checkpoint contents and the read's sampled_at; it is neither an atomic snapshot of every artifact nor action authority. view.execution records the saved mode, launch ID and controller epoch and, for durable mode, the named transport. Service inspection is separate from the existing controller/liveness and completion evidence. Legacy absence never implies detach support.

docs.title: Asynchronous viewer direction (#1879; implementation pending)
docs.text:
Owner-approved direction, implementation pending (2026-10-23). The owner approved PR #1985's lifecycle direction in the Codex chat: "Approve the proposed lifecycle." The source inventory below was checked against master 348670930. Current runtime behavior remains in force until the dependent implementation qualifies. The field examples describe the agreed semantics; clients cannot assume they are exported yet. This decision and read-only attachment do not approve an individual task plan or authorize an additional model call.

Existing guarantees should be extended rather than replaced:

Foundation Existing evidence and limit Single controller/writer and surviving provider exclusion autocode_controller_owner, the run lock and autocode_checkout_lock; tests/test_controller_owner.py and tests/test_checkout_lock.py. A second viewer is not a second owner. These checks alone do not prove SSH survival. Checked liveness and unknown inspection autocode_liveness separates owner, keeper and provider; autocode_wait_command observes controller loss. Access failure is not proof of a dead worker. Boundary pause The current pause.next_command uses a client request ID; intervention tests cover identical retry and conflicting payload, including after application. This is not a blanket guarantee for other actions. Core Requirements conversation send_conversation and refresh_conversation bind message IDs/revisions, reconcile saved acknowledgements and hold uncertain advances; tests/test_conversation_session_cli.py and tests/test_conversation_policy.py. Ordinary/legacy runs need not have this journal. Approval, recovery and restore Current plan/review/request tokens, recovery token and exact comparison control their own actions; see Commands, Exact stopped-run recovery and Saved code checkpoints. There is no universal retry receipt across all families. Responsive observation Bounded polling and its cancellation tests already exist. TUI history/verification display is E1; no whole-view freshness or durable detach guarantee follows from it.

docs.title: Agreed lifetime and authority
docs.text:
The agreed first delivery is opt-in durable local execution on persistent Linux, with a core-owned launcher and the ordinary task controller. The TUI observes it through this interface. The launcher must establish independent terminal/session lifetime, persistent output and a reconciliable launch identity before returning a durable-ready receipt; a separate process group alone is insufficient. A local user-service arrangement is the preferred first host adapter, provided its existing configuration survives SSH/session loss. A host without that demonstrated capability retains the current owned-worker mode. Enabling a service or changing host login/linger policy is a separate operator action, never a silent prerequisite installed by the TUI.

The launcher is part of the core runtime, not another task controller. It starts the existing loop under the existing locks and birth-bound ownership. A service name is not proof of ownership, and a lost launch receipt is reconciled by the core before any retry. At a human gate the controller can finish with its ready receipt; continuing later is another serialized invocation of the same run. The exact launch action/capability schema and host adapter must be reviewed with their deterministic qualification before this opt-in mode is exposed.

Event in the agreed durable mode Required outcome Normal viewer quit, Ctrl-D, SIGHUP, viewer SIGKILL or SSH disconnect Only the viewer leaves. It neither pauses nor signals the worker. Reattach is read-only and launches no provider. First or repeated Ctrl-C Request the currently named boundary pause; repeated keys do not escalate to an implicit worker kill. An unavailable pause offer is reported as such. Explicit pause Submit the existing request-ID-bound pause offer. Save the active step, then wait at the core's boundary. Explicit stop or interrupt Use a core-named action with its own confirmation and scope. No new immediate-kill control is included in the first delivery; missing controls remain unavailable. Stop, when offered, remains terminal for the conversation. Worker/controller loss while a viewer survives Show the current controller/liveness inspection and retained attempt. Use the existing reconciliation action only when offered; never infer a paid replay from a quiet log. Lost ordinary supervisor Fresh status may name private --reconcile-only - when owner, keeper and provider are positively dead. It classifies the retained unfinished attempt as uncertain under the run lock without provider setup, artifact adoption, settings changes or model calls. A changed checkpoint, live/unknown role or stop refuses, and status does not offer it while a stop is applied or still pending (the next relaunch applies that stop). Native visual workers and durable service actions remain outside this control. Archiving that uncertain attempt then follows as the core's own named --abandon-stage step; any retry is a separate named decision. Host reboot Work is interrupted, not transparently resumed. After reconnect, inspect ownership and attempts and expose the ordinary recovery boundary. Unknown provider outcomes stay uncertain. Two viewers act on one gate Both may inspect. The first current action admitted under the core's locks changes the run; a competing stale token is refused and refreshed. No client leader or second controller is introduced.

The current owned-worker Ctrl-C sequence remains documented for legacy mode until an explicit migration decision. It must not silently acquire durable-mode semantics. Multiple viewers initially share the same authorized local OS identity; this proposal adds no remote authentication service or Jira/RPC API. Jira/Fargate orchestration remains a separate layer using TaskRun.

docs.title: Observation, decision and attention requirements
docs.text:
Keep controller, liveness, status, needs, delivery, verification and the named actions authoritative for their existing meanings. Add only the missing capability and observation metadata, for example:

{
  "execution": {
    "version": 1,
    "mode": "durable_local",
    "detach_supported": true,
    "launch_id": "opaque-core-launch-id",
    "controller_epoch": "opaque-owner-receipt-id"
  },
  "observation": {
    "version": 1,
    "workspace": "/project",
    "run_dir": "/project/.autocode/runs/run-a",
    "checkpoint_token": "opaque-committed-checkpoint-token",
    "sampled_at": "2026-10-24T00:00:00Z"
  }
}

checkpoint_token identifies committed checkpoint bytes; it is not a sequence number or a token granting an action. controller_epoch distinguishes owner incarnations, not task completion. sampled_at describes the read, not meaningful progress or an atomic snapshot of every external evidence/log file. Existing attempt/log identities keep their narrower scopes. Clients bind each local read to its requested identity and request generation, discard cancelled/older local results and never order checkpoints by a wall clock or a hash. A failed read retains the last view as unavailable; it does not rewrite worker state.
