Before applying a decision, obtain a current view and retain the exact plan, question, review, recovery or comparison token the person inspected. A newer view cannot silently answer or approve on their behalf. Each action family needs its own conflict/lost-receipt contract:

Action family Required reconciliation rule Read, attach and detach No run writes, provider dispatch or approval. Detach is local viewer exit, not a new core task-state transition. Pause/intervention Reuse the existing request ID and exact payload; return its original receipt. A changed payload is a conflict. Core conversation send/refresh Reuse its existing request-ID/revision and acknowledgement rules. An unresolved advancing outcome holds rather than dispatching again. Plan/review approval and answers Validate the displayed token under the lock. Preserve existing per-family replay behavior; a missing command receipt requires fresh inspection, not a synthesized success. Feedback, follow-up and plan messages Verify their existing context/revision/request-ID coverage separately. Add missing conditional receipts in the core before claiming automatic reconnect retry for that family. Unsupported cases remain explicit handoffs. Retry, recovery and restore Keep the exact attempt/source/recovery/comparison binding and current cleanup evidence. A transport failure or reconnect grants no extra retry, model substitution or limit change.

Persistent attention (#1885) is exposed in view.attention and each runs --json row. Version 1 identifies a pending human boundary using the saved run incarnation and existing decision context. A completed outcome uses the existing same-chat turn receipt, so an identical follow-up's completion has a different ID. Missing saved identity means unknown; it is never invented from text or source equality. The item contains its workspace/run, kind, fixed label and bounded, redacted task snippet. It carries no answer or approval authority.

attention.acknowledge.next_command is an exact argument array for autocode attention ack --workspace W --run-dir R --item-id ID. TaskRun.acknowledge_attention(view) submits that offer without advancing the run. An acknowledgement never changes the task checkpoint, current question, plan token, delivery acceptance, provider attempts or budgets. New acknowledgements require the item still be current. Repeating an acknowledged ID returns its original receipt even after the task resolves; a different run cannot inherit it. A lost reply is uncertain until that same ID is inspected or explicitly retried. This reconciliation applies to acknowledgement only, not other action families.

The authorized local OS identity shares receipts across viewers. Storage defaults to $XDG_STATE_HOME/autocode/attention (otherwise ~/.local/state/autocode/attention); AUTOCODE_ATTENTION_HOME selects an isolated profile. It must be a private owned directory outside the editable task workspace; receipts are private atomic files bound to the local UID and run paths. Reads create nothing. Unavailable, corrupt, unowned, symlinked or unsupported storage projects unknown and offers no acknowledgement action. There is no remote identity service, notification service or workspace-owned acknowledgement file.

The TUI's F8 or /attention drawer restores current saved alerts, including after a viewer restart. Cold-start inventory is silent; a newly observed unread ID is announced once in that viewer's current bounded cohort. An acknowledged item stays inspectable while current but does not announce again. The selected run uses its own prompt and the global unread badge. Background runs and the prior run while composing a local new-chat draft receive the notice. Independently running viewers may each announce a newly observed item; delivery is not a universal exactly-once alarm guarantee. Resolved/superseded items disappear from current inventory; this is not an alert history journal. Unread storage is durable, while delivery of a notice is an observation. Completion says to inspect evidence, not that current delivery passed.

Inventory uses runs --all --json in the existing two-child bounded read pool, normally every ten seconds. Per-run status reads take precedence over an inventory started before them. The UI retains at most 256 rows and reports overflow; an empty runs --json inventory returns success with runs: [] rather than prose. /runs remains available for the full public list. Failed discovery retains a labelled last snapshot and shows unavailability. Drawer rows stay frozen until explicit refresh so incoming items cannot change which ID a queued key targets. Acknowledgements are asynchronous with a five-second viewer timeout; a slow receipt cannot block draft editing. Closing the drawer restores the draft/cursor and viewport without switching runs. Opening an item reads current status; submitting an answer or approval still uses the exact token the person inspected.

The terminal's /runs also uses that bounded pool for its project and global listings. The command returns immediately while a refresh is outstanding; its completion notice invites /runs to inspect the new snapshot. Displayed numbers appear automatically for the first requested list, then stay fixed until that explicit inspection, so a later read cannot retarget an /open N being typed. Listing a chat does not open a tab or subscribe to its individual status; only chats explicitly opened in this viewer join that set. An uncached /open N finishes its viewer navigation after fresh listings arrive. A newer navigation or a changed source chat/question cancels that pending open; a failed listing cannot complete it.

docs.title: Acceptance and rollout before implementation is enabled
docs.text:
Design case Required deterministic and supported-host proof A1: one worker, two viewers Both observe; competing starts/continues and token decisions admit one writer. Receipts reconcile the exact launch/action without a second provider call. A2: viewer, worker and host loss Kill each separately with an in-flight fake provider. Real PTY/SSH loss preserves a healthy durable worker; worker loss projects recovery; reboot never claims continued execution. Uninspectable ownership remains unknown. A3: stale/out-of-order data Hold an old read across a newer decision, refresh, run switch and controller epoch. Release it; it cannot replace the current view or authorize an action. Stale human tokens are rejected by the core. A4: old/new pairs Omit every proposed field independently. Legacy clients ignore additive fields; new clients show unknown and retain legacy lifetime semantics without advertising detach. A source/controller version change cannot rewrite a held provider attempt. A5: accepted request, lost response Lose launch, action and provider receipts at each persistence boundary. Inspect the same launch/request/attempt; no blind provider replay. Identical supported retries return their existing receipt, conflicts refuse, unsupported uncertainty holds.

Use fake providers and controlled clocks for authority/race cases, then actual terminal and SSH/service tests for host lifetime. No paid model is needed. Measure keyboard-command response and healthy-read completion while another read hangs; propose a controlled-host input target of 250 ms, report actual samples and load, and derive fairness from the configured subscription/read bounds rather than promising a fixed 25-run freshness number. No spinner, poll or notification acknowledgement counts as work progress.

Implementation order after owner agreement: #1881 owns durable launch/reattach and host capability; #1882 D2 owns active switching and per-run draft/cursor/view context; #1883 E2 consumes observation/identity metadata; #1885 owns durable attention and conditional decisions; #1884 F2 consumes separately approved stage policy; #1886 owns the integrated fault/terminal/SSH matrix. Existing E1/F1 and D1 results remain regression evidence, not proof of these new outcomes.

The consolidated owner decision above covers these lifetime/authority, metadata, first-host and response-target choices. Dependent issues should not ask the same policy questions again. Exact additive schema/actions, compatibility fixtures, host adapter and measured A1–A5 results are readiness evidence before enabling the opt-in capability, not a second owner approval gate unless the agreed semantics change. Keep current defaults and all saved routes, efforts, usage, limits, histories and approvals unchanged. Cross-host delivery, host administration and stage-selection policy remain separate decisions.

docs.title: First interaction timing
docs.text:
status()["interaction_timing"] reports the saved first useful interactions:

Field Meaning launched_at UTC timestamp at CLI main entry, before workspace setup and provider preflight. Interpreter startup and module imports precede this boundary. first_question_at First published question or decision request rendered for the caller. first_plan_at First approval-ready plan rendered for the caller. first_builder_at First successful Builder dispatch: provider supervisor launch in serial execution, or Builder worker process launch in parallel execution. first_question_seconds, first_plan_seconds, first_builder_seconds Wall seconds from launched_at to the corresponding event.

Builder dispatch measures the runner's job handoff; it does not claim the provider has accepted a request or emitted its first token. A parallel worker can still fail its own preflight after dispatch. Failed process creation, report repairs, dry runs and scheduling alone do not count as Builder dispatch.

The first timestamps are retained across repeated displays and resumes. Durations include human answer/approval time and time between invocations; compare automated runs with automated runs rather than treating human wait as model latency. Status reads do not stamp an event or perform a model listing. An unreached event is null, and all seven fields remain null for older runs without a recorded launch. A later resume does not fabricate their history. Canonical completion reports bind these facts and show them in JSON and Markdown. The generated reliability table lists dated samples and medians of recorded values, keeping fake and live profiles separate.

docs.title: Canonical completion evidence
docs.text:
Every newly completed task publishes evidence.json and evidence.md beside its state.json. The version 1 JSON schema is tools/autocode-schemas/evidence-report.schema.json. Markdown is rendered deterministically from that document. The report records the approved plan, checked source snapshot, criterion results, independent commands and their exit codes, artifact paths and hashes, roles/models and attempt durations, reported usage, regression proof and remaining gaps. The report of a build, bug-fix or design run (the run's workflow, or none for a run saved before workflow recognition) also has approvals: the status view's approvals rows when the report was written (who approved each plan and review, accepted completion, edited the plan or resumed a pause, with its recorded provenance, never verified), shown in the Markdown as an Approvals table after the intended outcome, or as None recorded for a run with none (Who approved). Review and discuss reports, which have no approval step, have no approvals field and no such section, even when the status view lists a resume. Neither do verification reports, nor reports written before AutoCode listed approvals, so older pairs still authenticate. A components report lists its child runs' approvals (below). An older build, bug-fix or design report gains the section when AutoCode saves the completed run again; reading its status does not. A task report whose approved plan is in the status view also has plan.goal_hash and plan.plan_file, copied from approved_contract (#720); the Markdown says them after the agreed plan's token. Reports written before AutoCode cited them have neither field and still authenticate; a completed run saved again rebuilds its pair with them. When the proof's mutation check left survivors, regression_proof.mutation_survivors lists them per test case, keyed like case_tests, and the Markdown names each one under the regression proof. For current task proofs, verification.changed_code_evidence binds execution, mutation observations and independently checked per-line reasons to the exact source/proof context. verification.changed_code_repairs retains the bounded Builder returns and Investigator handoffs. Legacy report-only proofs without this field grant no new changed-line evidence. Review-only mutation reports are kept separately in workflow_result.mutation_check, with survivors keyed by the reviewed tests' actual IDs. Local artifact paths are references, not hosted evidence. Unknown usage stays unknown; historical price estimates remain separate from provider-reported cost. Usage records the public accounting snapshot captured at the completed checkpoint, including its unknown quantities. It does not attest every later raw event-log byte. Inspection compares the report's bound evidence and accounting facts with the supplied current public projection; a changed finding, reproduced case, base revision, attempt or usage fact makes the report stale. Log timestamps and other inspection bookkeeping that do not change those facts do not rebind the report.

view = run.status()                         # small additive evidence_report metadata
report = run.evidence_report()              # authenticates current completion and both files
markdown = report["markdown"]               # exactly the bytes in evidence.md
document = report["document"]               # parsed evidence.json
historical = run.evidence_report(require_current=False)

status(inspect_evidence=True) includes the authenticated document and Markdown without writing files, launching a provider or replaying checks. Availability is missing, export_failed, recorded (historical), current, stale or invalid. The default evidence_report() raises TaskRunError unless the report pair, approved contract, completion and current source are authenticated. Historical inspection permits an intact old delivery record after source or approval changes; it conveys no authority to publish that record as current. A missing old report is never reconstructed by a status reader. Reports do not add approval or relax the existing completion gate. Read-only workflows can record job completion with explicitly unverified code checks.

Declare provider evidence when starting: --evidence-provenance live, fake, mixed or unknown. This is a caller disclosure, fixed at launch, not a model attestation. A fixture executable named codex remains fake when declared fake; provider names and model names cannot distinguish fixtures from real inference. Without a declaration, custom configurations and older runs are unknown. A resume cannot relabel their prior attempts live. The scenario harness declares fake, live or mixed according to the route it actually launches. Tests using a fixture must pass --evidence-provenance fake. Human plan approval remains a separate decision.

Completed component builds publish it beside .autocode-components/manifest.json; the component CLI summary and MultiComponentBuild.evidence_report() expose it. Aggregate documents reference authenticated child TaskRun.evidence_report() documents and retain simulated runtime/deployment scope and unknown totals. Their existing inheritance and integration gates authorize accepted historical child deliveries; the aggregate reader does not claim fresh child verification. Aggregate completion timestamps and elapsed wall time remain unrecorded when the coordinator has no owned timing record. A child's completion time does not stand for later integration checks or runtime smoke. An aggregate also lists, under approvals, the approvals each child's own report lists (#722): child by child, in its children order, each row as that report has it plus child, the child's id. Its Markdown shows them as an Approvals table with a Child column, and says what it leaves out: a components run does not list approvals of the architecture it was built from. That run's own report lists them. A program report an older checkout wrote (before autocode program moved to the archive/program branch) also says that its agreement records no approver and that it does not list the approvals of the plan run it was derived from. A child whose report lists no approvals, because it was written before AutoCode listed them, is named in the aggregate's not-verified list rather than taken to have recorded none. When no child's report lists approvals, the aggregate has no approvals and no such section, as before. For component --run-local, --runtime-evidence-provenance fake|live|unknown separately discloses the runtime smoke route. Its HTTP results and sanitized local receipt are included in the aggregate; simulated smoke does not prove real containers or database behavior. The harness supplies this known declaration.

autocode issue pr requires a current canonical report before staging source and embeds its exact Markdown in the PR body. Oversized reports are refused rather than truncated. The common writer masks text matching the shared credential policy before binding canonical JSON and Markdown; it discloses masking and preserves raw artifact/source hashes and plan bindings. Raw evidence is not rewritten. Readers refuse unsafe historical pairs, and issue delivery refuses any wrapper that the GitHub transport would change, including unsafe Git-quoted source names, before staging or pushing. Committing tested dirty source changes Git HEAD: the issue adapter records an owned delivery receipt with the tested manifest, plan/report bindings and resulting commit/tree. A later pr --open requires that exact clean tree and intact historical pair; changed bytes, modes, deletions, untracked source, approval or report digests refuse publication. The body distinguishes the tested snapshot from the later delivery commit and does not call historical evidence current. The owned evidence_export state field stores only paths, hashes, binding and publication error; the export adapter owns writes, while status and TaskRun consume it. Cross-run coordinators use public child reports, never child state.json.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
All commands take --workspace WORKSPACE; commands on an existing run add --run-dir RUN.

Step Command Exit status Start autocode "BRIEF" --in-place --no-chat [options] 0 complete, 2 stopped for input Status autocode --status 0; prints JSON, the view is under "view" Display brief autocode --show-goal 0; prints the current brief for human review Export the plan as a plan file (TaskRun.export_plan(path)) autocode plan --export PATH: the plan shown for approval, or the approved one, as the file a team reviews in a pull request (Workflow); changes nothing in the run 0 written, 2 refused (no plan yet, or the file cannot be written) Continue autocode --no-chat [options] 0 complete, 2 stopped for input Resume a pause autocode resume --no-chat [options]; after editing the design at PAUSED_DESIGN_CONFLICT, autocode --resume-paused --no-chat [options] 0 complete, 2 stopped for input Grant N recoveries after resolving the cause autocode --resume-paused --grant-recovery N --no-chat [options] 0 complete, 2 stopped for input Accept a changed OpenCode transport autocode --resume-paused --accept-transport-change --no-chat [options] 0 complete, 2 stopped for input Adopt an inspected interrupted Investigator report autocode --recover-job-report TOKEN [options] 0 applied, 2 rejected; no model launched Answer autocode --answer QUESTION_ID=TEXT --resolver-token TOKEN (--answer repeatable); a question with options takes only one of its option labels or its proposed_default, exactly 0 saved, 2 rejected Respond to an operational Resolver request autocode --resolver-request ID --resolver-token TOKEN --resolver-response provide_information --resolver-message TEXT; the next resume re-evaluates it once (below) 0 saved, 2 rejected Name the model a role stopped on quota, a content-filter refusal or an authenticated output limit continues on autocode --answer route-ROLE=MODEL --resolver-token TOKEN, then resume the pause 0 saved, 2 rejected Name the model a stopped workflow job continues on (retry_job with route) autocode --answer route-ROLE=MODEL --job-retry-token TOKEN, then retry the job with the new token 0 saved, 2 rejected Choose an effort the model declares for a role whose named effort it does not (PAUSED_EFFORT_UNSUPPORTED, TaskRun.assign_effort(role, effort)) autocode --answer effort-ROLE=EFFORT, then resume the pause 0 saved, 2 rejected Approve the plan autocode --approve-goal TOKEN 0 saved, 2 rejected Approve a review autocode --approve-review CRITERION --review-token TOKEN 0 saved, 2 rejected Reject a review (TaskRun.reject_review(criterion, token, note)) autocode --reject-review CRITERION --review-token TOKEN --review-note TEXT 0 saved as feedback for revision, 2 rejected Plan feedback autocode --feedback TEXT 0 saved, 2 rejected Follow up a finished run autocode --follow-up TEXT 0 saved, 2 rejected

Answers and approvals never launch a model; continue afterwards. A follow-up is the next request in the same conversation: on a finished run it records a new turn (turn in the status view) and reopens the run at Requirements, which names the kind of job again from the new message, with the earlier turn as context (its job, a review's verdict and finding counts, a design turn's documents), and continues in the same run directory (#1860). After a review, a follow-up that asks to act on the findings is a build planned from them: the review's blocking findings are the task list, so no requirements questions are asked, and the plan still goes to the user for approval. The rewritten task names what the previous turn wrote (its report or note, then the files its stages changed; at most eight paths). After a design turn, a follow-up that asks to build the design names that document, so the build goes from Requirements to checking it against the repository (check_design). The build is planned afresh from the design: the design turn's contract and requirements move to the run's history rather than being revised, and the new plan still needs approval. After a design review, a reply to it (an answer, a correction) is named design and the Architect revises the same review: concern ids are kept, settled concerns stay as resolved, and review/design-review.json records every revision (CLI). Only a finished run takes a follow-up, and a finished run takes no answer, feedback or edited plan: either mistake exits 2 and changes nothing (see CLI). A usage error also exits 2, with a message starting usage: on stderr; the client checks for it so a mistyped flag is not mistaken for a pause. A rejection also exits 2, starting Input rejected:, and startup can exit 2 before any run exists; TaskRun.start raises with the tail of the CLI's output so a startup failure is never mistaken for a pause. TaskRun.respond_operational() uses the separate Resolver response command; an operational request cannot be answered with TaskRun.answer(), except the model question of a quota stop or a content-filter refusal (needs.route, see Models): At a cross-model independence stop, TaskRun.answer() and assign_model() use the current status view's route question without a resolver token: the core derives that decision from saved routes and checks the replacement again. Other resolver questions still require their current request token.

TaskRun.assign_model(role, model) answers route-ROLE with a model a person named, updates every existing --ROLE-model MODEL or --ROLE-model=MODEL occurrence in the client's options, and leaves the run paused for resume_paused(). A refused model raises and leaves the run paused with the question open. At a stopped workflow job (retry_job with route, see Failed workflow jobs) the same call answers with the job's job_retry_token instead of a resolver token and leaves the run paused for retry_job() with the new token. That stopped job's view also names the answer as a command, needs.route.command, in the same shell-quoted form as next_command and carrying the job's token, beside the retry next_command names; a client that shows the retry as a yes/no takes a typed model through it (#2005). Each answer consumes the Resolver request whose token it carries, and the questions still open come back under a new resolver_token, so a token read before an earlier answer is rejected. Without resolver_token, TaskRun.answer() reads the status view and uses the current request's token after checking that the request lists the question. When a person chose the answer, pass the token of the view they saw, so it cannot apply to a request they never saw. A question that lists options is a choice AutoCode acts on, so its answer must be one of those labels or the question's proposed_default, matched exactly apart from surrounding spaces (#1013). Any other text is rejected with the valid labels (Input rejected:, exit 2; TaskRun.answer() raises): nothing is saved, the token stays current, and something the options do not cover goes in --feedback (/feedback in --chat, which asks again after a rejected answer). A question without options takes any nonempty text. The terminal CLI also shows the remaining question IDs and current Resolver token on stderr after each successful answer and on --status, and --status also prints the run's cost line there (Cost: ..., from the view's cost), then, when the run has escalated, one Escalations: ... line and a line per escalation (from the view's escalations); the status JSON on stdout and the returned TaskRun view keep their existing shape. TaskRun.accept_transport_change() uses the explicit transport-change command after a person inspects the new route and the saved run reports PAUSED_TRANSPORT_CHANGED. At an eligible OpenCode/Kilo pause with no retained attempt or report repair, needs.action and next_command name --resume-paused --accept-transport-change; needs.recovery_hint explains that confirming accepts the changed connection settings after model/billing checks. It requires a person's confirmation and does not approve a plan or replace selected role models. Separately selected per-role tools retain their immutable identities and receive no acceptance offer. Other engines, uncertain attempts and unrelated pauses keep their existing recovery; clients must use the current named action rather than add this flag themselves. TaskRun.accept_source_edit() uses --resume-paused --accept-source-edit when a repair is paused at PAUSED_STALE_HANDOFF because a person edited the source. The approved contract, task, budget, proof and evidence pins stay.

docs.title: Reviewed Figma input changes
docs.text:
Start with native references (--figma-file and repeatable --figma-additional-file) or a complete exported bundle (--figma-manifest) in start_options. Both inputs produce the same durable coverage and plan ownership, exposed in view.design. See figma.md for collection, responsive derivation and source receipts.

At a stopped, reconciled boundary, run.revise_design(manifest_path, view["design"]["manifest_hash"], reason) proposes a new complete bundle. It keeps the old references, approvals and independently recorded evidence, pauses for a new plan review, and launches no model. A changed hash, active worker or pending control rejects the correction. Resume through TaskRun.resume_paused() to review the updated coverage; existing plan and completion gates still apply.

docs.title: Exact stopped-run recovery
docs.text:
The additive view.recovery projection describes a saved pause: what happened, what is retained, recorded failure groups and specific next actions. Its token binds the run, task, scope, settings, attempts and failure history. It does not grant approval, increase limits or confirm that a human request is authorized. Current AutoResolver request and approval gates remain authoritative. Running and complete tasks have no recovery card. Unknown pause types retain inspection and corrective feedback rather than offering a guessed execution command.

A caller displaying this card can append --expected-recovery-token TOKEN to an existing --resume-paused or --abandon-stage command. The runner rechecks the token under its run lock before applying settings or writing the checkpoint. If the pause changed, it refuses: refresh and inspect the new card. Existing CLI callers can omit the flag; all ordinary liveness, scope and approval gates still apply. Abandoning an interrupted attempt preserves partial work and does not resume automatically. Stop remains terminal for that conversation.

Each card action that runs a control names its exact flags in args, for example ["--resume-paused", "--retry-builder", "M3"] or ["--abandon-stage", "004/builder-02"]. A repair paused on an edited source offers accept_source_edit with ["--resume-paused", "--accept-source-edit"], the same command needs.action names. At a recovery novelty hold, where needs is the AutoResolver request with a retry_action, the card also offers retry_failed_stage with ["--resume-paused", "--retry-failed-stage"]: the one explicit retry of the held step. Before that request is published (RESOLVER_PENDING), a plain resume would only hold again, so needs is a resume whose action and retry_action both name that retry, and the card offers the same retry_failed_stage (#1770). When the hold cannot take it yet, the card offers no retry and needs.retry_unavailable names what must happen first. A hold for an incident that repeated with nothing new does not reach the card while its source, settings and scope still hold: AutoCode takes that one scoped retry itself and, if the incident repeats again, ends the run with a recorded outcome (recovery.category stopped, recovery.outcome with its reason and evidence, #2485), so the card shows a finished, failed run and no retry. The view and --retry-failed-stage apply one shared admission rule (autocode_recovery_limits.scoped_retry_refusal), so the view never offers a retry the CLI refuses on saved state. A client runs autocode --run-dir RUN --expected-recovery-token TOKEN ARGS... and never derives flags from the action's kind, so a new action needs no client change. Inspection, feedback, decision and conversation actions have no args: they open a view or ask the person for input instead of running a command.

An operator changing the Resolver's model at its no-progress hold supplies --resolver-model MODEL (and optionally --resolver-reasoning-effort EFFORT) together with --resume-paused --retry-failed-stage. This records the exact Resolver route change alongside one invocation-local retry. The original incident, usage and spent allowances remain intact; changing another role, engine, source, contract or scope is refused. A model change alone cannot authorize a call, and a rejected combined change saves no settings. Clients continue to use only named view actions; this operator control does not add a client-side route override.

docs.title: Inspecting current verification
docs.text:
autocode --run-dir RUN --status --inspect-evidence performs a read-only source and evidence inspection. The additive view.verification field lists every planned criterion and method, its recorded result and current checked / failed / unchecked state. A normal status projection labels saved results not_inspected; a saved PASS alone never establishes current proof.

The inspection checks the report's source, task, plan and criterion identity, then hashes its pinned project-local evidence. It rereads the source and checkpoint to detect work changing during inspection. Missing, stale or unavailable evidence keeps current requirements unchecked while retaining the old report. Human acceptance remains a separately authenticated requirement. The inspection never runs tests, changes the checkpoint, approves work or substitutes for the full completion gate. The dashboard uses this supported inspection for selected task detail; list polling does not hash every project checkout.

docs.title: Status view
docs.text:
Produced by tools/autocode_run_view.py from the saved state. Fields may be added; existing fields keep their names and meanings, and schema changes if a meaning must change. schemas/status-view.schema.json describes the status payload --status and --json print, with this view under view: every field it requires is always present, and a consumer must ignore fields it does not know.

action() is the same composition of needs, pause_category and next_command that view() returns those three fields from, without the evidence, usage and completion accounting around them. A caller that only needs the next action takes it from here; a caller that needs any other field takes view(). Nothing else may derive a recovery command from saved state.

autocode events is this contract's streaming form: one JSON line per event the run recorded, and --follow ends the stream where action() says the run ended — exit 0 on a completed run, exit 2 with next_command named on stderr for a run that needs a person. The envelope is schemas/run-event.schema.json.

autocode wait is the contract's blocking form: it ends where action() says the run reached a person, or where COMPLETE says it finished — and, because a saved status is only a claim, it also ends when a fresh controller inspection finds nothing owning the saved RUNNING checkpoint. Every other read in this family surfaces that gap only after the fact.

task is the exact saved request text, including literal shell syntax and line breaks. task_sha256 is its UTF-8 SHA-256, also recorded when a new run starts or a follow-up rewrites its request. The read-only view computes the digest from saved text for legacy runs too; absent task text gives null for both fields. A legacy request that cannot encode as UTF-8 remains visible with a null hash. These fields identify what AutoCode received; they cannot recover text expanded by a shell before CLI invocation. Use --brief-file PATH or --brief - to read the original UTF-8 bytes without shell expansion.

{
  "schema": 2,
  "pause_category": "your_decision",
  "pause_category_label": "Your decision",
  "status": "AWAITING_GOAL_APPROVAL",
  "next_command": "AUTOCODE_APPROVE_GOAL_TOKEN=... autocode --run-dir RUN --approve-goal -",
  "done": false,
  "needs": {"kind": "approve_plan", "token": "..."},
  "phase": "AWAITING_GOAL_APPROVAL",
  "next_stage": "orchestrator",
  "iteration": 1,
  "stop_reason": null,
  "current_task": {"id": "task-1", "objective": "...", "milestone_id": "M1"},
  "workflow": "build",
  "turn": 1,
  "evidence": {
    "outcome": "...",
    "base_commit": "...",
    "acceptance": [{"id": "AC1", "criterion": "...", "status": "passed", "evidence": "...",
                    "validator_status": "PASS", "human_reviewed": false}],
    "validator_source_revision": "...",
    "findings": [{"id": "F1", "status": "resolved", "severity": "minor", "finding": "...", "source": "sol"}],
    "regression_proof": null,
    "unverified_risk_claims": []
  }
}

pause_category groups a stopped run's cause as your_decision, your_environment, model_or_provider or autocode; pause_category_label is its readable label. The exact status and every existing field retain their meaning. Both category fields and next_command are null for active or completed runs. A typed quota/refusal route retains the provider category; an operational request uses the additive needs.pause_origin when its published request names that cause.

next_command formats the current needs and existing recovery controls. It contains the owned run/workspace paths, and issued tokens travel through their paired environment variables with the - selector. Replace ANSWER, MODEL, N or GOAL_FILE with a decision; presentation never chooses one or grants approval. An uncertain attempt offers abandonment first; inspect status again before resuming. Missing issued tokens offer a noninteractive display, and a missing original source or immutable caller binding offers inspection. A terminal stop or dependency wait offers no recovery command. CLI gates still validate freshness and authority when a person executes any displayed command.

needs.command_inputs describes the one number a pause leaves to a person, so a client can ask for it instead of handing the command off (#2044). Every bound a budget pause names is described, with the same row shape:

Pause holding the run id flag label used reports PAUSED_TIME_LIMIT max_seconds --max-seconds Total active time (seconds) elapsed: active seconds PAUSED_COST_LIMIT max_cost_usd --max-cost-usd Cost cap (whole USD) known spend in USD PAUSED_ITERATION_LIMIT max_iterations --max-iterations Total iterations the current iteration PAUSED_MILESTONE_TIME_LIMIT, PAUSED_MILESTONE_BUDGET max_milestone_seconds --max-milestone-seconds Milestone active time (seconds) the milestone's counted seconds PAUSED_MILESTONE_STALLED max_milestone_replans --max-milestone-replans Milestone replans replans used PAUSED_NO_PROGRESS (its unchanged-batch bound only) no_progress_limit --no-progress-limit Unchanged implementation batches allowed unchanged batches counted

For each, minimum is one more than the larger of current (the saved bound; the cost cap may be fractional) and the count, maximum is the largest safe integer, and the command is --resume-paused FLAG N --expected-recovery-token - with the current recovery.token in AUTOCODE_EXPECTED_RECOVERY_TOKEN. The row is offered wherever that bound holds the run: at its own pause, after AutoResolver published its operational request for it, and once corrective information has been reviewed and held (not while that review is pending). It is not offered while the run is active, while an attempt or report repair is unreconciled, or where the need names another control (a retry, an edit, a model question, a new run).

Where next_command is that raise, the row binds to it. Where it is not, because the need is a plain --resume-paused or AutoResolver's operational response, the row also carries command: the raise itself, a complete command with the run's paths and the private token channel. A client fills the row's arg_index in that command and takes it, never in next_command or in a reply. The terminal chat offers it at the pause's yes/no and at the operational reply. The VS Code run details and sidebar chat show it as its own number and Raise limit and continue button beside the plain resume or the recovery reply, confirmed with the bound it changes. The browser dashboard's recovery card shows the one row needs.command_inputs describes, attached or separate, as a number entry once the saved pause is inspected; its backend re-reads the status, checks the recovery token the card showed and types the number only into the command the view names for it. The headless conformance client, the VS Code client and the dashboard validate the row the same way (tools/autocode_client_actions.check_input).

For the finite total-time recovery, for example:

{"id":"max_seconds","kind":"integer","flag":"--max-seconds","placeholder":"N",
 "arg_index":2,"label":"Total active time (seconds)","current":2700,"elapsed":2800.5,
 "minimum":2801,"maximum":9007199254740991}

The field is an array containing this one descriptor, and is offered only when the named action requires --resume-paused --max-seconds N. arg_index counts the arguments after removing the executable and owned --run-dir/--workspace pairs. The complete remaining command must be --resume-paused --max-seconds N --expected-recovery-token -, with the current recovery.token in AUTOCODE_EXPECTED_RECOVERY_TOKEN. A client validates the exact command, descriptor and token binding before substituting that one argument. A person must enter a whole number between minimum and maximum; there is no default and no extraction of numbers from chat. The minimum exceeds both the saved cap and consumed active time. An empty, zero, fractional, unsafe or out-of-range value grants nothing. An N with no row is a client gap.

This choice changes only the total active-time cap. It neither changes other limits or model routes nor approves a plan. Recovery freshness is rechecked under the run lock, including the saved active-time accounting. Ordinary CLI callers retain the existing --max-seconds 0 behavior; this finite input does not expose disabling the guard. Corrective information still authorizes no allowance: its pending deterministic review must first reach the held decision.

At a reconciled PAUSED_PLANNING_BUDGET checkpoint, the same array can instead describe the existing finite planning-review allowance:

{"id":"planning_review_call_limit","kind":"integer","flag":"--planning-review-call-limit",
 "placeholder":"N","arg_index":2,"label":"Total plan-review calls","current":2,"used":2,
 "minimum":3,"maximum":9007199254740991}

Only two exact remaining command shapes are supported, each followed by --expected-recovery-token - with the current token in the same private channel: --resume-paused --planning-review-call-limit N (index 2, explicit resume requested) and --planning-review-call-limit N (index 1, save only). The latter is the held operational-information action; a client must not insert Resume. Its next fresh status determines whether a separate continuation is available. Both inputs say "Set review allowance": even the explicit-resume form can save first and leave a separately named Resume. current is the saved finite allowance and used is the charged review-call count. Both are integers; the minimum exceeds both, and there is no default or unlimited choice. Planning accounting participates in the recovery token's freshness.

The person confirms the exact total number of calls. This uses the existing allowance setter and preserves charged calls, recovery history, other limits, routes and plan approval. It does not reset a cycle, change allowance policy or approve the plan. Ordinary CLI callers retain their existing explicit zero semantics.

An exhausted PAUSED_TIMEOUT_RECOVERY can name one additional finite choice:

{"id":"grant_recovery","kind":"integer","flag":"--grant-recovery","placeholder":"N",
 "arg_index":2,"label":"Additional recoveries","current":3,"used":3,"minimum":1,"maximum":3}

Its only remaining command is --resume-paused --grant-recovery N --expected-recovery-token -, using the same current private token channel. current is the existing fixed automatic-recovery allowance; used is counted spend, including the existing legacy fallback. The finite input accepts 1 through used, validated as safe integers, and never supplies a default. Pending corrective information must first reach its deterministic held decision.

This takes the existing grant action: choosing 1 replenishes one spent slot (for example, 3 counted becomes 2). It does not add to the fixed allowance or bank an excess grant. The existing action clears the consecutive-timeout streak, retains historical attempts and appends its ordinary grant receipt. Accounting, legacy fallback inputs and prior grant receipts are bound into recovery freshness. Routes, global time/spend/stage limits and plan approval remain unchanged.

evidence is what the run agreed to deliver and what supports it, for reports made outside the runner (such as a pull request body, docs/issues.md): the approved contract's intended outcome, the base commit, one row per acceptance criterion with its latest recorded outcome and evidence, the findings ledger, and, for bug fixes, the runner's own fail-before/pass-after regression proof (verdict, fail_to_pass, failures, unverified, commands, source_revision, and case_tests: each English test case's proving tests; null otherwise). Optional follow_up_baseline, when present on the proof, identifies the immutable completed-turn source freshly checked for new follow-up guards. Inherited regressions still use the original run reference; this field does not reuse a previous proof or approve a plan. Each acceptance row also carries validator_status: the latest saved validation's result for that criterion (FAIL, PASS or NOT_VERIFIED), or null when that validation has no row for it. A failed criterion must be distinguishable from an unchecked one; the decision report's own status is a separate field and a separate vocabulary (verified / not). validator_source_revision is the source revision that validation checked, or null before one. The view does not read the workspace: after rework, validator_status still reports that validation until a newer one replaces it, so compare validator_source_revision to the workspace before treating the status as current. test_cases lists a reproduced bug's regression tests in plain English (id, given, when, then; empty otherwise; see Bug fixes). check_replay is the current validation's checks as the runner itself re-ran them in a clean copy: verdict, source_revision and one row per command (command, exit_code, timed_out, output); null before a PASS validation and for validations that predate it (see Execution). It also carries the runner's own observations of promises a person declared: brief_acceptance (exact CLI output formats) and risk_acceptance (process recovery of a declared lease queue or transactional outbox, and a race between three interpreters when the request also promises atomicity under contention: verdict, source_revision, summary and one row per observation with its pinned supervisor transcript), each null when the request declares none. A failed risk_acceptance makes the replay's verdict FAIL even though the Tester's own checks passed (see Execution). Each findings row also has source: sol (Tester), astra (Completion Reviewer) or runner (a failed runner lifecycle observation or, in a --package run, the files changed outside the package, one blocking row naming each path (Monorepo packages)). No model report closes a runner finding: the runner closes it when a later check of its own passes, and a person can close one with --close-finding. Closing the package finding accepts nothing: the next check before review opens a new one, and --accept-completion refuses while the change is there. unverified_risk_claims lists the person's own sentences that promise durability or concurrency but that no runner protocol exercises (kind durability or concurrency, source_id, quote, reason); [] when there are none. It is a disclosure, not a check: a PASS never verifies them. For a completed code-review workflow, workflow_result.outcome and its artifact hash name the runner-derived verdict. Its optional review_attribution object contains pre_existing and inconclusive counts, submitted_verdict and verdict_adjustment. The summary distinguishes nonblocking pre-existing observations from blockers with inconclusive attribution. The findings artifact preserves each executable blocker's disposition (kind, reason, runner, inputs, base_proof, changed_proof); proof references carry path and sha256. Only a validated runner disposition of pre_existing exempts a blocking finding. Identical failures only support that exemption when the cited file and line range are verified unchanged in the actual applied scratch source; changed, unknown and out-of-range locations retain the blocker. Legacy findings and reviews without an explicit patch retain blocking behavior. This attribution applies to review findings, not the task's acceptance criteria. See patch attribution.

proof_stability is the proving tests' repeats: repeats, unstable (each test, which side, its kind and the run outcomes), unrepeated, next_step when a test disagreed, and note; null when the proof did not repeat tests. diff_coverage is the same proof's line coverage of changed product hunks (collected, tool, note, files, uncovered, unmeasured); null when the proof did not record it. The raw coverage report alone grants no completion authority. Current task proofs combine authenticated producing receipts with mutation evidence in verification.changed_code_evidence (#2474). mutation_check is the same proof's mutation check (#699, #2474, see Named test proof): collected, note, limit_per_file, budget_seconds, files (each path, notes, and mutants with line, operator, before, after, outcome killed, survived, timeout or not_run, and survived_tests) and, once collected, survivors, keyed by the same English test-case ids as regression_proof.case_tests (a diagnosis's T1 for a bug fix, the acceptance criterion's id for a planned build): each case's proving tests that still passed with a product line changed (test, path, line, operator, before, after, text), {} when every mutant that ran was killed. Every proof that did not pass, including one refused before any test ran, has the note not run: the proof did not pass and no survivors; null when an older passing proof had no due test case, or there is no proof. Current task proofs enumerate eligible Python sites within the existing command budget and require observed named-test failures; setup, collection, timeout and unrun outcomes never demonstrate a kill. verification.changed_code_evidence lists exact gap IDs, file hashes/lines, tested, reason_required or excepted, the reason/evidence, and the chosen fallback. Missing tools never trigger a project install: demonstrated per-line mutation evidence is the deterministic fallback, otherwise an explicit independent per-line judgment is required. Two direct repairs precede the existing Investigator path within saved run limits; no person question is added for these gaps. A review can instead report the original tests in its explicit patch: subject is reviewed_patch_tests, patch_path and patch_sha256 identify that patch, selected_files and selected_tests record the independently run pool, and survivors is keyed by actual test IDs. These are separate from reviewer-delivered finding tests, which must still fail on the reviewed code. Not-run notes never mean that all possible mutants were killed. The same report appears in workflow_result.mutation_check and the canonical document's Review test mutation check section; no named proof is manufactured for a review. regression_proof.unstable lists the same unstable tests. finding_scope_moves appears once an approved revision moved a criterion that open findings cite to another milestone: one row per finding it re-attributed (finding, from with the old milestone_id and criteria, to with every resulting finding's id, milestone_id and criteria, contract_token, at). A finding split across milestones appears in findings once per part (see Execution).

usage is the run's tokens and cost so far: stages (finished), active_stage (the stage running now, or null), tokens, cost_usd (reported, estimated, complete), unknown_stages and by_role (see Cost reporting). Unknown cost is not zero: complete is false while a stage has none or is running.

cost is the run's spend against its money cap (Money cap), priced at the dated table autocode models --prices prints: estimated_usd (stages priced from the table), reported_usd (stages whose provider reported a cost), inherited_usd (the spend a restored checkpoint carried from the run it was restored from), spent_usd (their sum, which the cap is compared with), cap_usd (the saved --max-cost-usd, or null for no cap), unpriced_stages (stages on a model without a rate, or with no token counts recorded; not counted), complete and prices_as_of. Each stage counts once. A null amount is unknown, never zero: estimated_usd and reported_usd are null when no stage has that basis, and spent_usd is null when no stage is known at all; while complete is false, spent_usd is a floor. usage.cost_usd keeps the frozen comparison rates its reports are bound to, so its estimated can differ from cost.estimated_usd.

cost.breakdown groups that same finished-stage ledger in three alternative ways: by_stage, by_process_outcome (completed, failed, interrupted, unknown) and by_billing (subscription, pay per token, unknown: how the stage's model bills, from the billing discovery saved for an automatically selected run, else the model ID's account; an OpenAI model's login is not recorded, so it is unknown). A subscription stage's estimated_usd is the API-equivalent figure, not the plan's bill. Each row has stages, spent_usd, reported_usd, estimated_usd, unpriced_stages, partial_stages, failed_stages, interrupted_stages and complete; stage rows also name the stage and routing-aware job. The groupings overlap and must not be added together. cost.breakdown.unpriced says why the finished unpriced stages have no cost (#1713): usage_missing (no input or output token count recorded), model_unknown (counts but no model identified) and rate_unavailable (counts, but the price table has no rate for the model), with those models in models_without_rate. They are counts of stages, never an amount. cost.breakdown.price_bases lists the dated rates the estimated stages were priced at, one entry per model and rate: model, input, output, cached_input where published, source, retrieved, until (the UTC date the rate stopped applying; null for the current rate) and stages. Each stage is priced at the rate in force when it finished. Each grouping plus inherited_usd reconciles with the known run total, subject to six-decimal rounding. Inherited spend has no stage attribution. Active attempts and unaccounted workers are excluded, just as in the money-cap ledger; the overall cost.complete remains false while they run. Unknown cost is not zero. A completed process may return a rejecting review, and another attempt may be required work: these labels do not claim acceptance or wasted spend. The cost line calls out repeated stages and failed/interrupted attempts. For observed repetition reasons, consult the existing efficiency.repeats projection.

escalation_outcomes counts the run's escalations and Builder retries by the outcome the runner stamped on them (passed, paused, open; tools/autocode_route_ladder.py). The runner stamps every one still open passed when the run completes on work a validation passed (including when completion is accepted via --accept-completion), or when the Completion Reviewer or Resolver assigns the next task while the last validation passed, and paused at the Builder's retry-limit pause. At that assignment it leaves the Builder's own (its climbs, its retries and its stronger attempt) open when the work was sent back after that validation's attempt started (a retry-policy charge or a correction task anywhere in the run; escalations takes the same two as a failure after a PASS of the escalation's own milestone), or when that attempt's start is not in the run's records, so a send-back cannot be ruled out. A stamp is the struggle's: every entry still open when the struggle ends takes its end, so a climb a later climb replaced reads passed there and failed_again as a row, and before the struggle ends a stamp is open while its row may read passed. Read a row's outcome for how one escalation ended. escalations lists each escalation the run made, oldest first (tools/autocode_escalation_view.py, #612): a role's climb on its effort ladder (kind effort_climb) and the Builder's stronger attempt (stronger_attempt; see Models). Each row has the route role that moved, the stage that struggled and its job as the screen names it (from the role when the stage is not known; null, never a code name, when neither names a job), at, trigger (validation_rework, rejected_output, no_progress or abandoned_attempt for a climb, execution_failure for the stronger attempt), detail, struggle_id, task_id (for the stronger attempt, the task of the failed attempt its decision names), the route it climbed from and to (model, reasoning_effort, profile), deferred_by_parallel_builder (a parallel Builder left the stronger attempt to this run, which made it serially), inherited, attempts, cost and outcome:

  • attempts are the role's stage records launched on the route it climbed to, from the escalation until the first of: a validation of its work that passed (that attempt included), unless one of its attempts was then charged as a failure (see outcome), or the role's next escalation of either kind (its next climb, the Builder's stronger attempt). The running one is included (active); dry runs and the runner's own stages are not attempts. A climb lasts for the rest of the run, so a later milestone's attempts on the climbed rung count until one of those ends it. A stronger attempt's attempts are this run's own Builder records: a parallel Builder's records the parent holds (worker_milestone) are its worker's, whose own stronger attempt is recorded only in its worker run. A validation judged an escalation's work when one of its attempts produced it, or, for the Builder, whose work another role validates, when the Builder's last attempt before it is one of its attempts. No other role is judged by another role's validation: a Tester PASS of the Builder's work is not the work of a Completion Reviewer's or Resolver's climb. Nor is a validation of another milestone's work, or of work on a route the role was moved to. The runner assigns every task, a rework included, a new id, so an attempt's milestone is its task's contract hash and milestone ids (current_task, task_archive): an attempt whose task is of another milestone than the attempt the escalation was made from (a later milestone, or a replanned contract's) is not its work, and for the Builder neither is a validation whose own task is: a replanned contract's first task may be a validate task, whose Tester runs before any Builder attempt. When either task is not recorded, they are not told apart. The Builder's retry policy's charge names the record of the attempt that failed: the Builder's own, or the Tester's or Completion Reviewer's that sent its work back, whose work is the Builder's last attempt for that record's task before the decision; when no Builder attempt of that task started before it (a validate task: unchanged work sent back to the Tester; a record that names no task), the Builder's last attempt of that task's milestone (of any, when it names none) before that record. A review that sends the work back also assigns a correction task (an implement task whose decision is REWORK), which charges the Builder's last attempt of that task's milestone before it was assigned: with the retry policy off (settings.workflow set, or builder_retry disabled), nothing else records that a review sent passed work back.
  • cost prices those attempts as cost prices a stage: usd (reported plus estimated), reported_usd, estimated_usd, unpriced_attempts, unrouted_attempts and complete. An attempt with no usage record is unpriced, never zero: usd is then a floor (complete false), or null when no attempt is priced. A stage record saved without a launch route (before 2026-10-01) cannot be shown to have run on the route it climbed to: the role's such records in that span are counted in unrouted_attempts, not listed in attempts, and no validation of them decides the outcome; while there are any, the cost is unknown the same way (complete false, usd null when no listed attempt is priced). An escalation whose attempt never launched (a cost-cap or time-budget stop before it) cost 0.
  • inherited is true for an escalation made before this run was created: in a checkpoint continuation (autocode checkpoint --restore), one the restored run made. Its attempts there are not in this run's stage records, so its cost is unknown, never zero: usd is null (a floor of its attempts since the restore, when it has any) and complete false. What that run spent is in cost's inherited_usd.
  • outcome is passed, failed_again, paused or running, and outcome_basis says what decided it, the first that applies: the first decisive record after it (validation: a validation of its work passed, unless one of its attempts of its milestone was then charged as a failure: by the Builder's retry policy, as it charges a review that sends passed work back, or by any correction task of its milestone assigned after that PASS, also one that sends back a later attempt that failed its own check; later_escalation: the role climbed again, the milestone made another stronger attempt, or the Builder made its stronger attempt after climbing, or climbed after it, from this escalation's attempt), the Builder's retry-limit pause (recorded: the runner's paused stamp, or the pause decision that charged one of its attempts of its milestone, since the runner does not stamp an escalation it already stamped passed), a validation of its work failing or blocked (validation), else such a charge (recorded: a retry, the stronger attempt, the retry-limit pause or a correction task charged to one of its attempts of its milestone), the runner's passed stamp (recorded), for a role other than the Builder, only when every attempt of its role since it, until the role's next escalation, ran on the route it climbed to and there was at least one, else the run's status now (run_status: complete is passed, running is running, any pause, wait or stop is paused). The runner stamps another role's open climb passed where the Completion Reviewer or Resolver assigns the next task while the last validation passed, whoever's work passed, so that stamp is not taken over a failure of its own work, once a person or the Builder's retry policy moved the role to another route, or when the role ran nothing since. Validations judge the Builder's work, and a run saved by AutoCode before this change (#612) may hold a passed stamp the runner wrote on the Builder's stronger attempt in the handler that made it, at the PASS the review just sent back, before that attempt ran, so the Builder's stamp is never taken. It is a projection of saved records, so it can change as the run continues.

A parallel Builder's own climbs and stronger attempts stay in its worker run's state, which the view does not read; a stronger attempt it leaves to the parent is listed once the parent makes it.

progress is how far the run has got, counted only from saved records (tools/autocode_progress_view.py; added by autocode --status, which supplies the accepted milestones, the valid review receipts and the state of the recorded workers). line is the one line a person reads, for example Builder working · 1 of 3 tasks done · 1 of 3 requirements checked, 1 failed · 1 open problem · nothing needed from you; its wording may change, so programs read the fields beside it:

  • headline: Complete, Waiting for you, Paused, Waiting for another run, <job> working, <job> finished (its report is saved but not applied yet), <job> finished · Next: <job> when the run already knows the job after that finished one (#1711), Next: <job>, <job> stopped without saving a report (the recorded workers are gone; see the top-level stale and next_action; a stopped runner check is named Runner check (...)), or the status in words when no stage is known. Job names come from autocode_roles; stage is that name.
  • needs_you: what a person has to do, in words: what needs asks for, the top-level next_action when the workers are gone, or plan approval needed while a saved plan waits to be shown for approval.
  • tasks: one item per milestone of the current plan, proposed or approved (number, id, label, state, current), with done and total. state is done (accepted under the current contract, or the run is complete), working (the run is on it now), waiting, or unknown when milestone checkpoints are off (known is then false until the run completes).
  • requirements: one item per acceptance criterion. Its state comes from the newest PASS or FAIL for it across the Tester results under the current contract (the current validation and the ones before it); NOT_VERIFIED and a missing row leave an earlier verdict standing. checked is a pass in the current validation with no different source recorded since; checked_earlier a pass from an earlier validation, or from one the source has changed since (rebuilt_since_check); failed; awaiting_review (a human-review criterion the Tester passed but no person has accepted yet); reviewed (a person's review receipt is valid for the current validation); unchecked otherwise, never checked. Each state has a count. Results under another contract, or with no contract hash under a contract, do not count. The view does not read the workspace.
  • problems: open counts the open findings (items: id, finding, source, severity, blocking) plus, for a code or design review and a design-conflict stop, the findings that job saved instead (reports: kind, blocking, advisory, report_path; a design review also has questions, the number of questions its report asks, and revision, 1 until a reply revises it). A design review's blocking and advisory count its open concerns: a concern a reply resolved is not a problem.
  • for_earlier_request: true after a --follow-up until the follow-up's own plan is drafted; the previous request's tasks, requirements and review findings are then left out.

No field is a percentage or an estimate from elapsed time.

displayed_plan is an optional structured approval projection: revision, hash, token, acceptance_criteria, constraints and permission_boundaries. It appears only when the last displayed token matches the current sealed contract. Missing, modified or stale contracts do not expose it. Criterion verification_method, human_review and the optional current_behavior (what happens today, from the bound diagnosis; #2133) values are copied without interpreting or coercing model-authored text. Where the body carries them it also includes milestones (each with at least id and objective) and end_to_end_flow: the completion order the approval binds, so a person approving a member plan can see a coordinator-owned joint-proof milestone in the milestone list instead of only in criteria summaries (#2434); sealed legacy bodies predate both fields and simply omit them, keeping every earlier field's shape. Automation must check these structured fields and bind the token to needs.token; do not infer approval authority by parsing headings or review labels embedded in --show-goal prose. This projection is not approval, execution permission or completion proof; the existing CLI approval checks remain authoritative.

approved_contract is the plan in force: the contract that was approved, for as long as that approval holds. It has revision, hash, token (the r<revision>:<hash> that was approved), task_id, approved_at, approval_source (skip_to_build when the person chose on starting the run to approve the reviewed plan, otherwise person) and body, the full approved contract body (outcome, deliverables, acceptance criteria, constraints, permission boundaries, end-to-end flow, technical approach, milestones and the rest) copied as saved. It also has goal_hash, the SHA-256 of that body (what autocode plan --check FILE prints for a file holding exactly this plan), and plan_file: null, or, when the plan was loaded with --goal-file and not approved, changed and approved again since, the file's path and goal_hash, the revision it was loaded as and the parts of the plan that changed since then, apart from the runner's records of the plan's review (#720). A malformed record gives null, never an absent approved_contract. It is absent until the current sealed contract carries an approval of exactly its token, once a newer draft revision replaces the approved one (a goal change, or the plan a --follow-up drafts), and while the contract itself records an open blocking question (approval refuses one); a question the run asks after approval does not remove it. An edited or stale contract does not expose it, and a completed run keeps it. Until a follow-up's own plan is drafted, and for a follow-up answered by a review, design or discussion, which drafts none, it is still the earlier request's approved plan; compare turn or progress.for_earlier_request. A follow-up that builds the design the previous turn proposed is the exception: when the design check passes, the design turn's plan is archived, so approved_contract is absent until the build's own plan is approved. The approval is normally the user's, but a small bug fix approved under the workflow policy the user agreed to (the short path for small fixes, off for now; see Bug fixes) shows it too, and the view does not say which. displayed_plan is what a person is asked to approve; approved_contract is what was approved. A coordinating layer reads a child run's approved criteria here, never from state.json. Like displayed_plan, it is neither execution permission nor completion proof.

approvals lists every plan and review approval, completion acceptance, goal edit and pause-releasing resume the run recorded, oldest first (#722): kind (plan, review, completion for --accept-completion, edit or resume), at, actor (user_cli for a person, workflow_policy for a small bug fix approved under the workflow policy), contract_token (the plan token approved, or the draft an edit installed; null for a review, a completion acceptance or a resume), criterion (the accepted criterion, null otherwise), pause_status (the pause a resume took the run out of, such as PAUSED_TIME_LIMIT, or the one a pause intervention interrupted; null otherwise), source (skip_to_build for a plan approved because the run was started with --skip-to-build; null otherwise) and provenance: git_user_name, git_user_email, host, command (autocode, the resume command word when typed, and the invocation's option names, never their values) and claimed_as (the --as name, or null). None of it is verified (Who approved). provenance is null for a record saved before AutoCode kept it and for a workflow-policy approval. It is a history: an approval stays listed after a newer plan or a rejection replaces it, so read what is in force from approved_contract and evidence.acceptance[].human_reviewed. It is empty until the first record.

routes maps every configured role to its saved model and engine, plus reasoning_effort (null when unspecified), resolved per-role provider, and job (its primary job's screen name from autocode_roles). These are configured assignments, not evidence a stage ran or a prediction of conditional routing or escalation. Several slots can serve the same job. The actual history is in usage.accounting.attempts: each attempt now also includes job, derived from its stage and workflow, alongside its recorded model and launch_route, and route_role, the slot whose route the stage launched when that differs from its unit role (null otherwise; #2114). Clients must keep configured assignments separate from actual attempts; changing a saved route does not rewrite an earlier attempt's model or reasoning effort.

The top-level provider names the provider those OpenCode-engine routes launch through (opencode, claude for the built-in Claude Code provider, or a configured tool's name); it is null when every role runs on Codex. route_assignments lists, oldest first, every model a person named for a role after its quota ran out or its provider's content filter refused it: kind (always route_assignment), role, job, from, to, engine, stage, attempt_id, events, pause_status, at, actor, via (answer or resume_flag) and, when via is answer, the request_id it answered. It is empty for runs that never stopped on quota or a refusal.

For a diagnosed criterion contradiction, an answer need may include recommended_revision with acceptance_criteria: [{id, criterion}] and recommended_revision_response: "Accept recommended revision". Present the request's current/proposed wording before submitting that exact response through TaskRun.respond_operational(request_id, token, text). Acceptance installs a draft; it does not advance the run or approve the plan. Follow the next published need through configured plan review and explicit approve_plan(new_token). The correction is limited to existing criterion text: at most 32 rows, with IDs up to 128 characters and wording up to 8,192 characters. All verification, human-review, source and permission fields are preserved. Replaying the identical response is idempotent. A stale request or changed diagnosis is refused, and other information keeps the ordinary hold.

information_review describes Resolver's one re-evaluation of the corrective information last sent to an operational request (--resolver-response provide_information), or is null: request_id, status, cause (the pause the request was for), scheduled_at, evaluated_at, decision (hold or continue), reason, action and receipt (the runner-owned decision record). status is pending until the next resume at that pause (autocode resume or --resume-paused with no other recovery flag) evaluates it once, with no provider call. A run that left the pause first (through another control, or to a newer request) never evaluates it, and status reads superseded. Otherwise it is held (still paused, action and needs.action name the control it requires, such as --resume-paused --grant-recovery N, a raised bound, --abandon-stage ATTEMPT or, at a parallel Builder member's quota or content-filter stop, --resume-paused --retry-builder M, which action also names while the review is pending; at PAUSED_PLANNING_BUDGET that is the planning_budget need's action), admitted (the run continued through the normal admission checks) or stale (the run, request, response or evidence changed after the response, so it was not evaluated and Resolver asks a fresh request). Information never raises a limit, resets a count or approves anything; a later resume repeats a held decision without evaluating again.

tool_containment says how built-in OpenCode stages other than planning run their tools: contained (inside the kernel tool boundary, see Execution) or uncontained_user_accepted (the run was started or resumed with --allow-uncontained-tools; those stages have OpenCode's own permission checks only, and each such stage record says uncontained_tools: true). It is null for runs that launch no such stage: the native Codex engine (unless its Investigator is pinned to an OpenCode model) and configured providers.

tool_containment_backend names the kernel boundary the latest contained launch ran in, read from that launch's own stage record (the running stage first), never from the machine reading the status: backend (seatbelt or bubblewrap; null if the record names neither), backend_version (the macOS release, or bwrap --version), and that launch's stage, iteration and started_at. A launch saved before backends were recorded reads as seatbelt with a null version, since Seatbelt was the only backend then. Launches without a boundary (planning, uncontained, configured providers, Codex) are passed over, so after a run turns uncontained this still names the last boundary that applied; tool_containment says whether the run's stages are contained now. It is null until a stage launches contained.

package is the repository directory a run started with --package works in, or null for a run of the whole repository; see Monorepo packages.

direct_rework_assignments records a repair assigned directly from a Completion Owner's accepted REWORK report. Each entry binds the original and assigned tasks, contract, source, report and evidence hashes, and the ordinary retry charged by the runner. It is assignment provenance, not a Resolver diagnosis or completion proof. The list is empty for runs that have never used this path.

Direct assignment is limited to the first ordinary repair of a single serial milestone, with an independent Tester's executed failure and a complete task within the same approved scope. Ambiguous or incomplete tasks, repeated failures, parallel/integrated work and recovery cases retain the Resolver path. Pending human decisions remain intact and hold the handoff before either route. Modified sealed evidence pauses before dispatch. Every assigned repair still requires fresh verification and independent completion acceptance.

workflow is the kind of job AutoCode recognized from the request, named by Requirements, the first stage of every new run and follow-up turn (#1846,

docs.title: 1860): one of build, bugfix, review, design or discuss (see
docs.text:
scenarios/README.md, "Workflows"). A flow without a Requirements stage (the v2 planning flow, a run without a Requirements role) still begins with the Job recognizer (recognize_workflow). It is null until that stage has run, and for runs that predate it. workflow_source is "model" when a model decided it (Requirements or the recognizer) and "user" when --workflow named it; workflow_reason is Requirements understood: <outcome> (Requirements named no job; planned as a build when its report named none), or the recognizer's one-sentence reason. Both are null whenever workflow is.

planning_depth shows how much planning the run chose and why (adaptive planning). It is always present:

Field Meaning adaptive Whether the run plans adaptively (--adaptive-planning, the default where it applies); false on the fixed sequence clarity "clear" or "vague": the judgment of the request text by the stage that names the job, Requirements (or the recognizer on a flow without Requirements); null on the fixed sequence, under --workflow, and before the job is named. It no longer skips Requirements; a small clear brief keeps its reduced plan-review depth requirements_skipped true only on a run saved before 2026-10-22 whose recognizer judged a build request clear and sent it straight to the Planner, false where such a run's judgment kept the Requirements stage; null on every newer run, which always runs Requirements first (#1860), and wherever clarity decided nothing plan_size "small", "medium" or "large", measured from the draft's milestones and the files they touch at its first review; null before that review size_signals The counts behind plan_size: milestones, affected_paths, acceptance_criteria, dependency_edges; null before the first review review_limit The plan-review call allowance set at the first review (0 is unlimited); a large plan gets one more call. A later --planning-review-call-limit changes the allowance in force, not this record challenges How many first-style reviews the Plan Reviewer has made approved_early true when the Plan Reviewer approved the Planner's draft at a first-style review, with no revision or final review uncited_sentences How many source sentences the latest Planner draft's criteria leave uncited, counted by the runner; 0 when none or unknown

The Plan Reviewer still reviews every build plan and you still approve it; these fields only report the decisions.

stage_policy records which planning path a bug-fix run took and why (compact planning). It is null until a bug-fix run's Investigator has reported (and for every other job); then:
