Stage contexts explicitly list current bundles, rejected captures with reasons, and unavailable inventory cases. The independent reviewer opens those candidates and compares them with the design. Exported-inventory reports copy the receipt into each design_results row alongside candidate_ref and comparison_ref. Native Figma reports use implementation_captures entries containing only capture_ref and capture_sha256, and cite their candidate images in criterion evidence. Partial nonvisual milestones can leave this array empty; whole-task visual acceptance cannot. An additional historical image in passing criterion evidence cannot be hidden beside a fresh receipt.

Report decoding and completion recheck provenance and pinned evidence. Source changes after capture, missing manifests, changed images/fixtures/build outputs, wrong reference/case/state/viewport and substituted candidates refuse acceptance. Older runs with unbound screenshots need fresh captures and independent review. Freshness never changes a FAIL or NOT_VERIFIED judgment into PASS.

This protocol assumes the project's fixture, build command and local tools are honest. It detects stale or inconsistent evidence; it is not an attestation against a malicious process fabricating every input and receipt. A native Figma reference hash binds the supplied URL, not the remote file's current contents; reviewers must still inspect that design. Selecting all required states and judging visual fidelity remain independent obligations.

docs.title: Verification without model spend
docs.text:
The regular suite includes scripted-provider completion tests and provenance guards. To also exercise real Chromium acquisition with an installed browser:

AUTOCODE_TEST_PLAYWRIGHT=/absolute/path/to/node_modules/playwright \
AUTOCODE_TEST_CHROMIUM=/absolute/path/to/chromium \
  .venv/bin/python -m unittest -v tests.test_visual_capture

Omit AUTOCODE_TEST_CHROMIUM to use Playwright's default installed browser. Set AUTOCODE_TEST_CAPTURE_EVIDENCE to a fresh ignored directory to retain the disposable browser test projects. Without the Playwright opt-in, these real browser tests are explicitly skipped; offline guard tests still run. These checks do not establish live Figma fidelity or model review quality.

docs.title: VS Code extension
docs.text:
← Back to README

Chat with AutoCode in the sidebar (issue #884). The extension starts the CLI, reads --status and registry list --json, and takes the actions the public task-run interface names. It imports no runner internals and never reads state.json.

docs.title: Chat in the sidebar
docs.text:
Open AutoCode → Chat, type a request, and press Enter. Shift+Enter adds a newline. Chat fills the sidebar, keeping the composer at the bottom. New chat starts another conversation; History switches to the Runs list so you can reopen one. Back to Chat returns to the current conversation and its draft. The selected conversation and each unsent draft survive reopening VS Code. When the same workspace is open in multiple VS Code windows, each window keeps its own selected run and drafts, so switching tasks in one window does not change the conversation shown in another. The Runs list in each window can still open any task registered for that workspace.

New sidebar chats start in the run mode shown on the Run mode chip beside the engine chip. AutoCode lists one mode, Full: every chat starts with the Requirements conversation (the Quick plan mode that skipped it was removed on 2026-10-22). The list and each mode's flags come from autocode modes list --json (Run modes for clients); the extension passes the chosen mode's flags unchanged. A choice is remembered for new chats in this workspace; one the list no longer names, such as Quick plan, starts Full. A chat that has started keeps the flow it started with, so the chip shows only on a new chat. An AutoCode without run modes shows no chip and starts the full flow.

In the full flow, new sidebar chats enable joint planning and the core's --spec-first flow. The Requirements agent answers your first message, whatever it is, and talks with you until it understands what you want done. A greeting or an off-topic question gets a short answer and a question about what to build or change. Answer in the same composer. Requirements reuses its provider session, retains prior replies and streams assistant text through the public status view; tool output and reasoning stay outside that stream. A reply still being written shows as AutoCode · writing… with provisional text, the same as the terminal chat, and status polls speed up while that extract is still growing. You can keep writing a draft while a reply arrives. The conversation does not show an empty task dashboard.

Once the requirements are clear, read the bound understanding and choose Approve understanding and prepare plan, or send a correction. This releases independent plan preparation/review. Requirements has already named the workflow (build, fix, review, design or discuss) with that understanding, and the approval starts it. It does not authorize implementation. Approve and build appears later for the concrete reviewed execution plan. Terminal users can answer the requirements review with plan.

The thread shows your messages, saved answers and completed-turn replies, with Markdown and code blocks for assistant replies. A fixed composer grows with your draft. New output follows the bottom until you scroll up or select text; Latest messages returns to the bottom. These composer and scrolling components are adapted from Kilo Code's open-source UI; the exact revision and attribution are in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.

Models & usage stays above the composer and starts expanded. Configured models lists every saved role assignment with its full model ID, provider and reasoning Variant (such as medium or high), even before that role runs. Models used groups recorded attempts by job, model, provider and variant, including retries and earlier models. Several stages or slots can serve the same job; configured assignments do not imply that all those stages will run.

Collapse the panel to a summary that still shows the current attempt (or Last used), variant, configured-role count, tokens and cost. Your expanded/collapsed preference survives polling, History navigation and reopening the chat. Values refresh with status polling and cover the whole run. Cache and reasoning are already included in input/output totals. Partial counts are labeled; unreported usage stays unknown.

Models & usage shows Cost counted toward cap from the core’s public budget accounting beside the configured cap. Partial totals say at least and name unpriced stages; unknown amounts stay unknown. The expanded breakdown keeps the historical comparison estimate separately. These figures describe recorded usage, not an invoice or a guarantee that the next step fits within the cap.

Stages sits above Models & usage once a run has launched one. Each stage takes a row for how it went (✓ done, ● working, ↻ retrying, ✗ failed), its time, cost and attempt number, and a second row for its model, reasoning level and tokens (+ when some are not reported yet). The newest four show; N earlier lists the rest. A report repair counts as the repaired stage's next attempt. When the working stage is retrying after a failed attempt, the working card shows a warning with which attempt it is, how long it has run and why the last one failed. A stage that runs again after succeeding, such as a second plan-review round, shows 2 runs and no warning. The toolbar shows the run's cost against its cap and its tokens; with two or more chats open it adds a total for all of them, which leaves out what a restored run carried over and ends in + while any chat has not been read yet. These figures are the same ones the terminal chat's stage panel reads: usage.accounting.attempts, cost.breakdown.by_stage, cost.spent_usd and usage.accounting.tokens.

A finished run closes with a card: its result, how many requirements were checked, the files its saved steps and acceptance tests changed, the time its stages ran and its cost, with Show changes (the saved code changes below) and Run details. A new chat opens with what AutoCode does and three example requests; choosing one only fills the message box. A tab shows ● while its run waits for you and ✓ once it has finished, and the status bar names the working stage and the run's cost.

Provider-reported cost and the core's historical comparison estimates are shown separately. These estimates are not current API prices or your token-plan bill. The extension reads the public accounting view and does not calculate its own prices. A new chat shows configured models once the core creates the run; actual model history appears as attempts are recorded. Older cores without the new display metadata still show available model IDs and leave missing variants unknown.

When a plan is ready, the thread lists what it will deliver, marks the items you check yourself, and shows its constraints and what it may do. Criterion IDs, verification commands and the plan revision stay in Run details. Send plan feedback and continue to revise it. Approve and build approves only the displayed plan, then continues the same run. A stale click is refused and the revised plan must be reviewed. Answer cards handle questions and model replacement choices.

After completion, sending a follow-up and continue reopens the same run for the next turn. Earlier messages and completed replies remain visible. A new build plan requires its own approval. While AutoCode works, you can compose a draft; sending becomes available when the core offers a message action.

While a run works, Pause takes the place of Send; Send stays beside it when the run also takes a message. Pause lets the current step finish and save, then the run pauses with nothing lost, and Continue resumes it where it paused. Until then the button reads Pausing after this step…. The button appears only when the status view names the pause (view.pause); a cancelled mid-step model call is not offered, and the run's terminal Stop stays outside the chat.

Saved code changes offers only the comparisons and restores named by the core. While this chat waits for one of its commands to finish, those buttons are disabled with an explanation. They become available again when the command finishes; inspecting a run started elsewhere does not disable a named comparison.

Run details opens the detailed progress panel. The Runs list reads the local registry and retains unavailable pointers with their diagnostic. Both surfaces use the core's named commands, including the optional view.chat.input offer. Commands use argument arrays; issued tokens stay in the child environment.

While a step works, the conversation shows the live agent log the status view names (view.chat.log): what each running agent thinks (∴), says (») and does ($, ±, ·), with its screen name. Like the terminal chat's /live, those entries are display only — a thought is not a report and a command shown is not a passed check. Where an older core offers only chat.activity, the conversation shows those tool marks instead.

Starting a new chat asks you to confirm model spend. Buttons that save an input and then advance explicitly say and continue; advancing uses the run’s saved provider and per-role routes. Person-only recovery decisions still require their separate confirmation (autocode.confirmPersonOnly). Free text cannot bypass an operational stop or approve a plan.

Change sets. For a run linked with runs in other repositories (scope.linked, autocode changeset link), Run details reads autocode changeset status --json and shows every run of the change set. While the set approval is offered it lists every run's plan, and Approve all N plans asks first, then approves them together. If a plan changes after the card was shown, nothing is approved. Once every run is complete and an integration check is due, Run the set's check asks first, then runs it. These are the only change-set actions the extension takes (change sets in clients).

docs.title: Run it from a checkout
docs.text:
cd vscode-extension
npm ci
npm run build
npm test
code .

Press F5 to launch the configured Extension Development Host. The AutoCode view appears in the Activity Bar. Point autocode.cliPath at your autocode, or set cliPath: python3, cliArgs: ["/path/to/autocode/tools/autocode.py"] for a source checkout. Provider execution needs a supported host; see testing.md.

For Kilo, set autocode.provider to kilocode, connect the selected providers with kilo auth, and put your per-role model routes in autocode.extraOptions. The CLI and Kilo must run on the same supported backend host. A Docker or remote wrapper must forward the argument array and issued token environment, and expose the same workspace paths. Point cliPath/cliArgs at that real CLI or wrapper; the qualification fixture is only a UI test backend and cannot conduct a model conversation.

PR #1425 was merged before full live qualification finished. Its draft Requirements follow-up has passed a real Kilo/token-plan greeting conversation; full build/test/completion qualification remains outstanding. The earlier full task attempt stopped on a MiMo network failure before building. See the qualification record. The jsdom tests alone establish neither editor-host nor live-provider compatibility.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning autocode.cliPath autocode The CLI to start. autocode.cliArgs [] Leading arguments, for a source checkout. autocode.provider "" --provider for new chats. autocode.extraOptions [] Extra engine and model flags for new chats. autocode.pollSeconds 5 Seconds between read-only status updates. autocode.confirmPersonOnly true Ask before acting on a pause the run stopped for a person.

Each status update is a new autocode process, which reads the whole workspace once before answering. On a large project, set AUTOCODE_SOURCE_HOST=1 in the environment the editor starts the CLI with, so the updates share one warm snapshot helper; see Execution just above "Who approved" for what it does and keeps.

docs.title: Remaining scope
docs.text:
This is an AutoCode chat client with selected Kilo UI adaptations, not the full Kilo, Cline or ZooCode extension. It displays saved task replies and status updates; token-by-token model output, file attachments, inline edit/diff acceptance and editing arbitrary plan files are not implemented.

At a total active-time pause, the core can name a finite total-time decision. Enter the desired total seconds explicitly in the blank field and confirm that total. It must exceed the saved cap and active time already consumed; chat text does not supply or authorize it. Other limits, models and plan approval still apply.

At a planning-review allowance pause, a core-named finite input shows the saved allowance and calls already used. Enter an explicit total above both and confirm the exact number of calls. Set review allowance takes only the named command and waits for the next status before offering any separate continuation. Even a named command containing Resume can save the allowance first. Used calls stay counted, other limits and models stay saved, and neither action approves a plan. Blank, zero, fractional or stale choices cannot run.

At an exhausted operational-recovery boundary, Additional recoveries is a separate blank finite input. It shows the existing recovery allowance and counted spend. Choose from 1 through the spent count and confirm Grant and continue. Choosing 1 replenishes one spent slot; it does not raise the fixed allowance or bank excess. History stays retained and the existing consecutive-timeout streak is cleared by that grant. Other limits, routes and plan approval still apply.

Plan editing (--edit-goal) and other actions with unresolved GOAL_FILE, untyped recovery N or explanatory placeholders remain explicit gaps. The client cannot invent those decisions. The separate core Requirements conversation journal is documented in task-run.md; this client uses ordinary task runs and their additive chat projection.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
Open Connections from the chat toolbar or AutoCode: Connections in the command palette. It lists installed and registered backends in the AutoCode CLI environment. Check connection checks saved credentials without launching a model. Sign in / Reconnect runs the backend's own sign-in in a terminal; finish there and check again. AutoCode does not ask you to paste credentials into chat. Credential presence does not establish selected-model access or a passing live qualification.

Use for new chats changes the default backend. Each backend's role/model options are saved separately, so switching back to Kilo restores its token-plan routes. Existing chats retain their saved backend, models and budgets. Company providers such as GoCode appear when registered; their optional connection commands are described in Providers.

docs.title: Stage models
docs.text: Open AutoCode: Stage Models from the command palette, or Stage models… in the chat's engine picker, to choose the model and reasoning level each stage of a new chat runs. Each stage shows what it does and the kind of model and level that suits it, with one dropdown for the model and one for the level; the level list follows the chosen model. A model the stage may not run beside the others (a Builder on the model its Tester runs, for example) is greyed out with the reason. Save keeps the choice for every new chat on that backend, and Use the default forgets it. Chats already started keep their own models. The panel reads autocode stages list --json and takes only the stage's own save or reset command (stage choices for clients), naming the backend when a provider or engine is chosen for new chats.

docs.title: No Kilo or OpenCode installed
docs.text:
The AutoCode · Direct connection card is always available in Connections. Choose Set up AutoCode to select MiMo, Z.ai, OpenAI or Claude and enter its API endpoint/key in a terminal, then refresh Connections. Use for new chats is enabled after local setup is complete; it does not mean live model access was verified. See AutoCode direct connections for credential storage, protocol support and qualification limits.

Credentials are never entered into the chat or its webview. Existing chats keep their saved backend. Model overrides, explicit external role transports and backend-specific containment options are kept with their original backend when switching connections, so Kilo settings do not become direct API settings.

docs.title: Native Windows
docs.text:
AutoCode supports Windows through WSL (install). Native Windows support is not planned: #698 was closed on 2026-10-16 and WSL stays the supported path. This page records what was audited, what is fixed and what is still open, for whoever takes native support up again.

OpenCode and Codex run natively on Windows, so the gaps are in AutoCode's own locking, file and process handling, not in the engines.

docs.title: Acceptance (if native support is taken up again)
docs.text:
• autocode doctor and one fake scenario pass on the Windows CI runner.
  • Install then drops the WSL-only line and names the supported shells (PowerShell, cmd) and what autocode doctor checks on Windows.

docs.title: CI
docs.text:
The windows-fast-suite job in .github/workflows/tests.yml runs on windows-latest: install, autocode --version, autocode doctor --json, then every fast test module (tools/run_suite.py --changed HEAD --all-fast --module-timeout 600). A module still running after ten minutes has its process tree ended and is reported as a timed-out failure, by name, so one hung module cannot hide behind the step limit (#1681). It is allowed to fail: every step and the job itself are continue-on-error, so it reports progress in the job summary and never fails the workflow. Make it required once it is green.

tests/test_windows_portability.py runs on Linux and fails when a runtime module gains a module-level import of a POSIX-only module (fcntl, termios, pwd, grp, resource, pty and similar), because one such import stops autocode from starting on Windows before any platform check runs. It allows no exceptions: the last ones were removed on 2026-10-16. It also loads the CLI and the thirteen modules that used to import fcntl in a fresh interpreter where import fcntl fails, so an import through another module is caught too.

docs.title: Audit (2026-10-15)
docs.text: Scope as proposed in #698: autocode_util (locks, snapshots, JSON files), the provider launchers in tools/providers/, and the activity watchdog. Process supervision is included because it decides the fake-scenario acceptance.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
Where Problem on Windows Fix autocode_util Module-level import fcntl: every module that imports the shared helpers failed to load. lock_file / unlock_file use fcntl.flock on POSIX and msvcrt.locking on Windows. workspace_lock and run_lock use them. autocode_util.lock_file (Windows) msvcrt locks are mandatory byte ranges: locking byte 0 would stop other processes reading a lock file that records its holder. Lock one byte at offset 2^30, past any content, and restore the file position. A busy lock raises BlockingIOError, as flock does, so callers keep their busy pauses. A blocking lock polls through autocode_util.sleep. autocode_util.atomic_json Syncing the directory after the rename opens it with os.open, which Windows refuses (PermissionError): every JSON state write failed. Skip the directory sync on Windows. The file's data is still synced before the rename. Thirteen runtime modules (below) Module-level import fcntl and direct fcntl.flock calls: loading any of them failed, and the CLI loads nine of them at start. They lock through autocode_util.lock_file / unlock_file, with blocking=True where they waited before. On POSIX each takes the same exclusive flock, blocking or not, raises the same BlockingIOError when busy and unlocks at the same points. autocode_registry and autocode_interventions now unlock only a lock they took: msvcrt refuses to unlock a range its handle never locked, which would have replaced their "busy" error after a timed-out wait.

The thirteen modules: autocode_checkout_lock, autocode_checkpoint_cli, autocode_controller_owner, autocode_conversation, autocode_conversation_session, autocode_dependencies, autocode_interventions, autocode_milestones, autocode_registry, autocode_usage, autocode_workspaces, autocode_worktrees, opencode_stage_router (2026-10-16).

docs.title: Open: autocode_junit at load
docs.text: autocode_junit computes os.O_DIRECTORY | os.O_NOFOLLOW and os.O_NOFOLLOW | os.O_NONBLOCK at module level. Windows has none of those flags, so loading the CLI raises AttributeError there. This is the next load failure now that fcntl is gone: found on Linux by removing os.O_DIRECTORY and os.O_NOFOLLOW before loading the CLI, not yet seen on the Windows runner. The import check above does not catch it. The module walks to a JUnit report one directory at a time with dir_fd and refuses links, which Windows does not support either, so it needs a Windows way to read the report safely, not only a default for the missing flags.

docs.title: Open: POSIX-only calls in those modules
docs.text:
They no longer need fcntl to load, but some of their calls still fail on Windows:

  • os.O_DIRECTORY and os.O_NOFOLLOW, which Windows lacks, raise AttributeError: autocode_workspaces.keep_out_of_git upgrading an existing .autocode/.gitignore, autocode_controller_owner reading its receipt and probing its lock, and autocode_conversation_session locking the selected folder before it creates a project there. That last one locks the folder itself, which Windows cannot open with os.open, so it needs a lock file on Windows.
  • autocode_checkout_lock.exclusive closes its handle without unlocking so that a surviving provider child keeps the checkout locked. That relies on flock, where a child that inherited the descriptor keeps the lock; whether a msvcrt lock survives that way is unverified. It matters only once providers can run natively (below).

The dashboard (tools/dashboard/) still imports fcntl in five modules.

docs.title: Open: needs a decision
docs.text: Supervised provider launches. Task-stage providers, fake ones included, run under the Linux kernel boundary in provider process ownership: start_new_session, os.killpg / os.getpgid, a /proc PID namespace and seccomp user notifications (linux-setsid-notify-v1). The decision recorded for #454 is to refuse any host without that boundary, with no portable fallback, so even with every import fixed a native Windows run refuses before the first stage, and "one fake scenario passes on Windows" cannot be met. A Windows boundary (for example a Job Object with kill-on-close and a recorded receipt) needs the owner's decision on whether it qualifies, before it is built.

docs.title: Checked, no change needed
docs.text:
• tools/providers/: launchers pass argument lists, never shell=True; env_prep joins PATH with os.pathsep; claude_stream installs SIGHUP through getattr and ignores a signal the platform lacks.
  • autocode_activity (the activity watchdog): parses the provider event stream and process rows it is given; it has no signals, paths or locks of its own. Its process rows come from the supervision layer above.
  • autocode_util.snapshot: Git names use /, which Path accepts on Windows.
  • autocode_process.interruption_handler adds SIGHUP only where it exists.

docs.title: To verify on the Windows runner
docs.text:
• Several of the thirteen modules release a lock by closing its file rather than unlocking it (autocode_checkpoint_cli, autocode_workspaces.creating, autocode_worktrees, autocode_dependencies, opencode_stage_router). Windows releases a msvcrt lock when its handle closes, but documents the timing as depending on system resources, so a lock taken again at once may briefly be busy.
  • autocode_util.snapshot records executable: from st_mode & 0o111. Windows derives those bits from the file extension, so a snapshot taken on Windows differs from one of the same tree on Linux. Snapshots are compared on one host, so this matters only for a run moved between hosts.
  • atomic_json uses os.replace, which Windows refuses while another process has the destination open without delete sharing (an antivirus scan, an editor).
  • tools/providers/opencode.py looks for OpenCode's managed configuration in /Library/Application Support/opencode (macOS) or /etc/opencode (others). The Windows location should be confirmed against OpenCode before it is added.
  • autocode_permission_recovery treats only /tmp/ and macOS temporary folders as temporary paths.

docs.title: Workflow: planning, approval, and handoffs
docs.text:
← Back to README

This page covers the end-to-end conversation flow: how a rough idea becomes an approved plan, how that plan is implemented and reviewed, and what Autopilot coordinates along the way.

docs.title: The flow
docs.text:
Start with a rough idea and discuss it with the Requirements. It helps define the smallest useful end-to-end product, asks focused questions, and drafts a versioned build brief. The Plan Reviewer challenges that draft; the Requirements revises; the Plan Reviewer finalizes. You can revise the brief in the same conversation. Implementation starts only after you explicitly approve it.

After approval, Autocode handles the handoffs:

You → Requirements first, on every run and follow-up turn: it names the kind of job (build, bugfix,
   review, design, discuss), saved as `workflow`; `--workflow KIND` names it instead (a pinned build
   still runs Requirements, any other kind starts its own first stage). A flow without Requirements
   (v2 planning, no Requirements role) has the Job recognizer name it first
   review → Reviewer only: findings written to review/findings.json, repository untouched, run complete
   bugfix → Investigator first: diagnosis written to docs/bugs/<name>.json, repository untouched;
            not reproduced → run complete;
            reproduced → the build pipeline below from the Planner on, planned from the
              diagnosis and the Requirements handoff: no second requirements gathering, but plan
              review and your approval
              (small or large; the short path for small fixes is off until the full path is dependable)
   design → Architect first: a design review is written to review/design-review.json (goals met,
            blocking/advisory concerns, questions for you), repository untouched, run complete;
            a request for a NEW design → the build pipeline below; its plan may not change a file an
            earlier turn of the same conversation wrote (a discussion's decision record) unless your
            newest message names it, so the design job writes its design and only reads the rest
   discuss → Analyst only: an answer with evidence tied to repository files (and the note the
            request asks for, written by the runner), repository untouched, run complete
   (a design review's or a discussion's questions do not hold the run: it completes, and you
    answer them with --follow-up, the next turn of the same run; a reply to a design review
    → the Architect revises that review in review/design-review.json as revision n+1, the same
    concern ids kept, settled ones marked resolved, the repository outside review/ untouched)
   build → the build pipeline below;
           implementing an APPROVED design document as written, or "Build it." after a design turn
             (the design that turn wrote) → Architect checks it against the repository first,
             repository untouched:
             conflicts (a frozen API, a documented invariant) → written to <design>.blockers.json,
               run stops (PAUSED_DESIGN_CONFLICT), nothing built, you decide;
             no conflicts → the design's binding decisions become a constraint and the pipeline starts
               at the Planner (no second requirements gathering; the Planner may not redesign or ask);
               after a design turn the earlier turn's plan is archived, so the Planner drafts a new
               contract for the build instead of revising the design job's
You → Requirements Gatherer: rough idea → saved requirements report
Requirements Gatherer → Planner: draft task DAG
Planner → Plan Reviewer → Planner revision → Plan Reviewer final → your approval

Autopilot → AutoCode task scheduler → independent Builders → combined validation

Builder → Tester → Completion Reviewer
   ↑                       |
   └──────── REWORK ───────┘

The Plan Reviewer owns final planning decisions. On new joint runs, the runner-owned Autopilot dispatches AutoCode to schedule independent milestone Builders after approval, falling back to one Builder when work cannot safely run in parallel. Each Builder implements one bounded task. A separate Tester independently inspects and tests the combined code, then the Completion Reviewer proposes completion or rework for Autopilot to evaluate. They all work from the same approved brief; you do not explain the product to each agent or relay their prompts. The runner saves decisions, tasks and evidence so it can resume.

docs.title: Reading a stop
docs.text:
A stopped run shows one category: Your decision, Your environment, Model or provider, or AutoCode. Its exact saved state and stop reason remain visible. The next command appears beneath the category; it uses the existing request, approval or recovery control and does not grant authority on its own. Resolve the stated prerequisite and supply any ANSWER, MODEL, N or GOAL_FILE value before executing it. Read autocode status again after the first step of a recovery; earlier request tokens cannot authorize a newer one.

autocode --help lists public commands and common options on one screen. autocode --help-all shows all accepted task/run options, and autocode COMMAND --help shows a subcommand's options. Compatibility console scripts remain internal; use autocode in new instructions.

docs.title: The job kind and the older settings
docs.text:
Three settings decide "which process runs". They answer different questions and do not override one another:

Setting Question it answers Where it applies Job kind (workflow.kind: build, bugfix, review, design, discuss) What you get back, and so which stages run at all. Every run. Named by Requirements from your request, or with --workflow. Fixed once named. Workflow mode (settings.workflow.mode: glm_first_v1, glm_final_audit_v2, or the legacy default) Who checks the build: which role reviews each milestone and which audits the whole task. Only inside the build pipeline, so only for build and a reproduced bugfix. review, design and discuss never reach it. Task-lane mode (ui or code on an item of autocode tasks) Which loop one lane task runs: the Figma design loop, or a normal code run. Only in autocode tasks. A code item is an ordinary run and gets its own job kind. A ui item uses the Figma path and has no job kind.

So the kind decides whether the build pipeline runs, the workflow mode tunes who checks inside it, and the lane mode picks between two loops before either applies. If two seem to disagree, the job kind wins: a review run never builds, whatever the mode says.

The kind is shown where you approve a plan (Job kind: build (Requirements understood: ...)), because the two mistakes are not equally bad. Reading "build" as "discuss" costs a little time; reading "discuss" as "build" writes code you never asked for. If the kind is wrong, do not approve: start a new run with --workflow KIND. A follow-up message on a finished run (--follow-up) starts at Requirements again, which names its job, and still needs its own plan approval.

docs.title: Four units controlled by Autopilot
docs.text:
The same repository contains four callable units:

Unit Owns Handoff Autoplanner Separate requirements, planner, and plan-reviewer sessions User-approved contract and task DAG Autocode Next-task planning, parallel Builders, implementation and integration Build candidate with source revision Autoreview Independent validation and completion-owner review Evidence-backed review result Resolver Read-only diagnosis of reviewer-requested rework Evidence-linked, bounded repair DAG and retests

autopilot is the deterministic workflow controller in tools/autopilot.py. It calls all four units, consumes their results, selects the next stage, coordinates recovery, pauses for approval, and enforces the final completion gate. Unit reports are proposals; Autopilot checks them against the approved plan and current evidence before advancing. Planning revisions, implementation handoffs, review outcomes and repair routing are applied by Autopilot. The shared runtime supplies provider calls, locking and persistence.

The public autocode command and the internal autocode-orchestrator compatibility alias delegate to the same controller, including dashboard launches. tools/autocode_orchestrator.py is a compatibility import. The saved stage named orchestrator remains the milestone scheduler inside Autocode so existing runs can resume. Autopilot owns the overall loop.

Each unit command stops successfully before dispatching another unit. Clarification, approval and blockers keep their existing explicit checkpoints. autocode --unit autoplanner|autocode|autoreview|autoresolver provides the same selection; omitting it runs all units.

Unit implementation lives in tools/units/. All four share a run directory and its authoritative state.json; they preserve separate model roles and sessions. Versioned JSON handoffs are saved under handoffs/<unit>/<hash>.json, with paths in the state's unit_handoffs field: approved plan, build candidate, and review result. These exports are inspectable snapshots, not standalone authorization tokens. Execution still checks the saved approval and current evidence; editing a handoff cannot approve a plan or pass a review. Existing runs acquire handoffs when they next progress, without migrating their approval or replaying completed stages.

In the standard workflow, a reviewer's REWORK decision routes to Resolver, then back to AutoCode and independent review. Resolver inherits the Plan Reviewer model configuration but has its own saved session. It cannot implement, approve or complete a task. Its first version emits one bounded repair task (a one-node DAG with depends_on: []), preserving integrated-batch accountability. It pins the reviewed source, task, contract and validation evidence; stale inputs pause instead of launching a writer. Requirements or permission changes still require a user decision and, where applicable, a revised approved plan.

Transport/report-format recovery and safety pauses remain runner-owned. Existing explicit alternate workflows retain their configured routing; this does not override their final-audit-only policy or automatically retry failed integration operations.

docs.title: Operational diagnosis
docs.text:
An operator can request the separate read-only astra_diagnose stage after a recorded repeated Builder report failure:

autocode --workspace /path/to/project --run-dir /path/to/run --resume-paused --diagnose-failed-stage

This is an alternative to --retry-failed-stage, not an automatic handler for every pause. Admission requires the approved task, stopped workers, current source and intact pinned evidence; unresolved user decisions and hard budgets still stop it. Repetition may stop a repair path before its configured repair allowance is exhausted.

Each fresh diagnostic provider attempt receives a durable reservation at final launch admission. Relaunches after a timeout, capacity or startup failure or a denied path, new blockers and new iterations consume new reservations. A diagnosis whose report was rejected is not relaunched for the same failure: it holds as PAUSED_NO_PROGRESS without another reservation. Reloading the same attempt does not consume another, and an ambiguous launch is not refunded. The default run-level diagnostic allowance is two; explicit resume does not reset it. Report-only format repair has its separate existing allowance and remains subject to the parent's time/token limits. The diagnostic limit is not a count of every internal model/tool step or separately budgeted report repair.

The model can recommend a bounded retry or escalation, not grant permissions, change approved requirements, implement a repair, or declare completion. The controller records the policy outcome before applying it. Escalation remains a durable pause; an admitted retry returns to the original owner and normal independent validation/review. It admits the Builder without a proposed source change, because a rejected report usually has none, until one Builder attempt returns a result. An attempt that automatic recovery archives without a report does not use it up; that recovery's own budget bounds the relaunches. (--retry-failed-stage differs: the attempt it admits spends it even if it times out.) Another attempt at the same unchanged failure needs new evidence or an explicit --retry-failed-stage. The Builder's repair plan carries the diagnosis and the recommendation. A proposed recovery_change the incident packet cannot attest goes in it as unattested_change, with the reason: advice for the Builder that neither blocks the retry nor counts as a new experiment.

docs.title: When a stage stops making progress
docs.text:
Before the runner pauses because a stage is not converging, it sends the run to the read-only investigate_stuck stage (tools/autocode_stuck_job.py) instead of stopping at once:

Pause After the Investigator PAUSED_REPEATED_FAILURE, PAUSED_INVALID_OUTPUT retry runs the stage once more; its failure history stays, so the same failure again extends the run of identical failures and a different one starts a new run (a spent report repair is archived). A Resolver repair's Builder retry continues from the in-scope work the rejected attempt kept, and is the one attempt recovery novelty admits for it (Evidence-bound repair) PAUSED_PLANNING_BUDGET retry grants one more review round (two calls from the challenge, one from the final review) PAUSED_NO_PROGRESS retry allows one more implementation batch PAUSED_COMPLETION_REVIEW retry asks the Completion Reviewer once more PAUSED_REPORT_REPAIR_LIMIT, PAUSED_BUILDER_RETRY_LIMIT, PAUSED_MILESTONE_STALLED, PAUSED_MILESTONE_REPLAN diagnosis only; these keep their operator resume flags

A rejected report pauses as PAUSED_REPEATED_FAILURE only after three consecutive attempts of the stage, at the same source, failed with the same error and left the same kind of output (tools/autocode_failures.py). Different problems that happen to share an exception type, such as missing responses to different concerns, pause as PAUSED_INVALID_OUTPUT.

The Investigator runs at high effort on a model different from the stuck stage's: in kilocode runs the first of the run's own direct routes (Plan Reviewer, Planner, Requirements, Completion, Tester, Builder) outside the stuck stage's model family, never a kilo/ gateway route; otherwise GPT-6 Sol, or GLM 5.3 when the stuck stage runs on Sol (GPT-6 Luna in native Codex runs, which have GPT models only). Never Astra by default. A gateway model needs --investigator-model. It runs on a fresh route and session. It reads the task, the saved state and the stuck stage's attempts and returns a diagnosis, then either guidance for one more attempt or the question only you can answer. --investigator-model MODEL (and --investigator-reasoning-effort) pins the Investigator's model for a run instead; a provider/model id such as openai/gpt-6-sol runs it through OpenCode even in a Codex run. Guidance goes into the retried stage's prompt: for planning, every planning stage until the plan is presented; otherwise that stage until it completes.

A retry is checked, not trusted. The Investigator states the diagnosed cause as a plain-English example ("Given the Planner's report cited docs/bugs/cent-drift.json (see note); when the runner validated code_refs; then it rejected the path as missing") and, unless it says in untestable why no command can, a probe: a command that exits 0 exactly when the files it cites in evidence_refs show that cause. Every cited file must exist, in the repository or in the run's directory, and a retry must cite at least one. The runner copies only the cited run files into a scratch tree, each at run/<name>, and runs the probe there: a probe that does not exit 0, or that needs a file the Investigator did not cite, rejects the report, and the original pause is restored with the reason. The probe also carries counterexample, one edit to a cited file after which it no longer shows the cause; the runner makes it in another scratch tree and the probe must fail there, so a probe that passes whatever the files say retries nothing (#1769). The probe's receipt, with its counterexample's exit code, is recorded with the investigation.

Bounds: one investigation per distinct stage and pause, three per run (settings.stuck_investigation.max_calls_per_run; 0 turns it off). A Builder failure the Investigator classifies does not count toward these three: it has its own budget per milestone (Models). A second failure of the same problem, a pause recommendation or a failed investigation restores the original pause, with the diagnosis in its reason. It never approves anything, changes requirements or criteria, weakens tests, grants permissions or extends budgets beyond that one attempt. Permission, scope, goal, criteria and spend pauses go straight to you, and so does a pause a guard re-raises on resume before any stage runs, or the outcome of a retry you authorized with --retry-failed-stage. Only full Autopilot runs investigate; a single-unit invocation (--unit) stops at its own boundary. A native visual run (VISUAL_REVIEW_PROFILE=), whose scope cannot run the Investigator, never sends a stalled stage to it, so that pause keeps its original reason and spends no investigation. A Builder failure that needs classification still queues the Investigator there; native authority refuses it, and the run pauses PAUSED_BUILDER_CLASSIFICATION at the Builder with that classification spent, as before. --diagnose-failed-stage below remains the operator's explicit, policy-ledgered alternative for a Builder.

docs.title: Joint requirements planning and review
docs.text:
This is the new-run default. Older mixed-CLI OpenCode runs move their Codex roles to OpenCode when execution resumes at a recovered stage boundary. The runner saves a checkpoint backup and archives those Codex session IDs; approvals, task history, evidence, limits, and existing OpenCode sessions are preserved.

autocode "Your rough idea"
# Or target another committed Git workspace:
autocode "Your rough idea" --workspace /path/to/project

You → Requirements Gatherer: clarify outcome, scope, constraints and definition of done
Requirements Gatherer → Planner: draft plan and task dependencies
Planner → Plan Reviewer → Planner revision → Plan Reviewer
    → you approve that exact plan
    → Builder → Tester → Completion Reviewer

Role defaults and escalation ladders are documented in Models.

The Requirements Gatherer saves a separate structured report under the run's iterations/ directory. The Planner receives that artifact, originates alternatives and a task DAG, and can push back on the Plan Reviewer using source evidence. Unanswered requirements questions cannot silently disappear from the draft. A handoff that has only questions so far, with no behaviors or acceptance tests yet (a vague request), stops the run for your answers before any Planner call, on every flow; Requirements then runs again with them.

Each question is classified by kind (discoverable, inferable, or decision), category, and delegable. A discoverable question, one the workspace can answer, is never shown to you. The first time the Requirements Gatherer or Planner asks one in a clarification episode, the runner holds that report back and re-runs the same stage once with the questions, the report that raised them, and its hash. That single pass must resolve each question from cited workspace files (a machine_resolution, accepted only for technical facts, never for cost, quota, permission, side-effect or outcome choices), keep it as a decision, or record an access_blocker when the source is missing. Anything still discoverable afterwards is shown to you as a labelled decision; there is no second pass. The episode, and so the pass, is renewed only by your own new input: a non-delegated --answer, --feedback, or --edit-goal. Delegating a default, rejecting an assumption, or the model regenerating question IDs does not renew it.

Whenever planning stops for your answers, the displayed brief starts with a Plan Preview bound to that exact revision and requirements handoff. It lists what you said (quoted requirements), what was read from the workspace, the assumptions the plan would rely on, and the decisions only you can make. Readiness is shown as counts only (blocking decisions, assumptions relied on, acceptance tests and criteria, open obligations), never as a score. Answering nothing leaves execution blocked; the preview never approves anything.

--reject-assumption A1 turns a structured assumption into an obligation the runner tracks until it is discharged; the rejected assumption may not reappear. If the assumption carried policy weight (cost, quota, permission, external side effect, or the requested outcome), it becomes your decision: the plan stays clarification-only and you are asked a question under the obligation's id. Otherwise the Planner may propose a remediation that still covers every requirement the assumption supported, and only a Plan Reviewer decision bound to the hash of that exact proposal discharges it; a revised proposal needs a new decision. Anything still open at final review comes back to you as a question, and the plan has no executable first task. Only your own answer to that question discharges it; feedback that merely mentions the obligation does not, and such a question cannot be delegated. A rejected assumption can never be restored, even after its obligation is resolved. Proposing a remediation under one intent does not carry over a change of intent: a new answer or feedback returns it to be proposed and reviewed again. Approval is refused while any obligation is open. --delegate-all and --reject-assumption act only on the revision you were shown, so both take its token with --review-token. Reviewer concerns have stable IDs; every concern requires a Planner response and a reviewer decision, including a concrete acceptance test. A row whose ID names no concern (a question ID, or an empty placeholder) answers nothing: it is not checked, and the saved report keeps only the concern rows. The final displayed brief includes the technical approach, milestones, and first bounded implementation task, all covered by its revision/hash. Approval dispatches that task directly, without a third Plan Reviewer call. The separate Completion Reviewer's later decisions use the normal execution budget.

The final review returns a reference to the revised plan rather than a copy of it. Inside that reference it may correct acceptance criteria only, as a delta on the retained rows (changed or new rows, removed IDs, corrected proofs); every other row is kept byte for byte. Each correction passes the same change-receipt, source-coverage and proof guards as a Planner revision, so a removed or reworded approved criterion still needs your saved answer or feedback. Milestones, the technical approach and permissions stay the Planner's: a problem there comes back to you as a blocking question.

A Planner revision that answers the Plan Reviewer's blocking concern may change one of its own lines without you while nobody has approved or edited the plan: a constraint it may reword or drop, a permission boundary it may replace. The line must be the Planner's (it repeats no sentence of your brief, your feedback or your answers), the change is declared as the Planner's own with its replacement, and the approval screen lists it under "Declared contract changes" with the concern that asked for it; the final review judges it. Required behaviors, scope exclusions, failure cases and any line that repeats your words still need your saved answer or feedback, and so does every line once a plan was approved or edited.

A fresh first-review receipt may also correct an exact failure-case inference that the model invented in an unapproved draft. That receipt can compose with independently permitted draft criterion wording, baseline observations and engineering proof corrections. It grants no authority over those adjacent fields: source citations, marked proofs, human review and approved obligations keep their existing guards. The corrected plan still receives final review and exact-plan approval; AutoCode does not ask you to approve its own draft corrections separately.

Planning defaults to two Plan Reviewer reviews per cycle. A review counts once it returns a report, whether or not the runner then accepts that report. An attempt that times out or whose provider fails returns no review, so it is given back before the next attempt; the repeated-failure limit, not this allowance, stops a review that keeps failing. Bounded recovery does not otherwise extend the allowance. Unresolved final decisions return to you as blocking questions. Once you answer them, planning starts a new cycle, and its first review receives the previous review's concerns, its decisions and your answers (previous_review), so it checks your answers instead of reviewing the plan from scratch. A technical question that AutoCode settles with the Planner's proposed default (a technical_decision, not an answer of yours) does not start a new cycle: the redraft that follows continues the cycle that asked, with its spent calls, its first review and its revision carried over (planning.inherited_review). The reviewer is told which answers were AutoCode's, and with one call left the final review decides on the redraft; what it cannot settle comes back to you as blocking questions. Only when the final review itself asked that question with no call left does the allowance grow by one call, once per run and never past a limit you set. Model output never renews the allowance; your answers and feedback do. If the budget is exhausted, the run pauses at PAUSED_PLANNING_BUDGET. After inspecting a reconciled checkpoint, an operator can permit one more attempt without discarding the accepted challenge and revision (for example, increase a total allowance of 2 to 3):

autocode --workspace /path/to/project --run-dir /path/to/run --planning-review-call-limit 3
autocode --workspace /path/to/project --run-dir /path/to/run --resume-paused --unit autoplanner --no-chat

The first command only saves an audited, finite total allowance for this cycle; repeating it does not add another attempt. Reviews that returned a report remain counted, unresolved provider work must be reconciled first, and final review and exact user approval remain mandatory. Unlimited allowances and decreases are rejected. A new cycle returns to the default of two attempts; its predecessor's allowance and exchange remain in history.

Alternatively, explicitly send --feedback '...' to request a new cycle. Answering final blockers, giving feedback, or editing the goal starts fresh joint review and requires fresh approval. Old exchanges remain archived. Ordinary resume preserves the cycle and its spent budget. With --planning-v2, the new cycle begins when Requirements hand over a changed handoff after your feedback, answer or follow-up (or a program's plan guidance); the same handoff again, or a Requirements report retried with nothing new from you, keeps the cycle and its spent reviews.

Before the plan is shown for approval, Resolver checks that it is the reviewed final plan and that the workspace has not changed since that review. If the check fails, approval is deferred and planning restarts with a new cycle. Planning restarts at most twice for the same reason since your last input. After that, the run pauses at PAUSED_APPROVAL_DEFERRED with the reason, instead of spending review calls on cycles that end the same way. --resume-paused runs one more cycle; --feedback restarts from requirements (in an adaptive run, from the Planner when a plan is shown for approval) and renews the allowance.

The default workflow uses OpenCode for every role. The Plan Reviewer, Builder, Tester, and Completion Reviewer use OpenCode's current ChatGPT OAuth connection; the Requirements Gatherer and Planner use separate sessions on the Z.ai connection by default. Changing the account in ChatGPT's browser or desktop app does not change OpenCode's login. To switch this workflow's ChatGPT account, reconnect OpenAI in OpenCode. Every role can select any available provider/model from opencode models. The role names describe responsibilities, not mandatory models.

Planning requests use fresh sessions and focused handoffs: the current brief, code references, alternatives, concerns, responses and changes since review. Full reports remain in the run's iterations/ directory. Codex planning uses its read-only sandbox. OpenCode planning uses a fresh, read/search-only agent with shell, edit, delegation, external-directory access and unlisted tools denied; workspace snapshots are also checked. These OpenCode restrictions are tool permissions, not an OS sandbox.

The existing --chat, --answer, --feedback, --show-goal, --approve-goal, status and resume commands work in this mode. Intermediate drafts cannot be approved. The saved planning object records the exchange, final approval token and Plan Reviewer call count; planning_history retains prior cycles. Existing runs keep their original routing, including earlier OpenCode-only runs and joint-planning runs that used the Requirements model for validation. Start a new run to use the current GPT Sol default in that case; saved sessions cannot move between CLIs. No global OpenCode or Codex configuration is changed.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
A bug report goes through the same conversation and every stage as any other task: requirements, planning, plan challenge, revision, final plan review, your approval, orchestrator, Builder, Tester and Completion Reviewer.

  • Job type. The Requirements Gatherer proposes task_kind (bugfix or build), the Planner writes it into the contract, and the Plan Reviewer confirms or challenges it. The brief you approve says "Job type: bug fix". It is part of the hashed contract, so changing it needs approval again. Saved runs without it are build and behave as before.
  • A defect-shaped plan. For a bug fix the planning stages keep the plan to the reproduction, the root cause, the smallest correct fix and a regression test in the project's own suite. The same stages run; they review less.
  • Runner-owned proof, no model call. Just before the Tester runs, the runner executes regression_proof against the run's base commit (the commit the run started from; for a run created before that commit was saved, the commit its first stage recorded, if the source still descends from it). An in-place run, including a new run in an earlier task's worktree, started with uncommitted or untracked files starts from a commit of HEAD plus those files (ignored files and untracked nested repositories left out), kept under refs/autocode/launch/RUN, so they count as original code rather than as the change; HEAD, the index and the files stay as they were. A run that finds the checkout busy records it once it holds the checkout. A later launch drops the ref of a run whose directory is gone, after a day's grace. Each suite run may take as long as the run's tool-call limit, at least 900 seconds and with no limit when the run turned that limit off; settings.regression.test_timeout overrides it. The new or changed tests must fail on the original code and pass on the current code, and every test that passed on base must still pass (not fail, be skipped or disappear). A repair that changes no test is proved by the tests the project already had: the base suite's tests that fail there and pass with the change. The checks run in clean scratch worktrees, never in the task workspace. The result is bound to the exact source revision and appears as a runner-owned step with zero tokens in the stage history.
  • Reviewers use it instead of repeating it. The Tester and the Completion Owner receive regression_proof. With a passing proof the Tester runs the regression command once as its own check instead of the whole suite. With a failing proof the Tester reports FAIL and the Completion Reviewer returns REWORK, which sends the proof's reasons back to the Builder.
  • The completion gate requires it. A bug fix cannot reach TASK_COMPLETE unless the proof passed for the current source. A refusal names the reason.
  • What happens today, beside the criterion. Each regression criterion (test:) carries a current_behavior box: the Investigator's observed behavior, copied from the diagnosis bound to the run whose probe the runner saw show the bug (an untestable reproduction is not evidence). The runner fills an empty box, and the plan shows it as "Today:" under the criterion. The box is not part of the agreed outcome: a revision that sets it to exactly the diagnosis text goes through with a receipt on the approval screen (current_behavior: C1 -> …) and no question, so a wrong note on today's behavior no longer costs a report repair and a second planning round (#2133). Any other change to it on a protected criterion still needs your saved answer, as a rewording of the criterion would. A planning report that leaves the box out has an empty one; that costs no report repair either.
  • Regression tests in plain English. When the Investigator reproduces a bug, it also writes the regression tests the fix must pass as test_cases in its diagnosis. Each case has an id (T1, T2, …) and given, when and then fields with exact values, for example:

T1: Given the timesheet entries for 2024-12-30 and 2025-01-02; when the weekly report runs; then both appear in one row for week 2025-W01.

You can check these without reading test code. They are saved in the diagnosis note under docs/bugs/. - "Reproduced" is checked. A reproduced bug also carries probe, a command that exits 0 exactly when the bug is present on today's code, for example python3 -c "from pager import page_count; assert page_count(5, 2) == 2". The runner runs it in a scratch copy and rejects the report if it does not exit 0, so the diagnosis rests on something the runner saw, not on the Investigator's word. The probe also carries counterexample, the one edit that removes the bug, and must fail in a scratch copy with that edit made: a probe that exits 0 whatever the code says, such as python3 -c 'assert 2 + 2 == 4', is not a reproduction (#1769). A bug no command can show here (a live registry, a race, a device) says why in untestable instead. The note records the probe that showed the bug in proven_by. - Contract criteria. Each case becomes an acceptance criterion of the small-fix contract. For a large fix, it becomes one the Planner must carry into the plan you approve. - Named tests. The Builder writes one test per case, named after the case id: test_t1_<what it checks>. - The runner's check. The regression proof also requires every case to have a test with its id in the name. The link is by name, so no model is involved. Names match as whole words, so T1 matches test_t1_… and TestT1… but not test_t12_…. - Restore and preserve cases. A case is kind: restore by default (and a case with no kind is one): behavior the fix restores, proven by a test that fails on the original code and passes after the fix. A case may instead be kind: preserve: behavior that already worked and must keep working — for example "an exact multiple still gives the same page count" — proven by a test that passes on the original code and after the fix. A preserve case without a test, or whose test fails on the original code (it describes restored behavior and is mis-tagged), fails the proof, which names the case. Nothing else is relaxed: a restore case whose test passes on the original code still fails, and every case needs its own named test. - Without per-test results (exit codes only), the cases cannot be matched and the proof is UNVERIFIED. - The Tester's check. The Tester reads each case's test (case_tests in the proof) and reports FAIL if the test does not assert what the English case says. - Where the cases appear. The status view's evidence carries the cases and the tests that prove them, and the pull-request body written by autocode issue lists them. - Compatibility. Runs whose diagnosis has no cases, including bug fixes planned without an Investigator and older saved runs, behave as before.

If same-chat feedback corrects a named case from restored behavior to preserved behavior (or the reverse), the old diagnosis cannot be superseded by a sentence in the plan. Before approval, AutoCode checks that the corrected draft cites the saved feedback and an admitted change record. With unchanged source and diagnosis evidence, it sends that exact correction through the Investigator once, then returns to planning and independent review. Old reports and usage remain saved; unaffected cases, file scope, reproduction checks and exact-plan approval remain required. An already displayed conflicting draft offers Resume instead of an approval that cannot succeed.

This refresh handles uniquely named case-kind contradictions. It does not infer arbitrary semantic changes or reinvestigate harmless wording. Missing authority, ambiguous names or changed evidence hold the run at PAUSED_STALE_DIAGNOSIS. Repeated resumes do not renew the same correction's allowance, and an approved plan still requires the ordinary explicit revision path.

docs.title: Features: tests in plain English
docs.text:
A feature gets the same kind of proof from its plan. The Planner writes every acceptance criterion a test can check as one concrete example, and sets its verification_method to name the test:

C2: Given calc.py with add(); when sub(5, 3) runs; then it returns 2 Verify: test: test_c2_subtracts

  • You approve the examples with the plan. The plan display says which criteria the runner will prove.
  • Criteria a test cannot check keep an ordinary verification. Examples are documentation, visual design and performance under real load; the Tester judges those as before.
  • Naming. The Builder writes one test per marked criterion, named with its id (test_c2_…).
  • The runner's check. Before the Tester runs, the runner checks each named test by the same regression proof as a bug fix, with one difference. The test must pass with the change and must not have passed without it. For a feature, "not passed" includes failing to import the new code on the original revision, because the code didn't exist yet. A bug fix still needs a test that runs and fails. As for bug fixes, no test that passed before may fail now.
  • Completion. It is refused until every marked criterion has its test.
  • Several milestones. A test criterion is listed under the milestone that delivers it. At each milestone checkpoint the runner proves:
  • the tests of that milestone, or of every member of a parallel batch
  • the tests of milestones already accepted under the approved plan

It never proves a later milestone's tests, so a milestone's tests must not depend on a later one. A test criterion that belongs to no milestone is proven once every milestone is current or accepted, which is at final completion. A milestone with no test criteria due runs no proof step. A proof made for a smaller set of due tests is never reused after the set grows.

The matching and the rules are in tools/autocode_test_cases.py.

Test commands are detected (pytest, unittest, Go, Jest/Vitest/Mocha, RSpec, Cargo, make test); --test-command and --regression-command set them for a new run. With per-test results (pytest, unittest) a proof needs a named test that ran and failed on base and passed on the fix; a test that only fails to import on base is not a reproduction. Without per-test results exit codes decide. When nothing can be proven (for example no test command is found), the proof is UNVERIFIED and the bug fix cannot complete until a command is supplied.

For a feature with several milestones and named test criteria, a saved literal pytest or verbose unittest file/module list includes the run's cumulative new or changed Python test files at each proof. Earlier selectors, the interpreter, environment assignments and collection options remain in the executed command; the saved setting stays unchanged. A selected --test-root still bounds added paths. Filters such as -k and -m remain authoritative, so a filter that omits a required case still fails the proof. A missing, failing or deleted acceptance test also blocks completion. This accumulation does not apply to an explicit bug-fix regression command. Shell programs, unknown option arity, --pyargs and discovery commands retain their existing selection; correct an unsupported saved command at the reconciled pre-validation pause with --resume-paused --regression-command CMD.

docs.title: Scoped Python proof
docs.text:
Start a new run with --test-root components/api/ to detect and run the Python suite inside that workspace-relative directory. The caller chooses a literal directory, not an absolute path, parent path or glob. The root is saved at launch and cannot be changed on resume. Through TaskRun, pass it in start_options, not the options repeated on every advance (Task-run interface). Omitting it keeps ordinary whole-project detection unchanged.

Scoped detection honors current and pinned-base pytest policy within the root and its ancestors, including pytest.ini, .pytest.ini, pytest.toml, .pytest.toml, conftest.py and conditional configuration in pyproject.toml, setup.cfg and tox.ini. It never substitutes unittest because configured pytest is unavailable. Pinned policy links are resolved from Git blobs; current policy reads use non-following directory descriptors. Both use bounded, repository-local link resolution. Current policies over one MiB are unknown; unknown, unreadable, special-file or unsafe policy leaves scoped detection unavailable. Unittest package hooks and relative imports remain part of collection.

A first feature can prove its tests when the pinned base holds nothing under the root and the independently detected complete rooted suite passes. This is evidence for a first suite, not a claim that a baseline passed. Explicit suite or regression commands and arbitrary filtered caller-supplied frameworks get no such exemption. Existing passing tests still cannot fail, be skipped or disappear; source identity, command ownership and completion checks are unchanged.

Changes outside the selected root remain UNVERIFIED, even with explicit test commands. For an ordinary task this is test selection, not permission to write only that directory or a filesystem sandbox. An identified generated component brief also binds its declared affected paths and file deliverables to the caller's owned root. Its mandatory flow must be executable locally by that child; deferred container builds, Compose and cross-service checks belong to the separate integration owner, not the child's mandatory flow. A retained conflicting plan stops at PAUSED_COMPONENT_PLAN: use --edit-goal FILE or --feedback TEXT and freshly approve the corrected draft. An unchanged resume cannot repair it or invent missing caller scope for a legacy run.

The scratch worktrees use the project's own environment: its .venv, venv or node_modules is linked in, and the Python tests run with the project's virtualenv interpreter even though the task worktree has none. Build-generated source files that git ignores but that sit next to tracked code (such as a setuptools-scm or hatch-vcs _version.py) are copied from the project into every scratch tree, base and fix alike, so the package imports there. Ignored build output directories are not copied. Ignored files under vendor/ are copied the same way. An --in-place run's Builder edits that same checkout, so the run saves these files before any prerequisite or provider starts, and clean checks use only inputs that still match the launch bytes and modes (#529). Added ignored files are left out of test copies and noted. A captured generated or vendored file changed or removed since launch makes the proof UNVERIFIED; restore it, or start a new run after preparing the intended inputs. Missing, damaged or incompletely captured launch records also block proof. Older runs without a record copy none of these files and remain UNVERIFIED if the checkout has eligible ignored inputs. The older generated-only byte-hash record cannot authenticate the complete launch inventory and requires a new run. Planning prerequisites apply the same policy before provider dispatch, including on resume. Saved evidence is checked again before stage results advance the run, artifact reviews are accepted, or completion is accepted or reused. Status also marks completed evidence stale after a captured input changes. Separate task worktrees retain their project checkout dependency policy; shared virtualenvs and node_modules are outside this ignored-source inventory. In-place capture requires readable regular files with no symlink in their paths. Materialize ignored vendor file links before starting, including links to tracked files in the same checkout. An incomplete capture stays unverified after the files are changed or removed; correct the inputs and start a new run.

Planning reports that omit only a provenance list (such as code_refs or source_refs) now get an empty list instead of a report-repair model call; the raw report is kept and every semantic check still runs. Reports that omit a list carrying a decision (requirements, questions, concerns, responses) still go to report repair.

docs.title: Monorepo packages
docs.text:
Start a new run with --package packages/api/ when the task belongs to one package of a larger repository. The path is a plain directory relative to the repository root, in the same form as --test-root. It must hold files in the checkout the run uses: committed files for a new task worktree, which starts from HEAD, or files Git does not ignore for an --in-place run. The package is saved with the run and cannot be changed on resume. Through TaskRun, pass it in start_options (Task-run interface). --status shows it as view.package.

What the package changes:

  • Test detection reads only the package, as if it were the project root: its own pyproject.toml, package.json, go.mod, Cargo.toml and test files choose the runner. The detected suite runs from the package directory, and receipts show the command that ran, for example cd packages/api && go test -json ./.... The regression command derived from the changed tests, and the repeated runs of the proving tests, run there too, with per-test results as for a whole project. A test's name is relative to the directory its runner treats as the root, normally the package (test_greet.TestGreet.test_x), and a node:test file there that runs another test runner is still not named proof (#380). A feature that adds the first Go module in the package, on a base with no Go project, is not held to a base Go suite that cannot exist, as at the root (#685).
  • Only the package's existing tests are retained as original test gates, with the package suite as their command unless --test-command gives one, so a large repository does not bind thousands of unrelated tests. The replay of the package suite is read in the package as the same suite is read at the root.
  • In a bug fix, the Investigator's handoff names the package (package_scope) and, when the run has one, suite: the command the run tests the package with (the suite detected there, or --test-command). A reproduced diagnosis must name only files or directories inside the package in affected_paths and test_paths. One that names anything else (another package, a file at the repository root, a shared lockfile) is refused as invalid output and takes the path of any refused report: the Investigator is asked to repair it with the reason, and the run pauses rather than plan from a report that still names such a path. The diagnosis note stays under docs/bugs/ at the repository root, where the runner writes it. A bug whose fix is outside the package needs a run without --package: the Investigator is told to name the file it would change there anyway, so its report is refused and the run pauses rather than plan the fix.
  • The package is the Builder's write scope, and its handoff says so (write_scope). Apart from the Investigator, no other stage is told the package. Before each Tester and Completion Reviewer dispatch, in every package run, whether or not it owes a regression proof, the runner compares the candidate with the run's base, as the regression proof reads it. The Code Reviewer, Designer and Design Reviewer dispatches are not checked. A file added, modified (its content or its mode) or deleted outside the package (another package, a file at the repository root, a shared lockfile or workspace file; a rename counts on both sides) opens one blocking finding with source runner that names each path and what happened to it. A file restored with the same content but a different mode still counts as modified. The completion gate and a milestone's acceptance refuse while the finding is open; every stage sees it in open_findings, and a correction task is assigned it. Only the runner closes it, when a later check finds no change outside the package; no reviewer report can. Closing it with --close-finding accepts nothing: --accept-completion runs the same check once its own checks pass (a finished run, an unapproved plan or missing evidence is refused for that reason first) and refuses while the change is there, and the next check before review opens a new finding. A task that must change files outside the package, such as a root lockfile, needs a run without --package.
  • What the check does not count outside the package:
  • what the regression proof does not count either: AutoCode's own .autocode/ files, bytecode, the runner's dependency links, and an untracked file Git ignores, unless the approved plan names its path;
  • an untracked Git repository or a submodule's uncommitted work that the checkout already held when the run started, which the run's base cannot hold. Every new package run records what is there when its base is taken (none, in a new task worktree). While such a path is still a Git repository, it and everything under it are left out, so a later change inside it is not seen. An untracked repository that is later removed entirely was the person's own and names no change of the candidate: it does not hold the run. A deleted submodule, or a path that is no longer a Git repository (replaced by a file, or its .git removed), is named apart from the Builder's changes, and the finding tells the Builder not to delete, move or reset anything there: the person restores it. A package run saved before this record existed has none, so its check leaves out every nested Git repository and submodule work it finds outside the package rather than report the person's own as the Builder's;
  • the files the runner wrote for this run, while they are as the runner wrote them: a bug fix's diagnosis note under docs/bugs/ (compared with the investigation the run saved, whether or not it reproduced the bug), a review's or design review's report (its saved hash) and a design check's blockers file (its saved hash). Once changed, the finding names them apart and tells the Builder to put back what the runner wrote, not to delete them. A check of the same design that later passes removes the blockers file an earlier, stopped check wrote, so no stale one is left behind;
  • what an earlier, finished turn of the run left (a discussion's note, a design's documents, the other files the turn changed), and a blockers file a run saved before it recorded the hash, are recorded by path only: they are left out by path, so an edit to one is not seen.

The regression proof's list of changes outside the package leaves out the same paths, apart from the person's Git work that is no longer as it was. - A runner regression proof (a bug fix, or a plan whose criteria name tests) also leaves a change outside the package UNVERIFIED, because the package suite never ran it.

The feature-monorepo-package scenario (scenarios/README.md, Catalog) runs a build in one package of a two-package repository with --package and the scripted model. Its reference completes; its broken variant, which also edits the other package, stops with each of those files named in the open runner finding. bugfix-monorepo-package does the same for a bug fix: the Investigator runs first, the proof runs in the package, and the runner's diagnosis note under docs/bugs/ is not counted as a change outside it. Its scripted Investigator names only the package's files, as its handoff asks. Its broken variant also fixes the other package's copy of the bug and stops with that file named.

An explicit --test-command or --regression-command still runs from the repository root, exactly as given; write cd packages/api && … to run it in the package.
