A --test-command in exactly that form for the run's own package, with a runner AutoCode reads per test (python3 -m unittest, python3 -m pytest, node --test or go test), is read with that runner inside the package, as the proof reads such a command at the root. The proof, the named-proof preflight and the protected-test replay all read it that way. Another command written for the package, such as cd packages/api && make test, is read by the runner detected there in the proof and the named-proof preflight; the protected-test replay judges it by its exit code. --package cannot be combined with --test-root.

The learned test command in project memory belongs to the whole repository: a package run does not take it as a default, and does not save its own test command or framework there.

In every run, with or without --package, a command that AutoCode replays in a scratch copy (a check, a probe or the protected-test replay) and that has exactly the form cd DIR && RUNNER, with a plain relative directory (no quotes or trailing slash) and one of those runners, runs with that runner's per-test results read inside DIR. A run of zero tests, of only skipped tests or with incomplete results is then refused, as for the same runner at the root. A direct node:test command in that form always runs fresh and is never reused from the baseline cache, as at the root.

Not covered yet (#711):

  • Nothing limits what the Builder writes while it works: a change outside the package is found when the candidate is checked before review, not refused when it is written.
  • Detection in the package does not read pytest configuration in parent directories (a root pyproject.toml [tool.pytest] section, pytest.ini or conftest.py), so a package that relies on it is detected as unittest. Give --test-command 'cd packages/api && python3 -m pytest' instead. pytest then takes the repository root as its root, so test names stay relative to the repository (packages.api.test_basic::test_adds).
  • Detection in the package finds a Go suite only from the package's own go.mod, so it finds no suite in a package of a single Go module (one go.mod at the repository root, packages in its subdirectories). Give --test-command 'cd packages/svc && go test ./...'. A root-form command such as go test ./packages/svc/... is read per test by the proof, but the named-proof preflight of a --task-preflight manifest judges it against the suite detected in the package, finds none, and refuses it.
  • Native visual checks cannot run a command in the form cd DIR && RUNNER: such an approved check pauses with PAUSED_VISUAL_EVIDENCE ("foreign suite instrumentation"), in a run with or without --package. A package run's own suite has that form, so its native visual checks cannot run it.
  • The test environment still comes from the repository root: the Python interpreter is the root's, and only the root's node_modules, .venv or venv are linked into scratch copies. A package's own node_modules or .venv is not used.
  • A package run never reuses an earlier passing Python proof; it runs again.
  • The first-Go-module rule (#685) still looks for a Go project in the whole repository. A Go module, workspace or Go source in another package counts, so a first Go module in this package is then held to a base suite that cannot run, and the proof stays UNVERIFIED.
  • The Tester's acceptance tests, written before the Builder starts, still run with the suite detected at the repository root.
  • Diff coverage and the mutation report, which never change a verdict, are not narrowed to a package's commands and may be skipped.

docs.title: Reviews, discussions and designs: findings and claims shown by running code
docs.text: The review and discuss workflows produce findings and answers, not code. The same idea applies: a finding or a claim is stated as a plain-English example, and the runner, not a model, runs something that shows it.

docs.title: Review: every blocking finding has a failing test
docs.text:
• Example. Every blocking finding carries example, the defect as one concrete case: "Given …, when …, then … (expected …)". A blocking finding without one is rejected.
  • Test. The Reviewer delivers a test under review/tests/, named after the finding (F1 → test_f1_…). The report names the change's patch file in change_patch ("" when the change is already in the workspace).
  • The runner's check. It applies the patch in a scratch copy of the repository, never in the workspace, and runs the delivered tests there. Each blocking finding's test must fail on the changed code. A finding whose test passes, or has no test named after it, rejects the report: a finding that cannot be shown is not reported. The failing tests are recorded per finding (proven_by in review/findings.json, finding_tests in the run state).
  • Untestable findings. A blocking finding no test can show (a documented compatibility rule, a missing document) says why in untestable and needs no test. Advisory findings need none either.
  • Bad patches. A patch that does not apply rejects the report with git's message.

docs.title: Discuss: a claim may be shown by a probe
docs.text:
• A claim about what the code does may carry example (the concrete case in plain English) and probe: a shell command, run from the repository root, that exits 0 exactly when the claim holds.
  • The runner runs every probe in a scratch copy of the code as it is now, with a two-minute limit each. A probe that fails rejects the answer. A probe cannot change the workspace.
  • A probed claim also carries counterexample: the smallest edit to one repository file (file, find, replace) that makes the claim false. The runner makes that edit in a second scratch copy and runs the probe again; it must fail there. A probe that exits 0 whatever the code says, such as python3 -c 'assert 2 + 2 == 4', does not tell the claim from its opposite, so the answer is rejected and goes to the usual bounded report repair; it is never shown as a check that ran (#1769).
  • Claims without a probe stay grounded by their source file only, as before, and the answer lists them as read from the source, not run.
  • Probed claims are recorded in the run state (answer.probes, each with its counterexample's exit code) and shown in the answer's evidence list.

docs.title: Design: a concern about today's code carries a probe
docs.text:
The design workflow's Architect judges a document, so nothing is applied. The same probe rule as discussions applies to what it says about the code.

  • Reviewing a design (review_design). Every blocking concern carries example, the problem as one concrete case in plain English. A concern that rests on what the code does today (an ordering check, a charge per call) also carries probe, a command that exits 0 exactly when the code behaves that way. The runner runs every probe in a scratch copy and rejects the review if one fails. A concern about the design text alone (a missing rollback step) has no probe. Probed concerns are recorded in design_review.probes.
  • Checking an approved design (check_design). Every conflict carries example. A conflict with something the code enforces today carries probe; a constraint that lives in prose (a README rule) has none. The blockers file written beside the design records each conflict's proving probe in proven_by.
  • Counterexamples. As in a discussion, every probed concern and conflict also carries counterexample, the one edit after which the code no longer behaves as it says, and its probe must fail there. A concern or conflict blocks work, so a probe that passes whatever the code says rejects the report (#1769).

The scratch runs are autocode_verify.scratch_run. A Python test delivered into a project with no test suite of its own still runs under unittest.

docs.title: Conversation and approval
docs.text:
The first stage runs read-only requirements gathering and saves a structured JSON handoff without milestones. A separate Planner uses it to propose the task DAG and any material questions. Chat mode stays in the conversation; command mode saves and exits at the checkpoint. Intermediate drafts cannot be approved; the Plan Reviewer still has to challenge, the Planner revises, and the Plan Reviewer finalizes first. State, answers, brief feedback, contract history, user events, prompts, schema files, evidence and sessions remain in the target workspace's .autocode/runs/<run>/. No implementation starts from the initial prompt.

Run the following from the project or the task worktree; each acts on its unfinished run. With several unfinished runs, add --run-dir /path/to/run (see Which run a command acts on):

autocode --answer 'Q1=CLI only'
autocode --no-chat
autocode --feedback 'Keep the first milestone local only'
autocode --no-chat
autocode --show-goal
autocode --approve-goal 'r3:<full displayed hash>'
autocode --no-chat

--answer is repeatable. --feedback TEXT saves a correction and returns to Requirements discovery on the next invocation; a revised brief always needs fresh approval. In an --adaptive-planning run, feedback on a plan shown for approval goes to the Planner instead, which revises that plan (Adaptive planning). --delegate Q1 explicitly accepts that question's proposed default. Saved answers are included in subsequent interviews; an answered question ID cannot be requested again. Answers do not approve the task. The approval token must exactly match the current displayed contract revision. At the approval stop the brief says which plan revision (r3) waits and that approving it authorizes implementation, explains the token as a SHA-256 lock on that exact plan (any revision changes it), and ends with the limits in effect and the exact --approve-goal and --feedback commands. The full brief can run to hundreds of lines, so just above the limits it summarizes the decision, quoting the plan: its outcome and milestones, every permission boundary, the first three scope exclusions, each acceptance criterion with how it is checked (and whether it also needs your review), and what passing proves for this job. That is what --show-goal and autocode --details print.

The approval stop itself (autocode --no-chat, or the chat's approval question) shows only the decision (#2535): the summary first, the limits, one line naming --details (in the chat, /details) for the full brief with its contract diff, file hashes and request tokens, then the commands. No hash or token appears before that line except in the approve command, which still binds to the token of the plan shown. --json and the status view are unchanged. The stop reads:

Before you approve r3:
What it will do:
  Provide a deterministic greeting CLI
Built in 1 milestone: M1.
What it may change:
  - May edit only: greet.py, test_greeting.py
Out of scope:
  - Web service
Done when:
  [C1] `greet.py Ada` prints exactly "Hello, Ada" and exits 0
    Checked by: test: test_c1_greets_ada
What passing proves:
  - An independent check of the final source must pass every criterion above, and the runner itself re-runs that check's commands in a clean copy: each must exit 0.
  - The runner also runs the test each of these criteria names: C1 (test:) must pass with the change and must not have passed without it. No test that passed before may fail now.
  - Not proven: behavior no criterion describes, or inputs no check exercises.

Limits in effect: 12 h of active time for the run, 1 h per stage, no iteration ceiling, one Builder at a time.

The full plan, its changes since the last revision and the request tokens: autocode --run-dir RUN --details (in the chat, /details)

Plan revision 3 (r3) waits for your approval. Approving it authorizes implementation of exactly this plan: AutoCode may then change files in the workspace to build it.
To approve this plan: autocode --run-dir RUN --approve-goal r3:<hash>
To change it instead: autocode --run-dir RUN --feedback 'WHAT TO CHANGE' (the revised plan gets a new token)

State: AWAITING_GOAL_APPROVAL / AWAITING_GOAL_APPROVAL

The proof lines name the cases the runner's regression proof will require a test for (autocode_test_cases.proof_cases, the same list autocode_regression checks): in a bug fix, the diagnosis's test cases when the bug was reproduced, else the plan's test: and guard: criteria, each with what its test must show; a guard whose test cannot load on the original code is called out, because the proof accepts it with only a note. When no criterion is marked test: or guard: (or in a design job) it says that nothing shows a check would fail without the change. Approval saves READY_TO_EXECUTE; the next ordinary invocation begins execution. The approval records who gave it: the Git identity, host and command, plus an optional --as NAME on a shared machine (Who approved). A project can name the Git identities allowed to approve; any other approver is refused at the same stop (Required approver). User-input commands never launch an agent. This command-per-turn interface also works from scripts and other frontends; no continuously attached terminal is required.

Execution roles must consult saved answers before asking for permission. An exact repeated permission request under the same approved contract is returned once to the Completion Reviewer with its authenticated answer, including any refusal or conditions. It is not automatically granted or extended to a broader request. If the owner repeats it again, the runner pauses for reconciliation rather than creating another question or spending indefinitely. Older answers without the original request remain available in the prompt but are not automatically matched.

A technical report blocked solely on one required human acceptance criterion can be presented for that review. Completion still requires the explicit review event, current source and evidence hashes, passing automated criteria and checks, and a passing full flow. Human acceptance does not rewrite the independent report or waive other failures.

--edit-goal body.json loads the full contract body (the goal_contract.body shape from state), creates a new draft revision and displays its delta. It invalidates goal approval, validation and human reviews. Previous contracts/evidence stay archived. Approval can never be inferred from a model response or a generic --resume-paused.

The contract records outcome/user, the ordered end-to-end user flow, deliverables, behaviors and failures, exclusions, constraints/permissions, assumptions and their provenance, delegated decisions, stable criterion IDs with verification methods, human-review flags and open questions. It also includes a minimal technical approach and small implementation milestones, each linked to existing acceptance criteria; every required criterion is covered. All listed acceptance criteria are required. Optional enhancements go in the deferred backlog and do not participate in the completion gate.

See also: Execution and completion · Models · Providers

docs.title: Reviewing a plan in a pull request
docs.text:
On a team, what will be built is worth reviewing before any model builds it. autocode plan --export PATH writes the run's current plan, the one shown for approval or the approved one, as a Markdown file someone can add to a pull request:

autocode plan --export plans/refunds.md        # or: --run-dir RUN when the project has several runs
autocode plan --check plans/refunds.md         # prints its goal hash; exits 2 if the file cannot be read

The file starts with a front matter between two --- lines. It is the plan: the contract body exactly as the run holds it (each criterion with how it is verified and the test: or guard: name it cites, the request's exact-output examples, milestones, what is out of scope, the runner's records), its goal hash, and the plan revision it came from and whether that was approved. The front matter is JSON, which YAML front-matter readers also accept. The text under it is generated from the front matter so reviewers can read the plan.

The goal hash is the SHA-256 of the contract body: what the plan says, whatever run or revision holds it. A plan read back from the file has the same goal hash as the run's. The scenario runner (scenarios/run.py) checks this at every plan approval its catalog runs reach: it exports the plan and reads the file back with --check before it approves the plan (scenarios/README.md). The approval token is not in the file, so committing it approves nothing. Text that looks like a credential is masked before the file is written, with the same policy as autocode bundle; the export then says that the file's goal hash differs from the run's.

A reviewer edits the front matter, then runs autocode plan --render FILE to regenerate the text. --check then prints the new goal hash and the one it was exported as. It exits 2 when the text no longer matches the front matter, for example when only the prose was edited, and names the line. It checks the file, not the plan: whether a run accepts the plan is decided in that run.

Once the pull request is merged, load the file into the run that drafted the plan:

autocode --goal-file plans/refunds.md          # or: --run-dir RUN

The file's plan becomes the run's next draft revision, as a body given to --edit-goal does, and any earlier approval token approves nothing. AutoCode first checks it as it checks a planner's draft and refuses it, leaving the run as it was, when:

  • the file cannot be read, or its text no longer matches its front matter;
  • it still holds [REDACTED] where the export masked credential-shaped text: loading it would make the mask the plan's text. Restore the masked values (or reword that text) and render the file again;
  • the plan drops a literal the request states, such as todo.py complete ID or a format like ID TEXT [open|done] (the message is the one the planner gets);
  • a Go test the request names is not proved by a criterion under that name;
  • a check names git status, or plans a command the shell cannot parse;
  • the runner's records in it (brief_acceptance, risk_acceptance, source_trace) are not the run's current ones, because the file came from another run or from a plan revision the run has since replaced. Export again, or delete those keys from the front matter to keep the run's own.

It is refused too at an operational pause that does not offer feedback, as --edit-goal is.

Then the plan goes through ordinary approval. In joint planning the Plan Reviewer reviews it first, as it reviews any edit, so resume the run (autocode --run-dir RUN) to get to the approval stop. That stop names the file and its goal hash, and says whether the plan it asks you to approve is still the plan loaded from it. A review of an unchanged plan records the new review in the runner's records, so that plan's goal hash differs from the file's; any other change is named. The approval token locks the revision on the screen, as always. --goal-file revises a saved run; it does not start a new one.

When the run completes, its evidence report (evidence.md, and so the pull request body autocode-issue pr writes around it) gives the approved plan's goal hash, the one --check prints for a file holding exactly that plan. When the approved plan came from a plan file, the report also names the file, its goal hash and the plan revision it was loaded as, and says how the two differ: the approved plan is the file's plan unchanged (the two goal hashes are equal), differs from it only in the runner's records of the plan's review, or differs from it in the parts it names. A plan approved, changed and approved again after the load is the later approval's plan, so the report names no file for it. For example:

Plan goal hash: 3f1c… (what `autocode plan --check FILE` prints for a file holding exactly this plan).
Plan file: `/repo/plans/refunds.md` (goal hash 9a07…), loaded as plan revision 2; the approved plan differs from that file's plan only in the runner's records of the plan's review.

docs.title: A team's plan review
docs.text:
Put together, a team reviews a plan like this:

  1. AutoCode drafts the plan. A run stops with its plan waiting for approval. For a GitHub issue, autocode-issue start gets it there.
  2. A person opens a pull request with the file. autocode-issue plan ISSUE --open exports the plan, commits it as plans/issue-N.md on a branch of its own and opens a draft pull request (GitHub issues). Without an issue, run autocode plan --export FILE, then commit, push and open the pull request yourself.
  3. Reviewers edit it. They change the front matter, regenerate the text with autocode plan --render FILE and check it with autocode plan --check FILE. Merging approves nothing.
  4. The merged file goes back to the run that drafted it. autocode --goal-file FILE --run-dir RUN loads it as that run's next revision, and a person approves it at the approval stop as usual.

Not available yet: starting a new run from the merged file (autocode "TASK" --goal-file FILE), for example on another machine or once the drafting run is gone. A plan file carries the exporting run's records of the plan's review, and how a new run should treat them is still to be decided (#720). Until then, --goal-file revises a saved run; it does not start one.

docs.title: Task chat message intent
docs.text:
Task chat uses deterministic, context-first rules; it makes no model call to guess a destructive action. Each saved message includes its kind and rule version. The rules are evaluated in this order:

Context or text Saved kind Effect Reply sent with Send this answer inside a current question card Answer Saves the literal text, including words such as “Continue?”. A standalone control phrase such as “stop”, “pause after this step”, or “continue” Control Explains the composer buttons; executes no control. A question, a status request, or a question-word prefix Question Replies from saved status. It does not change the plan, queue feedback, or start a worker. Other reply explicitly linked to a current question by the composer Answer Uses the existing answer/delegate operation and current request token. A typed “yes” here is only an answer, never plan approval. Unscoped “yes”, “approve”, “go ahead”, or equivalent approval wording Approval guidance Points to the exact reviewed-plan approval card; does not approve or start work. Other prose, including “actually use SMS instead” and ambiguous instructions Proposed change Saves the text and displays a confirmation card. Nothing is submitted to the runner yet.

“Yes, change the plan” confirms that saved text against the same plan token. Only then is a correction queued through the existing durable feedback operation. During execution it waits for the next safe boundary; fresh planning, independent review and explicit approval remain required. “No, keep as a question” records that decision and replies from saved status. If the plan token changed, the old confirmation is refused and the user must submit a new message.

Replay uses the original request ID and saved decision. Failed or uncertain delivery retains the receipt and requires the existing explicit retry/reconciliation path. Historical feedback already submitted before these rules keeps its original authority on retry. Pre-task planning conversations remain draft discussions and cannot approve or control a task.

docs.title: Question cards and saved progress
docs.text:
Each pending question has its own answer field and suggested-answer button in chat. Drafts survive refresh and reload. A draft from an earlier request is labelled for review; submitting always requires the current request identity. Accepted adjacent answers collapse into a history summary that distinguishes written answers from accepted defaults. Failed deliveries stay visible. Re-asked question IDs begin a separate history group. Suggestions are accepted one at a time; there is no implicit bulk acceptance or plan approval.

The task header links to Work with saved milestone acceptance, requirement results and open problems. Unknown and prior-plan results stay unchecked. Requirement and problem links open their read-only details in Checks. On narrow screens the checklist opens in the existing details drawer. None of these reads can approve a plan, answer a question or continue a run.

docs.title: The run's own worktree
docs.text:
A new task runs in its own Git worktree under .autocode/worktrees/<run>/ on a branch autocode/<run>, started from the current HEAD. The person's checkout is never read after the start: snapshots, protected tests and the check replay all operate on the worktree (#724). --in-place keeps the old behaviour and runs in the checkout you started from.

When the run reaches TASK_COMPLETE, the delivered source is committed to the task branch. Bring it back into the branch you started from with:

autocode merge            # the only task worktree; or name it
autocode merge --into main

merge fast-forwards when it can and makes a merge commit otherwise. If the base branch moved after the run started, it refuses and tells you to re-validate on the current source first (the same rule --resume-paused applies). Then remove the worktree with autocode clean-worktrees --yes.

docs.title: Project conventions across tasks
docs.text: A completed run can record reusable conventions that the person actually answered. The next task includes them as historical Requirements context, so it can avoid repeating an unchanged question. It still defines its own criteria and requires its own approvals. See Project memory for the learned file, explicit-setting precedence, doctor and forget.
